The matrix intentionally avoids minute estimates and starter labels. It assigns a strongest current claim, then names the skill that could widen or narrow the role. It should be rewritten after the official roster appears and again after Duke has enough competitive possessions to distinguish planned experiments from stable structure. Lineup architectures to test The most balanced July baseline is Blackwell plus one organizer, two credible space/connect players, and Ngongba . It gives the offense a proven perimeter scorer, a separate possession manager, a conventional interior partner, and three players capable of making the second read. Its swing variable is whether the nominal wings create enough gravity that opponents cannot crowd Blackwell and Ngongba simultaneously. A three-guard structure with Blackwell, Boozer, and Foster offers the strongest demonstrated organization. It can move initiation between players and reduce the effect of pressure aimed at one handler. Its challenge is not ballhandling but size allocation and role clarity: one guard must screen, cut, or space rather than waiting for a turn. A freshman can displace one of the veterans by creating more first-line pressure, but only if he preserves the group's decision quality. A Scharnowski-at-center movement group could emphasize handoffs, early offense, and five-man connectivity. Its offensive ceiling depends less on Scharnowski becoming a high-volume shooter than on his defender being unable to sit at the rim. Four perimeter partners must cut and relocate around his catches. The cost belongs chiefly on defense and the glass, but offensively the test is whether passing produces rim attempts rather than aesthetically pleasing circulation. The Ngongba-Scharnowski two-big group can create seals, high-low reads, and offensive rebounding. It is the lineup most likely to be mislabeled from formation alone. If Scharnowski's defender retreats and Ngongba's defender stays home, the lane can vanish. Duke needs screening exchanges, elbow decisions, and strong weak-side shooting to make the pairing functional. It should be an opponent-specific tool until the defense proves it must guard both bigs outside the restricted area. A large-wing pressure group with Sarr and one or more freshmen can preserve size while surrounding a single big. Its offensive question is decision speed. Long wings who shoot, cut, and swing immediately can see over rotations and punish switches. Long wings who hesitate give the defense time to reload. The lineup should be judged by paint touches and advantage continuation, not by how imposing it looks walking onto the floor. What would verify or falsify the map The first official 2026–27 roster should resolve membership and listed measurements, not roles. Preseason comments can reveal intended experiments but are weak proof. Exhibitions can show who initiates and which combinations the staff wants to inspect; unusual opponents and scripted substitution patterns limit inference. Competitive games provide the first serious evidence. For each lineup, the Duke desk should record: who starts the possession; who produces the first two-defender reaction; what happens on the next catch; which defender is allowed to help; who screens and how the coverage responds; and where the shot or turnover comes from. Add late-clock ownership, turnover type, offensive-rebound responsibility, and free-throw shooting for closing groups. This chain is more diagnostic than raw usage or plus-minus. The map should change when a mechanism repeats. If Boozer organizes cleanly against several pressure teams, that is stronger than a single high-assist game. If opponents repeatedly go under Sarr and clog Ngongba's rolls, his spacing classification must remain limited even after a hot night. If Rippey forces two defenders and finds the second side against veteran competition, he has earned more than a prospect label. If Scharnowski's handoffs generate advantage without compromising finishing, his passing becomes a Duke mechanism rather than a Belmont résumé line. Why it matters Duke has enough reported talent to invite the wrong kind of certainty. A summer rotation can make every player look additive because it does not force the five-man group to divide actual possessions. The offensive role map imposes that constraint. It asks who organizes, who bends, who connects, who spaces, who screens, and who finishes—and whether the same lineup can cover all six without asking three players to do the same thing. That framework also makes development legible. Blackwell does not need to repeat 19.1 points to succeed if his pressure creates better team shots and he remains dangerous off the ball. Boozer can become more valuable without scoring much more if he organizes pressure possessions and attacks selective gaps. Sarr can transform the offense by turning ignored space into immediate cuts and decisions. Ngongba can increase impact through screens and passes that never enter his scoring average. Freshmen can earn roles through one dependable action before they become complete creators. Most importantly, the map preserves uncertainty honestly. July 2026 evidence supports candidates and experiments, not a finished offensive identity. Duke's strongest offense may be distributed without being leaderless: multiple initiators, one clear decision-maker on each possession, and enough complementary jobs that the defense cannot remove everything with one coverage. Sources Duke 2025–26 cumulative statistics — official completed-season player and team totals used for Boozer, Foster, Ngongba, Sarr, Cameron Boozer, and Evans; accessed July 10, 2026. Official Duke men's basketball roster — official roster selector; still displayed 2025–26 when accessed July 10, 2026. Duke–Washington State announcement — official statement that five players return, three transfers and the second-ranked recruiting class join them, plus named returning scorers; June 22, 2026; accessed July 10, 2026. CBS Sports Duke 2026–27 roster tracker — Cameron Salerno, May 1, 2026; independent newcomer identities, Blackwell and Scharnowski prior production, and roster context; accessed July 10, 2026. NCAA men's basketball statistics portal — authoritative national statistics entry point for later 2026–27 comparison and verification; accessed July 10, 2026. Open questions Who owns organization when Duke faces sustained full-court pressure rather than ordinary half-court defense? Can Blackwell force help and make the next read often enough to be both Duke's leading scorer and a scalable creator? Which two wings create genuine off-ball gravity around Ngongba rather than merely occupying perimeter spots? Does Scharnowski's passing translate quickly enough to make him a second offensive hub, and can that role coexist with Ngongba? Which freshman first demonstrates one repeatable action against veteran high-major competition? Who owns the late-clock possession, and does that player change according to coverage? Can Duke's most productive offensive group also defend and rebound well enough to close elite games?

title: Duke 2026-27 paint-touch conversion
deck: Duke's 2026–27 offense should judge paint touches by what they force and what follows, not merely by whether a ballhandler crosses an imaginary line in the lane.
headings: What qualifies as a paint touch
How Duke's personnel questions enter the model
Lineup spacing changes the meaning of a touch
text: Duke's 2026–27 offense should judge paint touches by what they force and what follows, not merely by whether a ballhandler crosses an imaginary line in the lane. Up: [[Duke men's basketball 2026-27]] · Related: [[Duke 2026-27 half-court shot creation]] · [[How Duke attacks compact defenses]] · [[Duke 2026-27 free-throw generation]] · [[Duke 2026-27 turnover economy]] As of July 10, 2026, Duke has no public 2026–27 game sample and its official roster page still displays 2025–26. The program has said at the aggregate level that five players return, three transfers arrive, and the nation's second-ranked recruiting class joins them. That establishes broad roster architecture, not a settled rotation or a measured offensive identity. This article therefore defines a conversion framework and testable hypotheses. It does not claim that an unplayed team already owns a particular paint-touch rate. The central distinction is between arrival and conversion . A paint touch is an arrival: the ball enters the lane by drive, roll, cut, post catch, offensive rebound, or another action. Conversion describes the advantage produced from that arrival. A touch can become a rim attempt, free throws, an open kick-out three, an interior dump-off, a productive repost, or a rapid second-side attack. It can also become a smothered pickup, a low-value fadeaway, a reset that allows the defense to recover, or a live-ball turnover. Counting all touches equally would mistake geography for offense. This distinction connects several existing Duke questions without duplicating them. [[Duke 2026-27 backcourt creation]] asks who can bend the first defender. [[How Duke attacks compact defenses]] explains how spacing and sequencing can move loaded help. [[Duke 2026-27 shooting and spacing]] owns the credibility of perimeter gravity. [[Duke 2026-27 free-throw generation]] owns foul pressure. Paint-touch conversion owns the chain between those functions: once Duke gets the ball inside, does the possession preserve and enlarge the advantage? What qualifies as a paint touch A useful ledger needs a definition strict enough to compare possessions. “Paint touch” should mean controlled possession of the ball in the lane or a controlled dribble that reaches it. A loose ball, a pass deflected through the paint, or a receiver who never controls the catch should not count. An offensive rebound controlled under the basket should count, but it should be tagged separately because it began from a missed shot rather than initial creation. A post catch should count only when the catch is in the lane; a catch several feet outside the block is an entry, not yet a paint touch. The entry route matters because it changes the defensive state. A straight-line drive against a set defense tests first-line containment. A roll catch usually means the ball screen has occupied two defenders or opened a seam. A baseline cut attacks vision. A transition touch may arrive before help is organized. A putback begins amid congestion and often carries immediate foul or turnover risk. Aggregating them can answer “how often did the ball enter?” but not “which mechanism worked?” Each touch should therefore carry at least five tags: initiator, entry route, defensive state, immediate reaction, and possession outcome. The defensive-state tag should distinguish set half court, transition or early offense, scrambled recovery, and offensive-rebound continuation. The reaction should record whether the defense stayed home, helped from the strong-side corner, tagged from the weak side, brought the rim defender upward, switched, collapsed multiple bodies, or fouled. Those observations make the statistic explanatory rather than decorative. The conversion tree The cleanest positive outcome is a controlled attempt at the rim. Even here, process matters. A layup against a displaced rim protector is not equivalent to a desperate extension over two set defenders. Record whether the attempt was uncontested, challenged by one defender, or crowded by multiple defenders; whether the finisher used the correct side of the rim; and whether a pass could have created an easier attempt. Results fluctuate. Repeated access to balanced, low-contest finishes is stronger evidence than a week of difficult makes. Free throws form the second branch. A touch that forces a defender to rotate late can generate a shooting foul, while a post seal can induce contact before the shot. Yet the ledger must not reward offensive fouls or reckless collision seeking. The valuable event is legitimate defensive compromise: the attacker wins an angle, keeps the ball protected, and makes the defender choose between conceding the finish and fouling. [[Duke 2026-27 free-throw generation]] should evaluate the roster-level sources and late-game implications; this page records whether paint entry caused the foul. The third branch is a direct interior pass. When a driver draws the center, a dump-off to a big may be the possession's highest-value decision. When the low defender tags a roller, a short pass to a cutter can exploit the vacated space. Timing is decisive. The receiver should catch before the helper can recover, preferably with the ball leading him into the finish rather than forcing him to gather below his waist. An “assist” can conceal the difference between a pass that creates the basket and one that merely arrives before a difficult make. The fourth branch is the kick-out. A pass from the paint is valuable when help has actually left a credible shooter or when the closeout creates a new driving lane. The three does not have to be taken immediately. If a defender flies past and the receiver attacks the open seam, the original paint touch initiated a second paint touch and a deeper rotation. Conversely, driving into a set crowd and throwing backward to a guarded teammate is not a successful conversion merely because the ball traveled from inside to outside. The fifth branch is continuation without an immediate shot: a quick swing, extra pass, relocation, repost, or second ball screen while the defense remains in recovery. This is where conventional box scores lose the possession's author. The first attacker may force help, the next receiver may move the defense, and a third player may finish. Duke should preserve that causal chain. Credit an advantage creation when the first touch forces a meaningful rotation, an advantage extension when the next decision prevents recovery, and a finish when the final action produces the shot or foul. The negative branches require equal attention. A turnover is most damaging when it is live-ball and exposes Duke's floor balance. A blocked shot can be a tolerable aggressive error or evidence that the attacker ignored a loaded rim. A bailout pass can technically retain possession while erasing the advantage. A slow pivot in traffic may invite a tie-up or three-second violation. A short contested jumper can represent capitulation if an open teammate was available. [[Duke 2026-27 turnover economy]] supplies the broader cost framework; the paint ledger identifies which entry routes and reads create those losses. Touch quality before outcome Conversion cannot be separated from the quality of the touch itself. A player who barely steps on the lane line with his dribble alive has different options from a player who reaches the restricted area with shoulders square. A receiver catching on two feet can pass or finish more reliably than one catching off balance. A driver who keeps vision on the weak side can punish the tag; one who buries his head may convert only by scoring. Tagging depth, balance, dribble state, and number of nearby defenders would make the ledger far more useful. “Deep and controlled” should describe a touch at or near the rim with the attacker balanced and able to choose. “Shallow but live” should describe lane entry with the dribble and passing windows intact. “Terminal” should describe a pickup or catch from which the player has only a difficult shot or bailout. Duke wants more of the first category, but a shallow live touch can still be excellent if it draws the nail defender and opens a clean pass. This is why raw paint-touch volume can mislead. An offense may inflate the count through repeated post catches against a defense content to guard one-on-one. Another may record fewer touches but force two defenders on nearly every one. The better comparison uses reaction rate —the share of touches that materially move a second defender—and advantage yield —the share that produce a good rim attempt, free throws, an open catch-and-shoot three, or a preserved closeout attack before the defense resets. How Duke's personnel questions enter the model The strongest verified returning guard evidence comes from Caleb Foster and Cayden Boozer. Duke's official 2025–26 statistics list Foster with 92 assists and 36 turnovers and Boozer with 113 assists and 51 turnovers. Those totals support ball-moving competence, but they do not reveal paint-touch depth, help reactions, or pass windows. Film coding must determine whether their next responsibility is generating more arrivals, converting arrivals more cleanly, or both. Foster's potential value is not limited to the initial drive. A guard who can receive a kick-out, attack a bent closeout, and make the next read may be the essential second creator. Boozer can be assessed similarly: does his speed create controlled lane access, and does he retain enough pace variation to see the low defender? The right question is not which player “runs point.” It is whether their touches connect rather than alternate. John Blackwell supplies the clearest individually established incoming-transfer case. He publicly committed to Duke and later withdrew from the NBA draft; Wisconsin's official 2025–26 totals show 678 points, 79 assists, 57 turnovers, 91 made three-pointers on 219 attempts, and 121 made free throws on 149 attempts. Those numbers establish scoring, shooting, and foul-line production in his prior context. They do not establish how Duke will deploy him or how often his prior paint touches created shots for teammates. Blackwell's conversion test should separate self-finishing from defense-bending. If his downhill attack forces the rim defender upward, can he deliver the pass before the low defender recovers? If help stays home, can he finish or draw a foul without needing a difficult bailout? His shooting matters because a defender who must chase him over a screen creates a different entry angle. But the completed-season percentages remain evidence of tools, not a guarantee that a new lineup will reproduce the same decision environment. Patrick Ngongba II gives the returning frontcourt a different conversion role. A screen can create the touch before he ever catches; a hard roll can occupy the low defender and open the corner. On the catch, his decision clock matters. Finish if the rim is available, pass immediately if the defense has collapsed, or establish a strong repost if the initial window closes. Holding the ball while cutters and shooters stand still converts an advantage into congestion. His evaluation should include screen-to-touch sequences, not only his own paint catches. The incoming freshman and transfer frontcourt remains less settled in official Duke materials. The responsible July posture is functional rather than declarative: identify which lineups supply vertical spacing, interior passing, shooting gravity, and offensive rebounding, then test how each function changes the conversion tree. A shooting big may pull the rim protector away; a rolling big may create a two-on-one; a second large forward may improve putbacks while shrinking driving lanes. Names and exact roles should follow the updated official roster and competitive evidence. Lineup spacing changes the meaning of a touch A five-out lineup can create a clean initial lane but may place no target behind the rim defender. A traditional center lineup can offer a lob and offensive-rebound presence while bringing an extra body near the basket. A two-big lineup may punish switches and own the glass, yet allow weak-side defenders to occupy gaps if neither big creates credible spacing. Paint-touch conversion is therefore a lineup statistic as much as an individual one. For every five-man group, Duke should track where the four off-ball players stand when the touch occurs. Is the dunker spot occupied on the same side as the drive, narrowing the baseline window? Are both corners filled? Does a spacer relocate behind the driver's line of sight? Does the screener roll into an already occupied lane? These details explain why the same ballhandler can look decisive in one unit and trapped in another. The best lineups will create multiple valid exits. If the rim protector steps up, the roller is available. If the low defender tags the roller, the corner is available. If the corner defender stunts and recovers, the receiver can attack the closeout. If the defense switches, a seal or favorable re-screen appears. Conversion quality is the offense repeatedly making the defender's choice wrong, not mechanically forcing one preferred shot. A practical game ledger The first review can use a possession table rather than a proprietary metric. Log game and time, lineup, initiator, entry route, touch depth, defensive reaction, first decision, resulting shot or turnover, and whether the defense fully reset before that outcome. Add a separate field for the player who created the initial advantage and the player who extended it. This avoids giving all causal credit to the final passer. After each game, report a small funnel: half-court possessions; possessions with at least one controlled paint touch; touches that forced meaningful help or a switch mismatch; touches converted before reset into a rim attempt, shooting foul, open three, or closeout drive; negative endings: live-ball turnover, offensive foul, blocked attempt into transition, or full reset. No universal benchmark should be invented before definitions and opponent contexts stabilize. Instead, compare Duke with itself across lineup types and defensive schemes. A game against switching may produce fewer direct drives but more post seals. A compact gap defense may concede above-the-break threes while denying the restricted area. A pressing team may yield transition touches that should not be mixed with set half-court creation. Opponent quality, score, foul state, and garbage time all belong in the interpretation. The ledger should also retain misses. If Duke creates ten clean corner threes from paint help and makes two, the process may be healthier than the score suggests. If it makes several contested pull-ups after shallow touches, the result may overstate the process. Over a larger sample, shot making matters; in small samples, separating access, decision, and execution prevents premature conclusions. Early tactical experiments One experiment is a two-sided ball-screen sequence. Begin with a high screen, place a credible shooter in the strong-side corner, and keep a second creator ready on the weak side. If the first action creates only a shallow touch, reverse immediately into the second action rather than resetting. The measurement is whether the first touch shifted the low defender enough to improve the second screen's lane. A second experiment is the empty-corner drive. Clearing one corner can remove the nearest helper and simplify the read between the rim protector and roller. Its risk is reduced spacing elsewhere and easier loading from the opposite side. Duke should compare who benefits: guards who need a clear finishing path, rollers who need a pocket window, or wings who can pass over the tag. A third is post-to-cut conversion. Against switches or smaller defenders, an interior catch may draw a dig rather than a hard double. Timed baseline and split cuts can turn that attention into a layup without asking the post player to manufacture a difficult shot. The key is whether the cutter moves when the defender's head turns and whether the passer delivers before the lane closes. A fourth is using a guard as the screener. A guard-guard screen can force a switch, create a short roll for a skilled decision-maker, or make defenders communicate through an unusual matchup. It is valuable only if the screener threatens something after contact. Slipping without drawing attention creates motion but not leverage. Record whether the action produces a deeper touch or merely rearranges defenders. Failure signals and decision rules The first warning is empty volume : many touches, few help reactions, and few quality outcomes. That suggests shallow entry, poor spacing, or personnel the defense is willing to guard one-on-one. The answer may be better screening angles or faster second-side action, not simply telling guards to drive more. The second is terminal congestion : attackers repeatedly enter with no live dribble, no passing window, and multiple defenders present. This can reflect late-clock necessity, but repetition early in possessions indicates a structural problem. Duke should alter starting locations, clear a side, or use the first touch as a trigger for relocation rather than a demand to finish. The third is advantage decay : the initial touch forces help, yet the next player holds the ball until the defense resets. Coaches often attribute this to “decision-making,” but the diagnosis should be specific. Was the pass late or inaccurate? Was the receiver ready? Did spacing leave no next drive? Was the shooter unwilling to take an appropriate attempt? Each cause implies a different correction. The fourth is conversion fragility by lineup . If one unit generates clean touches only when a particular creator is present, Duke may lack redundancy. If a large lineup converts only through offensive rebounds, it may struggle when opponents finish possessions. If a small lineup reaches the paint but cannot finish over length or rebound misses, its apparent creation may not survive stronger competition. [[Duke 2026-27 lineup scalability]] should own the broader matchup judgment; this ledger supplies the offensive evidence. What successful conversion would mean Successful Duke paint offense would not require one player to lead every category. One guard may create the first bend, another may excel against the closeout, a big may turn screens and rolls into vertical pressure, and a wing may make the weak-side pass. The offense becomes difficult to scheme when these jobs form a chain and can change owners across lineups. The season-level goal is a repeatable relationship: paint entry forces a defensive choice; Duke sees that choice early; the ball or attacker moves before recovery; and the possession ends with an efficient opportunity without sacrificing transition balance. When that relationship breaks, the ledger should show where—entry, reaction recognition, pass, reception, finish, or floor balance. That is more useful than proclaiming Duke a “paint-touch team.” Every competent offense wants access to the lane. The competitive question is whether Duke can convert access against organized, physical, scouting-aware defenses after the first option disappears. Until games exist, that remains an explicit test rather than a forecast dressed as fact. Wisconsin profile of John Blackwell — official prior-school biography and role context; accessed July 10, 2026. Open questions Which entry route produces Duke's highest reaction rate against a set half-court defense: drive, roll, cut, post catch, or offensive-rebound continuation? Which two-player sequence most reliably turns a first paint touch into a second advantage before the defense resets? Can Duke's larger lineups preserve both a roll target and credible weak-side spacing, or does a second big compress the conversion tree? Who makes the low-man read most accurately when the rim protector steps up, and who is the most dependable receiver on the resulting kick-out? How often do Blackwell's Duke paint touches create teammate attempts rather than only self-finishing opportunities? Does Foster's or Boozer's conversion quality change more through added touch depth, stronger finishing, or faster passing? What official roster, health, and practice evidence changes the functional lineup hypotheses before the first competitive game?

title: Duke 2026-27 passing windows
deck: Duke's 2026–27 passing problem is not simply finding one point guard; it is creating windows early enough, wide enough, and from enough different locations that several decision-makers can keep an advantage alive.
headings: The window is the unit of analysis
Five windows Duke should deliberately create
A verification ledger for the season
text: Duke's 2026–27 passing problem is not simply finding one point guard; it is creating windows early enough, wide enough, and from enough different locations that several decision-makers can keep an advantage alive. Up: [[Duke men's basketball 2026-27]] · Related: [[Duke 2026-27 offensive role map]] · [[Duke 2026-27 backcourt creation]] · [[Duke 2026-27 frontcourt combinations]] · [[How opponents pressure Duke's initiators]] The window is the unit of analysis As of July 10, 2026, Duke's public roster evidence supports a passing ecosystem more confidently than it supports a single dominant creator. The program has officially described a team with five returners, three transfers, and a highly regarded freshman class, but its live roster page still showed 2025–26 when checked. The completed-season statistics establish that returning guard Cayden Boozer recorded 115 assists against 55 turnovers, Patrick Ngongba II had 64 assists from the center position, and Caleb Foster supplied veteran handling beside 39 made threes. Official prior-school statistics establish that transfer big Drew Scharnowski averaged 2.6 assists per game at Belmont. Those facts identify possible passers. They do not yet prove that Duke can consistently produce the space in which their passes become useful. A passing window is the temporary lane between the ball and a productive receiving point. It may lead directly to the rim, to a roller, to a shooter, or merely to the next player who can attack a shifted defense. The window has four properties: location , width , duration , and value after the catch . A technically completed pass can still be a failure if it arrives late, forces the receiver away from the rim, or transfers the ball without transferring an advantage. A risky pass can be correct when the window is brief and the reward is a layup. Evaluating Duke by assists alone would erase these distinctions. The central July hypothesis is that Duke should build its offense around manufactured windows rather than asking one guard to improvise them on every possession. Screens, cuts, seals, handoffs, pace, and alignment can force defenders to reveal space. The passer then needs to recognize which window opened, deliver on time, and resist the more spectacular pass when a simpler continuation is available. This framing connects [[Duke 2026-27 turnover economy]] to shot quality: ball security is not minimizing ambitious passes; it is matching pass difficulty to the actual window. Five windows Duke should deliberately create The entry window The first test is whether Duke can enter an action cleanly against denial. An entry is not administrative. A wing catch one step farther from the basket changes the angle of a ball screen; a delayed post feed lets help establish position; a floating reversal gives a closeout time to arrive under control. Opponents described in [[How opponents pressure Duke's initiators]] can damage a possession before the nominal action begins simply by making the ballhandler retreat or by pushing every catch toward the sideline. Boozer's 2.09 assist-to-turnover ratio in 2025–26 makes him the clearest returning candidate to stabilize this phase, but his task should extend beyond bringing the ball over half court. Duke can use shallow cuts, guard-to-guard pitches, and early drags so that the entry itself changes a matchup. Foster's shooting makes him useful on either side of the pass: he can initiate, or his relocation can pull a defender away from the next window. Freshman Deron Rippey Jr. has an authoritative USA Basketball profile as a guard committed to Duke, but there is no college-possession evidence yet that establishes how quickly he will diagnose ACC denial. The coaching test is concrete: does Duke begin its first consequential action with at least 20 seconds on the shot clock and the intended spacing intact? If the answer is no, later assist totals may conceal an offense repeatedly solving self-created emergencies. The pocket and short-roll window Ball screens create Duke's most obvious vertical window. When the on-ball defender trails and the big steps toward the ball, a pocket pass can reach Ngongba or Scharnowski before the low defender rotates. The width of that lane depends on screen angle, ballhandler pace, the screener's departure, and the shooting credibility behind the help. It closes when the handler takes an extra dribble, the roller leaves too early, or a weak-side defender can stand in the lane without consequence. Ngongba's official 2025–26 line—.606 field-goal shooting, 70 offensive rebounds, and 64 assists—supports more than a finishing role. His passing total is evidence that possessions need not end when he catches between the arc and rim. The important projection, however, is not that he becomes a hub by declaration. It is that Duke can pass him into a four-on-three situation and measure what follows: immediate finish, one-dribble force, corner delivery, dunker-spot feed, or reset. The receiver's decision is part of the original pass's value. Scharnowski offers a different geometry. Belmont's official statistics list 78 assists in 30 games, 2.6 per game, alongside 10.7 points and 6.0 rebounds. That is a meaningful college passing signal for a big, but not proof of ACC translation. As a short roller he may receive slightly farther from the basket and use processing rather than burst. Duke should test whether his passes arrive before longer defenders recover and whether the lineup around him preserves two genuine outlets. In two-big units, one big must occupy or move the low defender; otherwise the pocket catch merely places the ball in congestion. The post-entry and split-cut window Ngongba's interior efficiency gives Duke a reason to feed the post, especially after switches. Yet a post entry is vulnerable to fronting, a baseline trap, or a guard digging from the nearest shooter. Duke can enlarge the window by entering from below the free-throw-line extended, screening the fronting defender, or using high-low alignment. The pass should reach Ngongba where he can score without first backing down a recovered defense. The second window opens after the catch. Perimeter players can split cut, screen for one another, or relocate behind a dig. This converts an interior touch from an isolation into a decision node. Foster's .398 three-point shooting in 2025–26 gives defenders a reason to hesitate before helping from him. Other returners and freshmen will have to earn the same reaction. If a defender can dig off a non-shooter and recover comfortably, the apparent kickout exists but has little value after the catch. Scharnowski may also create elbow-to-post windows. A high-low pass over a front can punish switching or denial without demanding that a guard thread the ball from the sideline. But this alignment requires timing: the low big must seal while the high big still owns a clear sight line. Holding the ball turns a seal into wrestling and lets the weak side collapse. The baseline and corner window Paint pressure is most valuable when the ballhandler can see the help defender's origin. A drive that forces the low man to tag the roller should expose either a corner shooter or a baseline cutter. This is where size and vision matter differently. A larger wing such as Dame Sarr may see over a compact defense, while a smaller guard may create a lower passing angle by getting closer to the rim. Neither advantage matters if the receiver stands still behind a defender's shoulder. Duke should pair the baseline drift with the drive rather than treat it as improvisation. When a driver reaches the lane line, the corner player can drift toward the baseline to widen the passing angle; when the defender turns fully toward the ball, a cut behind the head can create a layup. The passer must distinguish the two. Throwing to the original corner spot after the teammate has drifted is a live-ball turnover. Passing to a cutter who has not actually cleared the help is worse than keeping the ball. This window is especially important for John Blackwell. Wisconsin's official statistics establish his high-volume scoring and prior playmaking base, but Duke needs to learn what happens when elite help commits to his drive. His scalable outcome is not simply more assists. It is forcing the low defender to choose, then placing the pass where the recipient can shoot or finish without gathering into a recovery. The developmental measure should separate reads made on balance from bailout passes made after the lane has closed. The second-side window The best first pass often does not produce the shot. A pocket pass may draw the low defender; the roller then finds a wing; that wing attacks the closeout or makes one more pass. Duke's roster appears suited to this chain because Boozer, Foster, Blackwell, Ngongba, and Scharnowski can plausibly occupy different links. The risk is that “shared creation” becomes sequential turn-taking rather than connected advantage. A second-side window is usually wider but shorter than it looks. The receiver catches against a moving defense, yet every pause allows the shell to reset. Duke's wings therefore need a three-option rule on advantage catches: shoot a clean attempt, attack the defender's momentum, or move the ball immediately. Extra dribbles without new pressure destroy the value produced upstream. Boozer may be especially valuable here. His official assist and turnover record was built in a complementary role rather than as the only creator. Receiving after Blackwell or a big has bent the defense could let him use size and decision control without requiring him to win every first matchup. Foster can similarly move between organizer and finisher. The formation is less important than ensuring that the best quick reader receives the second pass while the best shooter or cutter occupies the next outlet. Who owns which read The July evidence supports provisional ownership, not fixed positions. Boozer has the strongest returning possession-management evidence and should own difficult entries, pressure releases, and many second-side connections. Foster can initiate basic actions, punish under-help as a shooter, and attack a tilted closeout. Blackwell should create the first defensive commitment and prove that his passing scales when help is faster and teammates are more talented. Ngongba should own roll catches, post decisions, and high-low seals. Scharnowski should be tested as a handoff, elbow, and short-roll connector. The freshmen remain projections. Rippey's guard identity supports early testing as an organizer, not an assumption that he is immediately Duke's primary point guard. Cameron Williams and Bryson Howard may supply large-wing sight lines and receiving gravity, but high-school reputation cannot verify college processing speed. The correct early-season question is not “Can the freshman pass?” It is “Which read can he execute repeatedly against a scouting report?” A player may be ready for the corner lift before the weak-side skip, or for the simple pocket pass before rejecting the screen and reading a rotating center. Player First July passing responsibility Window that can expand the role Evidence still needed Cayden Boozer Entry organization and second-side continuity Live-dribble pocket and cross-court reads Efficiency against concentrated pressure as usage rises Caleb Foster Basic initiation and fast closeout decisions Late-clock pick-and-roll creation Healthy, repeatable reads against switches and traps John Blackwell Force help and pass from scoring pressure Baseline/corner and opposite-slot deliveries Turnover-adjusted advantage creation at Duke Patrick Ngongba II Post, roll, and offensive-rebound decisions Short-roll playmaking against two on the ball Accuracy before low-man recovery Drew Scharnowski Handoffs and elbow connection Four-on-three short-roll orchestration Translation against ACC speed and length Dame Sarr Immediate swing, cut, or closeout attack Large-wing drive-and-kick reads A stable handle and quick decisions under pressure Deron Rippey Jr. Simple entries and pace organization Primary ball-screen reads College turnover rate and coverage recognition Cameron Williams / Bryson Howard Advantage catches and low-complexity continuation Skip passes and live-dribble creation Which reads remain dependable in competitive games Lineup architecture changes the pass In a three-guard lineup, Duke can place two release valves around the initiator. Pressure against Blackwell becomes less damaging if Boozer and Foster exchange into visible passing lanes rather than wait at static spots. The cost is that one guard must create value without the ball through screening, cutting, or gravity. Three handlers do not automatically create three windows. With Ngongba as the lone big, Duke can use conventional spread ball screens and place four possible receivers above or outside the lane. This is the clearest environment for pocket passes and corner decisions. Its effectiveness depends on whether the weakest shooter is positioned as an active cutter or screener instead of becoming the defender who tags the roll for free. With Scharnowski at center, passing can originate at the elbow through delay actions and dribble handoffs. The ball may move more, but circulation is useful only if it produces a defender facing the wrong direction or two defenders guarding one action. Duke should count rim pressure and open attempts generated from the hub, not touches at the hub. The Ngongba–Scharnowski pairing creates high-low and interior-offensive-rebound possibilities, while narrowing certain drive-and-kick windows. To function, the big away from the ball must screen, occupy the dunker spot dynamically, or lift high enough to move his defender. If both big defenders can see ball and assignment from the paint, the lineup has converted passing talent into smaller windows. A verification ledger for the season The first official roster update can verify membership and listed size, but not decision quality. Preseason practice comments identify intended roles, not successful ones. Exhibitions reveal alignments and preferred actions, yet opponent quality can make windows appear wider than they will be in ACC play. Competitive possession coding is the necessary next layer. For each half-court possession, the Duke desk should identify the intended first action, whether the entry arrived on time, which defender first committed to the ball, which window opened, whether the pass arrived before recovery, and the receiver's next action. Record failed reads as well as turnovers: a missed roller that becomes a contested make is still a passing failure; a correct corner pass that produces a missed open three is still good process. Add pass destination and delivery type—one hand, two hand, bounce, hook, overhead, or jump pass—only when those details explain whether the window was actually usable. Four rates would make the framework operational: On-time entry rate: intended actions begun with spacing intact and at least 20 seconds remaining. Advantage-transfer rate: passes after a defensive commitment that leave the receiver with a shot, drive, or immediate two-on-one. Window-loss rate: possessions in which a visible productive pass disappears because of an extra dribble, hold, or inaccurate delivery. Receiver-conversion rate: useful outcomes after an on-time pass, separated into rim attempt, open three, foul, continued advantage, reset, and turnover. These measures should be split by passer, receiver, lineup, coverage, and opponent quality. A raw aggregate can flatter a player who makes safe reversals while hiding the guard asked to attempt narrow, high-value reads. Conversely, turnover rate without window difficulty can punish the only player generating rim chances. Film and outcome must remain connected. What success would look like Duke does not need every player to become an advanced creator. It needs enough complementary readers that a defense cannot end the possession by removing one route. Against ball pressure, a guard-to-guard outlet should preserve the entry. Against a hard hedge, a big should become a short-roll decision-maker. Against deep drop, the handler should reach a pull-up or pocket lane without drifting sideways. Against switching, the group should feed the seal or attack the mismatch before the defense scrams out. Against compact help, the baseline and second-side windows must turn paint pressure into valuable catches. The strongest version of this team would therefore have a hierarchy of reads rather than a monopoly of touches. Blackwell could force the first commitment, Boozer make the second decision, Ngongba finish or connect, and Foster punish the final rotation; on the next possession those jobs could rotate. The weak version would feature the same players exchanging the ball without changing the defense, then asking one scorer to rescue the clock. Passing windows make that distinction observable. They prevent a made shot from excusing a late read and a missed shot from condemning a correct one. More importantly, they show how roster construction becomes offense: size changes sight lines, shooting changes help distance, screening changes duration, and decision speed determines whether temporary space becomes a durable advantage. Wisconsin 2025–26 cumulative statistics — official prior-season statistical baseline for John Blackwell; accessed July 10, 2026. Belmont 2025–26 cumulative statistics — official 30-game scoring, rebounding, assist, and turnover baseline for Drew Scharnowski; accessed July 10, 2026. Deron Rippey Jr., USA Basketball — authoritative player identity, guard designation, listed size, school, and Duke commitment; accessed July 10, 2026. CBS Sports Duke 2026–27 roster tracker — independent roster and transfer-production cross-check; May 1, 2026; accessed July 10, 2026. Open questions Which guard owns the first entry against full-court denial, and does Duke preserve at least 20 seconds for its intended half-court action? Can Blackwell deliver to the corner or opposite slot before elite help recovers, rather than only after his scoring path closes? Does Ngongba's passing scale from post and connective possessions to repeated short-roll four-on-three reads? Can Scharnowski's 2.6 assists per game at Belmont translate when ACC defenders shorten the window with greater length and recovery speed? Which freshman read becomes dependable first: pressure release, pocket pass, baseline delivery, or second-side skip? In Ngongba–Scharnowski lineups, can Duke create high-low value without losing the drive-and-kick windows needed by its guards? What share of Duke's turnovers come from wrong reads, late reads, inaccurate delivery, or receivers failing to complete the route?

title: Duke 2026-27 point-of-attack defense
deck: Duke’s 2026–27 point-of-attack defense should be judged by whether its guards reliably steer the ball into the planned coverage, survive screens, and recover without forcing the back line into emergency rotations—not by steals, reputation, or a presumed summer matchup hierarchy.
headings: What is known, and what is only a projection
Containment is an angle, not a shutout
Keep the first drive out of the middle
Navigate the screen without abandoning the play
Guard without creating a foul crisis behind the ball
Finish the recovery and rejoin the shell
Cayden Boozer: event production versus disciplined pressure
John Blackwell: physical option with workload tradeoffs
Deron Rippey Jr.: pressure upside that must become discipline
Dame Sarr and the large-wing exception
Coverage changes who should take the assignment
text: Duke’s 2026–27 point-of-attack defense should be judged by whether its guards reliably steer the ball into the planned coverage, survive screens, and recover without forcing the back line into emergency rotations—not by steals, reputation, or a presumed summer matchup hierarchy. Up: [[Duke men's basketball 2026-27]] · Related: [[Duke 2026-27 defensive role map]] · [[Jon Scheyer's defensive evolution at Duke]] · [[Duke 2026-27 lineup scalability]] What is known, and what is only a projection As of July 10, 2026, Duke has announced the broad shape of the next roster but has not published evidence of its 2026–27 defensive assignments. The program says five players return, including Cayden Boozer, Caleb Foster, Patrick Ngongba II, and Dame Sarr; three transfers and the nation’s second-ranked recruiting class join them. Duke’s official roster page still displays 2025–26. Any claim that a particular player has already been assigned the opponent’s lead guard, has improved laterally over the summer, or is fully healthy would therefore exceed the public record. The completed statistics provide narrower facts. Foster played 816 minutes, Boozer 872, and Sarr 893 for Duke in 2025–26. Foster recorded 10 steals, Boozer 31, and Sarr 37. Wisconsin’s official ledger credits incoming transfer John Blackwell with 38 steals in 1,145 minutes. USA Basketball identifies incoming freshman Deron Rippey Jr. as a 6-foot-2 guard committed to Duke. Those figures identify candidates and experience levels. They do not measure screen navigation, matchup difficulty, the help behind a defender, or whether a gamble broke the scheme. This note therefore does not name a settled stopper. It maps the containment jobs Duke must fill, assigns provisional candidates on defensible evidence, and specifies tests that can overturn the projection. The broader division of all six defensive jobs belongs in [[Duke 2026-27 defensive role map]]. The center of this page is narrower: what happens between the moment a handler receives the ball and the moment Duke’s help structure must engage. Containment is an angle, not a shutout Point-of-attack defense is often narrated as a duel: defender versus scorer. Duke’s actual problem is relational. The on-ball defender must know the call, influence the handler toward the intended help, and remain connected enough that the helper can perform one job rather than choose among three threats. A defender can concede a difficult pull-up and execute correctly. He can also force a miss after opening the wrong lane and execute poorly. Outcome alone does not identify the mechanism. Against a right-handed guard in middle pick-and-roll, for example, Duke might ask the defender to chase over while Ngongba plays drop. The guard’s first job is to prevent rejection of the screen if that rejection escapes the coverage. At contact he must get narrow, avoid clipping the screener, and reattach to the handler’s back hip. Ngongba can then contain the ball and roller within a defined window. If the guard dies on the screen, Ngongba faces the pull-up, drive, and lob at once; the low man tags; the corner becomes vulnerable; and the possession may end in a foul or offensive rebound. The box score often assigns the consequence to the center even though the first failure occurred twenty feet away. “Keeping the ball in front” is therefore too blunt. Sometimes the scheme deliberately trails a shooter and relies on rear pressure. Sometimes it sends the ball weak, switches, or shows two defenders before recovering. The useful standard is whether the on-ball defender preserves the geometry of the called coverage. That includes four separable skills: stance and initial angle, screen anticipation, contact survival, and recovery discipline. The four perimeter jobs Keep the first drive out of the middle Middle penetration compresses every help assignment because the handler can pass to either side. Duke’s primary containment defender must shade without overcommitting, absorb a shoulder without opening his hips too early, and turn the drive toward a boundary or a waiting big. The defender need not steal the ball. He needs to reduce the handler’s options. Foster is the most plausible returning organizer for this task. Duke listed him at 6-foot-5 and 205 pounds in 2025–26, and three seasons in the program give him the strongest continuity case among the projected guards. That establishes familiarity and size, not superiority. His low steal total cannot prove poor containment, just as a higher total would not prove good containment. The first falsifiable question is whether Duke gives him the opening assignment on quick lead guards and whether those guards repeatedly reach the center of the floor before the screen arrives. Boozer offers a second continuity option. His 31 steals were the most among the returning quartet named in Duke’s June release, but steals combine anticipation, off-ball events, and gambles. The relevant translation is whether he can influence a live-ball creator without reaching himself out of position. If Duke consistently assigns him to lower-usage connectors while another guard takes the primary handler, that would weaken the projection that he is a first-line containment answer even if his steals remain high. Navigate the screen without abandoning the play Screen navigation is the roster’s decisive unresolved skill. A guard can be sturdy in isolation yet lose the possession at contact. Good navigation begins before the screen: hear or see the call, close the handler’s preferred setup angle, and choose the route demanded by the coverage. Going under, chasing over, top-locking, and switching are not grades. Each is correct only in context. Foster and Boozer deserve the earliest continuity presumption because they have defended Duke’s calls in college games. Blackwell deserves an experience presumption because he played 33.7 minutes per game at Wisconsin in 2025–26. Neither presumption establishes performance in Scheyer’s terminology or behind Duke’s centers. Rippey’s national-team background makes him an intriguing candidate, but USA Basketball’s profile verifies identity, size, and experience in its program—not college screen navigation. The best early measure is not how often a defender is screened. It is how often he remains functionally involved after contact. On each on-ball screen, record whether he arrives attached, is briefly detached but recovers before the second decision, or is removed from the possession. A defender who trails by half a step while taking away the pull-up may have executed. A defender who avoids contact by conceding a straight-line drive has not. Guard without creating a foul crisis behind the ball Perimeter pressure can become counterfeit aggression when it transfers fouls to the back line. Duke’s official totals credit Ngongba with 90 personal fouls in 701 minutes—about 5.1 per 40 minutes. Not all were caused by perimeter breakdowns, and the public totals do not classify them. The number nevertheless makes the dependency urgent. A guard who repeatedly releases the handler cleanly toward Ngongba forces the center to make high-risk decisions and may reduce the minutes of Duke’s most established rim protector. The point defender must also avoid his own avoidable fouls: reaching after being beaten, grabbing over a screen, or crowding a handler without legal position. Foul rate alone is inadequate because matchup difficulty and whistle context vary. Film coding should separate productive physicality from bailout contact and identify whether the first defender or the helper initiated the chain. This creates a useful alternative explanation for any apparent interior problem. If Ngongba’s foul rate falls, he may have improved his positioning; Duke’s guards may have improved containment; the staff may have changed coverage; or the opponents may pose less rim pressure. Only possession tagging can distinguish them. The same caution applies if the rate remains high. Finish the recovery and rejoin the shell The job continues after the ball leaves. A blitz, stunt, or drive may require the original defender to peel onto a roller, sprint to a shooter, or exchange assignments with the low man. Young defenders often complete the impressive first act—pressure the ball—then stop while teammates scramble. Duke needs guards who can make the second and third effort without confusing the coverage. This favors continuity conceptually, but experience is not proof. Foster and Boozer should recognize more of Scheyer’s vocabulary than newcomers; Sarr has a season in the system and can absorb some larger perimeter assignments. Blackwell brings major-conference experience, while Rippey brings a high-upside defensive prior. The correct hierarchy will emerge from communication and repeatability, not seniority alone. Candidate map, with explicit limits Caleb Foster: continuity baseline Foster is the cleanest July candidate to organize the first line because he combines program tenure with guard size. His offensive role also appears compatible with shared initiation, which could leave capacity for a difficult defensive assignment. But no public source establishes his current mobility, 2026–27 health, or staff-designated matchup. This note makes none of those claims. The Foster projection survives if he regularly opens on fast ball-screen guards, sends them toward the call, and stays in the play through repeated screens. It weakens if Duke protects him on lower-movement assignments, if opponents reject screens into the middle, or if his matchup repeatedly forces early help. His ten steals last season should have almost no weight in that judgment. Cayden Boozer: event production versus disciplined pressure Boozer’s returning production and 31 steals make him impossible to exclude from the competition. His value may be greatest as a physical secondary defender who can switch among guards, stunt from the nail, and rebound the possession rather than chase the smallest creator all night. That is a tactical hypothesis, not a limitation established by data. The discriminator is matchup allocation. Does Duke trust Boozer to take a primary handler through multiple screening actions, or use him on a connector so he can disrupt off the ball? Does his pressure force the ball toward help, or does it produce steals alongside middle drives and emergency rotations? A lower steal rate with fewer structural breakdowns could represent improvement. John Blackwell: physical option with workload tradeoffs Blackwell’s Wisconsin record is substantial: 34 starts, 33.7 minutes per game, 19.1 points, 5.1 rebounds, and 38 steals in 2025–26. It supports durability in a large role, physical guard rebounding, and experience against major-conference opponents. It does not isolate defensive matchup quality or forecast immediate command of Duke’s calls. His offensive burden complicates the assignment. Duke may ask Blackwell to create late-clock shots and therefore avoid spending his energy chasing an opponent’s quickest guard. Alternatively, his 6-foot-4, 203-pound Wisconsin listing may make him the most useful option against strong scoring guards. The tradeoff is empirical: compare his offensive efficiency and late-game decision quality across games in which he does and does not carry the primary matchup. Do not assume workload fatigue from one poor shooting night. Deron Rippey Jr.: pressure upside that must become discipline USA Basketball verifies Rippey as a 6-foot-2 guard and Duke commit. His pathway to early minutes may include speed and ball pressure, but public credentials do not establish execution against college screening, spacing, and strength. The temptation will be to treat steals or full-court harassment as proof that he is already Duke’s best point defender. The stronger test is bounded responsibility. Can he pick up the ball without being back-cut? Can he angle the dribbler toward the call, get over the first screen, and avoid gambling after losing contact? Can he execute the weak-side exchange after the ball moves? If those actions repeat against veteran handlers, his role can expand. If his pressure produces both highlights and four-on-three situations behind him, the staff may deploy him in bursts rather than as the default stopper. Dame Sarr and the large-wing exception Sarr is not the natural answer for every small guard, but his 6-foot-8 listing and returning experience make him relevant against large initiators and switch-heavy lineups. The question is whether his length can absorb the first drive without sacrificing screen recovery or rebounding position. Assigning him to a primary creator may also remove him from weak-side disruption, where length can have greater leverage. His usage should therefore be opponent-specific. If Duke faces a tall wing who initiates offense, Sarr may own the point of attack. Against a very quick guard, he may be better as the next defender in the chain. Successful possessions against one archetype should not be generalized to the other. Coverage changes who should take the assignment In a Ngongba drop, Duke needs a guard who can chase and apply rear pressure without leaving Ngongba in a permanent two-on-one. Foster’s continuity makes him the first candidate; Boozer and Blackwell must prove the same route discipline. Rippey could raise the pickup point, but pressure is useful only if the handler reaches the screen later and less comfortably. With Drew Scharnowski or another mobile big playing higher, the guard may need to recover under the show, switch briefly, or rotate onto the screener. That places more value on communication and physical rebounding after the exchange. The prior-school box score cannot determine who does it best. Switch-heavy groups change the job again. The first defender must call the exchange early, resist slipping actions, and survive if the offense screens him onto a larger player. Sarr and Blackwell may gain value because of size; Rippey’s speed may matter less if the possession ends with a post seal. A switch that prevents penetration but concedes an offensive rebound has not completed the defensive task. Pressure lineups can use Rippey or another quick guard to consume clock and steer the entry, then fall into a more conservative half-court coverage. This may be the best way to exploit youthful energy without requiring forty minutes of flawless screen navigation. The evidence gate remains the same: does the pressure simplify the next action, or merely move the breakdown farther from the basket? A falsifiable November test plan Duke’s demanding nonconference schedule supplies varied tests. The official program announcement lists Michigan State, Illinois, Connecticut, Florida, Michigan, Gonzaga, and Washington State among the 2026–27 opponents. Preseason labels about who is “elite defensively” should yield to possession evidence from those games. For every meaningful stint, record five items: the opening matchup, ball-screen coverage, first defender beaten or detached, first helper engaged, and final possession result. Add whether the defense secured the rebound. This permits several concrete tests: Middle-containment test: Against a quick lead guard, how often does the handler enter the paint through the middle before Duke’s planned screen coverage engages? Repeated early middle entry falsifies the claim that the assigned guard is controlling direction. Screen-survival test: On comparable high ball screens, how often is the defender still influencing the ball at the handler’s second decision? Being present matters more than avoiding the screen entirely. Back-line-cost test: How many Ngongba or weak-side rotations begin because the point defender lost the called angle? A decline in emergency help is better evidence than a rise in steals. Foul-chain test: Which fouls follow a point-of-attack loss, and which originate independently at the rim? This separates perimeter improvement from interior improvement. Matchup-trust test: Who receives the opening and closing assignment on small pull-up guards, strong downhill guards, and large wing initiators? Staff choices across archetypes reveal a role map more clearly than one starting lineup. Repeatability test: Does the same player execute across three to five games and against starting-caliber opponents? One exhibition, one weak opponent, or one highlight sequence cannot settle the question. Lineup-dependence test: Does a defender’s apparent success persist behind different centers and beside different helpers? If it disappears when Ngongba sits, the earlier result may partly belong to the anchor. These are diagnostic tests, not universal public metrics. Video access, camera angle, and ambiguous calls will limit precision. Uncertain possessions should be marked uncertain rather than forced into a category. The aim is a defensible sample of mechanisms, not false decimal-point authority. Alternative explanations and uncertainty Opponent shooting can distort defensive judgment. A guard may execute perfectly and concede a made contested pull-up; another may be beaten cleanly and benefit from a missed layup. Over a short sample, score and field-goal percentage can reward the worse process. Film grades should be kept beside outcomes, not replaced by them. Coverage can also make one player look better. A deep drop gives the guard a visible rear-contest role; an aggressive show may erase the initial advantage before viewers notice the guard’s recovery. Strong nail help can disguise poor containment, while weak communication can make a good on-ball stand end badly elsewhere. Any ranking that ignores the other four defenders will overclaim. Workload, officiating, opponent quality, and lineup spacing introduce further confounders. A primary scorer may defend differently late in games, but fatigue should not be inferred without repeated evidence. A physical guard may appear worse under a tight whistle. A freshman may dominate an exhibition matchup that never tests his screen reads. A veteran may look slow against an All-America candidate but remain Duke’s best available option. Finally, public roster and health information can change. The analysis should update when Duke publishes its final roster, official biographies, and availability information. Until then, it should not invent summer assignments, rehabilitation progress, or closed-practice results. Why it matters Duke’s point-of-attack defense controls the cost of every downstream choice. Reliable containment lets Ngongba protect the rim without constant foul exposure, lets Sarr stay attached to a large wing or operate as a calculated helper, and lets the weak side rebound instead of rotating through crisis. Poor containment converts a deep roster into a sequence of emergency substitutions and forces Scheyer to choose between offense, pressure, and interior protection. The July answer is therefore a portfolio, not a name. Foster owns the strongest continuity case; Boozer offers event production and physical secondary value; Blackwell supplies major-conference experience and size; Rippey offers a plausible pressure pathway; Sarr provides an opponent-specific large-wing option. Each case has a clear way to fail. Duke will have solved the role only when at least two guards can preserve the planned coverage against different creator types, allowing assignments to change without breaking the chain. That threshold is more demanding than finding one stopper and more useful over a season. Opponents will screen the preferred defender out of the action, hunt weaker links, and change creator archetypes. Duke’s best defense will not hide from those variations. It will have enough verified containment to choose who applies pressure, who navigates, who absorbs size, and who remains fresh for the next job. Official Duke men’s basketball roster — official listed sizes and roster status; still displayed 2025–26 when checked July 10, 2026. Wisconsin 2025–26 cumulative statistics — official Blackwell games, starts, minutes, scoring, rebounding, and steals; accessed July 10, 2026. John Blackwell’s Wisconsin biography — official prior-career and role context; accessed July 10, 2026.
