title: 2026 NBA offseason transaction verification ledger
deck: The safest 2026 NBA roster baseline is an event ledger that separates completed team actions from reported agreements; in the clearest Dallas correction, the Mavericks waived Tyus Jones on February 28 and Denver signed him on March 5.
headings: Why an event ledger beats a roster screenshot
text: The safest 2026 NBA roster baseline is an event ledger that separates completed team actions from reported agreements; in the clearest Dallas correction, the Mavericks waived Tyus Jones on February 28 and Denver signed him on March 5. Up: [[NBA and Dallas Mavericks]] Direct summary This ledger answers a narrow but consequential question: what transaction state can be treated as verified when building a 2026-27 NBA roster, minutes forecast, or team analysis? It records the event, effective date, evidence tier, resulting roster implication, and any remaining uncertainty. It does not treat a social-media report, an NBA.com roundup of reported agreements, an outdated roster page, or a writer's inference as equivalent to a completed club transaction. The first fully adjudicated case is Tyus Jones. Dallas's official 2025-26 game notes list “2/28: Waived Tyus Jones.” Denver then published a dated club announcement on March 5 saying that the Nuggets had signed him. Denver's official team-information history also labels him “Signed on 03/05/26,” and Denver's playoff game notes place the signing in the club's recent-transactions chronology. Those independent official surfaces agree on the sequence. Therefore Jones must receive zero projected Dallas minutes after February 28, 2026. His later Denver status must be evaluated separately because the NBA's July offseason trackers describe a reported one-year return, while the currently indexed Denver roster page labels him a free agent. A reported July agreement is not promoted here to a completed signing without a club announcement or official transaction entry. As of: July 10, 2026, America/New_York. This is a verification state, not a claim that every 2026 offseason move has been collected. Verified transaction ledger Effective date Player From To / disposition Event Verification state Roster consequence 2026-02-28 Tyus Jones Dallas Mavericks Waivers Dallas waived Jones Verified completed by Dallas's official game-notes transaction chronology Remove Jones from every post-February 28 Dallas roster, depth chart, lineup, cap, and minutes model 2026-03-05 Tyus Jones Free agent / waivers cleared or otherwise available Denver Nuggets Denver signed Jones Verified completed by Denver's dated announcement, team-information history, and game-notes chronology Assign his remaining 2025-26 club state to Denver, not Dallas 2026-07-02 reported Tyus Jones Free agent after 2025-26 Denver term Denver Nuggets Reported agreement to return on a one-year deal Reported, not yet promoted to completed in this ledger ; NBA.com offseason pages attribute the agreement to reports, while Denver's indexed roster labels him a free agent Do not use the reported deal as a completed-contract fact until an official Denver or NBA transaction surface confirms it The first two rows form one verified chain, but they remain separate events. Dallas's waiver proves only that Jones left Dallas. Denver's announcement proves where he next signed. Neither event, by itself, establishes the terms of his March contract, whether it extended beyond 2025-26, or whether the reported July agreement has become an executed 2026-27 contract. Why an event ledger beats a roster screenshot Roster pages are snapshots assembled for presentation. They can lag a waiver, retain a player through caching, switch to offseason “free agent” labels, or omit the effective mechanics behind an acquisition. A transaction is an event with a date and an issuer. The durable research object is therefore not “Jones appears on page X today,” but “Dallas recorded a waiver on February 28; Denver announced a signing on March 5.” That distinction matters because a roster model is path-dependent. If an old Dallas page or third-party depth chart still contains Jones, a model may allocate him 15–20 minutes, reduce minutes for Ryan Nembhard or Marcus Sasser, and infer a level of ball security that Dallas does not actually possess. The initial identity error then contaminates lineup combinations, usage estimates, guard-depth conclusions, cap assumptions, and even prose about coaching choices. [[Dallas Mavericks roster and minutes ledger]] should consume the verified event chain, not re-litigate it from display pages. The Denver evidence also demonstrates why a second official source is useful even after a club announcement. The March 5 article is a contemporaneous declaration. Denver's official team information later preserved “Signed on 03/05/26,” and its playoff notes included “3/5/26 ... Signed Tyus Jones” in recent transactions. Agreement across a dated announcement, roster history, and game notes sharply reduces the possibility of a headline mix-up, publication-date confusion, or similarly named player error. It also distinguishes Tyus Jones from Denver forward Spencer Jones, whose contract conversion appears elsewhere in the same transaction chronology. Evidence hierarchy The ledger uses the following order when sources conflict: Official transaction announcement or official transaction log. A dated team release explicitly saying “signed,” “waived,” “traded,” or “converted” is the strongest ordinary public evidence of a completed action. Official game notes or team-information transaction history. These are retrospective operational records. They are especially valuable for waivers that did not receive a durable standalone news release. NBA-published official trade announcement or league transaction surface. This can settle multi-team structure and formal completion. NBA.com news roundup that explicitly labels a move reported. This is strong evidence that an agreement was publicly reported, but its own wording prevents treating the contract as officially executed. Current official roster display. Useful corroboration, but weaker than a dated event record when caching, free-agency transitions, or page maintenance create a mismatch. Established reporting and databases. Valuable for discovering candidates and contract detail, but a discovery lead is not the same thing as official completion. This hierarchy is not a judgment about journalistic quality. It answers a narrower database question: what public artifact establishes that the team or league actually recorded the roster action? A reporter can be correct hours or days before a club release, yet the proper state remains “reported agreement” during that interval. Context and mechanism Jones's Dallas tenure began amid deadline churn. NBA.com reported that Orlando sent him to Charlotte, which then sent him to Dallas on February 5. Dallas's own February 9 feature described the unusual three-team, two-day movement and identified him as a new Mavericks guard. Denver's March announcement later summarized his 2025-26 Orlando-and-Dallas total as 56 games, including ten starts, and credited him with a 7.68 assist-to-turnover ratio among qualifying players at that moment. The relevant mechanism on February 28 was a waiver , not a trade. A waiver removes the player from the waiving team's active roster and exposes his contract to the league's waiver process; if unclaimed, the player generally becomes a free agent. Public sources reviewed for this ledger establish Dallas's act and Denver's later signing, but they do not establish every intervening procedural detail or the financial terms. The defensible statement is consequently simple: Dallas waived Jones on February 28, and Denver signed him on March 5. It is unnecessary—and unsafe—to invent the exact clearance time, cap treatment, guarantee, or exception used. The March 5 Denver announcement establishes a signing but does not state contract length or salary. That omission matters in July. A March signing for the remainder of 2025-26 could end at the league-year boundary, making Jones a free agent, while a multi-year agreement would produce a different status. Denver's currently indexed roster page shows “FA / Free Agent” beside Jones, and NBA.com's July 2 offseason roundup says he “returns” to Denver on a reported one-year deal. Together those pages support the interpretation that a new agreement was required, but the conclusion remains an inference unless contract terms or a completed July signing are officially posted. This is why one player's history can contain three different truth states without contradiction: the February 28 Dallas waiver is completed and verified; the March 5 Denver signing is completed and verified for the 2025-26 context; the July Denver return is reported but not yet verified here as a completed 2026-27 signing. How to use this ledger For a roster snapshot, begin with the last verified completed event for each player, then apply only later events whose evidence clears the same gate. Do not fill silence with a previous team's roster page. Record the as-of timestamp because an offseason ledger can become outdated within minutes. For projections, convert each row into a state transition: That chain should feed [[NBA roster churn as projection uncertainty]], [[Dallas Mavericks 2026-27 roster construction dossier]], and [[Dallas guard creation after roster turnover]]. It does not answer how good Jones was, how Denver used him, or what role he would have in 2026-27. It only prevents those analyses from beginning with the wrong employer. For cap work, do not infer salary, guarantee, Bird status, exception type, or tax effect from the word “signed.” Those require contract-specific evidence and the applicable collective-bargaining rules. For lineup work, do not interpret a reported future agreement as availability for opening night; execution, medical review, later transactions, and final roster decisions can still matter. Why it matters The Jones correction is small in transaction volume and large in downstream effect. Point guard is a high-leverage role in a Dallas roster already requiring careful distinctions among primary creation, secondary handling, and low-turnover organization. Leaving Jones in Dallas would make the guard room look more stable than the verified roster warrants. It could cause an analyst to understate the creation burden on Kyrie Irving and Cooper Flagg, misclassify Nembhard or Sasser's opportunity, and explain away a roster need that remains real. It also illustrates a general 2026 offseason research problem. “Official website” is not a single evidentiary category. An official team news release can confirm completion; an official roster can lag or shift labels; an NBA.com news-services story can repeat a report while conspicuously stopping short of official confirmation. Good transaction research preserves those verbs. Agreed , reportedly agreed , signed , waived , and appears on the roster are not interchangeable. Maintaining that discipline makes later revisions cheaper. When Denver publishes a new Jones announcement or its transaction history adds a July date, the third row can be promoted with one citation and timestamp. No surrounding prose needs to be rewritten, because the distinction between March completion and July reporting is already explicit. Verification notes Identity checked: Tyus Robert Jones, NBA player ID 1626145; not Spencer Jones or another similarly named player. Dallas waiver date checked: February 28, 2026, in Dallas's official game-notes transaction list. Denver signing date checked: March 5, 2026, in a dated Nuggets announcement; corroborated by Denver team information and game notes. Sequence checked: Jones appeared in official NBA game-book material for Dallas on February 26 and for Denver on March 25, consistent with the transaction chain, though game participation is corroboration rather than the controlling transaction proof. July status bounded: NBA.com calls the one-year Denver return reported; the indexed Denver roster calls Jones a free agent. This ledger does not upgrade the report to an executed contract. Duplicate checked: Existing Dallas notes already state the waiver/signing correction. This page adds the missing canonical evidence hierarchy and state-transition ledger rather than creating another general roster overview. Sources Dallas Mavericks 2025-26 game notes — official Dallas transaction chronology recording “2/28: Waived Tyus Jones”; accessed July 10, 2026. Nuggets sign Tyus Jones — official Denver announcement dated March 5, 2026; accessed July 10, 2026. Denver Nuggets team information and roster history — official NBA team surface recording Jones as signed on March 5, 2026; accessed July 10, 2026. Denver Nuggets 2026 playoff game notes — official recent-transactions list corroborating the March 5 signing; accessed July 10, 2026. NBA free-agency roundup — NBA.com report tracker describing a reported July 2 one-year return to Denver; accessed July 10, 2026. NBA offseason deals by team — NBA.com tracker labeling Jones's one-year Denver agreement as reported; accessed July 10, 2026. Denver Nuggets roster — official current roster display showing Jones with a free-agent label in the indexed page; accessed July 10, 2026. Tyus Jones trade chain to Dallas — NBA.com News Services account of the February Orlando-Charlotte-Dallas sequence; accessed July 10, 2026. Dallas feature on Jones's three-team movement — official Mavericks context published February 9, 2026; accessed July 10, 2026. Open questions Will Denver publish a standalone announcement confirming the reported July one-year agreement, and what effective date will its official transaction history use? What were the term, guarantee, and cap mechanism of Jones's March 5 contract? The reviewed official announcement does not say. Did any official league transaction record publish the precise waiver-clearance timing between Dallas's February 28 action and Denver's March 5 signing? Which other 2026 offseason roster pages currently conflict with completed event records and therefore need the same adjudication?

title: 2026-27 NBA cap and apron thresholds
deck: The NBA's final 2026–27 system levels put the $164.961 million salary cap at the bottom of a five-line decision map whose higher thresholds govern tax payments and which roster-building tools a team may use.
headings: A hard cap is triggered, not universal
Team Salary and Apron Team Salary are not always identical
Maximum salaries and exception amounts scale from the cap
Verification matrix for live roster work
text: The NBA's final 2026–27 system levels put the $164.961 million salary cap at the bottom of a five-line decision map whose higher thresholds govern tax payments and which roster-building tools a team may use. Up: [[Basketball]] Related: [[NBA apron mechanics and roster building]] · [[Second-apron draft-pick penalties in practice]] · [[Dallas Mavericks roster and minutes ledger]] The official numbers On June 30, 2026, the NBA announced the levels that took effect at 12:01 a.m. ET on July 1. These are final league figures, not the estimates that cap sites and reporters used before the league year opened. 2026–27 system level Official amount Distance from salary cap What the line primarily controls Salary cap $164.961M — Ordinary room and the baseline for cap exceptions and maximum salaries Minimum team salary $148.465M −$16.496M The required minimum payroll, equal after rounding to 90% of the cap Luxury-tax level $200.428M +$35.467M Whether a team owes tax, subject to the CBA's tax calculations First apron $209.015M +$44.054M A hard-cap line for specified transactions and a gateway to tighter trade rules Second apron $221.686M +$56.725M A higher hard-cap line for specified transactions plus the most restrictive trade and draft consequences The same release set three mid-level exceptions: 15.044 million for the non-taxpayer MLE, 6.064 million for the taxpayer MLE, and $9.366 million for the room MLE. Those amounts matter because an MLE is not simply extra spending permission. Which version a club uses can impose an apron ceiling for the rest of the cap year. The spacing between the upper lines is also useful. The first apron is 8.587 million above the tax line. The second apron is another 12.671 million above the first apron and $21.258 million above the tax line. A team can therefore be a taxpayer without being an apron team, or be above the first apron without being above the second. Calling every expensive team a “second-apron team” collapses materially different operating regimes. Five lines, five different questions The cap is soft. A team below it ordinarily has room equal to the cap minus its Team Salary. A team above it cannot simply sign any free agent for any amount, but the CBA supplies exceptions: Bird rights, Early Bird rights, non-Bird rights, rookie-scale and minimum-salary exceptions, the several MLEs, and others. This is why most NBA payrolls can exceed the cap without violating it. The minimum team salary points in the opposite direction. The CBA requires a team to reach a payroll floor. It is not a competitive-balance ceiling and should not be confused with the cap. For 2026–27, 148.465 million is roughly 16.5 million below the cap. A rebuilding club can have meaningful cap room while still satisfying the floor. The tax level is a payment threshold, not by itself a hard cap. Crossing $200.428 million can create a luxury-tax bill; it does not automatically make the roster illegal. The tax calculation uses its own rules, rates, and repeater status. A team may consciously accept a tax bill while retaining tools that disappear only at an apron. The aprons are different. They connect transaction choice to a ceiling. Under the NBA's CBA 101 guide, a team may not complete a listed transaction if its adjusted “Apron Team Salary” would exceed the applicable apron immediately afterward. Once it completes such a transaction, it cannot exceed that apron for the remainder of the salary-cap year. This is the mechanism commonly called being hard-capped. The resulting hierarchy is best read as a permissions map: The cap asks whether the club has ordinary room or needs an exception. The tax line asks whether the club owes a tax payment. The first apron asks whether certain powerful acquisition tools remain available and whether the club has triggered a first-apron hard cap. The second apron asks whether the narrowest trade rules and longer-horizon draft consequences apply, and whether a second-apron transaction has hard-capped the club there. Those questions overlap, but they are not interchangeable. A hard cap is triggered, not universal “The NBA has a hard cap at $209.015 million” would be wrong. The league has a soft salary cap, while particular actions impose an apron hard cap. The official CBA 101 transaction table identifies the relevant triggers. At the first apron, the listed actions include using the bi-annual exception, using the non-taxpayer MLE, acquiring a player in a sign-and-trade, signing certain higher-salaried players waived during the regular season, and using the expanded traded-player exception. If a team uses one of these tools, its applicable Apron Team Salary cannot finish the transaction above $209.015 million and its Team Salary cannot later rise above that line during 2026–27. There is a narrow MLE accounting exception: if a team nominally uses the non-taxpayer MLE only for contracts of no more than two seasons whose aggregate first-year salary does not exceed the taxpayer MLE, and it undertakes no other first-apron-triggering transaction, the CBA can deem the team to have used the taxpayer MLE instead if it later exceeds the first apron. That exception is one reason to test the exact contract and sequence rather than infer the hard cap from the name of an exception alone. At the second apron, the table includes acquiring a player with a pre-existing standard traded-player exception generated in a prior year, acquiring with an aggregated standard traded-player exception, paying cash to another team in a trade, acquiring a player with a traded-player exception generated by sending out a sign-and-traded player, and using the taxpayer MLE. Those actions impose the $221.686 million ceiling. The ordering can feel counterintuitive. The larger non-taxpayer MLE is a first-apron trigger, while the smaller taxpayer MLE is a second-apron trigger. That is deliberate: the richer exception is available only to a team that stays under the lower line. A club cannot use the larger tool and then spend through the first apron. Apron status also changes trade math even without a team voluntarily selecting an exception. The CBA's traded-player rules progressively remove flexibility. Above the first apron, the $250,000 salary-matching allowances are reduced to zero. Second-apron teams face still tighter constraints, including the inability to aggregate outgoing salaries to create an aggregated standard traded-player exception. [[NBA apron mechanics and roster building]] develops these roster-building effects; the present note's narrower job is to establish which 2026–27 number governs each decision. Team Salary and Apron Team Salary are not always identical Public cap tables often show several totals because the CBA asks different accounting questions. The official guide defines Apron Team Salary as Team Salary with adjustments: it excludes free-agent amounts and first-round draft-pick holds, includes certain incentive compensation excluded from Team Salary, and makes other CBA-specified changes. That means a simple sum of guaranteed player salaries may not answer whether a transaction is permissible. Cap holds preserve exceptions and room calculations. Likely and unlikely incentives can be treated differently. Waived salary, roster charges, two-way arrangements, trade bonuses, and timing can also affect the appropriate ledger. A public “payroll” number may be useful without being the controlling apron number. This distinction is especially important near a line. Suppose a cap site lists 208.8 million, about 215,000 under the first apron. It would be unsafe to conclude that the club can use the full non-taxpayer MLE. The proposed signing itself adds salary; the relevant calculation is Apron Team Salary immediately after the transaction; and the team must preserve room for a legal roster and later moves. Cap management therefore uses a buffer, not merely a screenshot showing one dollar below a threshold. The CBA also has special rules from the day after the regular season through June 30. For specified transactions, the league examines the following salary-cap year as well as the ending one. The official guide says the projection assumes options are handled in prescribed ways, no additional transactions occur, higher-max possibilities take their specified treatment, and—before the next levels are known—the subsequent cap and aprons equal the current figures. The basic lesson is that an offseason trade can constrain two accounting periods; “the new league year has not started” is not a loophole. Why final figures displaced projections The CBA calculates the cap from projected Basketball Related Income, projected player benefits, and the league's 30 teams. Its public summary describes the cap formula as 44.74% of projected BRI, less projected benefits, divided by 30, subject to adjustments. The other system levels then rise at the same rate as the cap. No system level can fall from the prior year or increase by more than 10%. Before June 30, independent cap trackers necessarily worked with projections. Spotrac, for example, published a 166 million 2026–27 projection earlier in 2026. The final 164.961 million cap is $1.039 million lower. That difference is small relative to a whole payroll but large at the margin: it can be most of a minimum contract, the difference between retaining and renouncing a cap hold, or the buffer needed to complete a trade. The correct research practice is therefore temporal. A projection is legitimate when labeled with its date and source. Once the NBA announces final figures, canonical threshold notes and scenario models should replace projected system levels with the official values while preserving uncertainty in team-specific payroll assumptions. Spotrac remains valuable as independent specialist corroboration and for live team ledgers, but the league release controls the system levels. Maximum salaries and exception amounts scale from the cap The cap is also a denominator. The usual first-year maximum salary bands are 25%, 30%, and 35% of the salary cap for players with 0–6, 7–9, and 10 or more years of service, subject to the CBA's higher-maximum and prior-salary rules. Applied mechanically to 164.961 million, those percentages are about 41.240 million, 49.488 million, and 57.736 million. These are teaching values, not a substitute for a contract-specific calculation: a player's service time, eligibility for a higher maximum, 105% prior-salary protection, extension structure, and timing can change the answer. Many exception scales also grow at the cap's annual rate. The NBA's final release is therefore more than five headline numbers. It resets rookie-scale values, minimums, cash limits, trade allowances, and other dollar amounts governed by the CBA's growth rules. A roster model that updates only “salary cap” while retaining an old MLE or apron can produce internally inconsistent advice. A practical classification workflow For any proposed 2026–27 move, work through the lines in order. First, establish the controlling ledger and date. Use the team's Apron Team Salary rather than a generic payroll total when testing apron transactions. Mark options, non-guarantees, cap holds, draft holds, incentives, waived money, and incomplete reported deals. Do not treat a verbal agreement as an executed contract. Second, identify the mechanism. Is the player signed into room, re-signed with Bird rights, acquired through an MLE, claimed on waivers, obtained in a sign-and-trade, or traded into a specific exception? The same incoming salary can be legal under one mechanism and prohibited under another. Third, identify the threshold the mechanism invokes. Ordinary use of the non-taxpayer MLE is not tested against the tax line; it is a first-apron trigger, subject to the limited taxpayer-sized, two-season deeming rule described above. The taxpayer MLE is a second-apron trigger. A pure Bird re-signing may take a club above an apron even though many outside acquisition routes are unavailable there. Fourth, calculate the post-transaction position and remaining roster needs. A legal move that leaves no room to reach the minimum roster size may be practically unusable. Include expected minimum contracts and other required charges. Fifth, separate tax cost from basketball permission. “The owner will pay” answers the tax question, not whether the CBA permits aggregation, a sign-and-trade, or an exception. Conversely, getting below the tax line can save money without being necessary to legalize a move whose controlling ceiling is an apron. Finally, preserve scenario ranges. Team salary changes with waived guarantees, unlikely incentives, trade bonuses, and order of operations. Near an apron, report the assumed sequence and buffer rather than one falsely exact “space” number. Verification matrix for live roster work The thresholds themselves are now the least uncertain part of a 2026–27 cap analysis. The NBA's June 30 release fixes the five system levels and three MLE amounts, and the league's key-dates page fixes the July 1 start of the cap year and July 6 end of the moratorium. Most remaining uncertainty sits in the transaction ledger. A reported agreement, an official team announcement, a league-approved trade, and a cap-table entry are four different evidentiary states. For committee work, each input should therefore carry both a status and an effective date: Input Preferred evidence Safe use System level NBA's final annual cap release Treat as controlling for the named cap year CBA permission or restriction Governing CBA, then the NBA's official CBA guide Identify the transaction mechanism and controlling apron Completed player movement Team release or NBA tracker explicitly identifying an official deal Move the player between canonical roster ledgers Reported agreement Attributable report, clearly labeled Build a conditional scenario; do not treat it as executed Team salary or apron salary Reconciled contract ledger with stated assumptions Estimate room only after checking holds, incentives, waived money, and roster charges Future roster action Explicit scenario and order of operations Test legality and flexibility; never present as a completed move This matrix resolves a common contradiction in July coverage. A leaguewide offseason page may still label a move “multiple reports” after the participating team has issued its own completion release, or a team roster grid may lag the completed transaction. The canonical article should use the most direct dated evidence for the specific claim rather than treating every NBA-owned page as equally current. In Dallas's July 2026 case, the official acquisition announcement controls the player movement while [[Dallas Mavericks roster and minutes ledger]] preserves the lagging roster display as a provenance warning. The matrix also prevents cap language from outrunning evidence. Knowing that the first apron is $209.015 million does not prove Dallas is below it, above it, or hard-capped there. That conclusion requires a reconciled Apron Team Salary and the mechanism used in every relevant transaction. Likewise, a public payroll estimate below the second apron does not establish access to the taxpayer MLE if another action already imposed a lower ceiling. The proper output is a conditional statement: given this ledger, this transaction mechanism, and this order, this threshold controls. Arithmetic recheck The published differences in this note were independently recalculated from the NBA's final figures on July 10. The first apron minus the tax level is 8.587 million; the second apron minus the first is 12.671 million; the second apron minus the tax level is 21.258 million; and the first apron minus the salary cap is 44.054 million. The minimum team salary is $16.496 million below the cap. These checks confirm the table's subtraction, but they do not substitute for team-specific accounting. What the 2026–27 ladder means strategically The $44.054 million interval between cap and first apron appears large, but it can disappear quickly on a star-heavy roster. Two 30% maximum salaries mechanically consume about 60% of the cap; add a 25% maximum and the nominal core reaches 85% before the rest of the roster. Bird rights allow the team to retain that core above the cap, but the aprons make external improvement progressively harder. That creates an asymmetry between retention and acquisition. A club may often re-sign its own players and become expensive, yet lose flexible routes for adding outsiders. The CBA does not impose a simple ban on spending. It makes repeated high-end spending increasingly dependent on drafting well, developing minimum-salary contributors, sequencing transactions carefully, and deciding which players merit long-term slots before the roster becomes rigid. For Dallas or any other contender, the right question is thus not merely “How far below $221.686 million are we?” It is “Which transaction tools does the plan require, which line does each tool invoke, what is the adjusted post-move salary, and what flexibility remains afterward?” Thresholds are constraints on a sequence, not labels attached once to a roster. Sources NBA, “NBA sets salary cap for 2026-27 season at $164.961 million” (June 30, 2026) — official final cap, floor, tax, apron, and MLE figures. NBA, CBA 101: Highlights of the Collective Bargaining Agreement (2024–25 edition) — official system-level formula, exceptions, apron accounting, hard-cap triggers, trade rules, and draft-pick penalty summary. NBA and NBPA, 2023 Collective Bargaining Agreement — governing agreement and union-hosted CBA access. Spotrac, 2026–27 NBA team salary-cap tracker and apron tracker — independent specialist ledgers; team figures remain sensitive to transaction timing and assumptions. Spotrac, “Updated 2026 Cap Space and Spending Power Projections” — dated pre-announcement projection, useful for showing why final official levels should supersede estimates. Open questions Which 2026–27 team cap tables have fully reconciled incentives, dead money, draft holds, and newly executed July contracts rather than reported agreements? How much operating buffer does each contender preserve below its controlling apron after accounting for minimum roster charges? Which Dallas transaction sequence uses the least scarce exception while preserving a later in-season move?

title: Availability risk in NBA projections
deck: NBA projections should model availability as a distribution over games, minutes, performance states, and replacement lineups—not as a single games-played discount applied to healthy player value.
headings: Availability is part of team strength
Replacement minutes are the causal pathway
Injury reports are state evidence, not ground truth about health
text: NBA projections should model availability as a distribution over games, minutes, performance states, and replacement lineups—not as a single games-played discount applied to healthy player value. Up: [[NBA and Dallas Mavericks]] Related: [[Dallas Mavericks availability scenarios]] · [[Lineup fit is not the sum of player value]] Availability is part of team strength A player projection usually begins with an estimate of value per possession or per minute. A team forecast needs a different quantity: how much of that value will actually reach the floor, in which games, at what workload, and alongside which replacements. A brilliant 65-game player and a merely good 80-game player can have similar regular-season totals while creating very different tails, rotations, and playoff paths. The simplest expected-value approximation is E[V_i] \approx E[m_i]E[r_i], where m_i is minutes and r_i is value per minute. The product of expectations is exact only when minutes and per-minute value are uncorrelated. In general, E[m_i r_i]=E[m_i]E[r_i]+\operatorname{Cov}(m_i,r_i). That covariance can matter because a player may return under a restriction, play through an injury at reduced effectiveness, or receive his heaviest workload when healthiest. His absence also changes teammates' roles and the lineup's fit. The better conceptual object is E[V_{team}] = E\left[\sum_g \sum_i m_{ig}r_{ig}(S_g,L_g)\right], where S_g is the game-specific availability and health state and L_g is the feasible lineup environment. The sum is over the games and players in one simulated season state; the outer expectation averages over those joint states. This formulation makes clear why availability belongs inside [[NBA team season projection model]], downstream from [[NBA player forward projection model]], rather than being hidden inside a player's healthy per-100 rating. [[RAPM evaluation and uncertainty]] already separates measurement error, player forecast uncertainty, and season outcome uncertainty. Availability is a major bridge between the latter two. It changes both the amount of star value realized and the identity of the replacement minutes that generate the team outcome. Four states that “games played” collapses Availability has at least four dimensions. The first is binary participation: active or inactive. This is what games played records most directly. The second is workload: a player can be active for 18 minutes or 38. The third is conditional effectiveness: “available” after surgery or during a recurring injury may not mean the same movement, shot profile, or defensive range as the healthy baseline. The fourth is recurrence and clustering: ten isolated missed games differ from a ten-game block because the latter forces a stable replacement rotation and may coincide with a difficult schedule segment. Historical games played alone mixes all four. It also mixes injury, illness, rest, suspension, personal absence, organizational decisions, and roster status. Those mechanisms have different persistence. A forecasting model should preserve reason codes when credible data permit, while resisting medical certainty that public evidence cannot support. Clinical NBA studies illustrate why coarse labels are inadequate. Leaguewide injury epidemiology finds large variation by injury type in incidence and games missed. Return-to-play studies often find that participation can resume without a uniform performance path. These results are population descriptions, not player-specific diagnoses. They support wider and mechanism-specific forecast distributions; they do not authorize an analyst to predict an individual's recovery from a public injury label. Expected games are not enough Suppose two players are each projected for 65 games. Player A has a narrow distribution centered near 65: managed absences are likely, but a full-season loss is unlikely. Player B has a mixture distribution: perhaps a substantial chance of 75 games and a meaningful chance of only 30. Their expected games may match, while their teams' outcome distributions do not. The distinction matters because wins are nonlinear around thresholds. A concentrated absence can knock a team out of home-court contention, force play-in games, or reduce the probability that a preferred lineup develops continuity. A long-tail injury to a star creates more downside than the same expected missed games spread across low-leverage reserves. Variance also interacts with roster depth. If a star's backup is a competent approximation of the same role, the team loses less structure when the star sits. If the backup changes the offense from five-out to two-nonshooter lineups, or removes the only point-of-attack defender, the replacement penalty exceeds a simple player-value difference. [[Lineup fit is not the sum of player value]] is therefore part of availability modeling: the absent player changes the constraints on everyone else. A projection should report at least the mean and a meaningful interval for games and minutes. For high-leverage players, it should also represent asymmetric scenarios: healthy season, managed season, delayed return, recurrence, and low-probability severe loss. Exact scenario probabilities should come from a declared model or be labeled judgmental. Replacement minutes are the causal pathway When a player misses 1,000 minutes, those minutes do not disappear. They flow to backups, two-way players, smaller lineups, heavier starter workloads, or newly acquired players. Team impact therefore depends on the replacement tree. A naive wins model may subtract the star's per-minute value times missed minutes. That assumes replacement value is zero on the model's scale and ignores role changes. A better calculation assigns the minutes explicitly: \Delta V \approx m_{missed}(r_{star}-r_{replacement}) + \Delta V_{fit} + \Delta V_{workload}. All terms must use the same value units and time horizon. The replacement term may be shared by several players. The fit term captures a change in spacing, creation, rim protection, rebounding, or scheme that is not already embedded in the player ratings. The workload term captures the possibility that healthy starters absorb more minutes, improving immediate replacement quality while increasing fatigue or leaving bench units exposed. As in any decomposition, unclear boundaries can double count the same consequence, so an implementation should define which effects live in r , lineup strength, and the workload state. This is why depth should be evaluated by function, not roster count. A team may have twelve NBA-caliber players yet no second organizer. Another may have only nine trusted players but multiple wings who can cover adjacent roles. Availability risk is concentrated where one player supplies a scarce function. The 2026–27 cross-team briefing found exactly this pattern across several projections: the largest downward challenges often involved older stars, post-injury workload uncertainty, or rotations whose depth collapsed if one high-leverage player disappeared. That local synthesis is not a clinical dataset and should not set injury probabilities. It is evidence that availability assumptions and replacement structure repeatedly drive human disagreement with additive team priors. Role elasticity is availability insurance Role elasticity is the ability to remain useful as usage, position, matchup, or scheme changes. It lowers availability risk at the team level even when it does not change the probability that anyone is injured. A wing who can defend two through four, space the corner, screen, and make a second-side pass can fill several replacement branches. A guard who only functions as the primary initiator may be excellent in his normal role but difficult to insert when the absent player is a defensive stopper. A center who can play drop and switch preserves more matchup options than one whose value depends on a single coverage. Elasticity should not be assumed from body type or reputation. It needs evidence from actual roles, preferably over enough possessions to separate ability from emergency noise. Still, a projection can label which substitutions preserve the team's architecture and which require a new one. That qualitative map is often more honest than assigning spurious decimal-point bonuses. Role elasticity also affects recovery. A returning star may initially avoid the hardest defensive assignment or reduce on-ball load. Teammates who can absorb those jobs allow the player to contribute before he reaches his full role. Thus return-to-play is not a switch from zero to the healthy projection; it can be a sequence of lineup states. Dependence between player risks Many simulations draw each player's games independently. That is convenient and often wrong. Availability can be correlated through shared schedule stress, contagious illness, team rest policy, playoff position, training practices, and role compensation. One absence can raise another player's workload. Two players may also be managed together or alternate rest to preserve a functional lineup. Independence errors are most damaging in the tails. If a veteran-heavy team collectively rests more on back-to-backs, simultaneous weakness is more likely than independent Bernoulli draws imply. If a team carefully staggers its creators, simultaneous absence may be less likely. A single expected-games table cannot express either policy. Correlation should be modeled cautiously. There is rarely enough public data to estimate every pairwise dependence. A practical compromise is to simulate team-level latent states—normal, schedule-stressed, outbreak, late-season management—and let those states modestly shift several players' availability. The parameters should be validated on historical seasons and shrunk heavily toward independence. Schedule context matters here. Back-to-backs, travel, and dense stretches can affect rest decisions and workload, but observational associations do not by themselves establish injury causation. The model may use schedule features for predictive calibration without claiming a medical mechanism. Injury reports are state evidence, not ground truth about health Official NBA injury reports are the best public source for current participation designations because the league requires teams to report statuses and enforces the rules. They remain operational disclosures, not complete medical records. The same designation can cover different uncertainty, and statuses change as game time approaches. For a daily game forecast, the model should timestamp the report, preserve the designation, and convert it into a calibrated probability of playing plus a conditional minute range. “Questionable” should not mechanically mean 50 percent unless historical calibration for the relevant reporting regime supports that number. A player declared active may still face a workload cap. For a preseason forecast, official reports are only one input. Surgery announcements, team statements, and credible return timelines can identify a starting state. Longer-run recurrence and effectiveness should come from population evidence, the player's history, age and workload features, and wide uncertainty. Public analysis should clearly separate official status, reported timeline, model inference, and unknown medical detail. The league's enforcement actions also show why timing matters. A designation can be accurate when filed and later change, or a team can violate reporting requirements. A frozen forecast should retain the information set available at prediction time rather than overwrite it with what became known later. Building an availability model A robust architecture has several linked layers. First, estimate a baseline participation process. Features may include age, recent games and minutes, rolling workload, prior absences by broad reason, offseason procedures, and current status. Use temporal validation: training only on information available before the predicted period. Historical availability features are a known leakage risk if season totals accidentally enter earlier dates. Second, model absence duration rather than only next-game status. A hurdle or multi-state model can separate whether an absence begins from how long it lasts. Survival methods are natural for time to return, while recurrent-event models can represent repeated spells. No method eliminates the sparse-data problem for rare injuries. Third, estimate conditional minutes after return. The first active game, the first back-to-back, and a gradual ramp may differ. This layer should be team- and role-aware without memorizing one coach's short sample. Fourth, connect states to player effectiveness. The default should shrink toward the healthy projection because public data often cannot identify a distinct injured-performance coefficient. Apply a decrement only when historical or population evidence supports it, and widen the interval when it does not. Fifth, allocate replacement minutes through a feasible rotation. Enforce 240 team minutes per game, positional and role constraints, and plausible workload caps. Recalculate lineup strength rather than merely removing a name. Sixth, simulate the season. Draw player states, lineups, opponent and schedule context, and game noise. Preserve the joint draws so the output can explain whether a wide win interval comes from rating uncertainty, availability, or ordinary game variance. Finally, calibrate. Score predicted play probabilities, games distributions, minute intervals, and team wins separately. A season model can have a reasonable win mean while its player availability probabilities are badly miscalibrated because errors cancel. A public-safe state-vector contract The model needs an explicit interface between evidence collection and season simulation. Without one, an analyst can update a player's “injury risk” while silently changing several different assumptions. A compact player-game state can be written as Z_{ig}=(A_{ig},M_{ig},E_{ig},R_{ig},C_{ig}), where A is participation, M is minutes conditional on participation, E is effectiveness relative to the healthy player projection, R is the basketball role, and C is the reporting-confidence state. The first four affect the basketball forecast. The fifth governs how aggressively the first four should move when new public evidence arrives. This separation prevents several common errors. An official active designation raises confidence in participation for that game, but it does not by itself establish ordinary minutes or healthy effectiveness. A coach's statement that a player will be “limited” narrows the workload branch without quantifying a medical recovery curve. Film showing that a returning guard is not reaching the rim may inform the effectiveness state, but only after the sample, opponent, and tactical context are stated. A change in role—moving from primary initiator to spacer—can alter observed efficiency even if physical capacity is unchanged. Every update should therefore record five fields: Observation time: when the evidence became public, not when a later article summarized it. Evidence class: official status, team statement, attributable reporting, observed game role, model inference, or unknown. State affected: participation, conditional minutes, effectiveness, role, or dependence with another player. Direction and magnitude: a declared numerical update when model-generated; otherwise a labeled qualitative pressure. Expiration or review trigger: the next report, practice stage, game sample, schedule phase, or roster move that could make the update stale. The confidence state is not a claim about whether a team or reporter is honest. It measures how directly the evidence identifies the model variable. An official injury designation is authoritative about the designation and its timestamp, but only indirect evidence about exact probability, workload, or long-run performance. A full-game workload is direct evidence that the player handled those minutes once; it is weaker evidence that the workload is sustainable across a dense month. This contract is also a privacy boundary. A public model should use official releases, attributable reporting, observed play, and declared statistical priors. It should never imply access to imaging, private medical records, or individualized recurrence estimates that the sources do not provide. “Unknown” is a valid state, not a defect to conceal with a point estimate. Scenario matrices before win totals For high-leverage players, the rotation should be solved inside a small set of coherent scenarios before those scenarios are mixed into one win distribution. A useful minimum is unavailable, active with a restriction, active in a modified role, and functionally normal. Those branches should not differ only in the focal player's minutes. Each branch needs a complete 240-minute allocation, a role map, and a list of lineup functions that are preserved or lost. Consider a primary creator returning under a workload cap. The direct change is additional creator minutes. The indirect changes may include lower emergency usage for a young forward, fewer possessions initiated by a reserve guard, a different closing lineup, and easier shot quality for a rim-running center. If the returning player cannot yet defend the hardest perimeter action, the team may also change matchups or coverages. Assigning the player's old per-minute rating to 22 minutes would miss both the positive role relief and the remaining defensive constraint. The replacement tree should be exhaustive rather than optimistic. If the first replacement also has an availability distribution, the model needs a second branch. If the only backup preserves scoring but not point-of-attack defense, the lost function must appear somewhere else in the lineup. If no feasible lineup covers every task, the simulation should retain the weakness instead of granting an abstract depth adjustment. Scenario weights can be learned, judgmental, or a mixture. Learned weights require a clearly dated training set and temporal validation. Judgmental weights should be shown as ranges and stress-tested. In either case, the public forecast should reveal which assumption drives the tails. A statement such as “the team projects for 46 wins” is less informative than showing that the median is similar across models while the lower tail is largely a joint availability-and-replacement outcome. The scenario matrix should update asymmetrically. A single practice can eliminate the branch in which a player has not begun basketball activity, but it cannot prove the functionally normal branch. One normal game can raise near-term workload expectations while doing little to settle recurrence or dense-schedule tolerance. Evidence accumulates through stages; the model should not jump directly from uncertainty to certainty because one visible milestone is encouraging. Forecast evaluation and accountability Availability models should be judged before the outcomes are known. Freeze preseason distributions, record hashes or immutable versions, and score them after the season. Useful diagnostics include Brier score or log loss for next-game activity, calibration curves by official designation, mean absolute error for season games and minutes, interval coverage, and continuous ranked probability score for full distributions. Evaluation must be time-aware. Random train-test splits leak the same player's later health state and a season's eventual games total into earlier examples. Expansion-window or rolling-origin tests better match deployment. Major rule or schedule changes may create regime shifts, so aggregate calibration should be accompanied by season-level results. Team forecasts need counterfactual baselines. Compare the full availability simulation with fixed expected minutes, independent player draws, and simple historical games-played averages. Complexity earns its place only if it improves out-of-sample calibration or produces decisions and explanations the simpler baseline cannot. The local RAPM project's season benchmark is a reminder of this hierarchy. Game-margin evaluation using realized minutes tests rating quality conditional on who played; it is not a strict pregame forecast. Preseason season scoring is harder because it must forecast the roster and minutes states themselves. Good realized-minute accuracy cannot validate availability assumptions. Common failure modes The first is false precision from medical labels. Public reporting rarely supports a confident player-specific recovery curve. The second is recency overreaction: one healthy season does not erase a long history, and one injury does not prove permanent fragility. Partial pooling and aging-aware baselines help. The third is double counting. If a forward player projection already incorporates reduced minutes or post-injury performance, a separate availability adjustment can penalize the same evidence twice. The model contract must state whether r_i is conditional on health and whether m_i carries the absence risk. The fourth is survivorship bias. Players who leave the league or never return are easy to omit from return-to-play samples, making recovery look better. The fifth is treatment-selection bias: surgery, rest, and workload management are chosen in response to severity and context, so observational comparisons do not identify their causal effects without strong assumptions. Recent research finding no reduced subsequent injury risk after games missed for rest or load management should not be read as proof that rest never helps; it describes the studied observational setting. The sixth is ignoring incentives. Late-season shutdowns, playoff seeding, development priorities, and transaction strategy affect availability without being injuries. A model trained on “games missed” should not silently call all absence medical risk. Why it matters Availability is often the largest reason a team forecast differs from the sum of its healthy player ratings. Modeling it well does not mean predicting injuries with certainty. It means representing uncertainty honestly, distinguishing participation from workload and performance, routing missed minutes to real replacements, and preserving the dependencies that shape downside. The result is more useful than a point estimate. It can show that two teams with the same projected wins have different risk structures: one is stable but capped, another is a contender when healthy with a long lower tail. It can also identify what evidence would move the forecast—an official return, demonstrated workload, a credible backup, or a lineup that survives without a scarce role. Open questions Which public absence reason codes are stable enough across seasons to train a recurrence model without creating label drift? How much does joint team-level availability modeling improve calibrated win tails over independent player draws? What return-to-play minute-ramp features predict future workload without leaking information unavailable at forecast time? How should organizational shutdown risk be modeled separately from health risk for rebuilding teams?

title: Cooper Flagg and two-big lineup creation burden
deck: Two-big lineups can amplify Cooper Flagg's size and defense, but they help his offense only when the second big creates space or decisions; otherwise they transfer too much first-advantage creation onto a 19-year-old whose pull-up shooting is not yet a proven coverage breaker.
headings: The question is not whether Flagg can play with two bigs
Creation burden has four separate layers
Flagg with one traditional center is the clean baseline
Aldama beside a center makes size additive
Flagg with Washington and a center is balanced only with guard skill
Two traditional centers create the wrong laboratory
Why this is the development hinge
text: Two-big lineups can amplify Cooper Flagg's size and defense, but they help his offense only when the second big creates space or decisions; otherwise they transfer too much first-advantage creation onto a 19-year-old whose pull-up shooting is not yet a proven coverage breaker. Up: [[Dallas Mavericks 2026-27 season]] · Context: [[Dallas frontcourt geometry]] · Development: [[Cooper Flagg year-two development]] · Spacing: [[Dallas shooting and spacing allocation]] · Health: [[Dallas Mavericks availability scenarios]] The question is not whether Flagg can play with two bigs Cooper Flagg is himself a large forward. Therefore, almost every Dallas lineup with Flagg and a conventional center is “two-big” in the broad positional sense. That label is too loose to explain the offense. The useful distinction is functional: how many players need to operate near the rim, how many force a defender to remain outside it, and who can create the first rotation when the defense is set? As of July 10, 2026, Dallas has several frontcourt partners with different answers. Dereck Lively II and Daniel Gafford are traditional centers whose strongest offensive value comes from screening, rolling, finishing and offensive rebounding. P. J. Washington is a forward who can space and attack a moving defense. Newly acquired Santi Aldama is a seven-foot shooter and connector who can play beside a center or, in selected matchups, function as the offensive five. The same “big” label therefore describes very different environments for Flagg. The official baseline shows why the environment matters. Flagg won 2025-26 Rookie of the Year after averaging 21.0 points, 6.7 rebounds and 4.5 assists in 70 games. He led Dallas in all three categories plus steals, and after the Anthony Davis trade he averaged 22.4 points, 6.7 rebounds and 5.2 assists in 23 games. Those are facts about a remarkably productive rookie. They are not proof that Dallas should make him solve every half-court possession. His full-season three-point line was 29.5 percent on 3.5 attempts per game, and he said after the season that he wanted to improve off the dribble and make higher-level reads. The combination points to an exceptional creator whose most important developmental work remains unfinished. This creates the central team-building rule: a large lineup should reduce or diversify Flagg's decisions, not merely give him more size to compensate for. When two frontcourt teammates occupy interior space and neither can manufacture an advantage, Flagg becomes responsible for beating the first defender, forcing help, identifying the help, and delivering the ball before the lane closes. When one of those bigs shoots, passes, or screens in motion, the same nominal size can make his decisions easier. Creation burden has four separate layers “Creation” is often treated as a synonym for shot attempts or usage. For lineup analysis, it should be divided into four jobs. Entry creation gets the offense into an advantage. It includes turning the corner against a set defender, forcing two defenders to the ball, drawing a switch that can be attacked, or creating a deep seal before the defense is organized. This is the hardest job to replace. A stationary shooter can finish an advantage but usually cannot create the first one. Decision creation converts pressure into the correct next action. The handler must read whether the low defender tags the roller, whether the nail defender stunts at the drive, and whether the center is in drop, switch, show or zone. Flagg's 4.5 assists per game show real playmaking output, but assists alone do not identify the difficulty or accuracy of every read. Shot creation turns the remaining matchup into a viable attempt. A pull-up jumper, post move, finish through contact, or closeout attack can all end the chain. Flagg already demonstrated unusually high scoring peaks, including a 51-point game, but repeated late-clock self-creation against a loaded floor is different from attacking a defense already displaced by Kyrie Irving or a screening action. Recovery creation rescues a possession after the first action fails. This can be a second pick-and-roll, a quick handoff, a short-roll pass, or an offensive rebound that produces a new advantage. Skilled large lineups can excel here because several players can continue the chain. Cramped lineups often return the ball to Flagg with fewer seconds and no new geometry. Dallas should measure Flagg's burden across all four layers. A lineup may lower his shot volume while increasing his difficulty if teammates cannot start or continue actions. Conversely, a high-usage night can be developmentally healthy if his catches come against rotation, the reads are legible, and another creator can organize possessions when he tires. Flagg with one traditional center is the clean baseline A Flagg–Lively or Flagg–Gafford pairing is structurally coherent when the other three players provide enough shooting and at least one additional organizer. The center supplies vertical gravity: if his defender steps toward Flagg, a lob or pocket pass becomes available; if the defender stays attached to the roll, Flagg receives a path toward the rim or short pull-up. The center also creates physical advantages through screening rather than requiring Flagg to win every matchup in isolation. The burden changes with the center. Lively's best projected version can continue an action as a passer after catching on the short roll. That gives Flagg permission to surrender the ball when trapped because the possession can still produce a corner pass, lob, or handoff. But this is partly projection, not a claim about current readiness. Lively appeared in only seven games in 2025-26 before right-foot surgery, and Dallas had not established a normal 2026-27 workload by this article's cutoff. Gafford offers a more direct exchange. His screen, dive and finishing can punish a defense after the handler creates separation. His 2025-26 statistical profile—9.5 points and 6.9 rebounds in 21.7 minutes, with no three-point attempts—supports the traditional-finisher description used in [[Dallas frontcourt geometry]]. The limitation is not that Gafford lacks value. It is that a Gafford action more often needs the ballhandler to deliver the decisive pass. If the defense goes under a Flagg screen because it does not fear the pull-up three, the action may never force the second defender to commit. This is why Irving's availability matters to Flagg's two-big life. An elite guard can make the center's vertical gravity real, shift Flagg to the second side, and let him attack a closeout rather than a loaded shell. Without Irving, Dallas needs another guard to get paint contact or Flagg must do the entry work himself. The same Flagg–center pairing can therefore move from balanced to overburdened without any frontcourt substitution. Aldama beside a center makes size additive The most credible true two-big construction uses Aldama beside Lively or Gafford, with Flagg functioning as a jumbo wing or initiator. Dallas officially acquired Aldama on July 8. In 2025-26 he attempted 4.7 threes per game and made 35.0 percent while averaging 2.9 assists. Those figures do not guarantee that every opponent will guard him tightly or that he can act as a primary creator. They do establish a different offensive proposition from pairing two non-shooting centers. Aldama can help Flagg before receiving the ball. Positioning him above the break removes a large help defender from the direct driving lane. Using him as the screener can force the opponent's center to defend farther from the basket. Letting him catch at the slot creates a handoff, swing pass, or one-dribble continuation rather than ending the possession. The center can remain a vertical threat while Aldama supplies horizontal spacing and a second decision point. The lineup's challenge is role compression elsewhere. A group with Flagg, Aldama and a conventional center has only two perimeter slots. If Irving occupies one, the remaining player may need to be the best point-of-attack defender and a respected high-volume shooter at once. If Irving is absent, the group may lack a second entry creator. Aldama's passing can move an advantage, but his box-score assists do not prove he can consistently create one against a set NBA defense. The coaching answer should be action design rather than an abstract demand that Flagg “be the point guard.” Dallas can use Flagg–Aldama inverted pick-and-rolls, with Flagg screening first and then receiving against a shifted defense. It can place the center in the dunker spot while Aldama screens higher, provided the weak-side shooters hold their defenders. It can run Chicago action—a pindown into a handoff—to give Flagg movement and a live dribble before he sees the primary rim protector. It can also let Aldama initiate a dribble handoff while Flagg cuts or seals a smaller switch. Each design changes who makes the first difficult read. The concept works only if Aldama's defender behaves as the geometry assumes. A nominal stretch big who is ignored does not provide spacing. Dallas should track whether defenders close out hard, switch a smaller player onto him, or remain in the lane. Defender response is stronger evidence than a small sample of made threes. Flagg with Washington and a center is balanced only with guard skill Washington is not a traditional big, but a Flagg–Washington–center frontcourt is another large configuration likely to matter. Its defensive appeal is clear: Washington can absorb stronger forwards, Flagg can take a varied assignment, and the center can protect the rim. Offensively, Washington can space, cut and attack a closeout. The group becomes fragile when those complementary skills are mistaken for primary creation. If the two guards can bend the defense, Washington's role is appropriately narrow and valuable. He can punish help rather than manufacture it. Flagg can alternate between initiating, screening and attacking the second side. The center can roll without colliding with another permanent interior player. This is a plausible regular structure. If one guard is a weak shooter and neither creates paint pressure, the nominal balance disappears. Opponents can go under Flagg's ball screens, stunt from the least dangerous perimeter player, and keep the center's defender near the rim. Flagg then faces three linked tasks: generate separation without a respected pull-up, throw a precise pass through a contracted lane, and recover the possession if the first read closes. Washington may receive the ball, but that does not mean the lineup redistributed creation. Dallas should avoid evaluating these groups only by whether Flagg scores. A 25-point game can conceal a high-cost offensive structure if the points required difficult late-clock attempts and the team created few clean looks. A lower-scoring game can represent progress if Flagg repeatedly forces two defenders and the resulting pass produces an open shot one action later. Two traditional centers create the wrong laboratory Lively and Gafford together would produce an extreme version of the creation problem. Neither has demonstrated perimeter shooting gravity. Both are most valuable near the basket. Add Flagg, whose rookie three-point percentage invites defenses to test his jumper, and Dallas could give three defenders permission to remain near the lane or go under screening actions. There are situational reasons to use the pairing: a final defensive possession, an opponent with unusual size, emergency foul trouble, or a brief zone. Those reasons do not make it a sound developmental base. Offensive rebounds and lob targets cannot compensate if Flagg has no runway to force the original rotation. Two rollers are not twice the vertical gravity when one defender can monitor both because the ball never penetrates. The developmental cost matters. A difficult environment can teach a young creator to solve congestion, but persistent congestion can also train bad counters: early contested pull-ups, predetermined passes, or excessive dribbling while waiting for a lane that the alignment cannot produce. Dallas should challenge Flagg with complex reads after providing a viable action, not confuse poor spacing with useful difficulty. The best actions distribute cognition For Flagg's year-two growth, the ideal large-lineup possessions should make the first read demanding but bounded. Empty-corner pick-and-roll gives Flagg and the center one side of the floor. The defense must choose between containing the ball and tagging the roll without a corner helper. Aldama or Washington can occupy the weak-side slot. This tests Flagg's pacing and pocket passing without placing five bodies in his driving lane. Inverted ball screens use Flagg as the screener for a guard, then let him short roll into a four-on-three decision. He receives the ball after two defenders have already committed, which develops passing and touch without requiring him to create the initial separation every time. It also punishes a switch by giving him a smaller defender in the post. Delay action through Aldama or Lively starts with the big above the arc or at the elbow while Flagg cuts, screens away, or receives a handoff. The big becomes a temporary organizer. This creates motion before Flagg's first dribble and prevents the defense from loading to a static isolation. Flagg as a ghost screener can force two defenders to communicate while he slips to space. It is especially useful when paired with Irving, because switching creates a mismatch and trapping frees Flagg as a short-roll playmaker. The action will be less threatening if the guard cannot punish the coverage. Post split and elbow hub actions can exploit size without parking everyone on the block. Flagg can receive at the elbow while a shooter cuts off the center or Aldama screens away. The aim is not a stationary post-up; it is to make the defense process two threats simultaneously and give Flagg a passing window. Across these actions, the principle is the same: another player should create movement, occupy help, or make a consequential read. The offense becomes healthier when Flagg is the best decision-maker in a chain, not the entire chain. A burden scorecard for 2026-27 Traditional usage rate will not answer whether Dallas has built a productive two-big environment. The team and outside analysts should instead watch a small set of possession-level indicators. First, how often does Flagg begin his attack against a set defense versus a tilted one? Second, how frequently does a ball screen produce two defenders committed to the ball? Third, after Flagg passes, does the next player shoot, drive or make another advantage pass, or does the ball return to him unchanged? Fourth, how often is the center's defender able to protect the rim without leaving the roll man? Fifth, which teammate initiates possessions during Flagg's high-minute stretches? Shooting response belongs beside those questions. The important signal is not merely whether Flagg improves from 29.5 percent. It is whether defenders alter coverage: going over more screens, closing space earlier, and staying attached when he plays off the ball. A modest percentage increase with stronger defender respect could transform the lineup. A hot percentage on low volume that opponents still ignore may not. Turnovers also require classification. A pass that correctly reads the low defender but arrives late is a developmental error. A turnover caused by two teammates occupying the same lane is partly structural. A risky live-ball pass forced after the lineup failed to create an advantage for 18 seconds is different from a careless early-clock giveaway. Treating all three as the same number would hide whether Flagg or the lineup needs correction. Finally, Dallas should compare the same frontcourt across creator contexts. Flagg–Aldama–center minutes with Irving are not evidence for the same trio without him. Flagg–Washington–center minutes against a switching bench are not interchangeable with minutes against a starting defense in drop. Opponent quality, game state, health and the identity of the other two players must travel with any lineup claim. Fact, inference and forecast Established facts: Flagg averaged 21.0 points, 6.7 rebounds and 4.5 assists while shooting 29.5 percent from three as a rookie. Dallas acquired Aldama on July 8. Aldama's 2025-26 production included credible three-point volume and secondary passing. Gafford did not attempt a three in 2025-26, and Lively's season was limited to seven games before foot surgery. Basketball inference: lineups with Flagg, Aldama and one traditional center have a more plausible offensive geometry than Flagg with two traditional centers because Aldama can occupy and act from perimeter space. Flagg plus Washington plus one center can be balanced when guard creation and shooting are present. These conclusions follow from player functions and spacing principles; they are not verified lineup results for a roster that had not yet played together. Forecast with uncertainty: Dallas is likely to use Flagg with one traditional center as a base and experiment with Aldama as the second big. Whether that experiment lowers Flagg's creation burden depends on Irving's availability, Lively's recovery, Flagg's shooting response, Aldama's defensive survival and the skill of the fifth player. No 2026-27 lineup evidence existed at the cutoff, so predicted starters, closing groups and minute allocations would be false precision. Why this is the development hinge Flagg's rookie production established that Dallas can ask him to create. Year two should determine how deliberately it asks. The objective is not to protect him from hard possessions. It is to give those possessions informative structure: a real screen, a spaced floor, a second reader, and a counter when the first action fails. Large lineups can support that objective. Lively or Gafford can create vertical pressure. Aldama can move a large defender away from the lane and continue the possession. Washington can preserve defense while punishing rotation. But size becomes counterproductive when the roster uses Flagg's versatility as permission to omit guard skill and shooting. In that version, he is not merely developing as a creator; he is covering the lineup's missing functions. The right two-big question is therefore diagnostic: after Dallas adds size, who makes Flagg's next decision easier? If the answer is the screener, connector, shooter or primary guard, the lineup may accelerate his development while competing. If the answer is still Flagg at every stage, the lineup has transferred its design problem to its youngest star. Open questions Which 2026-27 lineups make opponents go over Flagg's ball screens rather than concede the pull-up? Does Aldama's defender stay attached when he shares the floor with Flagg and a traditional center? Can Lively resume enough movement and contact work to supply both defensive anchoring and short-roll continuity? Who becomes the reliable second entry creator when Irving is unavailable or limited? How often can Dallas use a Flagg–Aldama–center frontcourt without sacrificing point-of-attack defense? Does Flagg's turnover profile improve because his reads sharpen, or because Dallas creates cleaner first advantages? Which opponent archetypes punish Aldama as a second big strongly enough to erase the offensive spacing benefit?

title: Cooper Flagg year-two development
deck: Cooper Flagg's second season should be judged by whether the same difficult possessions become easier for him—not by counting production that may rise because his role, teammates, or lineups changed.

What the rookie season actually established
Seven indicators of genuine skill growth
