Open questions When does Lively progress from non-running to unrestricted practice, and what workload does Dallas publicly assign him? Which Flagg lineups cause defenders to stay attached at the arc rather than load the lane? Can Aldama-at-center groups protect the rim and finish possessions against starting-caliber size? Does Washington's shooting hold up well enough to anchor defense-first frontcourts? Which non-Irving creator produces enough first-side advantage to maximize Gafford or Lively as a finisher? What minimum sample and opponent-quality controls should Rome require before treating a five-man result as lineup evidence? Which third-frontcourt configuration lets Dallas preserve two trusted shooters without assigning Flagg every high-load job?

title: Dallas guard creation after roster turnover
deck: Dallas can distribute ball security, passing, and secondary scoring across several players, but the post-turnover roster still has no verified replacement for Kyrie Irving's ability to create the first advantage and a credible late-clock shot against a set defense.
headings: The turnover removed the easy veteran answer
Ryan Nembhard is the clearest organizer
Marcus Sasser adds scoring possibility, not certainty
Cooper Flagg is the highest-upside secondary engine
Christie, Marshall, and the frontcourt are advantage extenders
What would count as an answer
text: Dallas can distribute ball security, passing, and secondary scoring across several players, but the post-turnover roster still has no verified replacement for Kyrie Irving's ability to create the first advantage and a credible late-clock shot against a set defense. Up: [[Dallas Mavericks 2026-27 season]] · Roster context: [[Dallas Mavericks 2026-27 roster construction dossier]] · Availability: [[Dallas Mavericks availability scenarios]] · Baseline: [[Basketball/NBA team briefings 2026-27/DAL_2026_27_briefing|Dallas Mavericks 2026-27 Research Briefing]] Current state — as of July 10, 2026: the verified Dallas guard-creation group is built around Irving, Cooper Flagg, Ryan Nembhard, newly acquired Marcus Sasser, and secondary handlers such as Max Christie and Naji Marshall. Tyus Jones is not a current Maverick: Denver officially signed him on March 5 after his eight-game Dallas stop, and the NBA's July offseason tracker lists his agreement to return to Denver. Any Dallas depth chart that still assigns Jones minutes is using a stale roster state. Why it matters Guard creation is the hinge between Dallas's apparent depth and its usable depth. The roster can put size, defense, shooting, passing, and vertical finishing on the court, but those skills do not activate themselves. Someone must make the first defender lose the play. Without that pressure, a center's lob gravity has no passer to exploit it, a shooter receives a stationary rather than rotating defense, and a wing who excels at attacking closeouts instead catches against a balanced opponent. The shortage also changes the developmental bargain around Flagg. Productive creation repetitions can teach him to diagnose coverages and become a larger offensive engine. Emergency possessions created by an imbalanced lineup can instead ask him to rescue late clocks through difficult isolation. Those two workloads may produce similar usage totals while teaching different lessons. Dallas therefore needs to evaluate not only how often Flagg handles the ball but whether the lineup gives him organization, spacing, and a second decision-maker. Finally, the issue is nonlinear with Irving's health. Losing an ordinary rotation guard redistributes minutes. Limiting the only proven elite creator promotes every other player into a harder job at once: Flagg faces the primary stopper more often, Nembhard must create rather than organize, Sasser receives more difficult attempts, and finishers must handle longer touches. A projection that subtracts only Irving's expected points misses this cascading role cost. Creation is four different jobs Calling every player who can dribble a “creator” hides the Mavericks' actual problem. Half-court offense asks for at least four separable functions: Organizing: advancing the ball safely, calling the action, delivering passes on time, and preventing empty possessions. Creating the first advantage: forcing the on-ball defender or a helper to move far enough that the defense enters rotation. Extending an advantage: attacking a closeout, making the next pass, or converting a four-on-three after someone else bends the defense. Producing scoring pressure: threatening a shot or drive strongly enough that a defender cannot simply stay home, especially late in the clock. The first and third jobs can be shared relatively well. The second and fourth become scarce against good defenses. A low-turnover point guard can organize without forcing help. A wing can punish a tilted floor without being able to tilt it himself. A shooter can create gravity without being able to navigate a trap. Conversely, a high-volume scorer can bend the defense while making unstable reads. Dallas's task is therefore not to identify one nominal “backup point guard.” It is to assemble lineups in which the four jobs coexist. Irving is the only current Maverick who has already demonstrated the full package at a high NBA level. He can bring the ball up against pressure, manipulate a screen defender, score from every level, make the help defender commit, and manufacture a contested attempt when the planned action dies. His ACL recovery makes the question unusually urgent: the team must prepare both for ordinary non-Irving minutes and for a branch in which his availability or effectiveness is limited. Those are different workloads, but the same functional shortage appears in each. The turnover removed the easy veteran answer Dallas's guard room has changed twice in a few months. The February 2026 Anthony Davis transaction sent D'Angelo Russell, Jaden Hardy, and Dante Exum to Washington while returning several players and assets. Dallas separately acquired Tyus Jones at the deadline, but his stay lasted only eight games before Denver signed him in March. The July 8 six-team transaction then sent AJ Johnson out and brought Marcus Sasser in from Detroit. The net effect is important. Dallas did not merely exchange one bench guard for another. It lost or moved several players who could absorb possessions, then entered July without Jones, the veteran organizer whom some local summaries still treat as part of the roster. The current fallback hierarchy is younger and more specialized: Nembhard supplies organization; Sasser supplies pull-up and shooting possibility; Flagg supplies large-scale wing initiation; Christie and Marshall are better suited to attacking advantages than creating them from neutral; and Irving supplies the only proven elite primary package. That distinction also corrects the apparent depth-chart comfort. “Irving, Jones, Sasser, Nembhard” looks like four point guards. The verified roster is “Irving, Sasser, Nembhard,” with Flagg performing major initiation and wings contributing selective handling. Removing the stale Jones entry does not make Dallas devoid of passers. It does make the gap between orderly possession management and playoff-grade advantage creation harder to ignore. Ryan Nembhard is the clearest organizer Nembhard's rookie line establishes a real NBA skill rather than a theoretical one. NBA.com credits him with 6.6 points and 5.3 assists in 19.5 minutes across 60 games, with 1.4 turnovers per game and a 3.72 assist-to-turnover ratio. In 27 starts he averaged 9.4 points, 6.8 assists, and 2.9 rebounds while shooting 40.4 percent from three, according to the Mavericks' own offseason material. Dallas converted his two-way deal to a multiyear standard contract in March and exercised his 2026-27 team option in June. Those facts support a specific claim: Nembhard can organize NBA possessions. He sees passing windows, keeps the ball moving, and can preserve structure when the first option is unavailable. The season-ending 23-assist game against Chicago—the NBA's highest single-game assist total of 2025-26 and a Mavericks rookie record—shows his upper-end passing vision, even though one April game cannot establish a normal offensive level. Organization is not the same as pressure. Nembhard used only 17.3 percent of possessions in his minutes, and NBA.com lists a 49.2 true-shooting percentage for the season. His 5-foot-11 frame gives opponents an obvious place to test Dallas defensively and may make it harder for him to finish or pass over switching size. A defense that does not fear his pull-up or rim attack can go under screens, keep the weak-side defender attached, and invite him to become the scorer. In that response, a clean assist-to-turnover profile does not by itself create a quality shot. The best Nembhard role is therefore as a possession steward beside a player who generates pressure. With Irving, he can reduce the burden of ball advancement and let Irving begin actions from more dangerous locations. With Flagg, he can call the set, deliver the entry, relocate, and make the next read while Flagg attacks the defense's strongest wing. In bench groups, Nembhard needs either Sasser's pull-up threat, Flagg's downhill size, or enough movement shooting that the scheme creates the first opening for him. Asking Nembhard to be Irving would misuse evidence of one skill as proof of another. Marcus Sasser adds scoring possibility, not certainty The July trade adds a different type of small guard. Sasser has played 166 regular-season games across three Detroit seasons. NBA.com lists career averages of 7.0 points and 2.7 assists in 15.8 minutes, with 38.6 percent three-point shooting. In 2025-26 he played 38 games, averaged 5.2 points and 2.0 assists in 12.0 minutes, and shot 41.5 percent from three on 2.8 attempts per game. That profile matters because shooting and pull-up willingness can force a different coverage than pure organization. A guard who will punish a defender for going under a screen can begin to create an advantage even before reaching the paint. Sasser can also attack a second side after Flagg or Irving draws two defenders. Compared with a low-usage caretaker, he offers a more plausible route to self-generated points. But the evidence has strict limits. Sasser's NBA role has been small, he has started 17 career games, and his 2025-26 sample was only 456 minutes. His career scoring average and free-throw volume do not describe a guard who has repeatedly lived at the rim or carried a primary burden. At 6-foot-1, he may face the same defensive size questions as Nembhard, particularly if Dallas plays them together. Three-point percentage in a reserve sample does not prove that the shot will hold when attempts become more difficult, the best perimeter defender changes assignments, or a playoff opponent switches length onto him. Sasser should initially be treated as a scoring-pressure candidate and an advantage extender , not a verified lead creator. Camp and preseason should test whether he can reject screens, reach the paint, manipulate the low man, and pass accurately after drawing a second defender. If he only converts open threes and takes pull-ups without shifting help, he can still be a useful rotation scorer. That outcome simply would not solve the non-Irving creation problem. Cooper Flagg is the highest-upside secondary engine Flagg is the roster's best internal path to reducing dependence on Irving. As a rookie he averaged 21.0 points, 6.7 rebounds, and 4.5 assists in 70 starts, leading Dallas in total points, rebounds, assists, and steals. After the All-Star break, the Mavericks reported 5.4 assists against 2.5 turnovers per game across 21 appearances. Dallas had already used him as a point forward, and his size lets him see and deliver passes that the smaller guards cannot. Flagg creates pressure in a different way from Irving. He can drive through a smaller defender, attack a mismatch from the elbow, grab-and-go in transition, and draw help with force rather than with Irving's change of pace and handle. That allows Dallas to invert the offense: Nembhard can technically occupy point guard while Flagg performs the possession's decisive creation. It also makes Flagg a natural hub for split cuts, handoffs, and short-roll decisions in a passing-oriented Dusty May system. The unresolved part is half-court repeatability. Flagg shot about 29 percent from three as a rookie. If defenders can go under his ball screens or station a strong wing in the driving lane, his first move may not create the same rotation against a prepared defense. Increasing his initiation also raises the difficulty of his reads and may reduce the energy available for demanding defensive assignments. His strong counting production proves he can carry substantial offense; it does not yet prove he can solve every late-clock or postseason coverage. The developmental target should be co-creation , not immediate substitution for Irving. Flagg should receive possessions in which he initiates against a set defense, but lineups should give him an organizer, shooting, and a vertical target. Nembhard can get the ball to the right place. Sasser or Klay Thompson can punish under-help. Dereck Lively II or Daniel Gafford can screen and finish above the rim. Santi Aldama can space, pass, or run a second action. These supports allow Dallas to learn whether Flagg can bend the first defender without forcing every possession into a referendum on his jumper. Christie, Marshall, and the frontcourt are advantage extenders Christie's 2025-26 scoring growth does not automatically make him a primary guard creator. He averaged 12.3 points but only 2.0 assists. NBA tracking data offer a sharper role clue: on attempts after touches shorter than two seconds, he shot 46.1 percent from the floor and 43.5 percent from three; after holding the ball six seconds or longer, he shot 34.1 percent overall and 12.9 percent from three. Those splits are descriptive, not causal, and difficult late-clock attempts likely populate the long-touch group. Still, they strongly favor using Christie as a quick-decision finisher—catch, shoot, drive, or move it—rather than asking him to dominate the ball. Marshall fits a similar conceptual bucket. He can handle in transition, drive a closeout, punish a mismatch, and make connective passes. Aldama can receive at the elbow, attack a slow big, and keep a possession flowing. Lively and Gafford create vertical pressure as screeners. Thompson creates off-ball gravity. Each can make the offense harder to guard, but most require the initial matchup displacement to come from Irving, Flagg, Sasser, or the scheme. This is not a semantic demotion. Advantage extension is how good offenses turn one opening into a high-value shot. It becomes a problem only when Dallas mistakes a roster full of capable second-side players for a roster full of first-side creators. Against ordinary regular-season defense, pace, passing, and talent may blur the difference. Against switching size or a playoff opponent that has removed transition, the distinction becomes the offense. Functional lineup architecture The cleanest way to allocate creation is by complementary pairs rather than by nominal position: Pairing Organization First advantage Scoring pressure Principal risk Irving + Flagg High Elite/proven from Irving; high-upside from Flagg High Irving workload and Flagg shooting Nembhard + Flagg High Primarily Flagg Medium Defense can load toward Flagg and ignore Nembhard Sasser + Flagg Medium Shared, still unverified at lead scale Medium-to-high if Sasser's pull-up translates Turnovers, size, difficult decision load Nembhard + Sasser High Uncertain Medium Two small guards and no large primary initiator Irving + Christie Medium-to-high Irving High Christie must stay in quick-decision role Flagg + Christie/Marshall Medium Flagg Medium Too much burden on Flagg if spacing slips These pairings suggest three rotation principles. First, stagger Irving and Flagg whenever health permits so that at least one meaningful advantage creator is on the floor. Second, pair Nembhard with pressure rather than asking his organization to masquerade as pressure. Third, give Sasser controlled primary repetitions to determine whether his scoring translates upward, but preserve a second organizer or passing hub while the answer is unknown. The table should not be read as a permanent hierarchy. It is a test map. A Sasser–Flagg pairing becomes materially different if Sasser consistently draws two defenders. A Nembhard–Flagg pairing becomes more forceful if defenders can no longer duck under Nembhard's screen actions. An Irving–Flagg pairing may be excellent in short closing stretches while still being too demanding as an every-night workload during Irving's return. The relevant unit of evidence is the role inside the lineup, not the lineup label alone. May's stated interest in pace and passing can improve the environment. Early offense reduces the number of possessions in which Dallas must beat five organized defenders. Multiple initiators can keep Irving from laboring through every ball advance. Movement can make Christie's quick decisions and Aldama's passing more valuable. Yet scheme redistributes hard possessions; it does not abolish them. Every close game still produces possessions after the opponent switches the first action, denies the preferred entry, and leaves eight seconds on the clock. Dallas needs evidence about who owns those possessions when Irving sits. What would count as an answer Summer League cannot answer the entire question because opponent quality, roster continuity, and defensive game planning differ from the NBA. It can clarify Nembhard's command and whether young guards create separation. Training camp can reveal May's preferred functional pairings. Preseason can show who initiates against NBA size. The strongest evidence will come in regular-season non-Irving minutes and, eventually, against defenses that deliberately take away the first option. The useful indicators are role-based rather than merely scoring-based: Can Nembhard preserve his decision quality when opponents pressure him full court or switch size onto him? Does Sasser force screen defenders above the level, reach the paint, and create passes after help—not merely make open threes? Can Flagg create efficient first advantages when defenders go under screens or load the nail? Do Christie and Marshall remain efficient when limited to fast decisions, and does the offense deteriorate when their touches lengthen? Can Dallas keep one of Irving or Flagg on court without overloading Irving's return or depriving Flagg of developmental repetitions? Which lineups survive defensively if two small guards play together? Until those questions are tested, the most defensible conclusion is asymmetric. Dallas has credible organization behind Irving because Nembhard proved he can pass and protect possessions. It has plausible secondary scoring because Sasser can shoot and Flagg can carry offense. It has abundant advantage extension through Christie, Marshall, Aldama, and its finishers. What it does not yet have is a verified second player who combines advantage creation, scoring pressure, and late-clock reliability against high-level set defense. That is why Irving's health matters beyond his box score and why Flagg's year-two development is the roster's most important offensive swing. If Flagg becomes a dependable primary or co-primary initiator and either Nembhard or Sasser complements him, Dallas can cover non-Irving minutes by committee. If not, the offense may look orderly without being forceful: clean entries, low turnovers, and competent passing that still end in difficult shots once the defense refuses to rotate. Fact, inference, and forecast Verified facts: Dallas officially acquired Sasser in the July 8 transaction and sent AJ Johnson out. Denver officially signed Jones on March 5, so Jones is not part of the Dallas solution. Nembhard played 60 games as a rookie, Dallas converted him to a multiyear standard contract, and the club exercised his 2026-27 option. Irving is the roster's established high-level veteran creator. Flagg produced 21.0 points and 4.5 assists per game as a rookie. Sasser's three-year NBA record includes 38.6-percent three-point shooting in a reserve role. These are roster and performance observations supported by the official sources below; they do not establish future roles or lineup quality. Evidence-based inference: Dallas has more players capable of organizing or extending an advantage than players proven to create the first advantage against a set NBA defense. Nembhard's passing and turnover profile support an organizer classification more strongly than a pressure-creator classification. Sasser's shooting supports a trial as a secondary scorer, not an assumption that he is a lead guard. Flagg's production and size make him the best internal co-creation candidate, but his rookie shooting and the increased difficulty of primary reads leave repeatability unresolved. The lineup architecture above is an interpretation of those skills, not a report of results from a team that has not yet played together. Forecast, not fact: Dallas's best path is likely to stagger Irving and Flagg, use Nembhard to stabilize possessions, and test Sasser's pull-up pressure beside a larger initiator. If Flagg's jumper and manipulation improve while one small guard supplies a complementary strength, the team can cover many non-Irving possessions collectively. If Irving is limited and no secondary option forces help, the offense is likely to become more dependent on transition, offensive rebounding, and difficult Flagg attempts. Training camp cannot settle that forecast; role-specific regular-season evidence against set defenses can. Open questions What workload and effectiveness can Irving sustain after ACL reconstruction, separately from whether he is active? Does Sasser's pull-up shooting force NBA defenses to change coverage when he receives more primary possessions? Can Nembhard's organization survive playoff-style pressure and switching size without another elite creator beside him? Which half-court actions does May use to create the first advantage when both Irving and Flagg sit? Does Flagg's jumper improve enough that defenders must chase him over screens rather than loading the lane? Can any two-small-guard pairing create enough offense to offset the defensive matchup cost?

title: Dallas Mavericks 2026-27 roster construction dossier
deck: Dallas has assembled a large, defense-capable roster around Cooper Flagg, but its competitive ceiling still depends on uncertain lead-guard health and on turning frontcourt abundance into lineups with enough creation and spacing.

text: Dallas has assembled a large, defense-capable roster around Cooper Flagg, but its competitive ceiling still depends on uncertain lead-guard health and on turning frontcourt abundance into lineups with enough creation and spacing. Up: [[Dallas Mavericks 2026-27 season]] · Live record: [[Dallas Mavericks roster and minutes ledger]] · Baseline: [[Basketball/NBA team briefings 2026-27/DAL_2026_27_briefing|Dallas Mavericks 2026-27 Research Briefing]] The roster must be reconstructed from events, not one webpage This dossier asks a deceptively basic question: what team has Dallas actually built for 2026-27? As of July 9, the answer cannot be copied safely from the Mavericks' roster grid. The grid was still showing Khris Middleton and AJ Johnson after Dallas had officially sent them away, while omitting newly acquired Santi Aldama and Marcus Sasser. That is a publication-lag conflict, not evidence that the transaction failed. The Mavericks' announcement and the NBA offseason trade tracker identify the completed six-team transaction; those event records control until the roster display catches up. The verified July 8 Dallas side is straightforward. Dallas acquired Aldama, Sasser, and the NBA rights to Tarik Biberovic. It sent Middleton to Washington and Johnson to Memphis, along with a protected 2030 first-round pick and Dallas-controlled second-round compensation. Biberovic's rights are not the same thing as a roster contract. Reports about a future agreement remain reports until Dallas announces a signing or the NBA transaction record shows it. Any depth chart that automatically inserts him into the rotation is therefore premature. This distinction matters because three different populations are easily collapsed into one “roster.” First are players under NBA contracts or otherwise displayed by current public roster sources. Second are acquired draft rights, which create negotiation control but no active-player status. Third are Summer League, Exhibit 10, two-way, or camp candidates whose presence does not guarantee a regular-season place. A useful construction analysis must keep those groups separate. The stable basketball core visible across official and established roster sources is Kyrie Irving, Cooper Flagg, P. J. Washington, Naji Marshall, Max Christie, Klay Thompson, Caleb Martin, Dereck Lively II, and Daniel Gafford. The offseason transaction adds Aldama and Sasser. Dallas's June 29 team report also says it exercised Ryan Nembhard's 2026-27 team option. Tyus Jones is not part of the current group: Dallas's official game notes record that it waived him on February 28, and Denver officially announced his signing on March 5. By contrast, the NBA's pre-draft team profile listed Dwight Powell and Marvin Bagley III as free agents, while ESPN's roster display included Bagley and Moussa Cisse when accessed. The research packet also contains draft or development names including Morez Johnson Jr., Sergio de Larrea, Tobi Lawal, and Vsevolod Ishchenko. Those names and third-party roster-grid appearances should not all be treated as equal-status members of the opening-night team; contract type and final roster disposition remain verification tasks. The resulting conclusion is narrower but more reliable than a twenty-name depth chart: Dallas has a confirmed star-development centerpiece in Flagg; a high-leverage but medically uncertain primary creator in Irving; several proven forwards and centers; and a group of secondary guards whose ability to organize an NBA offense is not established at lead-creator scale. The construction problem begins at point guard Irving is the roster's only demonstrated high-end half-court initiator. That does not mean every possession must begin with him. Flagg's rookie production—21.0 points, 6.7 rebounds, and 4.5 assists in the baseline research packet—supports a larger year-two creation role, and Dusty May has publicly emphasized pace, passing, and using Irving as a foundational veteran. But “can create some offense” and “can stabilize an NBA offense against set defenses” are different jobs. Irving's last competitive game preceded ACL reconstruction, and Dallas announced in February 2026 that he would miss the rest of 2025-26. The team's newer offseason language treats him as part of May's foundation, while an NBA draft profile said he should be ready for the start of the season. Those are encouraging organizational signals, not a verified workload guarantee. They do not establish that he can immediately absorb his old minutes, usage, burst, or back-to-back schedule. Sasser helps the guard inventory without resolving the central question. He is a smaller scoring guard with NBA experience, useful pull-up potential, and a plausible second-unit role. The acquisition gives Dallas another ballhandler and shooter, but the evidence does not warrant treating him as a full substitute for Irving's manipulation of switches, late-clock shot creation, or playoff-caliber decision making. Nembhard may organize units after Dallas exercised his option; Christie can defend wings and attack advantages; Flagg can become a point-forward hub. Each covers a portion of the job. None is a verified replacement for a healthy Irving's full creation burden. See [[Dallas guard creation after roster turnover]] for the corrected post-Jones guard map. That makes guard creation a portfolio problem. Dallas should ask which combinations supply four functions: bringing the ball up under pressure, bending the first defender, making the second read, and producing a credible shot late in the clock. A Jones-led group may be orderly but still lack Irving's scoring pressure. A Sasser–Christie pairing may provide handling and defense but need Flagg's passing. A Flagg-led bench group may need Thompson or Aldama to pull help defenders away. A Nembhard-led group may also organize possessions while remaining less forceful at the rim. The roster can cover the functions collectively, but the combinations are sensitive to shooting and health. Frontcourt abundance is both insurance and congestion Dallas has several real frontcourt options: Flagg, Washington, Marshall in larger wing configurations, Aldama, Lively, Gafford, Powell, and possible depth from Bagley, Morez Johnson, or Cisse depending on final status. This is valuable because Lively played only seven games in 2025-26 before foot surgery, and late-June public reporting in the research briefing said he had not yet progressed to running. A team with that medical uncertainty should carry more than one playable center. Yet extra bigs do not automatically produce a good defense. Lively offers the highest theoretical combination of rim protection, vertical spacing, mobility, and short-roll passing. Gafford supplies force at the rim, offensive rebounding, screening, and dependable regular-season center minutes. Powell is a veteran systems player. Aldama is the most important geometry changer because he can handle, pass, and shoot at forward or small-ball-center size. Washington can defend across frontcourt matchups and is a credible spacer. Morez Johnson projects as an energetic defender and rebounder but enters with rookie uncertainty. The problem is overlap. Two traditional non-shooting centers cannot share ordinary NBA minutes without severely compressing the offense. Flagg's rookie three-point percentage, cited in the Dallas briefing at 29.5 percent, means Dallas cannot yet assume that every Flagg-plus-center lineup has four respected shooters. If Washington, Marshall, or a young guard is also ignored, the lane narrows and Irving or Flagg sees extra bodies before creating an advantage. Aldama changes those constraints more than his raw scoring average suggests. NBA.com lists 14.0 points, 6.7 rebounds, and 2.9 assists in 43 games for Memphis in 2025-26. At seven feet, his willingness to pass and operate away from the rim can allow Dallas to keep size without assigning every frontcourt player to the dunker spot. He can play beside Lively or Gafford, replace them in offense-first stretches, or join Washington and Flagg in a nominally centerless skill lineup. The defensive viability of the last option is matchup-dependent; Aldama should not be described as a direct substitute for Lively's rim deterrence. This is why a roster that appears “too crowded” up front may be rational. The players are not interchangeable. Lively is the ceiling defender, Gafford the sturdy vertical center, Aldama the skill-and-spacing connector, Washington the two-way forward hinge, and the younger bigs insurance and development bets. The coaching challenge is not simply allocating minutes fairly. It is choosing which property the lineup needs and accepting the property it gives up. Flagg is the bridge between timelines The franchise's construction has two clocks. Irving, Thompson, Powell, and the established centers are oriented toward immediate competence. Flagg, Christie, Morez Johnson, Sasser, and other young guards represent development and optionality. Aldama and Washington sit between those groups: experienced enough to help now, young enough to remain relevant through Flagg's rise. Flagg makes the clocks compatible because he does not need to be hidden while he develops. His rookie scoring and playmaking establish a high baseline, and his size lets May test him at several functional positions. But the roster should not use versatility as an excuse to leave him without a defined developmental burden. His most valuable year-two questions are whether defenses must respect his three-pointer, whether he can create efficient advantages against set half-court coverages, and whether he can carry difficult defensive assignments without blunting his offense. The ideal veteran structure helps answer those questions rather than merely chasing a few extra wins. Irving can teach Flagg how to manipulate help and can reduce late-clock burden. Lively can supply a lob threat and defensive backstop. Washington and Aldama can preserve size while opening passing lanes. Christie and Marshall can take perimeter assignments. If those players are available, Flagg receives demanding repetitions inside coherent lineups. If they are not, he may accumulate counting production while being forced into tasks that obscure which skills are actually improving. The transaction price reveals the front office's bet Dallas did not acquire Aldama merely by clearing a stale veteran contract. The official trade accounting includes AJ Johnson and meaningful draft compensation, including a protected 2030 first. The protection matters, but so does the principle: the front office exchanged future optionality for a frontcourt player who better fits Flagg's age line and skill environment. That bet can succeed in several ways. Aldama can become a high-minute connector, improve non-Irving offense, and make larger lineups playable. Sasser can become a trustworthy rotation guard. Biberovic's rights can eventually yield a player without requiring an NBA roster commitment today. The bet can also disappoint without any player being “bad”: Aldama's defensive limitations could restrict postseason matchups, Sasser might remain a small scoring specialist, and the rights may never turn into an NBA contributor. The deal also clarifies the new leadership's approach after the February Anthony Davis trade and May's hiring. Dallas appears to be moving away from dependence on aging, famous names and toward a wider band of playable size around Flagg. That is an interpretation, not an official declaration, and it should be tested against subsequent contracts. A large expenditure on another aging star would complicate it. For now, the Aldama move is consistent with a roster that wants to compete while reopening a younger timeline. A role-range map, not a false depth chart The following construction map intentionally uses roles rather than exact minutes: Function First option if available Secondary coverage Main constraint Primary half-court creation Kyrie Irving Flagg by committee with Sasser or Nembhard Irving health; secondary guards do not duplicate his scoring pressure Wing initiation Cooper Flagg Aldama, Marshall Spacing around the initiator Point-of-attack/wing defense Christie, Marshall, Flagg Washington, young guards Keeping enough creation on court Rim protection Lively Gafford Lively recovery and workload Vertical spacing Lively, Gafford Powell Non-shooting overlap Frontcourt shooting/passing Aldama, Washington Flagg, Thompson in wing-sized groups Defensive rebounding and rim protection Movement/gravity shooting Thompson, Aldama Christie, Sasser Whether shooting survives defensive targeting Developmental upside Flagg Christie, Sasser, Morez Johnson and young guards Role stability and NBA readiness This map supports several plausible identities. A healthy version can start Irving with two large wings, Flagg, and one center, creating a balanced defense with enough playmaking. A conservative-health version can make Flagg the central organizer and use Aldama as the second frontcourt passer. A defense-first version can deploy Christie, Marshall, Flagg, Washington, and Lively, but it must prove it can score. An offense-first version can use Irving, shooting guards, Flagg, Aldama, and one mobile big—or Aldama at center—while accepting more pressure at the rim. The key is that Dallas does not possess one obvious five-man answer. Its roster is a menu of tradeoffs. That can be a strength under a coach who identifies matchup-specific functions, or a weakness if rotation choices are driven by reputation and nominal position. Why it matters The Mavericks' 34.4-win model prior is not contradicted by the roster's surface talent. It is a skeptical median for a team whose best creator and best defensive center have not yet demonstrated current availability, whose second-year star may be asked to scale rapidly, and whose depth is stronger at forward and center than at lead guard. The roster has a path above that median because Flagg can improve, Irving can return effectively, Lively can restore the defense, and Aldama can solve real spacing problems. It has a path below it because the same four propositions are correlated: missing creators worsens spacing, missing rim protection forces less skilled defensive lineups, and injuries push young players into unstable roles. The next good update is not a speculative trade target. It is a transaction-reconciled contract table, followed by evidence from camp and preseason about which players actually perform the four creation functions and which frontcourt pairings preserve space. Until then, role ranges are more honest than a precise depth chart. Sources Mavericks acquisition announcement — July 8, 2026; official Dallas transaction account; accessed July 9, 2026. NBA report on the six-team Aldama transaction — July 1 and updated with official structure; accessed July 9, 2026. NBA 2026 offseason trade tracker — official transaction chronology; accessed July 9, 2026. Dallas Mavericks official roster — accessed July 9, 2026; stale relative to the completed transaction at access time. ESPN Dallas roster — independent roster cross-check; accessed July 9, 2026. Kyrie Irving to miss the remainder of 2025-26 — Mavericks announcement, February 2026. Dallas 2026 draft profile — NBA roster context and preseason return expectation; accessed July 9, 2026. Dusty May begins with Kyrie as a foundation — Mavericks report on May's introduction; accessed July 9, 2026. Dallas Mavericks 2025-26 game notes — official transaction chronology recording the February 28 Tyus Jones waiver; accessed July 9, 2026. Nuggets sign Tyus Jones — official Denver signing announcement, March 5, 2026; accessed July 9, 2026. Santi Aldama NBA player page — official player statistics and history; accessed July 9, 2026. Open questions Which acquired or returning players have standard, two-way, Exhibit 10, or draft-rights-only status after all July transactions post? Does Irving participate fully in training camp, and what workload language does Dallas use? When does Lively progress to unrestricted running, contact work, and full practice? Which two non-Irving players can reliably initiate offense against pressure? Can Flagg's shooting command enough respect for defense-first lineups to maintain NBA spacing? Which frontcourt pairings survive defensively without sacrificing too much creation?

text: Dallas enters 2026-27 as a young-star development project with real size and defensive options, but its season range is unusually sensitive to lead-guard creation, center health, and whether Dusty May can turn frontcourt depth into coherent lineups. Up: [[Basketball/NBA/NBA and Dallas Mavericks|NBA and Dallas Mavericks]] · Baseline: [[Basketball/NBA team briefings 2026-27/DAL_2026_27_briefing|Dallas Mavericks 2026-27 Research Briefing]] · Construction: [[Dallas Mavericks 2026-27 roster construction dossier]] Current state — July 10, 2026 This is the canonical season hub, not a prediction frozen on one offseason morning. It records the verified state, routes each unresolved question to the article that owns it, and specifies what evidence should change the season view. The older research briefing remains a dated baseline; later facts should not be back-written into it. Official transaction state. Dallas completed a July 8 multi-team transaction in which it received Santi Aldama, Marcus Sasser, and the NBA rights to Tarik Biberovic. The Mavericks sent Khris Middleton, AJ Johnson, a protected 2030 first-round pick, and second-round compensation. The NBA transaction tracker and Dallas announcement establish the completed event. Biberovic's draft rights are not an NBA contract, so he does not belong in a projected active rotation without a later official signing. Roster-display conflict. The official Dallas roster grid lagged the completed transaction when checked during this research cycle. Event records control over a stale display. [[Dallas Mavericks roster and minutes ledger]] preserves the provenance conflict and distinguishes active contracts, draft rights, developmental arrangements, and unresolved free-agent status. Tyus Jones is not a Maverick: Dallas's official game notes record that it waived him on February 28, and Denver announced his signing on March 5. Any Dallas depth chart that still assigns Jones minutes is using superseded state. Leadership and coaching. Masai Ujiri leads basketball operations, and Dallas hired Dusty May on June 23 after Michigan's 2026 national championship. May has discussed pace, shared decision-making, role clarity, and development, while his Michigan teams supplied evidence of transition emphasis, read-and-react spacing, multiple ball-screen actions, and selective switching around a more traditional center. Those are documented prior principles, not yet a demonstrated Mavericks system. [[Dallas Mavericks under Dusty May]] owns the translation test. Health boundary. Kyrie Irving and Dereck Lively II remain the two highest-leverage availability questions. Dallas announced that Irving would miss the remainder of 2025-26 while continuing ACL recovery. Lively played only seven games before right-foot surgery ended his season. Public optimism about future participation is not equivalent to a verified workload, back-to-back policy, or return to prior performance. [[Dallas Mavericks health ledger]], [[Kyrie Irving return from ACL reconstruction]], and [[Dereck Lively II health and defensive value]] separate official milestones from inference. The season has two connected objectives Dallas is neither a clean rebuild nor a conventional win-now roster. The first objective is to build a durable environment around Cooper Flagg. The second is to discover how competitive that environment can be while Irving, Lively, and several younger players occupy wide outcome ranges. These objectives can reinforce each other, but only if the team distinguishes useful developmental responsibility from emergency overload. Flagg's rookie baseline—21.0 points, 6.7 rebounds, and 4.5 assists in the current research packet—justifies more year-two creation. It does not require Dallas to make him the full-time answer to every roster weakness. A healthy Irving can give Flagg possessions against a tilted defense rather than making every possession a test of self-creation. A healthy Lively can supply a lob threat and defensive backstop. Aldama and P. J. Washington can preserve size while creating more passing and shooting space. Max Christie, Naji Marshall, and other large wings can take difficult perimeter assignments. The development failure mode is easy to mistake for progress. Flagg could post larger counting numbers because he rebounds, initiates, creates late in the clock, guards the best wing, and compensates for cramped spacing. That workload may reveal his resilience, but it also confounds evaluation. [[Cooper Flagg year-two development]] therefore asks whether shooting, handle, passing reads, rim pressure, and defensive execution improve after controlling for role and lineup context. [[Cooper Flagg and two-big lineup creation burden]] separately tests when size helps him and when it transfers too many creation jobs onto him. The competitive objective depends on the same structure. Dallas can outperform a modest preseason median if Flagg improves, Irving returns effectively, Lively restores high-level center defense, and Aldama makes large lineups more skilled. Those propositions are partly correlated. Irving's absence increases Flagg's burden; Lively's absence changes the center rotation; weak spacing makes every creator's job harder. The roster's ceiling should therefore be evaluated as a scenario tree, not as four independent bonuses added to a point estimate. Guard creation is the first constraint Irving is the only player on the current verified core with a demonstrated record as an elite NBA half-court creator. “Primary creator” includes more than dribbling the ball up. It means bending the first defender, forcing the second defender to commit, making the next read, and producing a credible shot when the initial action fails. Dallas has several players who can perform parts of that chain, but no public evidence establishes another full substitute. Sasser improves the inventory. He can handle, pull up, attack a tilted floor, and defend within a smaller-guard role. His arrival matters because Dallas needs real second-side creation and a guard who can organize bench possessions. It would still be an evidence error to promote a limited-role sample into proof of lead-guard offense. [[Marcus Sasser as a secondary creator]] defines the narrower transferable case. Flagg can initiate from rebounds, the wing, or a ball-screen action. Aldama can connect actions and make the next pass. Ryan Nembhard can organize possessions if his roster status and role persist. Christie, Marshall, and Washington can attack advantages. Klay Thompson supplies shooting gravity more than primary initiation. These skills can form a portfolio, but only coherent combinations cover all four creation functions. This distinction changes how Dallas should be judged. A non-Irving lineup that produces a good shot through early offense, Flagg initiation, an Aldama connection, and a Sasser closeout attack has solved the possession collectively. A lineup that merely rotates several nominal ballhandlers before Flagg attempts a difficult late shot has not. [[Dallas guard creation after roster turnover]] owns the complete functional map and the tests for when May's shared-creation language becomes real offense. The season's first guard checkpoints are observable: who advances the ball after rebounds; whether the first action creates an advantage; who makes the second read; how often the offense reaches a late clock without leverage; and how far shot quality falls when Irving sits. These measures should be conditioned on opponent, lineup, and Irving's actual workload. One preseason burst from a young guard is evidence of a skill, not proof that the roster has solved initiation. Frontcourt depth is a geometry problem Dallas has more credible frontcourt options than lead creators. Flagg, Washington, Aldama, Lively, Daniel Gafford, Marshall in larger wing groups, and possible depth pieces provide size, rebounding, rim pressure, passing, and defensive flexibility. The players are not interchangeable, and “depth” becomes useful only when each combination preserves enough of the five essential properties: creation, spacing, rim pressure, rim protection, and defensive rebounding. Lively supplies the highest theoretical combination of vertical spacing, mobility, short-roll passing, and rim deterrence. Gafford supplies screening, finishing, offensive rebounding, and stable regular-season center minutes. Aldama changes the geometry because he can pass, handle, and shoot at frontcourt size. Washington is a two-way hinge who can defend larger assignments without automatically occupying the paint. Flagg can be a forward initiator, screener, cutter, or small-lineup big, but those labels conceal different workloads. Two-big lineups are not automatically large or defensive in functional terms. A combination that places two players near the rim can crowd Flagg's drives and give the opponent a designated helper. A combination with Aldama lifting or popping can preserve size while moving a big defender away from the lane. A Lively–Washington pairing may protect the rim and retain enough spacing; a Gafford–Aldama pairing may combine vertical force with passing; a centerless Aldama–Washington–Flagg group may improve skill while sacrificing some deterrence. [[Dallas frontcourt geometry]] evaluates those combinations rather than treating nominal positions as answers. Health makes this more than a stylistic exercise. If Lively is unavailable or restricted, Dallas must distribute his functions rather than search for a single replacement. Gafford can absorb conventional center minutes, but other lineups may need more nail help, low-man rotation, or collective rebounding. Aldama can improve offense at center without reproducing Lively's defensive ceiling. [[Dallas center rotation without full Lively availability]] maps those substitutions and their costs. The early evidence should be lineup-specific. Which player is the screener? Which frontcourt player occupies the weak-side corner or dunker spot? Whose defender helps from the lane? Can Dallas complete defensive possessions with rebounds after switching? Does an offense-first group survive at the rim? The answers determine whether frontcourt abundance is genuine optionality or merely several players competing for the same space. May's principles require NBA proof The strongest available evidence about May describes principles: play with pace, move from a good shot to a better one, use several ball-screen actions, switch comparable perimeter defenders, protect a distinct center role, communicate, and define responsibilities. The season should test whether those principles survive NBA spacing, scouting, schedule density, and player hierarchy. Pace should mean creating earlier advantages, not shortening possessions indiscriminately. Dallas has several forwards who can rebound and advance, which can reduce dependence on a single point guard. The useful measure is whether early offense produces rim attempts, open threes, free throws, or a defense forced into rotation. More possessions ending in rushed contested shots would falsify the intended benefit. Read-and-react offense also requires more structure than its name implies. Players must share reads, maintain width, know who replaces a cutter, and flow into a second action when the first is stopped. The roster's size makes this especially important. Two players making reasonable individual cuts can still destroy the spacing if they enter the same lane. May's task is to give Flagg, Aldama, Irving, and the centers complementary decision points rather than equal permission to occupy every spot. Defensively, selective switching could fit Dallas's large wings while keeping Lively or Gafford nearer the rim. It could also create rebounding mismatches and invite opponents to hunt the one exchange Dallas cannot make. The relevant evidence is not whether Dallas says it will switch. It is which positions exchange, how the center handles each ball screen, where help comes from, and whether the possession ends with a rebound. May's first NBA season should receive patience without immunity from measurement. Good results can arrive through unsustainable shooting; losses can occur despite a useful process. Repeated possession evidence, adjusted for lineup and opponent, is more informative than one result or one quote. The clearest confirmation would be a team that creates early advantages, reaches second actions, gives Flagg purposeful developmental reads, protects the center's defensive value, and maintains legible roles through health changes. A season scenario map The scenarios below are basketball states, not medical forecasts or precise win projections. State Observable evidence Basketball consequence Main evaluation question Irving and Lively broadly available Full practice, regular appearances, manageable restrictions Dallas can pair elite creation with its best defensive-center ceiling Does the supporting lineup preserve shooting and reduce overload? Irving limited, Lively available Guard workload restrictions with stable center defense Flagg and the secondary guards inherit more initiation while defense retains structure Can collective creation survive set defenses? Irving available, Lively limited Lead offense remains, but rim protection and center passing change Gafford and smaller groups cover center functions by committee Can Dallas defend and rebound without shrinking the offense? Both limited Multiple jobs transfer simultaneously Flagg's burden rises, lineup compromises compound, young-player roles destabilize Can May preserve coherent development rather than chase short-term patches? Young-player upside exceeds baseline Repeatable Flagg, Sasser, Christie, or other growth in stable roles Dallas gains value without relying solely on medical upside Which improvement survives opponent adjustment and role control? [[Dallas Mavericks availability scenarios]] provides the detailed update protocol. A new official designation changes the state; it does not justify an invented recovery probability. A minutes restriction can matter more than active/inactive status. A returning player may also change teammates' roles before his own box-score production stabilizes. What would move the season view The season outlook should move materially when evidence changes one of the roster's functional bottlenecks: Official roster reconciliation. Contracts, waivers, signings, two-way conversions, and draft-rights status should update the ledger before they update a depth chart. Full-practice and preseason participation. Irving and Lively milestones narrow the plausible availability states, while stated restrictions keep the range wide. Creation under pressure. Sasser, Flagg, Nembhard, or another guard repeatedly organizing offense against set NBA defenses would reduce dependence on one creator. Flagg's shooting and decision speed. Defenses respecting the shot, combined with faster correct reads, would improve both his individual projection and frontcourt lineup viability. Frontcourt pairing evidence. Repeated possessions can show which groups preserve space, protect the rim, and rebound rather than merely looking balanced on paper. May's second actions and coverage rules. Sustainable offensive counters and lineup-specific defensive rules would convert coaching hypotheses into team evidence. Conversely, silence is not positive evidence. A roster page that remains stale does not undo an official transaction, and an absence of injury news does not prove unrestricted participation. Training-camp praise is a source for intended roles, not a substitute for game evidence. Small samples should identify questions and mechanisms before they produce strong forecasts. Why it matters Dallas's season cannot be summarized by adding recognizable names. The roster contains a potential star initiator in Flagg, an elite but health-uncertain creator in Irving, a high-ceiling defensive center in Lively, several large two-way or connective forwards, and credible center depth. It also lacks a verified second elite organizer, carries correlated health and spacing risks, and is installing a first-time NBA head coach's system. That combination creates a wide but intelligible range. The high path is not simply “everyone stays healthy.” It is Irving returning effectively, Lively restoring defensive structure, Flagg improving in identifiable skills, Aldama helping large groups breathe, and May building actions that distribute decisions without pretending every creator is equivalent. The low path is similarly structural: health limitations transfer several jobs at once, compressed spacing magnifies the burden, and rotation instability makes development harder to interpret. The useful season coverage is therefore cumulative. Transactions update the roster ledger. Health milestones update scenario weights. Games update the guard-creation, frontcourt, coaching, and player-development articles. This hub records how those pieces change the season-level view without turning every small event into a new prediction. title: Dallas Mavericks availability scenarios
deck: Dallas's 2026-27 forecast should be expressed as a set of health-conditioned rotation scenarios because public evidence supports neither a clean-bill-of-health assumption nor a precise games-played prediction for Kyrie Irving and Dereck Lively II.
headings: Availability is a basketball variable, not a medical prediction
What is verified as of July 10
Scenario one: both core veterans are functionally available
Scenario two: Irving is available, Lively is delayed or managed
Scenario three: Lively is available, Irving is delayed or managed
Scenario four: both Irving and Lively are limited or unavailable
Scenario five: available bodies, reduced effectiveness
Converting scenarios into a minutes model
Evidence that should change the outlook
text: Dallas's 2026-27 forecast should be expressed as a set of health-conditioned rotation scenarios because public evidence supports neither a clean-bill-of-health assumption nor a precise games-played prediction for Kyrie Irving and Dereck Lively II. Up: [[Dallas Mavericks 2026-27 season]] · Roster context: [[Dallas Mavericks 2026-27 roster construction dossier]] · Health evidence: [[Dallas Mavericks health ledger]] · Method: [[NBA player forward projection model]] Availability is a basketball variable, not a medical prediction The Mavericks' roster creates an unusually large gap between “who is under team control” and “which version of the team can play together.” Kyrie Irving missed the entire 2025-26 season while continuing recovery from left-knee ACL reconstruction. Dereck Lively II appeared in only seven games before right-foot surgery ended his season. Dallas publicly expects both players to matter in 2026-27, but the available sources do not establish exact return dates, minute limits, back-to-back policy, or probability of recurrence. That evidence boundary should shape the analysis. This note does not diagnose either player, infer healing from silence, or assign a medically precise games-played distribution. It instead asks what Dallas's basketball structure looks like under observable states. The scenarios are conditional planning tools. They become more or less plausible as Dallas releases milestones such as full practice participation, preseason appearances, restrictions, or official injury designations. The distinction matters for forecasting. Availability does not merely subtract a player's projected value. It changes the jobs assigned to everyone else, the combinations a coach can use, and the environment in which young players develop. Irving's absence transfers initiation and late-clock creation. Lively's absence transfers rim protection, screening, and vertical spacing. If both are absent, Dallas cannot replace each independently without creating secondary costs. What is verified as of July 10 Dallas announced in February 2026 that Irving would not return during the 2025-26 season as he continued ACL recovery. The injury occurred in March 2025, and the long recovery means his absence was a deliberate team decision rather than an ordinary late-season designation. The NBA's Dallas draft profile subsequently described him as expected to be ready for the start of the next season, and Dusty May's introductory material spoke about building with Irving. Those later statements improve the organizational outlook, but they do not demonstrate competitive readiness or an unrestricted workload. Lively's public baseline is less encouraging. Dallas and NBA reports identify right-foot surgery and a season ending after seven appearances. The prior Dallas briefing records that, as of June 26, he had not progressed to running. That is a dated milestone, not a current diagnosis. It is enough to reject an assumption that he had already completed a normal offseason progression; it is not enough to project a particular return month. The two cases therefore differ. Irving's team-facing language has shifted toward expected return, after an intentionally prolonged recovery. Lively had a more recent negative functional milestone in late June. Neither case should be flattened into “healthy” or “out.” The honest categories are stages: not cleared for full basketball work, participating with restrictions, available but workload-managed, and available without a publicly stated restriction. Other players can miss games, of course, but Irving and Lively carry the largest structural leverage. P. J. Washington, Naji Marshall, Santi Aldama, Daniel Gafford, Cooper Flagg, Max Christie, Ryan Nembhard, and Marcus Sasser affect depth and lineup quality. The roster can absorb an isolated short absence from one of them more directly. Irving and Lively define capabilities the roster does not duplicate at the same level. Tyus Jones is not a current Maverick; Dallas waived him on February 28 and Denver signed him on March 5. Scenario one: both core veterans are functionally available In the best basketball scenario, Irving and Lively participate in training camp, enter the regular season without a material public restriction, and remain available often enough to establish lineup continuity. “Functionally available” does not require 82 games or peak-career minutes. It means May can plan rotations around them rather than treating each appearance as a special event. This version has a coherent starting architecture. Irving supplies first-side advantage creation and late-clock scoring. Flagg can expand as a secondary creator instead of being forced to organize every difficult possession. Lively screens, dives, passes on the short roll, and protects the rim. Washington, Marshall, Christie, Aldama, or another credible wing fills the remaining slots based on shooting and matchup. The offensive benefit compounds. Irving's defender cannot abandon him, which creates cleaner spaces for Flagg. Lively's lob gravity occupies the low defender, which makes Irving's pocket passing and Flagg's downhill attacks more dangerous. Aldama or Washington can stretch a frontcourt defender away from the paint. Dallas can then use Sasser as a scoring reserve rather than asking him to imitate a primary point guard. The defensive benefit is equally important. A functional Lively allows perimeter defenders to press higher and lets Flagg take aggressive assignments without every mistake becoming a layup. Gafford can remain a forceful second center rather than carrying all traditional-center minutes. Aldama can be used for his skill in favorable matchups instead of being pressed into every rim-protection possession. Even this scenario contains uncertainty. Irving will be 34 during the season after an extended absence, so “available” does not guarantee old burst or defensive tolerance. Lively must demonstrate that his foot can tolerate repeated NBA loading. The proper forecast response is not to restore each player's old rate and multiply by optimistic minutes. It is to use a broad effectiveness band inside the healthy-availability branch. For roster planning, this scenario supports balanced units: Irving–Christie–Flagg–Washington/Aldama–Lively as one conceptual shape, with Marshall, Sasser, Thompson, Gafford, and the remaining forwards supplying matchup depth. The names are illustrative, not a predicted starting five. What matters is the functional distribution: one elite creator, two or three large connectors/defenders, and one rim-running center. Scenario two: Irving is available, Lively is delayed or managed This may be the easiest partial-health scenario for Dallas to survive because the roster has multiple centers. Gafford can start and provide screening, finishing, rebounding, and some rim protection. Powell or another depth big can cover low-leverage minutes. Aldama can play small-ball center when offense is the priority. Morez Johnson or another young center can receive developmental minutes if his roster status and readiness justify them. The substitution is not neutral. Lively's defensive range and passing ceiling are distinctive. Gafford can protect the rim and finish powerfully but does not reproduce every coverage or connective read. Aldama improves skill and spacing but is not the same last-line defender. A rookie may supply activity while making positioning errors. Dallas can fill the minutes more easily than it can fill the exact role. With Irving active, however, those compromises are manageable. He can create efficient shots for Gafford and keep offense-first Aldama groups organized. Flagg can spend more energy as a defender and transition force. May can choose center types by matchup instead of choosing them solely to rescue a stagnant offense. The forecast effect should therefore include a modest direct downgrade plus matchup variance. Against teams that pressure the rim or punish small centers, missing Lively may be severe. Against switching or spacing opponents, Aldama-at-five groups could remain competitive offensively. A single points-per-game deduction would miss that distribution. The verification triggers are concrete: running, contact work, full practice, preseason participation, and official injury reports. A vague statement that Lively is “progressing” should not move the scenario much unless it identifies the stage. Conversely, an absence from Summer League or voluntary workouts has limited meaning for an established injured player unless Dallas explains it. Scenario three: Lively is available, Irving is delayed or managed This version preserves the defensive skeleton but exposes Dallas's thinnest offensive function. Lively can anchor the paint, Gafford can keep center minutes stable, and the team can build large lineups around Flagg, Washington, Marshall, Christie, and Aldama. Those groups may defend, rebound, and run. The central question becomes who creates a quality half-court shot after the first action is stopped. Flagg would carry a larger initiation burden. That can accelerate development, but it is not costless. Defenses can load toward him, test his handle, and go under screens if his shooting does not improve. Nembhard can organize the first action and protect the ball, but the evidence does not establish that he reproduces Irving's scoring gravity. Aldama can serve as a second-side passer and occasional handler. Sasser can take pull-ups and attack tilted defenses. Christie and Marshall can drive closeouts. None has Irving's proven ability to repeatedly manufacture advantages against a set defense. May can mitigate the problem through pace and collective passing. Defensive stops create transition chances before the opponent loads the paint. Early drag screens let Flagg or Sasser attack before matchups settle. Split cuts and movement shooting can create advantages without a traditional point guard. But scheme changes the frequency and location of hard decisions; it does not eliminate the need for someone to make them. The likely rotation implication is more ballhandling by committee and more shooting around Flagg. Thompson's gravity may earn situational minutes despite defensive decline. Aldama becomes more valuable because he can keep the ball moving from a frontcourt slot. A non-shooting perimeter defender becomes harder to play beside Lively because the lane already contains a center. This scenario is also where the distinction between “Irving plays” and “Irving restores the offense” matters most. A managed return could involve fewer minutes, fewer back-to-backs, and reduced rim pressure even while he is officially active. Dallas should be modeled with an intermediate branch in which Irving stabilizes some minutes but does not carry his prior offensive workload. Scenario four: both Irving and Lively are limited or unavailable This is the stress case, not a forecast. It reveals why Dallas's apparent depth should not be mistaken for redundancy. Without Irving, the team lacks proven top-end creation. Without Lively, it lacks its highest-upside defensive anchor. Replacing both forces Flagg to solve more possessions while also taking harder defensive responsibility. A plausible group might use Nembhard or Sasser with Christie, Flagg, Washington or Marshall, and Gafford. It can defend at several spots and maintain vertical pressure, but its half-court ceiling depends heavily on Flagg. Another version could use Aldama beside Gafford to add passing and shooting. A smaller offense-first version could put Aldama at center, but then rim deterrence and rebounding become vulnerabilities. These are functional sketches rather than a claim that an unverified depth chart is settled. The deepest consequence is role cascade. Nembhard moves from secondary organizer toward a larger creation burden; Sasser moves from reserve scorer toward more primary handling. Flagg moves from developing co-creator toward offensive engine. Gafford moves from a shared-center arrangement toward a heavier workload. Aldama becomes both spacing solution and backup organizer. Christie and Marshall receive more on-ball tasks. Each promotion can reduce the very skill that made the player valuable in the smaller role. Tyus Jones must not appear in this allocation: Dallas waived him February 28, 2026, and Denver officially signed him March 5. This is why availability shocks are nonlinear. Suppose Irving is worth a certain number of points above a reserve and Lively another number above a backup. Adding those two individual losses understates the combined effect if the backups cannot coexist cleanly or if Flagg's efficiency drops under extra usage. It can also overstate the effect in specific matchups if Dallas discovers a productive Flagg–Aldama offense. Scenario analysis preserves both possibilities. The model's 28-to-41-win p10–p90 band and four cold-start players are consistent with this structural uncertainty. The low branch is not simply “bad shooting luck.” It can represent the roster spending long stretches without one or both organizing pillars while inexperienced players absorb unfamiliar jobs. Scenario five: available bodies, reduced effectiveness Binary injury models often miss the most plausible middle. Irving and Lively may both be active yet below assumed effectiveness. Irving might protect his knee by reducing rim attacks or defensive change-of-direction. Lively might play shorter stints, avoid some coverage demands, or need recovery days. These examples are basketball possibilities, not claims about their medical state. This branch matters because official “available” status can tempt forecasters to restore full player value immediately. A better method separates participation, workload, and performance. For each player, ask three different questions: Is he active for the game? How many and what kind of minutes can he play? How effective is he within those minutes relative to the prior projection? The answers need not move together. Irving could be active for 24 controlled minutes and still transform Dallas's second unit. Lively could start but avoid long closing stints until conditioning returns. A model that records only games played will miss both the value and the limitation. Evidence should also be weighted by proximity. An official training-camp restriction is more informative than a June optimism quote. Repeated preseason workload is more informative than one practice clip. Regular-season back-to-back decisions are more informative than a generic statement that there is no formal minutes limit. The evidence ladder should update gradually rather than flipping the projection at the first positive headline. Converting scenarios into a minutes model The vault's older roster-context packet assigned Irving 56 expected games at 27.0 minutes and Lively 51 games at 25.8 minutes. Those are model inputs, not verified forecasts. The public evidence is insufficient to replace them with more precise point estimates. It is sufficient to test them against conditional branches. A practical approach begins with role-minute ranges rather than exact season totals: State Irving role range Lively role range Main beneficiaries of transferred work Both functionally available Primary creator; starter workload with possible management Starting defensive center; shared center workload Flagg develops as co-creator; Gafford stabilizes bench Irving available, Lively limited Primary creator Delayed, restricted, or absent Gafford center minutes; Aldama small-ball/skill minutes Lively available, Irving limited Restricted or absent creator Starting defensive center Nembhard organization; Flagg initiation; Sasser handling; Aldama passing Both limited No stable primary creator No stable defensive anchor Nembhard, Flagg, Sasser, Gafford, Aldama and young depth all promoted Both active but sub-prior Participation without full assumed effectiveness Participation without full assumed effectiveness Mixed; role cascade is smaller but performance remains uncertain For simulation, each branch should carry correlations. Irving's status affects Flagg's usage and the value of finishers. Lively's status affects Gafford's minutes and perimeter defenders' risk tolerance. Their joint absence should not be sampled as two unrelated additive losses. The model can represent this with branch-specific minute matrices and player-effect distributions, then weight branches only when evidence supports probabilities. Until Dallas supplies more evidence, the branch weights should remain broad and qualitative. Publishing “Irving will play 55 games” would create false certainty. Publishing “if Irving is workload-managed, these four functions transfer to these players” produces a falsifiable and useful planning statement. Evidence that should change the outlook Positive evidence for Irving includes full-contact participation, repeated preseason appearances, normal change-of-direction and rim pressure in games, and no stated restriction beyond ordinary veteran management. Positive evidence for Lively includes progression from running to basketball activity, full contact, repeated practice, and preseason minutes that show he can move through defensive coverages. Negative evidence includes delayed clearance, repeated non-contact status, an official timetable extending into the season, recurrent soreness identified by the team, or regular absences after return. A single rest day or conservative preseason scratch is weak evidence by itself. The NBA's regular-season injury reports become the authoritative status source once games begin; commentary can explain context but should not override the designation. Performance evidence must also be interpreted carefully. A few made jumpers do not prove Irving's burst has returned. One blocked shot does not prove Lively can sustain a starter workload. Useful early indicators are role and movement patterns over repeated possessions: Irving's ability to turn the corner, force low-man help, and defend changes of direction; Lively's ability to cover space, screen repeatedly, sprint in transition, and recover between efforts. Any film conclusion should state the sample. Why it matters Dallas's season cannot be understood through a single “healthy roster” depth chart. The team has enough frontcourt inventory to survive a Lively delay better than it can survive an Irving delay, but losing Lively still changes the defense's ceiling. It has enough secondary handling to distribute Irving's minutes, but not enough evidence to claim the creation job is replaced. Flagg is the swing bridge in every branch: better health lets him develop inside a balanced structure; worse health asks him to become the structure. This scenario frame also disciplines expectations. Organizational optimism is relevant because it signals planning, but it is not clearance. Old injury news is relevant because it sets the last verified milestone, but it is not a permanent status. The forecast should move when the evidence moves, and it should move the entire rotation rather than only the injured player's games-played cell.
