Oh Kangwon, “Go-Joseon and Its Periphery as Seen through Bronze (Dagger) Manufacture Technology of Liaoning and Northwestern Korea,” Hangukak Nonchong 47 (2017): 1–52, https://www.kci.go.kr/kciportal/ci/sereArticleSearch/ciSereArtiView.kci?sereArticleSearchBean.artiId=ART002200450 — specialist technological chronology and argument for shifting centers. National Museum of Korea, “Production Specialization of Liaoning-Type Bronze Daggers,” Journal of Korean Art & Archaeology 7, https://www.ijkaa.org/v.7/0/78/121 — artifact classification, production, and the limits of typological inference. National Museum of Korea, “Liaoning-type Bronze Dagger,” collection highlight, https://www.museum.go.kr/ENG/contents/E0403000000.do?relicId=4379&schM=relic_represent_view — authoritative object description and association with Gojoseon. Gina L. Barnes, “State Formation in Korea: Historical and Archaeological Perspectives,” Curzon Press / Korean Studies (critical overview), https://www.researchgate.net/publication/248654251_State_Formation_in_Korea_Historical_and_Archaeological_Perspectives — comparative framework for distinguishing archaeological processes from retrospective dynastic accounts. Open questions Which Liaoning and northwestern Korean site sequences can now be synchronized by radiocarbon dates rather than artifact typology alone? How much of the apparent eastward shift reflects political relocation, and how much reflects changing burial customs, excavation coverage, or scholarly classification? What can new metallurgical provenance studies reveal about workshops, exchange corridors, and elite control without turning material networks into ethnic maps? How should historians weigh textual passages whose surviving recension is later than the events they purport to describe? What comparative work across Chinese, North Korean, South Korean, Japanese, and Anglophone scholarship can expose national framing without assuming that all interpretations are equally supported?

title: Buddhist institutions in Goryeo state and society
deck: Goryeo Buddhism became politically powerful through institutions—monastic communities, clerical examinations and offices, land and labor, court ritual, printing, and patronage—whose roles changed across the dynasty and cannot be reduced to either piety or corruption.
headings: What it means to call Goryeo Buddhist
Ritual made Buddhism part of government
Text, print, and the protection of the realm
Land, labor, privilege, and the limits of the evidence
text: Goryeo Buddhism became politically powerful through institutions—monastic communities, clerical examinations and offices, land and labor, court ritual, printing, and patronage—whose roles changed across the dynasty and cannot be reduced to either piety or corruption. Up: [[Korean history (MOC)]] What it means to call Goryeo Buddhist Goryeo (918–1392) is often called a Buddhist kingdom. The label is defensible only when translated into mechanisms. Kings founded and endowed monasteries, sponsored assemblies, appointed eminent monks, and sought Buddhist protection for dynasty and realm. Elite households sent sons into clerical careers and paid for images, manuscripts, bells, and rites. Monasteries held land, managed dependants, offered ritual expertise, and anchored regional communities. The state examined and ranked monks. Large textual projects joined scholarship to royal defense. None of this means that a single Buddhist “church” governed Goryeo. Multiple doctrinal schools and Seon lineages possessed distinct bases of authority. Monasteries differed enormously in wealth and political access. Court patronage could strengthen a temple while exposing it to political reversal. Clerics debated practice and criticized institutional laxity. Local worshippers encountered Buddhism through funerals, festivals, vows, healing, images, and sacred sites, not only through court ideology. It is also misleading to set Buddhism against Confucianism as mutually exclusive state religions. Confucian learning supplied much of official education, remonstrance, historiography, and administrative ethics. Buddhism addressed merit, kingship, death, protection, and cosmic order. The same royal or aristocratic household could invest in both. The institutional balance and the arguments about it changed, especially after the 1170 military coup, Mongol intervention, and late-Goryeo reform. Monasteries as corporate places A Goryeo monastery was at once a religious community, a built environment, and an economic organization. It required halls, images, books, fields, fuel, food, cloth, tools, and skilled labor. Resident monks observed discipline, studied texts, meditated, taught disciples, performed rites, and managed property. Lay workers and dependants sustained activities that monastic biographies rarely foreground. Location mattered. Some temples stood close to the capital and royal court; others occupied mountains associated with Seon practice; still others served regional centers or sacred landscapes. A foundation’s relationship to the throne could bring land, titles, construction, and prestige. Ties to a great family could generate donations and clerical recruits. Regional patronage did not make a monastery merely “local,” since monks, texts, and gifts circulated across the peninsula and beyond it. Temples accumulated layered claims over time. A donor could pay for a hall, dedicate a field, commission an image, or establish a recurring rite. Such gifts were meritorious acts and material transfers. Endowments supported memorial services for royal and aristocratic dead and linked a lineage to a community of ritual specialists. Corporate continuity allowed a monastery to preserve those relationships beyond one patron’s life. This material foundation demands precision. “Temple land” was not one legal category, and a temple’s receipt of revenue did not always equal modern freehold ownership. Holdings could derive from royal grants, private donations, reclamation, purchase, or assignments for particular services. Rights to revenue, cultivation, and jurisdiction might be divided. Late sources that describe vast Buddhist wealth cannot simply be projected back across the whole dynasty. Clerical recruitment, rank, and office Goryeo incorporated monks into a state-recognized hierarchy. The seung-gwa , or clerical examination, selected monks within the doctrinal and Seon streams. Successful candidates could advance through clerical grades; exceptionally eminent figures received titles such as Royal Preceptor ( wangsa ) or National Preceptor ( guksa ). These honors gave rulers authoritative teachers and gave clerics access to the court. The system did not make monastic advancement purely meritocratic. Education, lineage, temple affiliation, patrons, and proximity to power shaped opportunity. Royal sons sometimes became monks, most famously Uicheon. Elite families could diversify their influence by placing members in both civil and clerical careers. A distinguished monk’s disciples formed another kind of lineage, transmitting teaching, institutional affiliation, and patronage. State recognition also implied supervision. Ordination defined legitimate membership and helped distinguish authorized clerics from people who claimed exemptions or wore robes without acceptance into established communities. Surviving sources do not permit a simple count of monks at all dates, and rules were not necessarily enforced uniformly. Still, examinations, titles, and ordination show that court and sangha were institutionally entangled. Court titles should not be confused with command over all Buddhism. A National Preceptor possessed prestige, not a papal jurisdiction. Authority remained dispersed among schools, monasteries, masters, court patrons, and textual traditions. The plural structure enabled intellectual variety while also producing rivalry over recognition and resources. Ritual made Buddhism part of government Royal ritual was not an ornamental addition to politics. Goryeo rulers sponsored Buddhist assemblies for protection, merit, rain, healing, the dead, and the security of the realm. Ritual gathered king, officials, monks, objects, music, offerings, and spectators into a public representation of ordered rule. It made invisible claims—karmic merit and cosmic protection—visible through coordinated expenditure and performance. The Lotus Lantern Festival ( Yeondeunghoe ) and the Festival of the Eight Vows ( Palgwanhoe ) became emblematic state observances. Their histories included pre-Goryeo elements, and their meanings were not exclusively doctrinal. They joined Buddhist devotion to royal display, seasonal celebration, and memories of the founding order. The Ten Injunctions attributed to Taejo treat their observance as dynastically important, although the injunctions survive in a later compilation and require the same source criticism as other early records. Ritual responded to emergency. Buddhist services addressed drought, disease, invasion, and political instability. Modern readers may divide “religion” from practical statecraft, but Goryeo actors did not necessarily do so. Mobilizing monks to recite scripture or commissioning a canon was a technique of protection within their causal world. It also redistributed material resources and advertised the ruler’s capacity to coordinate collective action. Funerary and memorial practices tied Buddhism to family life. Elites funded services for deceased relatives and dedicated works for their merit. Surviving Goryeo paintings often record dedicatory intentions, even though many now outside Korea were preserved through Japanese collections. Their refined materials demonstrate costly patronage; their iconography reveals devotional worlds that cannot be inferred from official chronicles alone. Text, print, and the protection of the realm Goryeo was a major center of Buddhist textual production. Printing did more than reproduce doctrine. It established authoritative texts, generated merit, displayed technical command, and connected Goryeo to wider East Asian Buddhist networks. Imported Chinese editions and catalogues supplied models, but Goryeo scholars collated and organized materials in their own projects. The first Goryeo Buddhist canon was carved in the eleventh century during conflict with the Khitan. Its blocks were destroyed during the Mongol invasions. The second project, now commonly called the Tripitaka Koreana or Goryeo Daejanggyeong , produced 81,258 woodblocks between 1237 and 1248 under dynastic sponsorship. The blocks are now kept at Haeinsa. The often repeated number is documented by the UNESCO nomination dossier, but should not be inflated into claims that every block or character is literally error-free. The project joined devotional and administrative capacities. Scholars compared editions; artisans prepared and carved wood; institutions procured materials and labor; the court framed the enterprise as a response to invasion. The blocks’ uniformity and the canon’s textual value testify to disciplined production. At the same time, celebrating them only as a technological marvel can hide wartime suffering and the fiscal effort demanded by the project. Uicheon (1055–1101), a son of King Munjong, traveled to Song China and collected Buddhist works. His catalogue and supplementary canon project sought to encompass East Asian commentarial literature that lay outside the standard canon. Uicheon advocated an integration associated with the Cheontae tradition and criticized rigid separation between doctrinal study and meditation. His royal birth opened extraordinary opportunities, but his work was intellectually substantive rather than merely court propaganda. Printing also complicates modern stories of national isolation. Goryeo Buddhism relied on transregional circulation among the peninsula, Song and later Yuan China, Khitan Liao, and Japan. Texts and teachers moved through diplomatic and maritime routes. Goryeo patrons adapted those resources to local political and ritual purposes. Schools, lineages, and reform Histories of Korean Buddhism often organize Goryeo around “doctrinal” ( gyo ) schools and Seon meditation traditions. The distinction mattered institutionally, including in examinations, but it was never an absolute separation between book learning and practice. Monks on both sides read texts and cultivated disciplined practice. Programs of synthesis emerged precisely because the categories were close enough to argue over. Uicheon’s project emphasized doctrinal learning while seeking to integrate contemplation. A century later, Jinul (1158–1210) developed an influential Seon reform in the changed political environment after 1170. Disturbed by the gap between monastic ideals and practice, he promoted a community of fellow cultivators and eventually settled at Songgwangsa. His teaching is commonly summarized as “sudden awakening, gradual cultivation”: insight into one’s nature does not eliminate the need for sustained practice that transforms ingrained habits. Jinul drew on Chinese Chan and Huayan writings but constructed a program suited to his community. He did not reject scripture in favor of an anti-intellectual spontaneity. His synthesis helped shape the Jogye tradition and Songgwangsa’s later prestige. Because later Korean Buddhism claimed Jinul as a formative figure, historians must distinguish his own writings and immediate community from retrospective institutional genealogies. The military regime altered patronage. The Choe rulers who dominated politics from 1196 to 1258 cultivated relationships with Seon institutions and leading monks. This did not mean a complete transfer from doctrinal schools to Seon, but it changed which networks enjoyed political access. Religious reform and political patronage could coexist: a disciplined community might criticize worldly monastic behavior while receiving support from powerful warriors. Land, labor, privilege, and the limits of the evidence Buddhist institutions needed an economic base, and that base made them targets of criticism. Temples held fields and other assets, received donations, and relied on labor by tenants, slaves, artisans, and dependants. Some clerics and monasteries engaged in lending, production, or exchange. Exemptions from particular obligations could make ordination or temple affiliation economically consequential. Yet a sweeping claim that “the temples owned most land” is not supported by adequate dynasty-wide measurement. Surviving evidence is uneven, terminology varies, and late-fourteenth-century reformers had reasons to portray temple wealth as excessive. The Goryeosa itself was compiled by the successor Joseon state. Its accounts preserve valuable information but often participate in an explanation of why Goryeo’s order failed. The right analytical unit is therefore the dated transaction or institution. Which monastery? What kind of land or revenue? Who cultivated it? Which grant, register, inscription, or lawsuit demonstrates the claim? Was an exemption formal, temporary, evaded, or retrospective? Without those questions, “monastic economy” becomes a vague synonym for wealth. The same caution applies to monastic slaves. Temples could possess nobi , but their legal and lived conditions varied, and elite sources make dependent people difficult to hear. Labor was not peripheral to Buddhist splendor: buildings, bronze bells, lacquered sutra boxes, paintings, and printed canons all depended on it. An institutional history must keep artisans and cultivators in view even where sources name patrons instead. Economic critique could also come from within Buddhism. Reformers’ emphasis on discipline and practice suggests recognition that status and patronage could distort monastic ideals. It would be a mistake to sort every monk into “spiritual reformer” or “corrupt beneficiary”; individuals and institutions could occupy both devotional and material worlds. Mongol intervention and transregional Buddhism The Mongol invasions beginning in 1231 destroyed temples, books, and communities. The royal court moved to Ganghwa in 1232 and remained there during decades of war. The second canon project was undertaken in this context. Buddhist protection did not prevent military catastrophe in a modern causal sense, but the project shows how the court interpreted and acted within catastrophe. After Goryeo’s submission, its kings and elites operated within the Yuan imperial sphere. Buddhist relations now included powerful currents associated with Yuan court culture, including Tibetan Buddhism. Goryeo royal marriages with Mongol imperial princesses and repeated residence at the Yuan court changed patronage and cultural circulation. This did not erase established Korean lineages. It layered new imperial connections onto them. Late-Goryeo Buddhism produced major intellectual and artistic achievements even amid political strain. Goryeo Buddhist painting, manuscript illumination, and ritual objects testify to wealthy patronage and highly specialized workshops. Their beauty should not be used as proof of general prosperity, just as evidence of corruption should not erase devotion. Objects answer different questions from fiscal records: they can reveal materials, iconography, donors, workshop practice, and devotional aspiration. From criticism to Joseon restriction In the fourteenth century, reform-minded officials increasingly attacked Buddhist privilege. Neo-Confucian thinkers argued that monks withdrew people from productive and familial obligations, that temples absorbed land and labor, and that costly rites burdened the state. These criticisms combined moral philosophy with a concrete struggle over fiscal registration and political power. The critique gained force because the late Goryeo state faced land concentration, military threats, and contested revenue. Temples were one class of corporate holder among other powerful interests, including royal, aristocratic, and Yuan-connected households. Reformers singled them out not only because they were wealthy, but because Neo-Confucian accounts of family, social reproduction, and legitimate ritual challenged Buddhist premises. Dynastic change in 1392 did not instantly eliminate Buddhism. The Joseon state progressively reduced recognized monasteries and clerical institutions, restricted monks’ public position, and redirected land and labor. Royal and private Buddhist patronage nevertheless continued. The sharper contrast between a “Buddhist Goryeo” and “Confucian Joseon” is useful at the level of official institutional priority, but misleading if taken to describe every subject’s beliefs or an overnight rupture. Successor-state criticism creates a circular danger. If historians use Joseon polemic to define late Goryeo as corrupt and then cite that corruption as the inevitable cause of Joseon, the conclusion has been built into the evidence. A better explanation connects ideological criticism to land registers, political coalitions, military control, and the institutional interests of the new dynasty. An institutional balance sheet Buddhist institutions helped Goryeo rule in at least six distinguishable ways. They legitimated kings through merit and protective ritual. They organized court and public ceremonies. They preserved and produced knowledge. They supplied clerical careers for men, including members of elite families. They managed durable property and labor. They linked local sacred places to peninsula-wide and transregional networks. Each capacity produced a corresponding tension. Royal patronage encouraged dependence on court factions. Clerical rank integrated monks into the state but rewarded hierarchy. Endowments sustained worship but concentrated resources. protection rituals created solidarity but demanded labor and expense. Textual projects preserved learning while displaying power. Transregional exchange enriched Goryeo culture while exposing it to unequal imperial relations. That balance explains why Buddhism was neither an ideology floating above society nor a parasite upon it. It was part of the machinery through which Goryeo people governed, accumulated, remembered, worshipped, and contested authority. Its institutions were resilient because they met real social needs; they were vulnerable because their material success made them legible targets for rival projects of rule. Placed beside [[Goryeo as a plural aristocratic and Buddhist polity]], this account clarifies the larger polity. Goryeo’s pluralism did not mean modern toleration or separation of religion and state. It meant that several forms of cultivated authority—royal descent, official learning, family standing, military command, monastic discipline, ritual efficacy, and imperial connection—operated at once. Buddhist institutions translated several of those forms into durable communities and resources. Reading the sources No surviving genre gives a neutral institutional inventory. The Goryeosa and Goryeosa jeolyo were compiled under Joseon from earlier materials. Monastic inscriptions and epitaphs preserve careers and patronage but are commemorative. Clerical writings tell us what reformers wanted practice to be, not automatically what every monastery did. Art objects disproportionately survive when made from durable materials and collected by elites. Modern heritage descriptions often emphasize national achievement rather than conflict or labor. Claims should therefore be triangulated. A clerical title in an epitaph can be compared with dynastic records; a temple’s patronage with land or donor evidence; a ritual prescription with reports of performance; a canon’s cultural meaning with the physical blocks and production record. Silence is not proof of absence, but neither should an evocative object carry a claim about the whole dynasty. Sources Sem Vermeersch, The Power of the Buddhas: The Politics of Buddhism during the Koryŏ Dynasty (918–1392) (Harvard University Asia Center, 2008). Robert E. Buswell Jr., The Korean Approach to Zen: The Collected Works of Chinul (University of Hawai‘i Press, 1983). National Institute of Korean History, A History of Korea: Understanding Korea Series , Goryeo chapters: https://contents.history.go.kr/resources/common/pdf/A%20History%20of%20Korea_The%20Understanding%20Korea%20Series.pdf Academy of Korean Studies, Exploring Korean History through World Heritage , sections on Goryeo Buddhism and the Tripitaka: https://www.aks.ac.kr/ikorea/upload/intl/korean/UserFiles/Heritage_eng.pdf UNESCO Memory of the World, nomination dossier, “Printing Woodblocks of the Tripitaka Koreana and Miscellaneous Buddhist Scriptures”: https://media.unesco.org/sites/default/files/webform/mow001/korea_tripitaka.pdf UNESCO Courier, “200 years before Gutenberg: The master printers of Koryo”: https://courier.unesco.org/en/articles/200-years-gutenberg-master-printers-koryo Metropolitan Museum of Art, Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History, “Buddhism and Buddhist Art” and collection records for Goryeo works: https://www.metmuseum.org/toah/hd/budd/hd_budd.htm Richard D. McBride II, Domesticating the Dharma: Buddhist Cults and the Hwaŏm Synthesis in Silla Korea (University of Hawai‘i Press, 2008), for the inherited institutional background rather than direct Goryeo coverage. Open questions Which surviving Goryeo land documents permit quantitative comparison between temple holdings and those of royal or lay elite households? How differently did capital, mountain, and provincial monasteries organize labor and relations with surrounding communities? What can colophons and donor inscriptions reveal about non-elite women’s participation beyond the aristocratic patrons best represented in art history? How did clerical examinations change after 1170 and under Yuan intervention in practice, not merely in formal regulation? Which features of the institutional history above rest mainly on Joseon compilations and most need epigraphic corroboration?

title: Catholic persecution and new social networks in Joseon
deck: Catholicism survived repeated Joseon persecutions because books, households, women, itinerant teachers, and sacramental contacts made a dispersed community—but those same ties also made believers legible to relatives, neighbors, and interrogators.
headings: From scholarly reading to a lay church
Why ancestral rites became a political fault line
1801: factional purge, institutional destruction, and dispersal
What made a clandestine community work
1839 and 1846: a transnational church under regency politics
Persecution changed the church it failed to destroy
text: Catholicism survived repeated Joseon persecutions because books, households, women, itinerant teachers, and sacramental contacts made a dispersed community—but those same ties also made believers legible to relatives, neighbors, and interrogators. Up: [[Korean history (MOC)]] The causal core Catholic persecution in Joseon was neither one continuous campaign nor a simple collision between “Korea” and “the West.” A religion first appropriated by Korean readers became an organized community before a resident foreign clergy existed. Its claims about one creator, salvation, the soul, and the moral equality of human beings gave converts reasons to form ties that could cross some inherited boundaries of lineage, locality, gender, and status. Its ban on sacrifices before ancestral tablets, however, struck at rites through which families reproduced hierarchy and officials recognized proper order. Secret meetings, unauthorized religious specialists, cross-border communication, and later European priests then supplied governments with further grounds for treating the community as an illicit association. Repression and network formation therefore drove one another. Kin sanctions and arrests pushed believers out of visible elite circles toward trusted households, mountain settlements, market routes, and relations of religious sponsorship. Books and memorized prayers allowed practice without priests. Women could host meetings, teach, carry messages, and maintain devotions within spaces less accessible to unrelated men. Lay leaders recruited and instructed others; guides moved clergy across the border; believers housed strangers because baptism created an obligation that could compete with lineage. Yet the network was never socially weightless. Converts depended on relatives, servants, tenants, and neighbors, and police learned to follow precisely those dependencies. Torture, denunciation, confiscation, and collective liability could turn a chain of trust into a chain of arrests. The best explanation is thus a feedback loop: Catholic texts and interpersonal teaching created small circles of conviction. Conflict over rites and authority exposed those circles to family discipline and state prosecution. Dispersion made the church less dependent on a few capital elites and encouraged portable, household-based practices. New sacramental and charitable obligations joined people who were not linked only by descent. Those ties enabled survival and expansion, while also giving investigators pathways to books, safe houses, catechists, and priests. Each major persecution altered the community inherited by the next; it did not merely repeat an unchanged “anti-Christian” policy. From scholarly reading to a lay church European learning reached Joseon through the Qing capital long before a Catholic missionary entered Korea. Korean members of tribute embassies encountered books, objects, and clergy in Beijing. Some late eighteenth-century scholars discussed the learning called Seohak , or Western Learning, within broader arguments over cosmology, ethics, and evidentiary scholarship. In 1784 Yi Seung-hun was baptized in Beijing and returned to a circle that included Yi Byeok and other Korean readers. They did not wait for a foreign mission to organize worship. Lay believers taught, baptized, selected leaders, and at one point improvised a clerical hierarchy before learning that Catholic canon law did not permit it. Calling this a “self-founded” or “lay-founded” church captures something important but can mislead. Chinese translations produced by Jesuits and other Catholic writers, the Beijing church, and the annual embassy route were indispensable. The new community was Korean-led, not untouched by transnational institutions. Its early recruits were also not a representative cross-section of Joseon. Literate men from interconnected families supplied access to books and argument. Their social capital accelerated diffusion, while factional association—especially with branches of the Southerners ( Namin )—made religious affiliation usable in court politics. The medium soon widened the audience. Oral teaching, vernacular prayer, and Korean-script texts reduced dependence on classical-Chinese literacy. Jeong Yak-jong's Jugyo yoji ( Essentials of the Lord's Teaching ) explained doctrine in Korean and became one of the works on which believers relied after 1801. A text was not a mass medium by itself: manuscripts and printed copies required money, copying, custody, readers, and teachers. But a portable book could outlive an executed leader and travel farther than an elite discussion circle. Repeated reading and memorization gave a household a small ritual archive that police could seize but not wholly eradicate. Why ancestral rites became a political fault line In 1790 the bishop of Beijing communicated Rome's prohibition on Catholic participation in ancestral sacrifices. The resulting crisis was not adequately described as private freedom of belief versus superstition. In Joseon, rites before ancestral tablets expressed filial duty, organized descent, distinguished legitimate lines, and connected household morality to state orthodoxy. Elite officeholders were evaluated as sons and ritual actors as well as administrators. Refusal could deprive kin of expected service and publicly suggest that canonical teaching was false. The 1791 Jinsan incident made the conflict concrete. Yun Ji-chung did not perform the prescribed rites after his mother's death and, with his cousin Gwon Sang-yeon, was implicated in destroying or setting aside the ancestral tablet. Both were executed. The affair divided the early circle. Some renounced Catholicism or tried to separate its moral teachings from prohibited practice; others treated obedience to the church as binding even against lineage demands. The episode exposed a mechanism that recurred: conversion was discovered at funerals, feast days, and memorial observances because nonparticipation could not remain purely inward. Ritual conflict was central, but it was not the sole cause of every persecution. Officials also used older legal categories for heterodox teaching, illicit gatherings, deceptive specialists, and offenses against hierarchy. Governments feared uncontrolled associations because teaching, money, travel, and loyalty could circulate outside registered institutions. The arrival of foreign clergy added violations of border and residence controls. In the age of Western gunboats, Catholic connections could appear inseparable from imperial coercion. Different regencies and court coalitions combined these concerns in different proportions. Nor did Catholic life abolish Confucian family feeling. Martyr narratives often represented filial affection, loyalty, chastity, courage, and posthumous honor through a vocabulary intelligible to Joseon readers. Converts could reject sacrifice while caring intensely about parents and kin. The conflict rearranged ritual obligation; it did not make believers socially detached individuals. 1801: factional purge, institutional destruction, and dispersal The Sinyu persecution of 1801 followed King Jeongjo's death and the accession of the child Sunjo under Queen Dowager Jeongsun's regency. The political fall of Southerner rivals and a campaign against Catholic teaching overlapped. Officials arrested leaders, searched for books, demanded apostasy, executed some believers, and exiled or punished others. Zhou Wenmo, the Chinese priest secretly in Korea since 1794, surrendered and was executed. Jeong Yak-jong was executed; other members of the extended Jeong family met death, exile, or lasting suspicion. The repression removed a great part of the capital leadership and interrupted translation and instruction. Hwang Sa-yeong's Silk Letter intensified the political meaning assigned to foreign connection. Hiding after the arrests, Hwang wrote an extensive report intended for the bishop of Beijing. It catalogued suffering and proposed extraordinary means of external rescue, including pressure by Western power. The letter was intercepted, Hwang was executed, and the court could present the document as evidence that Catholic allegiance endangered sovereignty. It would be wrong to make Hwang's proposals the secret program of all believers; a desperate individual's undelivered appeal was not a collective platform. It would be equally wrong to dismiss its effect. The state possessed a text that connected a clandestine domestic church to imagined foreign intervention. The surviving documentation requires source criticism. Interrogation records preserve names, routes, meetings, books, kin relations, and statements that may be unavailable elsewhere. They were created to convict. Answers were elicited under unequal and often violent conditions; scribes regularized speech into legal formulas; suspects minimized, redirected blame, recanted, or adopted the language of martyrdom. Later church compilations preserve indispensable testimony too, but their questions favored perseverance, sanctity, and sacramental correctness. A name appearing in both a judicial dossier and a beatification inquiry is not automatically an unmediated voice. The convergence can establish events while the framing of motive remains contested. The institutional effect of 1801 was paradoxical. The loss of concentrated leadership and priestly access damaged catechesis and sacramental life. It also dispersed survivors. Some moved into remote communities or joined older pockets of believers away from Seoul. A church embedded in a few prominent networks became harder to eliminate as it spread among commoners and socially marginal households. This was not persecution “causing growth” in a mechanical sense: executions, apostasy, fear, and lost books reduced the community. Rather, those who persisted developed forms of organization compatible with illegality. What made a clandestine community work The household was both refuge and danger. A trusted home could conceal a prayer meeting, catechism, traveling teacher, or priest. Marriage and kinship could join Catholic clusters across villages. Widows and unmarried women sometimes possessed more room than wives under a husband's ritual authority, though their economic vulnerability was greater. Female believers could instruct children and other women, prepare candidates, sustain common prayer, offer lodging, and transmit messages. The prominence of women in martyr records is evidence of agency, but also of the church's later selection of exemplary lives; it does not by itself yield a demographic census. Religious kinship supplemented descent. Baptismal names placed believers in a sacred history, while godparent-like sponsorship, instruction, confession, communion, and care for imprisoned members generated duties beyond the lineage. Catholics sometimes called one another siblings in faith. Teaching that all people shared a creator could challenge claims that moral or spiritual worth followed hereditary rank. People of lower status and women could become respected teachers or martyrs. Yet equality needs careful qualification. A universal soul did not automatically dissolve slavery, patriarchy, elite manners, or economic dependence. Literate men retained advantages in correspondence and leadership; priests later introduced another male hierarchy. Converts carried status expectations into Catholic communities even when doctrine made those expectations debatable. The new network crossed and bent social boundaries more often than it erased them. Material practices held it together. Catechisms, calendars, rosaries, sacred images, copied prayers, and memorized formulas standardized belief across distance. Couriers and guides connected villages to Beijing and, after 1836, to clandestine French missionaries. Contributions supported journeys, clergy, prisoners, and bereaved households. Markets and ordinary travel could mask religious movement. Remote settlements offered concealment but also exposed believers to poverty and denunciation. No single secret organization commanded the entire community; it was a layered web with strong local clusters and fragile long-distance bridges. These same mechanisms explain police success. Authorities seized addressable objects and questioned owners about their provenance. A captured guide exposed safe houses; a household head's arrest endangered dependents; a relative could be punished or pressured to denounce. Officials mapped affiliation through social questions long before “network analysis” existed: Who taught you? Who baptized you? Where did you meet the priest? Who kept the book? Persecution targeted relationships, not abstract belief alone. 1839 and 1846: a transnational church under regency politics After years without resident clergy, lay Catholics repeatedly sought priests through Beijing and Macao. Rome created the Apostolic Vicariate of Korea in 1831 and entrusted it to the Paris Foreign Missions Society. French missionaries entered secretly beginning in 1836, aided by Korean guides and safe houses. This changed Catholic organization. Priests supplied sacraments, trained leaders, counted adherents, corresponded abroad, and linked local communities to a global hierarchy. It also made the church more visibly transgressive of Joseon's border regime. The Gihae persecution of 1839 occurred amid a court struggle associated with the regency of the Andong Kim clan and the growing influence of the Pungyang Jo clan. Authorities arrested believers and executed three French missionaries—Bishop Laurent Imbert and priests Pierre Maubant and Jacques Chastan—along with Korean Catholics. The records show investigators moving through chains of hosts, catechists, relatives, and intermediaries. They also show that arrest did not produce one response: some confessed faith, some apostatized, some evaded, and some supplied information. Martyrdom is central to Catholic memory, but survival through compromise and flight was at least as important to the community's continuation. The Byeongo persecution of 1846 was smaller and belongs to a distinct political moment. Its best-known victim, Kim Taegon, had been ordained in Shanghai in 1845 as the first Korean Catholic priest. His work included navigating a maritime entry route for missionaries. Arrest therefore joined priestly identity to illegal mobility and foreign contact. Kim's execution and the killing of other believers again deprived the church of scarce personnel, while letters and testimony carried their stories abroad. The interval between 1839 and 1846, and the two decades before 1866, matters: persecution varied with court conditions and enforcement rather than operating at a constant intensity. 1866: security crisis and mass repression The Byeongin persecution began under the regency of Heungseon Daewongun early in King Gojong's reign. By then the international context had changed sharply. British and French forces had occupied Beijing in 1860; Russia pressed in Northeast Asia; missionaries' presence demonstrated that borders could be crossed; and the Taiping civil war made heterodox Christianity appear politically explosive even though Taiping religion was not Catholicism. Some Korean Catholics explored whether French missionaries could help mediate against Russia. When that possibility collapsed, the contact could look like proof of precisely the foreign entanglement officials feared. Authorities executed nine of the twelve French missionaries then in Korea and killed large numbers of Korean believers over a campaign that continued beyond its opening year. Exact totals remain uncertain and confessional estimates should not be treated as a complete state census. The scale, geographic reach, and duration nevertheless distinguished Byeongin from 1846. Arrests devastated communities, drove survivors into hiding and migration, and reinforced a Catholic geography of remote villages and refuges. Repression also became entangled with imperial violence. Missionary Félix-Clair Ridel escaped and reported the executions in China. A French naval expedition attacked Ganghwa later in 1866. As [[Foreign incursions before the opening of Korea]] emphasizes, the expedition followed the Catholic executions, not the General Sherman incident. French retaliation did not rescue the church. It validated official claims that foreign priests might bring foreign cannon, while subjecting Koreans to an unauthorized coercive response they did not collectively request. Hwang Sa-yeong's imagined rescue of 1801 and the expedition of 1866 were different events, but later memory could join them into a powerful suspicion. Persecution changed the church it failed to destroy Joseon's anti-Catholic campaigns succeeded in killing leaders, interrupting sacraments, destroying texts, inducing apostasy, impoverishing families, and restricting public organization. Survival should not be romanticized as victory. The costs fell unevenly: people without resources to flee or purchase help were exposed; dependents suffered for a household member's choices; denunciation fractured trust. A martyr-centered narrative can obscure those who recanted under torture, practiced intermittently, protected relatives by silence, or left no heroic dossier. But suppression did not restore the social world that preceded Catholicism. It helped produce a decentralized religious repertoire: household worship, lay catechesis, memorized prayer, clandestine hospitality, border guides, and support for prisoners and refugees. Successive losses transferred authority to new people and places. Women and lower-status converts did not become socially equal, yet the community gave some of them roles and sacred prestige unavailable through examination office or agnatic ritual. The church's global ties furnished resources and clergy, while repeatedly exposing it to plausible charges of illegal foreign connection. The causal lesson is broader than a story of tolerant ideas defeating an intolerant state. Joseon's government policed ritual because family order, political loyalty, and cosmic legitimacy were institutionally connected. Catholics formed alternative ties because doctrine required shared practice, not merely private assent. Persecution made those ties costly and clandestine; clandestinity made them resilient in some places and vulnerable in others. By the treaties of the 1880s, formal diplomatic relations and foreign pressure changed the legal setting, and toleration emerged unevenly rather than through a single decree. The communities that entered that new era had been remade by a century of selective violence. Why this matters This history explains why religion belongs inside, not beside, Joseon social and political history. The ancestral-rites dispute reveals how household practices constituted governance. Catholic books reveal that intellectual exchange could generate institutions without conquest or a resident mission. Persecution records expose the reach and limits of the state at village and household scale. The church's survival shows how networks can become robust through dispersal while remaining vulnerable at their bridges. It also complicates nationalist and confessional stories. Catholicism was neither simply a Western implant nor simply an indigenous democratic movement. Korean actors selected, translated, debated, and organized it; they also sought foreign clergy and sometimes foreign protection. The state was neither reacting to pure fantasy nor confronting a unified conspiracy. Real border violations and imperial danger were interpreted through court rivalry, ritual orthodoxy, and sweeping collective suspicion. Martyr archives preserve courage and community, but they are advocacy archives as well as historical evidence. Judicial archives preserve social relations, but through coercive categories. Reading them against one another makes the network visible without turning testimony into transparent fact.
