surviving explanations come through male leaders and later compilation? Which lines in the surviving scriptures can be securely dated to Choe's lifetime, and where did oral transmission or Haewol's editorial work shape the canon? How did local jeop organization vary by region before the large petition movements of 1892–1893? At what points did anti-Catholic language become anti-Western or anti-Japanese political action, and when is later nationalism being projected backward? How should historians translate gi , sicheonju , and gaebyeok without forcing them into either Christian theological or secular revolutionary categories?

title: Factional politics as institution rather than pathology
deck: Joseon factions were durable coalitions built through offices, scholarly reputations, recruitment, and kinship; they could discipline power and organize policy as well as monopolize posts and turn defeat into purge.
headings: The wrong question: why were Koreans so factional?
Recruitment turned learning into political capital
Purges were personnel actions with expanding stakes
Kinship helped coalitions endure, but did not determine them
Coalition durability came from repeated games and moral memory
From colonial pathology to institutional history
text: Joseon factions were durable coalitions built through offices, scholarly reputations, recruitment, and kinship; they could discipline power and organize policy as well as monopolize posts and turn defeat into purge. Up: [[Korean history (MOC)]] Related: [[The gwageo examination system in practice]] · [[Patrilineal transformation of the Joseon family]] · [[Local magistrates, clerks, and yangban power]] · [[Joseon land taxation from gwajeon to daedong]] · [[The Manchu invasions and Joseon's place in the Qing order]] The wrong question: why were Koreans so factional? Accounts of Joseon politics often become a procession of named camps— Sarim , Easterners, Westerners, Southerners, Northerners, Old Doctrine and Young Doctrine—followed by exiles and executions. Read that way, factionalism looks like a national vice or an inexplicable preference for doctrinal quarrels over government. The framing is misleading. It treats a political outcome as a cultural personality and strips away the institutions that made coalitions both necessary and visible. Joseon had no legally recognized parties, electoral constituencies, or cabinet responsible to a parliament. It did have a monarch, a highly literate civil bureaucracy, a small number of prestigious offices, formal organs of criticism, regular personnel evaluation, examinations and recommendations, royal lectures, and a political language in which the fitness of a policy was tied to the moral fitness of its advocate. Officials who wanted a proposal adopted, a colleague protected, or a successor promoted therefore needed allies inside a common arena. Those allies were connected by teachers, exam cohorts, service together, marriage, descent, native place, academies, memorial associations, and agreement on particular controversies. A bungdang was not simply a modern party under another name. It was a coalition inside the official and literati order, without a separate legal personality, permanent membership roll, mass electorate, or assured right to opposition. This distinction changes the explanatory task. The question is not whether factional conflict was “good” or “bad.” It is how Joseon's personnel and speech institutions converted networks into governing coalitions; why some coalitions survived exclusion from court; why moral disagreement could become a contest over appointments; and under what conditions competition became reciprocal criticism, winner-take-all displacement, or lethal purge. Offices made organized disagreement consequential At the center stood the king, but royal government did not mean that every decision was a private royal act. The State Council deliberated on major affairs; the Six Ministries administered personnel, taxation, rites, war, justice, and public works; the Royal Secretariat transmitted commands and memorials; specialized offices gathered information and executed policy. Officials obtained leverage from the jurisdiction and documentary routines of the posts they occupied. Control of a ministry mattered differently from access to the king's lectures or the power to challenge an appointment. Especially important were the institutions conventionally grouped as the Three Offices. The Office of the Inspector-General ( Sahonbu ) investigated official misconduct and guarded bureaucratic discipline. The Office of Censors or Censorate ( Saganwon ) remonstrated with the king and criticized policy. The Office of Special Advisers ( Hongmungwan ) kept books, drafted learned texts, advised the monarch, and participated in royal lectures; its scholarly authority gave its officials a platform for political speech. Boundaries and titles changed across the dynasty, and “Three Offices” should not imply a modern separated branch of government. Together, however, these offices institutionalized an unusual capacity: relatively junior literati in authorized roles could speak against senior ministers, personnel choices, and sometimes the king. Two practices made this more than advice. In remonstrance, officials framed criticism as loyal correction: because a ruler needed to cultivate judgment and hear unwelcome truth, silence could itself be disloyal. In personnel review, censorial officials could object to an appointment on grounds of character, reputation, procedure, or conflict. The precise force of an objection depended on period and circumstance; it was not an absolute constitutional veto. Yet repeated objections could delay an appointment, damage a career, force a royal response, and publicly define the issue recorded in court documents. The system rewarded coordination. A lone memorial could be dismissed as eccentric or self-interested. Convergent memorials from offices charged with public criticism carried institutional weight. Conversely, a king or senior coalition could neutralize critics by transferring, demoting, exiling, or prosecuting them and by installing more congenial officials. Personnel control and policy control therefore reinforced each other. A faction did not merely seek office because office brought private reward. It sought offices because occupants decided which allegations entered the record, which nominees were obstructed, which precedents were cited, and which policy acquired the appearance of a learned consensus. Royal lectures added another arena. They joined classical exposition to current affairs and brought selected scholar-officials into repeated contact with the king. The language was moral and historical rather than programmatic in a modern party sense, but that did not make it ornamental. An interpretation of proper kingship could justify scrutiny of favorites, restraint in punishment, a ritual decision, or a new personnel balance. Because political argument claimed to identify impartial principle, opponents rarely described themselves as one interested group among others. Each side was tempted to call its network the community of upright scholars and the rival network a selfish clique. Recruitment turned learning into political capital The civil examinations supplied a prestigious route into service but never allocated careers mechanically. Eligibility and preparation were socially unequal; the number of graduates exceeded desirable openings; protected appointment, recommendation, irregular examinations, family reputation, and royal favor coexisted with tested achievement. After entry, an official still needed postings, evaluation, promotion, and protection. As [[The gwageo examination system in practice]] shows, selection occurred repeatedly rather than at one meritocratic gate. That structure made relationships productive without making examination performance fictitious. A teacher could identify talented pupils and transmit an interpretive lineage. A successful senior official could recommend men whose scholarship and character he trusted. Men examined in the same cohort or employed in the same bureau acquired shared experience. A junior official's public defense of a censured teacher might display conviction while also locating him within a network. The resulting tie could be intellectual, affective, strategic, and material at once. Reducing it to “ideas” misses patronage; reducing it to patronage assumes that ideas never constrained conduct. The rise of Sarim scholar-officials illustrates this interaction. The term referred broadly to a “forest of scholars,” especially literati who cultivated claims to moral learning and local scholarly standing, not to a single disciplined party with continuous command. From the later fifteenth and sixteenth centuries, men associated with such networks increasingly entered the central bureaucracy, especially speech and advisory posts, and challenged established merit subjects and powerful officeholders often labeled Hungu . The familiar story of virtuous provincial scholars replacing corrupt capital grandees captures the actors' moral geography better than it maps two coherent social classes. Both categories contained officeholding families, and their boundaries shifted. What changed was partly the weight of new recruitment and reputational networks within the institutions of court. By the later sixteenth century, competition among literati no longer centered on a simple Sarim–Hungu opposition. The Easterners and Westerners emerged around a personnel dispute in 1575 and wider alignments among officials, teachers, and associates. Later divisions produced Southerners and Northerners, and eventually Old Doctrine ( Noron ) and Young Doctrine ( Soron ) within the Westerners. Names should not deceive: “east” and “west” initially referred to residences associated with protagonists, not stable geopolitical platforms. Splits often outlived their triggering controversy because a verdict affected careers, honor, and the status of teachers and the dead. Once an official had signed a memorial, prosecuted an opponent, or defended a condemned scholar, reversal could threaten his credibility and allies. Purges were personnel actions with expanding stakes The literati purges of 1498, 1504, 1519, and 1545 preceded the mature bungdang alignments but exposed the same institutional danger: criticism, historical writing, succession, royal affinity, and appointments could be fused into a criminal case. Purge was not simply a debate becoming rude. It involved the machinery of the state—interrogation, legal classification, confiscation, exile, execution, and sometimes retrospective punishment or rehabilitation. The 1498 purge, for example, turned an allegedly disloyal passage associated with Kim Jong-jik and recorded by his disciple Kim Il-son into a prosecution reaching through a scholarly network. Under Jungjong, Jo Gwang-jo's rapid promotion and reform program ended in the 1519 purge when royal confidence collapsed and opponents framed his coalition as dangerously exclusive. Two cautions follow. First, it is too simple to say that kings merely watched factions destroy one another. Monarchs selected officials, exploited counterweights, authorized punishments, and sometimes used attacks on censorial or scholarly groups to recover room for action. A purge could be a royal strategy against an institutional challenge as well as victory by one elite network. Second, a purge did not erase a coalition. Exile dispersed adherents but could preserve identity. Students maintained a teacher's texts; descendants sought restoration; local scholars commemorated the condemned; later governments reversed verdicts and bestowed posthumous honors. Martyrdom created moral capital that survivors could not have manufactured as easily in office. Later “changes of government” ( hwanguk ) under Sukjong demonstrate the destructive potential of a court in which factional alternation was not protected. In 1680, 1689, and 1694, sharp reversals displaced governing groups and brought executions, exile, and rehabilitation. Disputes over royal marriage, succession, and the status of consorts were not court gossip detached from institutions: designation of an heir determined the future source of favor, while ritual and legitimacy arguments gave officials grounds to intervene. But narrating these episodes through personalities alone conceals the mechanism. A new royal decision changed appointments; new officeholders reopened the conduct of predecessors; legal punishment made the personnel reversal harder to undo; and each side accumulated injuries that raised the price of coexistence. Kinship helped coalitions endure, but did not determine them Joseon political society became increasingly patrilineal over the dynasty. Elite descent groups compiled genealogies, concentrated ritual around male lines, maintained ancestral sites, arranged marriages, and developed durable local seats. These changes, treated in [[Patrilineal transformation of the Joseon family]], gave political networks memory and resources beyond an individual's career. A punished official's sons, nephews, affines, and disciples could preserve documents, pursue rehabilitation, or avoid a compromised alliance. Marriage connected officeholding houses, while a distinguished ancestor and record of examination success strengthened claims to standing. Kinship was nevertheless neither a complete faction map nor an automatic command structure. Large descent groups contained branches of unequal wealth and divergent politics. Affinal ties crossed factional lines. Officials sometimes broke with relatives or teachers over succession, ritual, diplomacy, or strategy. A lineage name could conceal different local bases, and later genealogies could tidy relationships that had once been uncertain. It is safer to treat descent and marriage as channels through which trust, resources, liability, and memory traveled. They made some coalitions cheaper to maintain and some betrayals more costly; they did not generate a political position by themselves. Private academies ( seowon ), local schools, community compacts, and shrine associations also connected central contests to provincial society. An academy educated students and honored selected sages; royal charters and tax privileges could enhance its authority. Scholars gathered around teachers and texts, communicated judgments about public men, and mobilized memorials. A faction excluded from central posts could thus retain a provincial audience and recruit a later generation. Yet no equation—academy equals factional branch office—is adequate. Academies had educational, ritual, economic, and local-status functions, and neighboring elite families could contest their control. Their political importance lay precisely in joining these functions. Coalition durability came from repeated games and moral memory Several mechanisms explain why factions lasted despite lacking formal membership. First, government was a repeated personnel game. Today's junior censor might become tomorrow's minister, examiner, or recommender; a coalition benefited from cultivating careers over decades. Second, Joseon's documentary culture preserved positions. Memorials, verdicts, biographies, genealogies, collected writings, and eventually the Veritable Records made it difficult to pretend that a consequential stand had never occurred. Third, Confucian commemoration extended politics across death. Decisions about posthumous title, shrine inclusion, or rehabilitation altered the moral genealogy claimed by living scholars. Fourth, exclusion sometimes strengthened boundaries. When one group monopolized desirable posts, outsiders had incentives to coordinate rather than defect individually. When rulers tried “impartiality” or tangpyeong policies, they did more than ask officials to be nicer. Yeongjo and Jeongjo sought to manage recruitment across factional divisions, distinguish legitimate principle from selfish party adherence, and restore royal control over personnel. Such balancing could broaden appointments and reduce retaliatory swings, but it also let the monarch define acceptable factional identity. It did not abolish networks or make all appointments neutral. Coalitions could also decay. Leaders died; disciples disagreed about the proper inheritance; policy shocks split allies; a long spell out of office weakened access to posts; and royal patronage elevated new intermediaries. The Northerners' association with Gwanghaegun's government made the 1623 coup especially devastating to them. The Westerners subsequently divided, while Southerners sometimes returned but did not regain equivalent central dominance after later reversals. By the nineteenth century, politics is often described through sedo or in-law government: a narrow set of affinal houses secured extraordinary access around young or weak monarchs. This was not the sudden replacement of institutions by family. It was a changed concentration within the same ecology of royal access, appointments, examination prestige, and kinship, with fewer effective counterweights. Who bore the costs? Most named faction members were male civil literati. That fact reflects both the distribution of formal office and the archive's categories, not the social boundary of political consequence. Purge could affect households through execution, exile, confiscation, blocked careers, and inherited stigma. Wives and other kin managed displaced households, property, ritual continuity, petitions, and marriage prospects, but court-centered records often make this labor visible only indirectly. Royal and elite women could be pivotal in succession and affinity politics while being represented through moralized accounts written by male officials. Provincial elite families gained or lost access to offices, academies, charters, and central patrons. Local rivals could translate a court verdict into control of a shrine, school, register, or community compact. Commoners, nobi , clerks, soldiers, merchants, and tenants rarely belonged to a bungdang in the same sense, yet factional governments made fiscal, military, legal, and relief policy that affected them. Competition could open investigation of a corrupt administrator; it could also paralyze appointments, protect an ally, or make local disputes more punitive. A general claim that “factionalism harmed the people” proves little unless linked to a particular decision and its enforcement. Social incidence therefore has to be traced policy by policy. The long debate over the Uniform Land Tax Law ( Daedongbeop ), for example, involved factional sponsorship but also regional transport, procurement, landholding, official finance, and contractor interests. [[Joseon land taxation from gwajeon to daedong]] shows why labeling one camp reformist and another conservative is insufficient. Coalition alignment affected whether a proposal reached office and survived turnover; it did not supply every participant with the same motive or determine implementation in every province. From colonial pathology to institutional history Factionalism acquired unusually heavy historiographical baggage. Late-Joseon critics themselves condemned selfish party spirit, so the pathology thesis was not invented from nothing. In the colonial period, however, Japanese scholarship and official ideology made endemic factional strife one sign that Koreans were supposedly incapable of autonomous, progressive government. A court-centered sequence of quarrels could then stand for the character of an entire people and help rationalize colonial rule. Some post-liberation narratives retained a moralized “national weakness” even while reversing the political judgment. Later scholarship has complicated that inheritance in several ways. Institutional history reconstructs the censorial, personnel, and monarchical structures that made alignment rational. Social history connects central officials to marriage, descent, local education, land, and status. Intellectual history takes ritual and classical argument seriously without accepting participants' declarations of pure principle at face value. Political history restores royal agency and shows that the balance changed by reign and crisis. Quantitative work on examination rosters, marriage, officeholding, and genealogies can test whether alleged groups actually clustered, although the survival and construction of those records introduce their own bias. Calling factional politics an institution does not mean celebrating it or claiming it was formally designed as a party system. “Institution” here means a recurring set of rules, offices, expectations, and relationships that structured action. It directs attention to variation. Censorial opposition could improve information or become coordinated obstruction. Coalition continuity could sustain a policy or enforce exclusion. Moral accountability could restrain a king or turn disagreement into a contest over the opponent's character. Purges were not the essence of all Joseon politics, but they were a recurrent possibility when institutional criticism, personnel monopoly, royal insecurity, and criminal sanction aligned. How to read the sources The Joseon wangjo sillok is indispensable for memorials, appointments, arguments, and chronological sequence. It is not a stenographic transcript or a neutral window into faction membership. Historiographers compiled reign records after a monarch's death from daily records and other documents; compilers worked within later political conditions. Recorded speech is selected and formalized. An accusation that someone formed a “party” is evidence that the accusation was politically available, not automatic proof of a bounded organization. The Seungjeongwon ilgi , diaries of the Royal Secretariat, can supply denser daily proceedings for the surviving later period. Official codes describe jurisdictions and authorized procedure, but repetition of a rule may disclose enforcement difficulty rather than compliance. Collected writings, letters, academy records, genealogies, and epitaphs reveal networks omitted by central annals, while also commemorating authors and ancestors selectively. Purge narratives and posthumous biographies are often written by beneficiaries of rehabilitation. Genealogies can clarify descent and marriage but may incorporate later corrections, exclusions, or prestigious inventions. A defensible analysis therefore separates at least four claims: an actor used a factional label; contemporaries coordinated on an appointment or memorial; a durable relationship connected named people across episodes; and those people shared a policy or philosophical position. These propositions often overlap, but none proves all the others. Network evidence should be dated, not projected backward from a later split. Most importantly, court evidence should not be made to represent society without local, fiscal, legal, and household evidence. That discipline replaces gossip with institutional explanation while preserving the coercion, inequality, and contingency of the politics itself. Academy of Korean Studies, Hongmungwan , institutional reference on the advisory and scholarly office and its place among the Three Offices. Academy of Korean Studies, Government organization ( gwanje ) , institutional reference on Joseon central offices and direct royal organs. James B. Palais, Politics and Policy in Traditional Korea (Harvard University Asia Center, 1975), a foundational study of late-Joseon court politics, faction, and policy; Harvard catalog record . Martina Deuchler, The Confucian Transformation of Korea: A Study of Society and Ideology (Harvard University Asia Center, 1992), on the construction of patrilineal elite society; publisher record . John B. Duncan, The Origins of the Chosŏn Dynasty (University of Washington Press, 2000), on elite continuity and institutional formation; publisher record . Donghyeok Choi and ChangHwan Kim, “Meritocracy with Multiple Rules: How Special Civil Service Examinations Reproduced Privilege in Joseon Korea” , Social Science History (2026), quantitative analysis of examination routes and elite reproduction. Sun Joo Kim, “Inventing Ancestors and Limited Empiricism in Chosŏn Korea” , Comparative Studies in Society and History 66, no. 2 (2024), on genealogy, patrilineal competition, and evidentiary limits. Henry H. Em, The Great Enterprise: Sovereignty and Historiography in Modern Korea , Duke University Press, 2013 — colonial knowledge, national historiography, and the stakes of historical “pathology” claims. Paek Chol, “King Yŏngjo's T'angp'yŏng Policy and Its Orientation” , International Journal of Korean History 16, no. 1 (2011), on royal management of factional balance. Open questions How closely do officeholding and marriage-network reconstructions match the faction labels used in memorials for each reign? When did local academy affiliation predict central alignment, and where did local rivalries cut across court factions? Which fiscal and military policies survived changes of governing coalition, and what protected them from reversal? How did women in exiled or rehabilitated households preserve political memory in sources not organized around formal office?

title: Forced labor and wartime mobilization
deck: Japan's wartime mobilization of Koreans was not one undifferentiated roundup: between 1937 and 1945 colonial authorities and firms escalated from pressured recruitment through state allocation to formal labor conscription, embedding coercion in law, police power, company discipline, debt, wage withholding, and the impossibility of freely leaving dangerous work.
headings: From labor shortage to escalating compulsion
text: Japan's wartime mobilization of Koreans was not one undifferentiated roundup: between 1937 and 1945 colonial authorities and firms escalated from pressured recruitment through state allocation to formal labor conscription, embedding coercion in law, police power, company discipline, debt, wage withholding, and the impossibility of freely leaving dangerous work. Up: [[Korean history (MOC)]] Related: [[Colonial Korea's changing administrative regimes]] · [[Korean migration within the Japanese empire]] · [[Military sexual slavery and the comfort women system]] · [[Liberation and the end of colonial rule in Korea]] What the terms do—and conceal “Wartime mobilization” is the broadest useful category. It includes industrial labor, military service, military civilian work, student and women's labor, savings and material drives, and the unpaid work demanded within Korea as well as movements to Japan, Sakhalin, Manchuria, the Pacific, and other war zones. “Forced mobilization” emphasizes that these programs operated under an unrepresentative colonial state whose officials could use police, schools, neighborhood bodies, rationing, and punishment. “Forced labor” asks a narrower question about the work relation: could a person give meaningful consent, refuse placement, leave, receive the promised pay, and live without violence or confinement? The distinctions matter. Long before 1939, Koreans crossed to Japan for wages, and ordinary migration continued during the war. A worker might initially respond to an advertised job yet encounter deception, confinement, withheld savings, or violence after arrival. Conversely, the formal legal category chōyō (labor requisition or conscription) applied only late in the war. Restricting “forced labor” to people drafted under that final ordinance mistakes a bureaucratic label for an account of freedom. Calling every Korean resident of wartime Japan a deportee erases both earlier migration and workers' varied trajectories. The historical task is to reconstruct the channel, the pressures at departure, and the conditions at the destination rather than infer experience from one aggregate number. This is also a legal and diplomatic vocabulary dispute. Imperial documents represented Koreans as Japanese subjects owing labor to a national emergency. Japan's postwar government stresses legal equivalence and the 1965 claims settlement. South Korean courts have treated Japan's colonial rule as incompatible with the Republic of Korea's constitutional order and have distinguished damages for illegal colonial forced labor from ordinary property claims. The International Labour Organization's supervisory committee concluded that the wartime mass conscription of Koreans and other Asians for private industry under deplorable conditions violated the Forced Labour Convention. These are not interchangeable judgments, but none makes close historical description unnecessary. From labor shortage to escalating compulsion The causal setting was total war. Japan's war in China after 1937, expansion across Asia and the Pacific after 1941, and military conscription removed Japanese men from mines, construction, transport, and heavy industry. The 1938 National General Mobilization Law gave the state sweeping powers over labor and production. Colonial Korea supplied food, savings, soldiers, civilian auxiliaries, and workers while remaining politically subordinated. Administrative capacity built during earlier colonial decades—household registers, police stations, village offices, schools, railways, and cooperating associations—made bodies legible and movable. Historians commonly distinguish three Japan-bound labor channels, although dates differ slightly by implementation and source: Company “recruitment” ( boshū ), from 1939 to early 1942. Japanese firms recruited allotted numbers with authorization and active assistance from the Government-General of Korea, local officials, police, and brokers. The paper form could appear voluntary. In practice, misleading promises, official pressure, economic distress, intimidation, and village-level quotas narrowed refusal. Authorities sought to prevent local resistance and deliver groups intact. The coercion did not begin only if a policeman physically seized someone; state-backed recruitment and deception could produce an unfree journey. Official mediation or allocation ( kan assen ), roughly February 1942 to September 1944. Government offices took a more direct role in selecting and assigning workers to firms. Local administrations received quotas and organized collection, transport, and surveillance. The distinction between a corporate recruiter and the colonial state became thinner because firms' manpower demands moved through administrative command. Formal requisition ( chōyō ), from September 1944 to surrender in August 1945. The National Labor Conscription framework was extended fully to Koreans. Orders now expressed legal duty openly; refusal could bring punishment. Yet the short formal phase does not mean coercive mobilization began only in 1944. It marks an escalation and juridical clarification of a system already restricting choice. These channels overlapped with military mobilization. Koreans entered the Japanese army first through a volunteer system for men from 1938 and through conscription implemented in 1944; naval volunteering began later. Others served as military civilian employees, guards, porters, and laborers. Because official datasets classified laborers, soldiers, sailors, and civilian auxiliaries differently, totals cannot safely be combined without identifying the denominator. A state–corporate labor regime The system joined public coercion to private production. Ministries and the Government-General planned allocations; provincial, county, township, and police personnel identified and assembled people; transport networks moved groups; and mines, construction contractors, shipyards, steelworks, and munitions firms put them to work. The Korea Labor Association and state-controlled Kyōwakai organizations helped administer, discipline, and assimilate Korean workers. Large conglomerates including Mitsui, Mitsubishi, and Sumitomo were prominent, but thousands of sites and subcontracting relationships make responsibility broader than a few famous corporations. At the worksite, compulsion took material forms. Managers commonly housed Koreans in segregated dormitories, monitored movement, imposed long shifts and hazardous tasks, and punished disobedience. Deductions for food, lodging, compulsory savings, family remittances, and other charges could consume wages. Promised savings or pay were sometimes withheld and never recovered. Violence, inadequate food, disease, industrial accidents, and poor medical care appear repeatedly in survivor testimony and police or company records. Conditions varied by site and period; variation does not cancel the structure. A worker paid some wages could still be forced, and a nominal contract could coexist with confinement and assault. Escape is especially revealing. Wartime records show high rates of flight from some mines and companies. Escape demonstrates agency and the porousness of control, not free employment. Workers risked arrest and punishment, and escapees depended on Korean communities, brokers, or irregular jobs to disappear. The combination of repeated flight and efforts to prevent it is evidence that many placements could not retain labor on ordinary contractual terms. Geography and unequal danger Mobilization began in Korean villages and cities but its geography was imperial. Many people worked inside Korea on mines, railways, airfields, military construction, factories, and local labor details. Others crossed through Busan and Shimonoseki into Japan. Coalfields in Kyushu and Hokkaido absorbed large numbers; workers also entered mines on Hashima and Sado, steel and shipbuilding centers, dams, tunnels, ports, and military installations. Specialist research finds Korean miners concentrated in particularly dangerous and labor-intensive sectors. Educational and class differences could influence placement: people with schooling had better chances of factory or clerical work, while poor rural men were disproportionately sent to mines and heavy construction. Still others went beyond metropolitan Japan. Karafuto/Sakhalin coal and industrial sites left Korean communities stranded when Soviet occupation and the collapse of the Japanese empire disrupted repatriation. Military labor took Koreans to Manchuria, Southeast Asia, and Pacific islands. Death could occur at work, under bombing, at sea, during the atomic bombings, or in the chaotic return after surrender. The failure to identify and repatriate remains is therefore not a marginal afterlife of mobilization; it is evidence of how an empire moved people without creating an adequate system to account for them as persons. Scale is hard to state in one number. A South Korean fact-finding commission operating from 2004 to 2015 documented 798,043 Koreans forcibly mobilized and sent to Japan between 1939 and 1945 and identified 1,589 worksites, according to Ágota Duró and David Palmer's synthesis of the commission's work. Other widely cited archival reconstructions give lower Japan-bound labor totals, often around 670,000–725,000, because they use different categories and surviving official series. The wartime Korean population in Japan exceeded two million, but that figure includes earlier residents, families, and migrants outside organized labor mobilization. The defensible conclusion is not a false precision: several hundred thousand Koreans moved to Japan through organized wartime labor channels, while the wider number mobilized across military, labor, and geographic categories was larger. Mortality is even less certain. The commission-derived estimate that more than 10 percent of the nearly 800,000 died or went missing would imply roughly 80,000, but Duró and Palmer stress that only 9,043 deaths in Japan had been identified by name in Takeuchi Yasuto's research and that the precise total is unknown. Destroyed or incomplete records, inconsistent categories, unmarked graves, cremation, post-surrender shipwrecks, and missing repatriation data prevent a secure death count. Estimates should be labeled as estimates, never converted into identified victims. Gendered mobilization The familiar image of a male miner captures only one part of wartime extraction. Colonial policy assigned men and women different duties through gendered ideals. Men were cast as soldiers, miners, construction hands, and household providers whose labor and bodies belonged to the emperor. Women were told to become “mothers of the empire,” maintain households under rationing, join patriotic associations, collect materials and savings, support soldiers, and replace absent men in production. These unpaid and undercounted activities sustained mobilization even when a woman never left Korea. Paid and compulsory female labor also expanded. Schools, the Patriotic Women's Association and its successors, youth bodies, employers, and officials directed girls and unmarried women into factories, military-related workshops, agriculture, nursing, and other work. The Women's Volunteer Labor Corps ( Joshi Kinrō Teishintai ; Korean Yŏja Kŭnro Chŏngsindae ) was formalized late in the war, but female labor mobilization preceded the ordinance. “Volunteer” again described an official form more reliably than a free choice. Young age, teacher or police pressure, deceptive promises of schooling or training, separation from family, and withheld wages appear in litigation and survivor accounts, including cases involving Mitsubishi aircraft factories in Nagoya. The labor corps must not be collapsed into the Japanese military's “comfort women” system. The former organized industrial and other labor; the latter was a system of military sexual slavery. Korean popular memory sometimes used chŏngsindae broadly, and fear that labor recruitment could lead to sexual exploitation shaped family responses. Individual paths could involve deception and abuse, but treating the two institutions as synonyms obscures how each operated and makes both harder to document. Gender analysis should instead show their place within the same militarized colonial order while preserving distinct recruitment structures, destinations, and forms of violence. Reading survivor evidence critically Survivor testimony is indispensable because official records encode the mobilizer's categories and often omit beatings, hunger, humiliation, fear, and family rupture. Testimony explains how a “recruitment” visit felt in a village, how advertised wages changed after arrival, why someone escaped, and what unpaid savings meant to a household. It also restores names and moral claims to aggregate labor tables. Testimony is positioned evidence, not a transcript immune to criticism. Many accounts were recorded decades later, through Korean or Japanese interviewers, activist projects, compensation applications, or lawsuits. Trauma, aging, translation, public vocabulary, and the legal questions asked can shape narration. A responsible method compares testimony with rosters, wage ledgers, police reports, transport lists, company histories, graves, temple remains, local newspapers, and other survivors' accounts. Discrepancies should remain visible. They may reveal faulty memory, but also aliases, clerical erasure, corporate record destruction, or categories designed to hide coercion. Official evidence needs equal source criticism. A personnel card can establish presence without revealing whether consent was meaningful. A wage entry can record earnings while omitting forced deductions. A company history may celebrate production and silence Korean deaths. Postwar deposits of unpaid wages and savings show that money remained outstanding, but incomplete names and the gap between nominal deposit and family receipt complicate restitution. Material and forensic evidence can correct paperwork, yet cremation and poorly documented grave excavation have foreclosed identification in many cases. No source genre is self-sufficient. Liberation without settlement Japan's surrender ended colonial sovereignty but not the consequences of dispersal. Workers improvised journeys home amid transport shortages, mine and factory collapse, discrimination, violence, and shipwreck. Some remained in Japan; many Koreans in Sakhalin could not return for decades. Families searched for missing relatives, wages, savings, pension deposits, and remains. Cold War division then fractured archives and claimant communities between North Korea, South Korea, Japan, and the Soviet sphere. The 1965 Agreement on the Settlement of Problems concerning Property and Claims accompanied normalization between Japan and South Korea. Japan provided grants and loans, and Article II declared property and claims questions between the states and their nationals “settled completely and finally.” Japan argues that this disposed of compensation claims. South Korea used much of the funds for national development and later created domestic compensation programs, but the agreement was negotiated by governments, not individual survivors, and did not produce a shared account of colonial illegality or company responsibility. South Korea's Supreme Court took a different route in 2012 and final 2018 judgments against Nippon Steel and Mitsubishi Heavy Industries. It held that claims for consolation damages arising from illegal colonial rule and forced labor were not the ordinary claims extinguished by the 1965 agreement. Japanese courts and government reject that interpretation, producing a conflict between domestic judgments and Japan's treaty position rather than a simple absence of law. In 2023 the South Korean government announced a foundation-funded “third-party reimbursement” plan for successful plaintiffs, using donations from South Korean companies rather than compelled payments from the defendant Japanese firms. Some victims accepted; others rejected a plan they believed removed apology and corporate responsibility. Compensation is therefore simultaneously about material repair, legal doctrine, diplomatic management, and who has authority to settle a survivor's claim. Memory, remains, and industrial heritage Memory politics concentrates at visible sites: Hashima, Sado, Hokkaido mines, company factories, temples holding remains, and museums interpreting Japan's industrialization. When Japan's Meiji industrial sites entered UNESCO's World Heritage List in 2015, the Japanese delegation said it would explain that a large number of Koreans and others were brought against their will and forced to work under harsh conditions at some sites. Subsequent disputes asked whether exhibitions fulfilled that commitment. The disagreement is not only semantic. A display that celebrates technology while moving coercion outside the site's “relevant period” divides industrial achievement from the colonial labor that sustained its wartime operation. Local Japanese and Korean researchers, Buddhist institutions, lawyers, unions, former dormitory staff, and families have recovered rosters, excavated graves, returned some remains, and recorded testimony when states and firms did not. Their work is a historical source and a political intervention. Duró and Palmer's study of Hokkaido shows both achievements and limits: community excavation forced forgotten deaths into view, but cremation and inadequate forensic protocols made individual identification and cause-of-death findings impossible in many cases. Commemoration cannot substitute for evidence preservation. What can be concluded The strongest synthesis avoids two shortcuts. The first says only the openly compulsory 1944 requisition phase was forced, treating earlier official pressure, deception, confinement, and inability to quit as irrelevant. The second treats every Korean migration or every workplace as identical, obscuring changes over time and differences among sites. Evidence supports a staged but connected regime: colonial state power and corporate demand increasingly organized labor from 1939; coercion existed throughout the organized program but changed in legal form and intensity; destination conditions ranged widely yet repeatedly included restricted movement, hazardous work, discriminatory control, and unpaid money. It also supports a wider view than male Japan-bound labor alone. Work inside Korea, female and student mobilization, military civilian service, imperial destinations beyond Japan, household extraction, and failed repatriation belong to the history. Precise totals remain category-dependent, mortality remains underidentified, and individual experiences require site-level reconstruction. Those uncertainties are reasons to preserve archives and testimony—not reasons to retreat to the mobilizers' euphemisms. Sources Republic of Korea, National Law Information Center, Agreement on the Settlement of Problem concerning Property and Claims and the Economic Cooperation between the Republic of Korea and Japan (1965) — official treaty text and status. International Labour Organization, Committee of Experts, observation on Japan and the Forced Labour Convention — official supervisory finding on wartime industrial forced labor and Japan's treaty-settlement position. Republic of Korea Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Facts Regarding the Issue of Forced Labor — official South Korean account of the litigation and claims dispute; read as a party's position. Ágota Duró and David Palmer, “Japan's Forgotten Korean Forced Laborers: The Search for Hidden Wartime Graves in Hokkaido” , International Labor and Working-Class History 106 (2024), 311–330 — open-access specialist study of mobilization scale, death estimates, remains, and forensic limits. William Underwood, “Names, Bones and Unpaid Wages (1): Reparations for Korean Forced Labor in Japan” , Asia-Pacific Journal: Japan Focus (2006) — source-rich synthesis of the three stages, worksites, escape, unpaid wages, and redress; its figures require attention to categories. Nikolai Johnsen, “Katō Kōko's Meiji Industrial Revolution—Forgetting Forced Labor to Celebrate Japan's World Heritage Sites, Part 1” , Asia-Pacific Journal: Japan Focus (2021) — specialist analysis of coercion during “recruitment” and industrial-heritage interpretation. Derek Kramer, “‘We Go on Our Own Boats!’: Korean Migrants and the Politics of Transportation Infrastructure in the Japanese Empire” , International Review of Social History 67, no. 1 (2022), 25–52 — specialist context distinguishing prewar migration, mobility control, and wartime traffic. Lee Song-jook, “The Actual Aspect of Female Labor Mobilization in Japanese Colonial Era: Focusing on 1937–1945” , Women's Studies Review (2019) — Korean specialist study of women's organizations, students, and expanding female labor mobilization. Janice C. H. Kim, To Live to Work: Factory Women in Colonial Korea, 1910–1945 (Stanford University Press, 2009), publisher record — specialist monograph distinguishing factory women, the Women's Labor Volunteer Corps, and the gendered wartime labor regime. Open questions How do South Korean commission case files revise aggregate counts when separated by labor, military civilian, military, and women's mobilization categories? Which surviving company wage ledgers can connect postwar Japanese government deposits to named workers and actual family receipt? How different were mortality, escape, pay, and punishment across mines, construction sites, shipyards, and factories? What evidence survives for labor mobilization inside northern Korea and for claimants who later became North Korean citizens? Which remains could still be identified through modern forensic methods without repeating the destructive excavation and cremation practices documented in Hokkaido?

title: Foreign incursions before the opening of Korea
deck: The French expedition of 1866, the United States expedition of 1871, and Japanese coercion in 1875–1876 formed a connected sequence of gunboat encounters, but only the last converted battlefield pressure into a durable treaty regime.
headings: 1866: persecution, the General Sherman , and French retaliation
1871: an American military victory without a diplomatic result
From the Meiji rupture to the Un'yō incident
The Ganghwa Treaty and the sovereignty paradox
Why Japan succeeded where France and the United States did not
text: The French expedition of 1866, the United States expedition of 1871, and Japanese coercion in 1875–1876 formed a connected sequence of gunboat encounters, but only the last converted battlefield pressure into a durable treaty regime. Up: [[Korean history (MOC)]] Related: [[Markets and monetization in late Joseon]] · [[Nineteenth-century tax disorder and peasant protest]] · [[How historians periodize Korean history]] · [[Gabo Reform causal map]] The problem was not simple “isolation” Late Joseon is often described as a “hermit kingdom” that refused all foreign contact until superior force opened it. That shorthand obscures the problem Korean decision-makers were trying to solve. Joseon maintained regular diplomatic relations with Qing China, sent missions to Beijing, received Qing envoys, exchanged missions with Tokugawa Japan, traded through designated border and port channels, and handled castaways. Its policy was better understood as regulated permeability : the court distinguished legitimate relations conducted through recognized institutions from unauthorized landing, proselytizing, surveying, commerce, and demands made by armed ships. See [[Markets and monetization in late Joseon]] for the economic side of that distinction. Western governments brought a different diplomatic grammar. They expected written treaties between formally sovereign states, accredited representatives, commercial access, protection for their nationals, and navigational practices that treated coastal surveying as ordinary. Joseon authorities understood unlicensed approach to the Han River—the route to the capital—as a security breach. Each side therefore interpreted acts such as sailing, sounding channels, exchanging letters, and firing warning shots through incompatible assumptions about jurisdiction. The three confrontations were not repetitions. France went to punish the killing of missionaries and contemplated regime-changing claims but lacked the authorization and force for conquest. The United States combined inquiry into a destroyed merchant ship with an attempt to open treaty negotiations; after a disputed survey encounter it mounted a punitive assault, won decisively on the ground, yet obtained no negotiations. Meiji Japan possessed something the two distant powers lacked: proximity, prior institutional relations, sustained political attention, knowledge of the peninsula, and the ability to return with a treaty mission backed by warships. It also adapted Western gunboat diplomacy after having experienced it itself. 1866: persecution, the General Sherman , and French retaliation The crisis year 1866 contained several different encounters that later became causally entangled. Early that year, the court launched the Byeongin persecution of Catholics. The policy arose from more than a timeless hatred of foreign religion. Catholic refusal of ancestral rites had long raised political and social objections; clandestine missionaries violated border controls; the Anglo-French occupation of Beijing in 1860 demonstrated Western military danger; and Russian approaches in the northeast sharpened fears about imperial penetration. A proposal to use French missionaries as intermediaries against Russia briefly seemed useful, then became politically dangerous. The government arrested missionaries and believers. Nine of the twelve French missionaries then in Korea were executed, along with many Korean Catholics. In August, the American-owned merchant schooner General Sherman , with a multinational crew, entered the Taedong River toward Pyongyang seeking trade. Korean authorities repeatedly indicated that unauthorized commerce was prohibited and ordered it away. The ship grounded or became trapped as the water fell. Accounts differ in detail, and later national narratives simplify responsibility, but the confrontation escalated after coercive acts that included detaining a Korean official and firing from the ship. Local forces and civilians destroyed the vessel by fire and killed its crew. The incident would become one American rationale for the 1871 mission, although Washington initially possessed fragmentary evidence about what had occurred. The French expedition followed the Catholic executions, not the General Sherman . Félix-Clair Ridel, one of the missionaries who escaped, carried news to French authorities in China. Henri de Bellonet, France's acting representative at Beijing, declared in July that the Korean king had forfeited his throne and suggested that France could dispose of Korea. That extraordinary threat exceeded what Paris had authorized. Rear Admiral Pierre-Gustave Roze had naval resources in East Asia, but not an army capable of conquering the peninsula or occupying Seoul. Roze first conducted a reconnaissance in September. His ships probed the difficult channels toward the Han and produced charts. The main force returned in October with seven vessels and roughly one thousand men. Rather than risk larger ships in the shallow, tidal, fortified approach to Seoul, the French occupied Ganghwa, the island commanding the western approaches to the capital. They seized the administrative center, arms, silver, records, and royal books. The occupation demonstrated a major technological imbalance: modern naval guns and percussion firearms could suppress fixed defenses and defeat troops armed largely with older weapons. Yet occupation of Ganghwa did not compel the court. Joseon mobilized forces, repaired defenses, and avoided conceding the central French demands. Korean troops contested French movement at Munsusan and elsewhere. On 9 November (dates can vary by calendar conversion), a French detachment attacking Jeongjoksanseong met determined fire from forces under Yang Heon-su and suffered enough casualties to expose the cost of moving inland. Roze withdrew later that month, taking plundered materials, including books from the Oegyujanggak royal library. Calling the result simply a Korean “victory” or French “victory” confuses levels of analysis. France won most direct engagements, occupied a strategically important island, and removed cultural property. It failed to overthrow the government, secure a treaty, establish religious protection, or open commerce. Joseon preserved its policy autonomy but could not prevent invasion, losses, or plunder. The court drew a politically powerful lesson: disciplined refusal and local resistance could outlast a limited expedition. That lesson was rational given the actual French withdrawal, even though it underestimated what a more persistent neighboring power might do. 1871: an American military victory without a diplomatic result The United States approached Korea through Qing diplomatic channels. Washington wanted information about the General Sherman , protection for shipwrecked sailors, and a treaty of amity and commerce. Frederick Low, the U.S. minister to China, and Rear Admiral John Rodgers led the mission. Their instructions and correspondence show an unstable combination: they described peaceful negotiation as the object, but brought a substantial naval force and assumed that a conspicuous display of power would make officials engage. The expedition arrived near Ganghwa in May 1871. Korean representatives and Americans exchanged communications without establishing shared rules. Language passed through interpreters and Chinese writing; the rank of intermediaries mattered because Joseon sought to keep unauthorized foreigners away from the royal government, while the Americans interpreted lower-ranking contacts as delay. Most consequentially, the Americans announced that they intended to survey the waters. They believed officials had received notice and had not explicitly objected. Korean authorities did not accept that notice as permission to send armed vessels through a defended channel toward the capital. On 1 June, American vessels entered the Ganghwa narrows to take soundings. Shore batteries fired; American ships returned fire. Both governments could represent the other as the aggressor because their premises diverged. The American report called surveying peaceful and treated fire upon the flag as an offense requiring apology. From the Korean position, armed foreign vessels were penetrating restricted waters past fortifications after the danger had been made evident. The ambiguity did not make force inevitable. It made escalation easier because neither side would accept the other's account of lawful movement. Low and Rodgers demanded an apology and waited about ten days. When no acceptable response came, Rodgers launched a punitive landing. On 10–11 June, sailors and marines captured a succession of forts, culminating at Gwangseongbo. Korean commander Eo Jae-yeon and many defenders were killed. American reports counted 243 Korean dead and twenty captured, while the U.S. force suffered three killed and ten wounded; exact Korean totals vary by source and counting method. The disparity reflected naval bombardment, modern firearms, and the vulnerability of fortifications once approached from the landward side. Korean soldiers nevertheless fought at close range rather than accept surrender, a fact American participants themselves recorded. Tactical success produced no treaty. The expedition held forts briefly and took the commander's flag, but it lacked a political partner willing and authorized to negotiate under those conditions. Captured Koreans were not useful bargaining assets; the court did not treat their recovery as grounds for concession. The Americans could raid Ganghwa, but marching on Seoul or maintaining an occupation would have required a different mandate and much larger commitment. They withdrew in July. The expedition thus exposed a central limitation of punitive gunboat diplomacy: punishment can demonstrate destructive capacity without creating compliance. Low and Rodgers assumed that defeat would raise the cost of refusal. Joseon officials could instead read withdrawal as proof that refusal had worked again. The United States did not return immediately to force the issue; a Korean-American treaty came only in 1882, after Japan had already opened the treaty-port era and Qing officials encouraged wider treaty relations as a strategic counterweight. The French and American expeditions also strengthened the domestic position of the Daewongun , the king's father and dominant political figure. The government erected anti-appeasement stelae ( cheokhwabi ) in 1871 declaring that failure to fight Western invasion meant making peace, and making peace meant selling the country. The slogan compressed a real sovereignty dilemma into a moral binary. Refusal protected jurisdiction in the immediate encounters, but it also made experimentation with selective treaties politically easier to denounce as treason. From the Meiji rupture to the Un'yō incident Japan's leverage developed through a separate diplomatic rupture. For centuries, Joseon relations with Tokugawa Japan had been mediated through established forms involving the Tsushima domain, Korean embassies, and carefully negotiated status language. The Meiji Restoration replaced the shogunate and announced a new imperial government. Japanese communications used titles and diplomatic formulations that Joseon officials regarded as incompatible with the existing order—most controversially characters associated with imperial sovereignty. Joseon refused to accept some of these documents. Japanese leaders debated responses, including the coercive project later called Seikanron (“debate on conquering” or chastising Korea). The 1873 political crisis did not produce an immediate invasion, but it did not restore the old relationship either. Japan was now building a centralized conscript state and modern navy while revising its place in a treaty system imposed by Western powers. Korea mattered not only as a commercial opportunity but as a nearby strategic space. Japanese officials feared rival influence on the peninsula, sought recognition of the Meiji order, and increasingly treated Korean refusal as an affront to the emperor and an obstacle to national security. Domestic political competition also made a Korean settlement useful: decisive external action could display the new government's authority. In September 1875, the Japanese gunboat Un'yō approached Ganghwa while ostensibly surveying and seeking water. Its movement reproduced a critical feature of 1871: an armed foreign vessel entered sensitive waters guarding the capital and presented hydrographic activity as normal navigation. A Korean battery fired. The Un'yō returned heavier fire, destroyed the position, landed men, and attacked Yeongjong Island, where Japanese forces killed defenders and seized weapons. Whether described as a deliberate provocation or an aggressively conducted reconnaissance, the voyage created a usable incident. Japan framed Korean fire as an unprovoked insult to its flag and demanded redress. The resemblance to the American encounter makes the different outcome especially revealing. Joseon's coastal-defense doctrine had not changed enough to distinguish between American and Japanese armed surveying. But Japan could connect the clash to a sustained diplomatic campaign. In early 1876, it sent Kuroda Kiyotaka and Inoue Kaoru with warships and troops to Ganghwa. Negotiations occurred under an evident threat of renewed violence. Qing officials offered advice but neither controlled Joseon's decision nor intervened militarily. Within Joseon, opinion was not uniform: rigid refusal risked a war the government was poorly prepared to fight, while negotiation risked legitimating demands that would weaken control of ports and foreigners. The Ganghwa Treaty and the sovereignty paradox Signed on 26 February 1876, the Treaty of Peace and Friendship—usually called the Ganghwa Treaty—declared in Article 1 that Joseon was “an autonomous state” enjoying equal rights with Japan. Read in isolation, that language appears to affirm Korean sovereignty. In context, it served two purposes. It provided a formally equal basis for direct Japan-Korea relations, and it challenged Qing claims or conventions of suzerainty that might justify Chinese intervention. Formal independence could therefore be used as an instrument of unequal leverage. The treaty opened Busan and provided for two additional ports, allowed Japanese diplomatic representation, gave Japanese vessels freedom to survey Korean coasts, established assistance for shipwrecks, and placed Japanese subjects in the opened ports under Japanese jurisdiction. The treaty and its August regulations also created permissive commercial conditions, including tariff arrangements unfavorable to Korean fiscal control. Some operational provisions were elaborated after February, so the treaty and its implementing regulations should not be collapsed into one text. Together, however, they created a durable structure rather than a one-time settlement. This was an unequal treaty , but that does not mean Joseon ceased to be sovereign in 1876 or that annexation in 1910 was already determined. The court made a constrained choice among dangerous options. Signing avoided immediate war and created space to learn from Japan and other states. It retained a government, diplomacy, armed forces, taxation, and the capacity to make later treaties. At the same time, extraterritoriality removed foreigners from ordinary Korean jurisdiction, port opening limited control over entry and commerce, and hydrographic access normalized a practice previously treated as an armed intrusion. Those were real erosions of sovereign capacity. The treaty also transformed the strategic environment. Joseon later sought relations with the United States and European powers partly to diversify external ties; Qing officials likewise encouraged some of these relations to counter Japanese predominance. Reformers used missions abroad to gather knowledge, while defenders of established institutions feared that trade and religious access would dissolve political order. The choice after 1876 was no longer “closed” versus “open.” It was how to distribute access, jurisdiction, revenue, expertise, and force among competing powers while rebuilding state capacity. Why Japan succeeded where France and the United States did not Four differences explain the sequence better than a story in which repeated defeats finally broke Korean will. First, the coercers wanted different things. France's maximal rhetoric outran its practical expedition, and punishment followed by withdrawal could not create a treaty. The United States wanted negotiation but allowed a survey dispute to redirect the mission toward retaliation. Japan arrived in 1876 with a specific diplomatic settlement, commissioners empowered to negotiate it, and military force staged as leverage. Second, geography shaped commitment. France and the United States operated from regional squadrons with many responsibilities. Japan faced Korea across a narrow sea and could return repeatedly. Its preexisting relationship through Tsushima supplied channels, personnel, and knowledge even as the Meiji government rejected the old diplomatic form. Third, tactical force mattered only when joined to credible persistence. French and American weapons took forts but did not make their governments willing to occupy the capital or sustain a costly war. Japan did not need to conquer Joseon in 1876. It needed Korean officials to believe refusal might bring a larger and continuing conflict. The Un'yō attack, the subsequent warships, and memories of 1866 and 1871 made that threat legible. Fourth, Joseon politics changed. The Daewongun lost power in 1873, and King Gojong and Queen Min's political network had greater room to consider controlled accommodation. This did not produce consensus or make the treaty voluntary in an unconstrained sense. It altered which risks appeared tolerable. Earlier resistance had protected immediate autonomy; by 1876, leaders also had to reckon with Japan's permanence, military modernization, and the danger that another refusal would produce a war without reliable Qing rescue. Why it matters The decade shows that military superiority did not automatically “open” Korea. Coercion succeeded when it was attached to a practicable political objective, sustained proximity, an empowered negotiating mission, and divisions or adaptations within the target government. Joseon's choices were neither passive isolation nor free consent. In 1866 and 1871, resistance preserved treaty autonomy at severe human and material cost. In 1876, negotiation preserved peace and the state while accepting institutions that constrained jurisdiction and invited deeper competition. The distinction prevents two errors. One is triumphalism: repelling limited Western expeditions did not eliminate the strategic danger revealed by their ships and guns. The other is inevitability: the Ganghwa Treaty did not contain a predetermined road to annexation. It opened a new arena in which Korean officials, reformers, soldiers, merchants, religious communities, Qing statesmen, Japanese factions, and other powers made consequential choices. Later loss of sovereignty must be explained through those subsequent conflicts, not projected backward as the automatic result of a single treaty.
