title: Agentic trading evaluation pitfalls
deck: Most agentic-trading results are hard to trust unless they specify timing, costs, universe construction, and reproducible closed-loop evaluation.
text: Most agentic-trading results are hard to trust unless they specify timing, costs, universe construction, and reproducible closed-loop evaluation. The 2026 survey [[Agentic Trading]] is useful because it is skeptical. It reviews 77 studies and finds that the field is rich in architectures but weak in comparable evidence. The practical lesson for an AI trading pet project is: make the dashboard an evaluation instrument, not just a P&L display. Common traps Look-ahead bias : using information that was not available at decision time. Training-cutoff leakage : evaluating LLMs on events inside their pretraining memory. Survivorship bias : testing only assets that survived or remained liquid. Unspecified execution timing : pretending a signal at bar close could trade at the same close. Ignored transaction costs : fees, spread, slippage, and minimum order sizes. Overfit agent prompts : repeatedly tuning prompts against the same backtest. No benchmark : reporting returns without BTC, ETH, equal-weight, cash, and no-trade baselines. No uncertainty accounting : acting on point forecasts with no calibration history. Feedback loops : letting agents trade on signals that include their own published forecasts or prior trades. Dashboard-friendly fixes Log every input with timestamp and source. Store immutable forecast objects before deliberation. Store final forecasts after deliberation. Store blocked trades and the guardrail that blocked them. Mark every decision as paper, simulated fill, or real fill. Use latency-aware execution: decision at time t , executable at t + \Delta . Score forecasts separately from trades. Report P&L net of fees and slippage. Show benchmark-relative returns and drawdowns. Freeze prompts by version and annotate changes. Sources Agentic Trading TradingAgents PolySwarm ForecastBench Open questions What is the smallest evaluation period that makes a live crypto-agent dashboard intellectually meaningful? Should agent prompts be versioned like trading strategies, with frozen deployment windows? How should a toy project report uncertainty when the number of resolved trades is tiny?

title: DUOT memo
deck: DUOT is the most direct AI-infrastructure microcap in the set, but the thesis now depends on proving Hydra GPUaaS economics before dilution, customer-credit risk, and project-finance risk dominate.
text: DUOT is the most direct AI-infrastructure microcap in the set, but the thesis now depends on proving Hydra GPUaaS economics before dilution, customer-credit risk, and project-finance risk dominate. Scorecard Category Score AI/product fit 16/20 Customer/revenue traction 14/20 Financial survival and dilution risk 11/20 Liquidity/tradability 8/10 Valuation/asymmetry 12/15 Fraud/promotion/accounting/listing safety 7/15 Total 68/100 Moonshot upside: 8.5/10. Kill risk: 7.5/10. Evidence DUOT is pivoting from AI rail inspection and machine vision into modular edge data centers, GPUaaS, colocation, and infrastructure procurement. Nasdaq showed 10.24 per share and roughly 301M displayed market cap on 2026-07-06, but pro forma dilution from recent issuance and pre-funded warrants likely puts economic market cap higher. The bull case is unusually tangible for a microcap: the Hydra Host agreement is expected to generate about 176M over 36 months, with an 18M customer prepayment, 4.3 MW of deployment, and projected high gross margin. DUOT also disclosed project financing for NVIDIA B300 GPUs through a bankruptcy-remote subsidiary. The weak point is that Q1 2026 hosting revenue was only about $30K, Q1 total revenue fell 45% YoY, and much of the 2025 growth came from unusual New APR/asset-management economics rather than mature GPU hosting. Deepening pass Nasdaq's July 6, 2026 snapshot showed 10.24 per share, 301.0M displayed market cap, and about 719k average volume. That displayed market cap likely understates the true economic equity because recent common issuance, pre-funded warrants, preferred conversion, warrants, and options can put rough fully diluted shares closer to 41.3M before equity-plan reserves. At 10.24, that implies roughly 423M fully diluted market cap, or about $446M including the plan reserve. The Hydra/GPUaaS contract is the whole thesis now. It is described as about 176M over 36 months with 80%+ projected gross margin and about 40M annual EBITDA potential, but the actual contract is not public. Public investors cannot inspect termination rights, customer acceptance milestones, payment schedule, SLA penalties, cure periods, or amendment risk. The 10-Q also says GPUaaS revenue comes from a single customer, DUOT bears full customer nonpayment risk, and Hydra does not guarantee customer credit. The 98.1M GPU asset-backed financing improves the first-deployment survival story, but it does not remove execution risk. DUOT had already disclosed about 145M of GPU infrastructure commitments and a $35.42M Hydra deposit as of March 31, 2026. The proof gate is not the financing press release; it is clean delivery, installation, facility closing, revenue commencement, and customer payment evidence in Q2/Q3 filings. Bear case The stock may be capitalizing press-release EBITDA before operations exist at scale. The unnamed end customer, related-party revenue history, preferred/warrant complexity, and repeated equity issuance make the forward contract less bankable than it first looks. Falsifiers Q2/Q3 filings do not show GPU delivery, customer acceptance, and revenue ramp. Another equity, preferred, or warrant financing arrives before clear cash generation. Customer nonpayment, contract amendment, GPU impairment, or rail-business slippage appears. Verdict Active research. DUOT deserves the first full memo because the upside is directly tied to AI infrastructure, but it must be attacked through customer credit, GPU residual value, financing closure, and dilution. Sources DUOT Q1 2026 10-Q Hydra Host agreement release June 2026 offering 8-K NVIDIA blog on Duos rail AI Nasdaq DUOT quote API Open questions Who is the ultimate GPUaaS customer, and can credit quality be independently checked? How much pro forma dilution exists after all preferred, warrants, and pre-funded warrants? What is the realistic residual-value risk on the GPUs?

title: GSIT memo
deck: GSIT is a technically credible AI-chip moonshot with real cash runway, but it should not be promoted until Gemini-II creates named production revenue rather than validation work.
text: GSIT is a technically credible AI-chip moonshot with real cash runway, but it should not be promoted until Gemini-II creates named production revenue rather than validation work. Scorecard Category Score AI/product fit 17/20 Customer/revenue traction 7/20 Financial survival and dilution risk 14/20 Liquidity/tradability 8/10 Valuation/asymmetry 6/15 Fraud/promotion/accounting/listing safety 9/15 Total 61/100 Moonshot upside: 8/10. Kill risk: 7/10. Evidence GSI Technology is a legacy high-performance SRAM company trying to turn Gemini-II, a compute-in-memory Associative Processing Unit, into an edge-AI hardware platform for defense, drones, smart-city surveillance, vector search, SAR, and low-power inference. FY2026 revenue was about 25.1M, up 22% YoY, with 54.5% gross margin and a 13.2M net loss. Cash was about $67.2M at March 31, 2026, no debt, and pro forma cash may be higher after ATM completion. The problem is explicit: company filings say APU revenue has not been material and about 99% of revenue is SRAM. Government funding, the Sentinel POC, Army SBIR work, Taiwan smart-city Phase I, and third-party benchmark work are validation, not production revenue. Deepening pass Nasdaq's July 6, 2026 snapshot showed 6.82 per share, 261.6M displayed market cap, and about 1.98M average volume. The balance sheet gives GSIT time: about 67.2M cash, no debt, and roughly 70M working capital at March 31, 2026. That is the strongest survival feature in the thesis. The technical case is real but narrow. Gemini-II looks most interesting for data-movement-bound edge workloads: vector search, RAG retrieval, SAR/image/sensor processing, GPS-denied navigation, object detection, smart-city video analytics, and low-power inference where time-to-first-token matters more than cloud-scale throughput. The Cornell/MICRO/arXiv work is the best independent technical evidence, but it does not prove broad replacement of NVIDIA Jetson/Thor, Qualcomm edge NPUs, AMD/Xilinx/Intel FPGA paths, Hailo, Ambarella, or custom defense silicon. The investment case fails if validation never becomes procurement. FY2026 revenue was 25.1M, gross margin was 54.5%, and net loss was 13.2M, but APU revenue remained immaterial and SRAM supplied about 99% of revenue. Avnet concentration and end-customer swings still matter while R&D rises toward Plato and future APU work. Bear case This may be a technically elegant architecture that never beats NVIDIA, Qualcomm, Jetson, FPGA, or custom ASIC ecosystems in actual procurement. If Gemini-II remains a demo platform, the market can reprice GSIT as a slow memory business plus cash. Falsifiers FY2027 passes with no named Gemini-II production customer or material APU revenue. SRAM revenue rolls over while quarterly burn stays high. Sentinel, Taiwan, or Army programs fail to produce follow-on orders. Verdict Active research, but behind DUOT and LTRX in practical urgency. GSIT is one of the few true AI-hardware moonshots here, but promotion requires signed Gemini-II orders above $5M and then visible repeat APU revenue. Are POCs funded procurement paths or only validation work? How much additional capital would Plato or a next-generation APU require?

deck: LTRX is the strongest risk-adjusted operating company in the group, but its edge-AI/drone story still needs FY2027 guidance to prove it is more than a hardware-heavy turnaround.
text: LTRX is the strongest risk-adjusted operating company in the group, but its edge-AI/drone story still needs FY2027 guidance to prove it is more than a hardware-heavy turnaround. Q3 FY2026 revenue was about 30.2M, and management raised FY2026 drone revenue expectations to about 10M-$14M. Nine-month FY2026 revenue was down YoY, but operating cash flow was positive at about 8M, cash was about 23.5M before later offering proceeds, and debt was manageable. Post-offering liquidity improves survival odds. The weak point is dilution and mix. The company established a $30M ATM, issued shares through it, then sold more shares in an underwritten offering. Product revenue still dominates, while software and services remain a small share. Deepening pass Nasdaq's July 6, 2026 snapshot showed 5.81 per share, 223.4M displayed market cap, and about 1.34M average volume. That displayed market cap likely trails pro forma dilution after the ATM and underwritten offering; mechanical pro forma market cap is probably closer to the mid-$200M range depending on final incremental share count. LTRX is the cleanest operating story in the top three. Q3 FY2026 revenue was 30.2M, gross margin stayed near 43%, operating cash flow was positive for the nine-month period, debt was manageable, and the June offering added roughly 32.3M net after full option exercise. The drone business is real enough to track: management raised FY2026 drone expectations to 10M- 14M and suggested FY2027 drone revenue can roughly double. The bear case is also straightforward. Nine-month FY2026 revenue was down 4.6% YoY because a prior Gridspertise program disappeared, and Software and Services was still only 7.6% of nine-month revenue. If drones are mostly hardware modules and payload integration while customers capture the strategic value, LTRX remains an industrial IoT hardware company with AI-adjacent upside rather than a platform. Bear case LTRX may be a hardware turnaround with AI vocabulary rather than a high-multiple AI platform. If drone revenue fails to scale or software/services do not expand, the equity is less moonshot and more cyclical small-cap hardware. Falsifiers FY2027 guidance fails to show double-digit growth. Drone revenue misses the 10M- 14M FY2026 range. Software/services and deferred revenue fail to expand. Verdict Active research as the risk-adjusted anchor. LTRX is not the flashiest candidate, but it gives the basket one name with real revenue, improving liquidity, positive operating cash flow, and identifiable drone/edge-AI exposure. title: AI microcap stock research
deck: AI microcaps should be researched as public-market venture bets where disclosure quality, dilution, liquidity, and promotion risk matter as much as the AI thesis.
text: AI microcaps should be researched as public-market venture bets where disclosure quality, dilution, liquidity, and promotion risk matter as much as the AI thesis. Define the universe Separate three buckets: Small/mid-cap AI-adjacent companies: real businesses, still volatile, usually not "penny stocks." Exchange-listed microcaps: more disclosure and listing standards, but often fragile. OTC microcaps/nanocaps: highest information risk, liquidity risk, and promotion risk. The SEC describes microcaps as companies often under roughly 250-300 million in market capitalization, and nanocaps as often under 50 million. Penny stocks are usually low-priced shares, often under $5, but "penny stock" and "microcap" are not identical. Source stack Use screeners only to discover names. The actual research should come from primary documents: SEC EDGAR: 10-K, 10-Q, 8-K, S-1/S-3, DEF 14A, Form 4, 13D/G. OTC Markets page: market tier, disclosure status, warnings, quote/liquidity context. Company materials: investor deck, website, product docs, customer case studies, pricing, demos. Independent checks: customer references, patents, GitHub activity if relevant, job postings, litigation search, management history. Promotion checks: paid newsletters, social media spikes, press-release mills, unexplained volume. AI reality test For every company claiming "AI," answer: What is the actual product? Is the model core to the business, or a marketing adjective? What proprietary data, distribution, workflow integration, regulation, or switching cost could create a moat? Are there named customers, recurring revenue, deferred revenue, retention data, or paid pilots? What are the inference/training costs, and do gross margins survive real usage? Why would this company beat hyperscalers, incumbents, open-source models, or better-funded startups? If the answer is mostly press-release language, assume the market is selling theme exposure rather than business quality. Financial survival test The core question is not "could this 10x?" It is "can this company survive long enough without destroying shareholders?" Check: Cash runway: cash divided by recent operating cash burn. Gross margin and whether AI usage makes it better or worse. Share count history over several years. Warrants, convertibles, toxic financing, ATM programs, equity lines, and preferred shares. Auditor language: going-concern warnings, internal-control weaknesses, auditor changes. Related-party transactions and executive compensation. Reverse splits, name changes, and repeated pivots into hot themes. Fully diluted market cap matters more than share price. A stock at $0.50 can be expensive if the capital structure is a mess. Market microstructure test For a speculative position, the ability to exit matters. Use average daily dollar volume, not just share volume. Check bid-ask spread as a percentage of price. Use limit orders. Avoid positions that would take multiple normal trading days to exit without becoming the market. Treat sudden volume on no fundamental news as a warning until proven otherwise. Hard-no filters Immediate rejection is reasonable if any of these show up: No current, credible public financials. The AI claim cannot be tied to a product, revenue line, or technical asset. Paid promotion is louder than business execution. Insider or promoter selling is the main visible activity. Liquidity is too thin for the intended position size. Dilution is structurally built into the financing. Management has a pattern of failed reverse mergers, name changes, sanctions, or promotional pivots. Before-buy memo Every buy should fit on one page: Ticker, market cap, fully diluted market cap, cash, debt, burn, runway. What the company actually sells. Why the market might be mispricing it. The next two catalysts. What would falsify the thesis. Maximum dollar loss. Exit rule for success and failure. Date for review. This turns the speculation into a small research lab, which fits the [[Quant research]] path better than impulse trading does. Sources SEC: Microcap Stock, A Guide for Investors Investor.gov: How to Read a 10-K/10-Q SEC: Search Filings FINRA: Artificial Intelligence and Investment Fraud OTC Markets: Pink Limited and OTCID context Open questions What AI subtheme is most worth learning first: infrastructure, edge inference, autonomy, security, vertical SaaS, robotics, or data centers? What daily dollar volume cutoff should match the intended position size? Should the research be kept as a spreadsheet, a small database, or one Obsidian note per ticker?

title: Backtesting political forecasts without leakage
deck: An honest political-forecast backtest reconstructs what each forecaster could have known at a fixed historical cutoff, scores a prospectively defined event universe, and treats repeated forecasts about the same political contest as dependent observations.
headings: The backtest is a historical information experiment
Write the estimand before touching results
Synchronize comparators rather than handicapping them
Score events, horizons, and forecast paths separately
Dependence is not a cosmetic standard-error choice
text: An honest political-forecast backtest reconstructs what each forecaster could have known at a fixed historical cutoff, scores a prospectively defined event universe, and treats repeated forecasts about the same political contest as dependent observations. Up: [[Political prediction markets]] Related: [[Prediction-market calibration]] · [[Proper scoring rules and market forecasts]] · [[From event-contract prices to probabilities]] · [[Agentic trading evaluation pitfalls]] · [[From forecasts to positions in agentic portfolios]] The backtest is a historical information experiment A backtest asks a counterfactual question: if a fixed evaluation procedure had been running at time t , what forecast would it have recorded, and how would that forecast have scored after resolution? It does not ask how well an analyst can reconstruct a plausible probability today. The distinction is decisive in politics because contract wording changes, polls are revised or reweighted, model pages are overwritten, markets open after news, and analysts learn which races ultimately became interesting. The experimental unit should therefore be an immutable forecast record, not a present-day chart. At minimum, each record needs an event identifier, forecast source, forecast probability or executable interval, observation timestamp and timezone, forecast horizon, exact proposition, resolution rule, information cutoff, later outcome, and a provenance pointer to the archived artifact. For a market, add venue, contract identifier and version, bid, ask, last, depth at a stated size, fees, and settlement convention. [[From event-contract prices to probabilities]] explains why a displayed price is not automatically an executable probability. This design is prequential : predict first, observe the outcome later, then score. Historical reconstruction can approximate it only when artifacts prove what was public at the cutoff. A current webpage bearing an old chart is insufficient if the underlying series, definitions, or methodology could have been revised. When the archive cannot establish a field, mark it missing rather than infer it from the outcome. Write the estimand before touching results “Which forecaster is best?” is not an estimand. A defensible protocol specifies all of the following before scores are inspected: Target universe. For example, all major-party US Senate general-election winner contracts opened by a named date, rather than “important races” selected afterward. Forecast origin. A named venue and contract field, poll-to-probability model version, published expert forecast, or archived model output. Cutoff rule. A fixed horizon such as 30 days before the scheduled election, with a prospective fallback when no admissible quote exists. Outcome rule. The designated official result and a policy for recounts, cancellations, substitutions, postponements, and unresolved or void contracts. Primary score. Binary Brier loss, log loss with prospectively fixed clipping, or another justified proper rule. See [[Proper scoring rules and market forecasts]]. Comparator. A contemporaneously available baseline with the same target semantics and cutoff. Dependence unit. The contest, election cycle, jurisdiction, or larger political shock at which uncertainty will be clustered. Missingness policy. Whether absent, stale, illiquid, or semantically unmatched forecasts count as coverage failures, exclusions, or prespecified imputations. This specification prevents the analyst from changing horizons, samples, scores, and liquidity filters until a preferred winner appears. A dated protocol or code commit—or a cryptographic hash anchored to a trusted timestamp—is stronger evidence than a prose claim that choices were made “in advance.” A fully prospective study should publish the protocol before outcomes. A retrospective study cannot truly preregister history, but it can blind outcome labels while the universe and transformations are frozen, then timestamp the frozen manifest before scoring. Build a point-in-time event manifest Start with a manifest of eligible events generated by a rule that did not depend on later excitement or resolution ease. Preserve every candidate event and an exclusion reason. Political markets list salient questions selectively; a sample of listed contracts is not a random sample of political events. Likewise, a model may publish only races it judges competitive. Coverage is part of performance, not housekeeping. Give each proposition a semantic version. The proposition should include actor, office or action, jurisdiction, deadline, resolution authority, tie and recount treatment, candidate-withdrawal treatment, and void conditions. Hash the normalized terms or retain a dated rules artifact. If wording changes materially, terminate the old series and begin a new version; do not splice prices across different claims. Map related contracts to a common event family . A presidential popular-vote contract, Electoral College winner contract, party-to-win contract, and conditional nomination contract do not share an outcome merely because they mention the same candidate. Conversely, fifty state winner contracts and the national winner are not fifty-one independent political experiments. The manifest needs both a contract-level identity and a higher-level contest or cycle cluster. Outcome collection comes last conceptually even if it is convenient technically. Record the official resolution authority named by the protocol, the outcome timestamp, and whether the event resolved yes, no, void, disputed, postponed, or remained unresolved at the analysis freeze. Do not silently delete nonbinary terminal states. Ordinary binary scores may be undefined for them, but their frequency and concentration reveal whether a forecast source systematically chooses fragile questions. Enforce the as-of join Every input must satisfy an availability test: could a user following the written procedure have obtained this exact value before the cutoff? This requires at least three times: event time , when the underlying political or economic fact occurred; publication or exchange time , when the source made it public; ingestion time , when the research system captured it. The admissible value is the latest version whose publication time is no later than the cutoff, not the latest value stored today. This is an as-of join, commonly written as “take the record with maximum available-at time subject to available-at \le t .” Retain the raw source timestamp and the normalized UTC timestamp so daylight-saving and midnight-boundary errors are auditable. Polls require field dates, release time, sample definition, question wording, and the version of any poll-average transformation available then. A poll completed before the cutoff but first published afterward is future information. A historical poll average rebuilt with pollster ratings or house effects estimated using later elections is also contaminated unless those parameters are refit within each training window. Economic predictors require release vintages. The Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis's ALFRED system and FRED vintage API explicitly distinguish dates on which observations were released or revised. Using the latest unemployment or income series in an old election model can let later revisions enter an apparently historical forecast. The same rule applies to redistricting files, candidate rosters, incumbency status, fundraising filings, and expert ratings that were corrected or overwritten. Market data add microstructure problems. A last trade may precede the cutoff by days; a midpoint requires live two-sided quotes; an interface “probability” may be rounded; and an empty side cannot be converted to zero or one. Fix an admissibility rule prospectively—maximum quote age, minimum displayed depth at a specified size, maximum spread, and fee treatment. If both sides are executable, preserve bid and ask as an interval and state how a point forecast is derived. Never use the eventual settlement payout, closing quote, or post-cutoff trade to fill a missing historical observation. Synchronize comparators rather than handicapping them A market, poll, and statistical model must forecast the same proposition using information available at the same cutoff. Erikson and Wlezien show why comparing an election market's election-day expectation with an unadjusted contemporaneous trial-heat poll is conceptually uneven: the poll measures current preference, while the market targets the future result. A fair poll comparator needs a prospectively specified transformation from current polling to election-day outcome, estimated without the test election. Useful baselines become progressively harder to beat: the unconditional event base rate, estimated only from prior eligible events; a simple constant such as 0.5 for balanced binary questions, when substantively defensible; an incumbency or fundamentals model trained on earlier cycles; a poll-based probability model using only polls available by the cutoff; the other forecasting system observed at the identical horizon and semantic target. Hyperparameters, calibration mappings, clipping thresholds, liquidity filters, and forecast-combination weights must be learned inside the training period. For election-cycle evaluation, use expanding-origin validation: train on cycles before year T , choose all transformations within those earlier cycles, predict cycle T , then advance. Randomly splitting daily rows places later observations from the same race in training and earlier observations in testing, an especially direct form of leakage. If a comparator was not historically published, label it a reconstructed baseline. Its point-in-time inputs and code may still make it valuable, but it does not become a contemporaneous public forecast. Conversely, an archived published forecast may be scored even when its internal model cannot be reproduced, provided its timestamp and target are clear. Score events, horizons, and forecast paths separately For a binary event with probability p_i and outcome y_i\in\{0,1\} , mean Brier loss is \overline L_B=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}(p_i-y_i)^2. Log loss is \overline L_{\log}=-\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\left[y_i\log p_i+(1-y_i)\log(1-p_i)\right]. Lower is better. Log loss strongly penalizes failed near-certainties, so any clipping away from zero and one must be fixed before outcomes and reported as a sensitivity analysis. [[Prediction-market calibration]] explains why an average score alone does not establish reliability, discrimination, or sharpness. One fixed-horizon forecast per event gives each event equal weight. Scoring every hourly or daily tick instead answers a different question: how accurate was the forecast path across time? It also gives long-running or frequently sampled contracts much more weight. Both estimands can be useful, but they should appear in separate tables. For path scores, first average within event and horizon band, then average across events, or publish explicit weights. Do not allow API sampling frequency to determine scientific importance. Report performance by prospectively meaningful horizon bands, such as 180–91, 90–31, 30–8, and 7–1 days. Exact bands depend on the application. Avoid searching dozens of cutoffs and reporting only the one where a venue wins. If horizon is the research question, display the whole prespecified curve with uncertainty. Calibration plots should use bins defined before outcome inspection or smoothing whose tuning is isolated from the test set. Report bin counts and outcome counts; a smooth-looking line from a handful of correlated elections is not strong evidence. Decompose performance only with care: reliability and resolution estimates can be noisy and depend on grouping choices. Dependence is not a cosmetic standard-error choice Political forecasts share shocks. Candidate contracts within one primary are mutually exclusive. State outcomes within one presidential election respond to the same national environment. Repeated quotes for one race share the same final outcome. Senate and House markets can react to the same macroeconomic release or candidate event. Treating all rows as independent makes uncertainty intervals far too narrow and turns one election wave into hundreds of apparent replications. Choose the inferential population explicitly. If the intended claim is about future US presidential cycles, the effective number of independent cycles may be tiny even when the dataset contains millions of ticks. Cluster paired score differences at least by contest; for national generalization, cluster or resample by election cycle. A hierarchical bootstrap can sample cycles, then contests within cycles, while preserving all linked contracts and forecast dates inside a sampled contest. With few clusters, emphasize the distribution of cycle-level effects and leave-one-cycle-out sensitivity rather than relying on asymptotic significance. Compare systems on matched event-cutoff pairs. For pair i , define d_i=L(p_{A,i},y_i)-L(p_{B,i},y_i) . Summarize the mean or median paired difference, its cluster-aware interval, and how many distinct cycles and contests support it. A lower unpaired average can merely reflect that system A forecast easier events. When coverage differs materially, publish both matched-pair skill and a coverage table; neither substitutes for the other. Nested or mutually exclusive contracts invite additional checks. Probabilities for exhaustive candidates should sum coherently after accounting for spreads and fees, while conditional and unconditional questions must obey probability bounds. These constraints can diagnose data errors, but do not retroactively “repair” forecasts using outcomes. Any coherence projection must be fixed prospectively and scored as a distinct derived forecast. Leakage audit Before opening the outcome column, audit each transformation against common failure modes: Outcome leakage: resolution status, official results, certification dates, or post-election labels enter features or filters. Timestamp leakage: a release is assigned its field date rather than its public release time; a daily observation accidentally contains the closing value. Revision leakage: latest macro data, poll weights, candidate metadata, or model parameters replace historical vintages. Semantic leakage: today’s contract wording is imposed on an earlier version, or unmatched propositions are treated as identical. Selection leakage: only resolved, liquid, competitive, famous, or correctly forecast events survive the sample. Training leakage: calibration and hyperparameters use the test cycle, directly or through random row splits. Horizon leakage: the analyst chooses a favorable snapshot after observing results or substitutes a later quote when the scheduled one is missing. Comparator leakage: a “baseline” incorporates polls, ratings, or model code unavailable to the market at the comparison cutoff. Dependence failure (pseudoreplication): multiple timestamps or correlated subcontracts are presented as independent evidence, reusing the same outcome and overstating the effective sample size. Automated tests should assert , one semantic version per series segment, no outcome fields in feature tables, no test-cycle records in fitted transformations, and deterministic inclusion from the frozen manifest. Manually inspect a stratified sample of winners, losers, voids, missing forecasts, wording changes, and extreme probabilities. Data checks can prove internal consistency; only archived provenance can establish historical availability. A reproducible reporting package A credible backtest should ship, or at least describe, five artifacts: a frozen event manifest with inclusion and exclusion reasons; a raw provenance table and immutable archived references; a transformation log that maps raw records to forecast probabilities without outcomes; a scoring specification with weights, clusters, missingness, voids, and sensitivity analyses; and a results table reporting coverage, matched pairs, event and cycle counts, primary and complementary scores, cluster-aware uncertainty, and all prespecified horizons. The headline should match the evidence. “Lower mean Brier loss on 86 matched Senate races at a 30-day cutoff” is supportable if the protocol and uncertainty agree. “Markets beat polls” is usually not: it suppresses target construction, horizons, venue selection, political domain, coverage, and dependence. A single election can be a case study, not a general performance estimate. Negative results remain informative. If semantics cannot be aligned, the correct output is a basis-risk finding rather than a score comparison. If historical quotes lack depth or timestamps, report that the market forecast is not recoverable. If only three independent cycles exist, show them without converting rows into false precision. The purpose of leakage control is not to make a forecasting system look weak; it is to ensure that any apparent skill could actually have been achieved in real time. Sources Glenn W. Brier, “Verification of Forecasts Expressed in Terms of Probability” , Monthly Weather Review 78(1), 1950, pp. 1–3 — original probability-score formulation. Tilmann Gneiting and Adrian E. Raftery, “Strictly Proper Scoring Rules, Prediction, and Estimation” , Journal of the American Statistical Association 102(477), 2007, pp. 359–378 — theory and use of proper scores. Robert S. Erikson and Christopher Wlezien, “Are Political Markets Really Superior to Polls as Election Predictors?” , Public Opinion Quarterly 72(2), 2008, pp. 190–215 — demonstrates the target mismatch between election-day market forecasts and raw trial-heat polls. Joyce E. Berg, Forrest D. Nelson, and Thomas A. Rietz, “Prediction Market Accuracy in the Long Run” , International Journal of Forecasting 24(2), 2008, pp. 285–300 — long-run Iowa Electronic Markets evidence and evaluation context. Francis X. Diebold and Roberto S. Mariano, “Comparing Predictive Accuracy” , Journal of Business & Economic Statistics 13(3), 1995, pp. 253–263 — paired loss-differential framework and dependence-aware forecast comparison. Peter Reinhard Hansen, “A Test for Superior Predictive Ability” , Journal of Business & Economic Statistics 23(4), 2005, pp. 365–380 — guards against data-snooping when many models are compared. Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis, ALFRED: Archival Federal Reserve Economic Data and FRED series vintage-dates API documentation — authoritative infrastructure for release and revision vintages; accessed July 10, 2026. Iowa Electronic Markets, Market Data — academic prediction-market historical-data entry point; accessed July 10, 2026. Open questions What minimum archival evidence should make a reconstructed market quote admissible when a full order-book snapshot is unavailable? Should Rome's primary political backtest weight each event equally, each election cycle equally, or report both as separate estimands? How should an executable bid–ask interval be scored without inventing a midpoint probability? Which political event families are sufficiently stable across cycles to justify claims beyond a single historical episode? Can contract coverage and forecast skill be combined in one proper evaluation without rewarding indiscriminate listing or hiding missingness?

title: Bid-ask spreads as probability uncertainty
deck: A prediction-market bid and ask define an executable probability interval, but the interval mixes uncertainty about the event with trading frictions and therefore is not a statistical confidence interval.
headings: Order-processing, fees, and minimum price increments
Spread is not a confidence interval
Size turns one interval into a curve
Midpoints: useful, conditional, and easy to misuse
text: A prediction-market bid and ask define an executable probability interval, but the interval mixes uncertainty about the event with trading frictions and therefore is not a statistical confidence interval. Up: [[Political prediction markets]] A binary event contract makes probability look unusually tangible. A Yes share pays 1 if a specified event occurs and 0 otherwise, so a price in dollars resembles a probability. Yet an order book normally offers at least two prices: the highest price somebody will pay now, the bid b , and the lowest price somebody will accept now, the ask a . If the best Yes bid is 0.58 and the best Yes ask is 0.64 , the immediately executable evidence is not a single 61% forecast. It is a two-sided market in which a seller can hit roughly 58 cents and a buyer can lift roughly 64 cents, before fees and subject to the displayed quantities. That distinction is the practical bridge between [[From event-contract prices to probabilities]] and research-grade political forecasting. The midpoint is a useful summary. The spread is useful information. Neither, without more structure, identifies a true probability or measures the forecaster's statistical confidence. The executable interval Let V\in\{0,1\} be the contract payoff, with V=1 when the contract's exact resolution condition is satisfied. In a frictionless risk-neutral benchmark with common information, no funding cost, and unambiguous settlement, the fair price would be p^*=\mathbb{E}[V]=\Pr(V=1). In a live limit-order book, the best quotes instead define a no-immediate-trade region. If m denotes a candidate latent value that would not by itself imply crossing the posted book, then b \leq m \leq a, This inequality does not establish that one unique “true” market valuation lies inside the quotes; it merely records the range within which a marginal valuation would neither sell at the bid nor buy at the ask. The midpoint and quoted spread are q=\frac{a+b}{2},\qquad s=a-b. Calling [b,a] an executable probability interval is useful shorthand. It says what prices are available to a marginal seller and buyer at a timestamp. It also refuses false point precision: a 58–64 book supports a weaker public inference than a deep 60–61 book, all else equal. But the word “probability” requires caveats. Bid and ask are reservation prices for particular quantities under a contract rulebook. Risk aversion, fees, capital constraints, market-maker inventory, access restrictions, and resolution risk can move them away from a common expected payoff. The interval is also directional. Someone who already owns Yes can immediately sell at the bid. Someone seeking Yes can immediately buy at the ask. The midpoint is normally not executable. It is an analyst's interpolation between two orders posted by potentially different people. A chart that treats q as though a trade occurred there converts a useful descriptive statistic into fictional execution evidence. On Kalshi, the public order-book response makes the binary complement explicit. Its current fixed-point response returns and bid arrays rather than redundant ask arrays; prices and quantities are strings, the arrays are ascending by price, and the final element is the best bid. A No bid at n implies a Yes ask at 1-n , so a_{Yes}=1-b_{No},\qquad s_{Yes}=1-b_{No}-b_{Yes}. An analyst who reads the highest Yes bid as “the price,” without reconstructing the complementary ask, discards half of the executable information. Polymarket's documentation similarly distinguishes best buy and sell prices from the midpoint. It states that its interface displays the midpoint when the spread is no more than ten cents but switches to the last traded price when the spread is wider. Consequently, the same visual field can represent two different estimators depending on market state. A stable data pipeline must store bid, ask, midpoint, last trade, display convention, and timestamp as separate fields. Why a spread exists The spread is often described casually as “uncertainty.” That is directionally helpful but mechanically incomplete. Several forces can widen it, and they imply different things about the underlying event forecast. Adverse selection A liquidity provider who posts both sides risks trading against someone with better information. If an informed buyer is especially likely to arrive when the contract is truly worth more than current public estimates, a market maker who sells Yes at an undifferentiated price loses on those trades. The ask must rise relative to the maker's conditional estimate. Symmetrically, an informed seller is more likely to hit the bid when Yes is worth less, pushing the safe bid down. This is the central mechanism in Glosten and Milgrom's sequential-trade model. Competitive, risk-neutral market makers can quote a positive spread even with zero expected profit because a trade's direction is informative about asset value. The ask is an expectation conditional on observing a buy; the bid is an expectation conditional on observing a sell. A larger chance that the next trader is informed, or more consequential private information, can widen the gap. Political event contracts fit the intuition imperfectly but usefully. Some participants may process a poll release faster, understand a party rule better, possess superior local reporting, or model correlated races more carefully. A maker cannot know whether an incoming order reflects that edge or merely entertainment, hedging, or noise. Around debates, court rulings, candidate withdrawals, counting updates, and ambiguous resolution news, the composition of order flow can change abruptly. A wider spread may then be a rational defense against informed flow rather than a direct statement that the election itself became intrinsically harder to predict. Kyle's model emphasizes a related object: market depth. Informed trading is camouflaged by noise trading, and price responds to net order flow through a liquidity parameter. The key lesson for event contracts is that tightness and depth are separate. The best quotes might be only one cent apart while very little quantity rests there; a modest market order can consume those levels and move the price sharply. Conversely, a visibly wider top-of-book spread can coexist with substantial depth farther out. Spread alone cannot describe how much capital is required to change the apparent probability. Inventory and risk bearing Even without private information, a market maker may not want unlimited exposure to one political outcome. If customer flow leaves the maker long Yes, the maker can lower both bid and ask to encourage buyers of No or sellers of Yes. If hedges are unavailable or only approximate, carrying the position through volatile news consumes risk capacity. The quote may therefore move or widen even when the maker's central event estimate is unchanged. This matters more for contracts with few natural cross-hedges. A presidential winner contract might be partially hedged through nomination, popular-vote, state, or party-control markets, but differing resolution terms create [[Prediction-market resolution risk]]. A contract on a cabinet appointment, court action, or procedural deadline may have no close hedge. Inventory compensation then contaminates any attempt to read the spread as pure belief dispersion. Order-processing, fees, and minimum price increments Posting and maintaining quotes consumes infrastructure, attention, capital, and sometimes explicit venue fees. Makers also face cancellation latency, failed hedges, chain or rail costs, and the opportunity cost of collateral locked until resolution. These costs can create a spread even if everybody agrees on the probability. The tick size places a mechanical floor under observable precision. If a particular market requires one-cent increments, a latent value of 60.4 cents may appear as a 60 bid and 61 ask even in a highly competitive book. Tick size is a market field, not a safe venue-wide constant: Polymarket's order-book response exposes it explicitly, while Kalshi's current fixed-point API supports price strings and documents subpenny pricing. A one-cent spread near 50 cents and a one-cent spread near 99 cents have the same dollar width but not the same proportional significance for the cheap side or the same attainable payoff geometry. The bounded [0,1] price scale also makes conventional percentage-spread measures unstable near zero. Fees widen the economically relevant no-trade region beyond the raw quoted spread. If a buyer pays the ask plus a transaction charge, the buyer's break-even probability exceeds a . If a seller incurs a fee or sacrifices collateral yield, the seller's threshold differs from b . Exact adjustment depends on the venue, fee schedule, price, order type, and holding path. Public reporting should therefore label [b,a] “before fees” unless the transformation has actually been calculated. Sparse participation and stale orders A wide spread can mean that informed traders disagree, but it can also mean that almost nobody is paying attention. Old orders can remain after public information changes. One side may be empty. A maker may quote token size to preserve optionality without inviting a meaningful trade. A newly listed or obscure contract can have a wide interval simply because the expected reward from improving it is too small. This is why spread should be read alongside recency, depth, volume, and trade activity. Historical volume is not current liquidity. Open interest is not an executable quote. A last trade is not a current consensus. An interval whose best levels each contain one contract is a statement about one-contract execution, not a robust probability range for institutional size. Spread is not a confidence interval A statistical confidence interval is generated by a specified sampling procedure and has a coverage interpretation under repeated samples. A Bayesian credible interval is generated by a posterior distribution and has a probability interpretation conditional on a model and prior. A bid-ask interval has neither property by default. It is generated by submitted orders. If a Yes contract is quoted 58–64, one cannot say there is a 95% chance that the true probability lies between 58% and 64%, or that market participants assign all plausible probability mass to that range. A trader might believe the event is 70% likely but be unwilling or unable to buy because of fees, position limits, legal access, capital costs, or correlated exposure. Another might believe 50% yet decline to sell because short-side mechanics or collateral are unattractive. Orders outside the best quotes are hidden from a top-of-book snapshot, and beliefs held without orders are invisible entirely. Nor is spread width a monotone measure of event uncertainty. Consider two contracts: Contract A is an election six months away, with genuinely diffuse possible outcomes but intense market-making competition. It trades 49–50 with deep size. Contract B concerns an administrative announcement tomorrow that almost everyone thinks has a 70% chance, but only two small traders participate. It trades 55–85. The first event may have more irreducible outcome uncertainty even though its market is tighter. The second book reveals less about its participants' central estimate because liquidity is poor. Market uncertainty, event uncertainty, and estimator uncertainty are different objects. The spread can nevertheless serve as an identification warning . Under a strong benchmark—matched contract meaning, competitive quoting, negligible fees, fresh orders, meaningful two-sided depth, and no severe constraints—a narrow interval supports using its midpoint as a compact market forecast. As those conditions fail, the analyst should weaken the claim: report the executable interval, avoid point scoring, or classify the market as not presently research-grade. Size turns one interval into a curve The top of book answers only the smallest executable-size question. For a buy quantity Q , define a volume-weighted ask A(Q) by walking up the sell orders needed to fill Q . Define B(Q) analogously by walking down bids for a sale. The size-specific executable interval is [B(Q),A(Q)]. Usually A(Q) rises with Q and B(Q) falls, so the effective spread widens with size. Reporting “60–61” without quantities may be defensible for a one-contract observation and misleading for a $10,000 comparison. A depth-aware snapshot should preserve multiple levels or calculate standardized intervals at fixed quantities. Price impact adds a dynamic dimension. A market order both consumes liquidity and potentially conveys information. Makers may cancel or revise remaining orders after observing it. The realized cost of a large trade therefore need not equal the cost computed from a stale snapshot. For research, this is a reason to call order-book calculations quoted or instantaneous depth, not guaranteed execution. Political comparisons need a common size convention. If one venue has a 60–61 top-of-book interval for ten contracts and another has 59–63 for ten thousand, declaring the first venue more precise mistakes tightness for capacity. A reasonable tracker can publish the top of book plus intervals for several fixed notional sizes, while marking unavailable quantities rather than extrapolating. Midpoints: useful, conditional, and easy to misuse The midpoint q is attractive because it produces one number for charts, calibration bins, and comparisons with polls. Under symmetric trading frictions and competitive two-sided quotes, it can be a sensible estimator of latent value. Midquotes also avoid the mechanical bid-ask bounce that appears when successive trades alternate between sides. But symmetry is an assumption. Inventory can shift both quotes. One side can be stale. Tick constraints can make the midpoint jump mechanically. The book may be crossed only in economically equivalent Yes/No representations that a data pipeline failed to reconcile. A platform's displayed number may switch to last trade in wide markets. The midpoint can even represent a price at which neither participant is willing to trade. Rome should use a midpoint only under a written admissibility rule established before outcomes are known. A possible research protocol is: retrieve the official order book and contract rules at a precise UTC timestamp; reconstruct both Yes sides correctly, including the complement relation where applicable; require live bids on both complementary outcomes and record their quantities; store best bid, best ask, midpoint, spread, last trade, and several depth levels separately; calculate fixed-size intervals and note whether fees are excluded; use the midpoint for a point forecast only when spread and depth pass preregistered thresholds; otherwise preserve an interval and exclude the observation from point-score comparisons or apply an explicitly preregistered interval-scoring method; retain the raw snapshot so later changes in venue field definitions can be audited. There is no universal five-cent or one-cent cutoff. An acceptable threshold depends on forecast horizon, contract family, sample size, intended comparison, and tick size. Choosing the cutoff after seeing which markets resolved correctly would create selection bias in [[Prediction-market calibration]]. The rule belongs in the study design, not in the postmortem. Why it matters A narrow, deep, fresh spread supports a limited claim: at the stated timestamp and size, competitive orders bracket a marginal transaction in a small range. That makes the midpoint a more defensible market summary than it would be in a wide, thin, stale book. It does not prove that the midpoint is calibrated, unbiased, manipulation-resistant, or superior to polls and models. A widening spread supports another limited claim: immediacy became more expensive or two-sided liquidity deteriorated. It does not by itself identify why. The cause could be adverse-selection risk before news, inventory imbalance, a maker outage, fee or incentive changes, stale orders being cancelled, resolution ambiguity, or genuine disagreement. Establishing a political explanation requires synchronized event timing, book depth, trades, comparator forecasts, and ideally evidence that distinguishes rival mechanisms. A wide spread also sets bounds on honest prose. If a contract is 40–70, “the market gives the candidate a 55% chance” overstates precision. “The displayed midpoint is 55%, but executable Yes quotes span 40–70 before fees at the captured size” preserves the evidence. If one side is absent, even an interval may be impossible; the correct result is “no two-sided executable estimate.” Finally, the interval inherits the contract's semantics. Tight quotes around the wrong interpretation are not precise forecasts of the event a reader has in mind. Before comparing spreads across venues, match resolution language, source, deadline, cancellation provisions, payout, participant access, collateral, and timestamp. Apparent precision cannot repair [[Prediction-market resolution risk]]. Sources Kalshi API documentation, “Orderbook Responses” — official explanation of fixed-point Yes/No bid arrays, ascending price order, complementary asks, and spread reconstruction; accessed July 9, 2026. Kalshi API documentation, “Get Multiple Market Orderbooks” — official order-book endpoint and field description; accessed July 9, 2026. Polymarket documentation, “Prices & Orderbook” — official CLOB, displayed-midpoint, execution-price, and wide-spread display conventions; accessed July 9, 2026. Polymarket documentation, “Orderbook” — official best-price, midpoint, spread, and streaming-market documentation; accessed July 9, 2026. Lawrence R. Glosten and Paul R. Milgrom, “Bid, ask and transaction prices in a specialist market with heterogeneously informed traders,” Journal of Financial Economics 14 (1985), 71–100 — primary market-microstructure model of information-based spreads; DOI links to the publisher record. Albert S. Kyle, “Continuous Auctions and Insider Trading,” Econometrica 53 (1985), 1315–1335 — primary model connecting informed order flow, noise trading, price impact, and depth; DOI links to the archival record. Open questions Which spread and fixed-size depth thresholds should Rome preregister for political-market calibration samples? How should interval-valued forecasts be scored without replacing them by outcome-informed point estimates? Can public order-book histories distinguish adverse-selection widening from inventory withdrawal around political news? How should tick size and fee schedules be normalized when comparing spread quality across venues and probabilities near zero or one?

title: CFTC 2026 prediction-market proposal
deck: The CFTC's June 2026 proposal would create a contract-review framework, but it remains proposed regulation and does not settle every political contract's status.
text: The CFTC's June 2026 proposal would create a contract-review framework, but it remains proposed regulation and does not settle every political contract's status. Up: [[Political prediction markets]] · Related: [[Kalshi]] · [[Prediction-market resolution rules]] Proposed framework The Commission proposes factors and procedures for deciding whether event contracts involving activities enumerated in the Commodity Exchange Act are contrary to the public interest. The document follows a March 2026 advance notice and roughly 3,500 comments, about 300 of which the CFTC characterized as detailed. The proposal contemplates review after a market submits or self-certifies a contract, possible requests to suspend listing or trading during review, and consolidated treatment of similar contracts. The CFTC acknowledges that contracts could trade before an adverse determination and positions could consequently be closed. Relevant proposed factors include suitable settlement criteria and dispute resolution, surveillance, customer identification, and controls on traders likely to possess nonpublic information. These are regulatory considerations, not evidence that any price is calibrated or manipulation-free. Why it matters Rule uncertainty is part of contract basis risk. A political market can have clear election semantics yet still carry listing, suspension, closeout, jurisdiction, and access risks that impede cross-venue comparison. Sources CFTC proposed prediction-markets rule — Commission-approved pre-publication version, June 2026; accessed July 9, 2026. CFTC prediction-markets guidance — accessed July 9, 2026. Open questions What changes in the final Federal Register version? Which political contract families could be reviewed together? How would a venue disclose closeout treatment after trading begins?

title: Conditional political probabilities
deck: A conditional political probability answers “how likely is outcome A if condition B holds?”, but extracting it from event contracts is valid only when the contracts implement the same event algebra, information cutoff, and settlement convention.
headings: Three structures that labels often blur
Four ways to obtain a conditional estimate
1. Divide a joint estimate by a marginal estimate
2. Compare a nested event with its parent
text:
A conditional political probability answers “how likely is outcome A if condition B holds?”, but extracting it from event contracts is valid only when the contracts implement the same event algebra, information cutoff, and settlement convention. Up: [[Political prediction markets]] Related: [[Logical coherence across prediction markets]] · [[From event-contract prices to probabilities]] · [[Prediction-market resolution risk]] · [[Cross-market arbitrage and contract basis risk]] · [[Forecast combination with polls models and markets]] The object being estimated Political reasoning is full of conditional questions. What is the probability that a party wins the presidency given that it nominates a particular candidate? How likely is unified government if the party wins the presidency? What is the probability that a bill passes if one party controls both chambers? These questions differ from ordinary forecasts because they hold one event fixed and ask about uncertainty inside that branch of the world. For events A and B , with P(B)>0 , the ordinary conditional probability is P(A\mid B)= rac{P(A\cap B)}{P(B)}. The identity is simple; implementing it with market prices is not. It requires a contract for the joint event A\cap B , a contract for B , and a defensible interpretation of both prices as probabilities measured at the same time. It also requires that “ B ” mean exactly the same thing in the numerator and denominator. If one nomination contract resolves on acceptance at a convention while another presidential contract names a person regardless of ballot substitution, the ratio is not estimating a single coherent conditional. Suppose, purely as an arithmetic illustration, that aligned contracts imply P(N)=0.40 for a politician to become the nominee and P(W\cap N)=0.18 for that politician both to become the nominee and win the general election. Then P(W\mid N)=0.18/0.40=0.45. That calculation does not mean a 45% market price is executable. A trader may have to buy one claim and sell another at bid and ask, post collateral until different settlement dates, pay fees, and bear separate resolution risk. It is first an inference about a probability model, not an arbitrage quotation. Three structures that labels often blur A joint claim A joint claim pays only when both A and B occur. Its idealized probability value is P(A\cap B) . A contract titled “Candidate X wins the nomination and the presidency” is a joint claim if its rules really require both events. Dividing its probability by a separately estimated P(B) can produce P(A\mid B) , subject to all the price and semantic caveats below. A branch-conditional claim A genuinely branch-conditional claim is designed to report on A inside the B branch. One possible payoff convention pays 1 if A\cap B , pays 0 if 
eg A\cap B , and cancels or refunds if 
eg B . That resembles a bet activated only when B happens. But cancellation makes the security's cash flows and opportunity cost state-dependent. Its market price need not equal the ratio of two ordinary binary-contract prices, especially when B is unlikely or when capital is tied up until the condition is known. The word “conditional” therefore does not determine the payoff. Rules might instead settle the claim at a fixed value when B fails, use an oracle to select an outcome, or define A so that A logically implies B . The full resolution tree is the instrument. A technological “condition” token Polymarket's documentation calls its infrastructure the Conditional Token Framework. In that framework, a binary market has fully collateralized Yes and No tokens, a complete pair can be split from collateral or merged back into collateral, and the winning token is redeemable after resolution. Here “condition” identifies an oracle question and its outcome slots. It does not , by itself, mean the quoted market estimates P(A\mid B) for two political events. This distinction prevents a category error. Tokenizing “Will A occur?” as a condition produces ordinary outcome claims on A . To elicit “Will A occur if B occurs?”, the market's question, payout vector, invalid-state treatment, and resolution rules must explicitly implement that conditional object. Four ways to obtain a conditional estimate 1. Divide a joint estimate by a marginal estimate The direct estimator is \widehat P(A\mid B)= rac{\widehat P(A\cap B)}{\widehat P(B)}. This is attractive because it uses ordinary binary claims. It is also fragile. If P(B) is small, a modest error in either input creates a large change in the ratio. Using the delta method as a rough diagnostic, the sensitivity to the joint estimate is 1/P(B) and the sensitivity to the denominator is -P(A\cap B)/P(B)^2 . Rare conditioning events amplify noise. Prices should therefore enter as intervals, not false-point precision. If executable, semantically aligned intervals are P(A\cap B)\in[j_L,j_U] and P(B)\in[b_L,b_U] , a conservative first bound is P(A\mid B)\in\left[ rac{j_L}{b_U}, rac{j_U}{b_L}ight], with the probability constraint then imposed on the upper endpoint if necessary. This is not a license to hide incoherence: if j_L>b_U , no joint distribution represented by those intervals can satisfy P(A\cap B)\leq P(B) , so the analyst should report a semantic, timestamp, or executable-price inconsistency rather than clip the result to [1,1] . If only j_U>b_L , capping the upper conditional bound at one is a conservative probability restriction, not a repair of the inputs. Even this calculation assumes the intervals can be treated as probability bounds and ignores dependence in estimation error. Bid-ask spreads, fees, depth, and the fact that both legs may not be executable simultaneously can make the honest interval wider. 2. Compare a nested event with its parent Sometimes contract logic supplies the joint automatically. If A implies B , then A\cap B=A , so P(A\mid B)= rac{P(A)}{P(B)}. “The nominee wins the presidency” can have this nested form only if the presidential-win rules guarantee that the person was the relevant party's nominee under the nomination contract's definition. Write-in victories, replacement candidates, deadlines, party labels, withdrawal, death, and disputed certifications can break the implication. Logical nesting must be proved from rules, not inferred from natural-language shorthand. 3. Trade an explicitly conditional market A venue can list separate claims on A under B and on A under 
eg B . This can make the desired question legible and lets traders express information about different political branches. Wolfers and Zitzewitz note that conditional markets can reveal beliefs about relationships between outcomes, while warning that correlation remains distinct from causation. The design creates thin-market problems. Trading interest fragments across branches, the unlikely branch may receive little informed participation, and traders who influence or anticipate the decision that selects a branch may have unusual incentives. The reported conditional can be less stable than an unconditional market even when its label is more precise. 4. Recover a coherent joint distribution A richer contract family can be viewed as fragments of one joint distribution. For a candidate C , nomination N , and victory W , a coherent model assigns probabilities to mutually exclusive states such as N\cap W , N\cap
eg W , and 
eg N . Conditional probabilities follow by normalization within the relevant branch. In practice, independently traded contracts may violate adding-up and monotonicity restrictions because of spreads, fees, separated collateral, participant access, or different wording. A researcher can fit the closest coherent distribution subject to the rules, but that fitted distribution is a model output. The objective function, price inputs, weighting by liquidity, and timestamp must be disclosed. It should never be presented as a directly traded consensus. Conditional is not causal The most consequential error is reading P(A\mid B) as the effect of making B happen. A market may show that a party has a higher probability of winning the presidency conditional on nominating Candidate X than conditional on nominating Candidate Y. That difference does not establish that choosing X would cause the higher win probability. Selection into the nomination can reveal information. X may become nominee mainly in worlds where the economy, opposition, scandals, health, or primary turnout already favor the party. Traders may condition on those correlated states. In causal notation, P(W\mid N=X) 
eq P(W\mid do(N=X)) in general. The left side is observational: it concerns worlds in which X is nominated. The right side concerns an intervention that sets the nominee to X while defining what else is held fixed. Ordinary event contracts usually identify, at best, the left side. This matters for “decision markets,” which aim to advise a decision-maker by eliciting outcome forecasts under alternative actions. The decision rule affects what gets observed and how forecasters are paid. If the principal chooses the action with the best reported forecast, reports can change the probability that their own branch is selected and scored. Othman and Sandholm show that natural combinations of decision rules and scoring rules can create manipulability; Chen, Kash, Ruberry, and Shnayder likewise analyze incentive problems and propose designs for decision markets. These are mechanism-design problems, not cosmetic details. A political conditional can still be useful without a causal interpretation. It can describe how market participants sort possible worlds, expose assumptions inside an electoral narrative, or provide an input to scenario planning. The safe wording is “market-implied belief about A among worlds where B occurs,” followed by the contract and price caveats. Calling it “the effect of B on A ” requires an independent causal design. Information feedback and endogenous conditions Political conditions are often endogenous to the market itself. A visible nomination probability can affect donors, volunteers, media coverage, endorsements, and candidate withdrawal. A conditional general-election market can influence elite arguments about “electability,” which may influence the nomination whose consequences it purports to forecast. The object can change as people react to it. This feedback does not make conditional probabilities meaningless, but it fixes their interpretation to a market and institutional regime. The estimate is conditional on information available at time t , the existence and visibility of the contracts, expected reactions to their prices, and traders' beliefs about those reactions. It is not a timeless property of a candidate. Decision-linked markets add a further missing-data problem. If only the chosen branch resolves naturally, forecasters on unchosen branches cannot be scored against an observed outcome. Designs may cancel those claims, use randomized action selection, or alter payments to preserve incentives. Each remedy changes participation, variance, and ethical or legal feasibility. A public election market should not be casually described as a validated decision market merely because several “if” contracts exist. A contract-level audit Before reporting any political conditional, record the following for every input leg: Event definitions. Transcribe the exact criteria for A , B , and A\cap B ; include deadlines, jurisdiction, named resolution authority, recount and postponement treatment, substitution, withdrawal, death, and invalid-market rules. Payoff algebra. State what each claim pays in all four states A\cap B , 
eg A\cap B , A\cap
eg B , and 
eg A\cap
eg B . Mark impossible states only after proving the logical implication from the rules. Matched time. Capture bid, ask, last trade, midpoint, spread, depth, volume or open interest, and timestamp from the same information cutoff. Do not divide a current numerator by yesterday's denominator. Execution and financing. Report whether both inputs were executable at the stated size, applicable fees, collateral requirements, settlement dates, and cancellation refunds. A probability identity is not a zero-cost trading strategy. Price interpretation. Explain whether prices are last trades, quotes, midpoints, or fitted probabilities. Manski shows that binary-contract equilibrium prices do not generically reveal a simple average of heterogeneous beliefs; Wolfers and Zitzewitz provide sufficient conditions and argue prices are often close to mean beliefs, but potentially biased. A ratio inherits the weaknesses of both inputs. Coherence checks. Verify 0\le P(A\cap B)\le P(B) and P(A\mid B)\in[0,1] . Across a partition B_1,\ldots,B_k , check the law of total probability: P(A)=\sum_i P(A\mid B_i)P(B_i). Failure can reveal semantic mismatch, stale or thin quotes, or true trading frictions; it is not automatically arbitrage. 7. Comparator and uncertainty. Compare the result with a poll model, historical base rate, or expert forecast only when the conditioning event and information cutoff match. Publish an interval and sensitivity analysis when the denominator is small. Worked diagnostic example Imagine three synchronized, hypothetical estimates: P(N_X)=0.30 for Candidate X to be nominated; P(N_X\cap W_X)=0.12 for X to be nominated and then win; P(W_P)=0.52 for X's party to win with any nominee. The derived quantity is P(W_X\mid N_X)=0.40 . It is coherent with the two X contracts because 0.12\le0.30 . It does not imply that nominating X reduces the party's chance from 52% to 40%. The 52% marginal averages over possible nominees and over political states correlated with their selection: P(W_P)=P(W_P\mid N_X)P(N_X)+P(W_P\mid 
eg N_X)P(
eg N_X). If the first term uses 0.40 and the marginal is 0.52, then the other branch would need an implied value of approximately 0.571, assuming exhaustive, aligned definitions. That 17-point branch contrast might reflect candidate strength, but it might instead reflect selection: X could be nominated disproportionately in adverse environments. Now suppose executable quotes imply intervals of [0.10,0.14] for the joint and [0.27,0.33] for the nomination. The elementary ratio bound becomes roughly [0.303,0.519] . The “40%” midpoint calculation conceals a much less precise market statement. If the contracts settle months apart or differ on replacement rules, even that interval is too confident. The correct publication would identify the claims as hypothetical or give permanent real identifiers, display the interval and timestamp, say that the result is observational rather than causal, and list the edge cases that could break nesting. It would not announce that “markets say nominating X costs 12 points.” Why it matters Conditional probabilities are the bridge from generic forecasting to political scenario analysis. They let a researcher decompose an unconditional election outlook into nomination, turnout, chamber-control, policy, or personnel branches. Used carefully, they expose hidden assumptions: two analysts may agree on the nomination probability but disagree sharply about general-election performance conditional on nomination. They are also where prediction-market overclaiming becomes most dangerous. A neat ratio can disguise incompatible contracts, illiquid denominators, non-executable midpoints, state-dependent cancellation, and causal selection. Because conditional figures sound like answers to policy questions, readers may treat them as prescriptions rather than descriptions. The durable practice is to start with the state-contingent payoff table, prove the event relationships, preserve executable intervals, and label the inferential object. Only then should arithmetic convert joint and marginal beliefs into a conditional. A conditional market can organize thinking about possible worlds; it does not, without additional design, tell political actors what their intervention will cause. Sources Justin Wolfers and Eric Zitzewitz, “Prediction Markets,” Journal of Economic Perspectives 18(2), 2004: https://www.aeaweb.org/articles?id=10.1257%2F0895330041371321 Charles F. Manski, “Interpreting the Predictions of Prediction Markets,” Economics Letters 91(3), 2006: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.econlet.2006.01.004 Justin Wolfers and Eric Zitzewitz, “Interpreting Prediction Market Prices as Probabilities,” NBER Working Paper 12200, 2006: https://www.nber.org/papers/w12200 Robin Hanson, “Decision Markets,” IEEE Intelligent Systems 14(3), 1999: https://mason.gmu.edu/~rhanson/decisionmarkets.pdf Abraham Othman and Tuomas Sandholm, “Decision Rules and Decision Markets,” AAMAS 2010: https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~sandholm/www/decision%20rules%20and%20decision%20markets.AAMAS10.pdf Yiling Chen, Ian A. Kash, Mike Ruberry, and Victor Shnayder, “Decision Markets with Good Incentives,” WINE 2011: https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/wp-content/uploads/2016/02/wine11-decision-markets.pdf Polymarket documentation, “Conditional Token Framework,” accessed 2026-07-09: https://docs.polymarket.com/trading/ctf/overview Gnosis, “Conditional Tokens,” framework documentation: https://conditional-tokens.readthedocs.io/en/latest/ Open questions Which public political venues, if any, currently implement a genuinely branch-conditional payout rather than merely listing related ordinary binary contracts? How should a researcher propagate bid-ask, depth, and semantic uncertainty through ratios when the two input markets share traders and liquidity shocks? Can randomized decision selection make a political decision market incentive-compatible without imposing unacceptable institutional or ethical costs? What minimum probability and depth should a conditioning event have before its derived conditional is stable enough for a public tracker?

title: Contract-set coherence diagnostics
deck: Contract-set coherence diagnostics test whether synchronized, rule-aligned political contracts admit one common probability model; they identify semantic or statistical contradictions without mistaking stale, shallow, or non-executable quotes for arbitrage.
headings: Build the state and evidence tables first
Diagnostic 1: mutually exclusive and exhaustive sets
Diagnostic 4: overlapping and Boolean contract families
text:
Contract-set coherence diagnostics test whether synchronized, rule-aligned political contracts admit one common probability model; they identify semantic or statistical contradictions without mistaking stale, shallow, or non-executable quotes for arbitrage. Up: [[Political prediction markets]] Related: [[Logical coherence across prediction markets]] · [[Political prediction-market contract families]] · [[Conditional political probabilities]] · [[Dependence across political event contracts]] · [[Fees and executable probability intervals]] What a diagnostic should establish A coherence diagnostic is a reproducible claim about a set of contracts at a specified time. It asks whether one probability distribution over the contracts' rule-defined terminal states could produce all the quoted values or intervals. It does not ask whether an individual price is accurate, whether a trader can profit, or whether the contracts will resolve correctly. Those are separate questions about calibration, execution, and adjudication. The distinction is essential in political markets. A dashboard can display mutually exclusive candidates, a candidate's nomination and election contracts, party-control markets, and state-contingent policy markets as if they were comparable percentages. Yet each may use a different deadline, resolution authority, void rule, outcome universe, or price convention. Even aligned contracts can be observed at different times or at negligible size. Arithmetic performed before those differences are recorded creates a polished but unauditable result. The unit of analysis should therefore be a versioned snapshot: D=(C,R,T,Q,S,F,X), where C is the contract set, R the frozen rules and identifiers, T the observation window, Q the bids and asks, S the available sizes, F the applicable fees and financing assumptions, and X the state-to-payout matrix. The result is valid only for that object. A later rule clarification, added candidate, shifted book, or changed fee schedule creates a new diagnostic. This page is the operational companion to [[Logical coherence across prediction markets]], which owns the general probability logic and interpretation. Its independent contribution is a reproducible diagnostic protocol: relation manifests, state-to-payout matrices, interval witnesses or infeasibility certificates, minimal conflicting subsets, controlled classifications, and execution evidence. It does not re-establish the canonical note's conceptual case; it specifies what an analyst must freeze, solve, save, and report so another researcher can rerun a contract-set finding.
