The market forecast was closer to the eventual two-party vote split 74% of the time and had its clearest relative advantage more than 100 days before election day. The comparison supports the claim that the market incorporated information useful beyond a single poll—possibly other polls, fundamentals, anticipated campaign effects, and corrections for known survey patterns. But forecast superiority is only indirect evidence of aggregation. The market could reuse a public polling average plus a good adjustment model. The set of elections is small, observations within an election are highly dependent, and a vote-share contract is not the same object as a winner-take-all probability. A fair conclusion is that these political markets produced useful composite forecasts in the studied settings, not that every displayed political price is a sufficient statistic for all public and private evidence. Field markets can also reveal which participants matter. The 1988 study reported that traders' political preferences and biases did not mechanically determine the final forecast; price-setting activity by better-calibrated traders could counter the average participant. This endogenous correction is an advantage over an unweighted survey of opinions. It also creates a selection question. If the few corrective traders leave, hit position limits, or cannot take the opposite side, the same crowd can yield a worse price without any visible change in head count. Organizational markets and shared error Internal corporate markets test aggregation where useful knowledge is dispersed across teams. Bo Cowgill, Justin Wolfers, and Eric Zitzewitz studied Google's prediction markets, which asked employees about project completion, product demand, and other organizational outcomes. The markets conveyed useful information, but they also documented optimistic bias. New hires were especially optimistic, optimism was stronger when Google's stock price rose, and trading was correlated among employees who sat near each other or shared social and work relationships. These findings cut both ways. An internal market can make organizational information visible without requiring a manager to know who possesses it. At the same time, participation was not representative of the workforce, and social proximity made signals less independent than a “wisdom of crowds” story might assume. Ten traders repeating a team's shared narrative are not equivalent to ten independent measurements. The price may efficiently aggregate the orders submitted while still underweighting facts held by nonparticipants or lower-status employees. Political markets have analogous dependence. Traders read the same polls, follow the same accounts, and may copy the same model. A rapid consensus can therefore mean either efficient synthesis or synchronized attention. Counting traders, trades, or dollars does not reveal the effective number of independent information sources. A rigorous analyst asks what evidence could have entered, who could trade, and whether apparently separate beliefs share an upstream source. Why full revelation is impossible as a general rule The Grossman–Stiglitz paradox supplies the central theoretical limit. If market prices perfectly and costlessly revealed all costly information, nobody would pay to acquire that information, because there would be no profit left from trading on it. Without acquisition, the fully informative price could not exist. Informational efficiency must therefore be an equilibrium with some residual error or reward that compensates informed participation. This point changes the right standard. The relevant question is not “Does the price contain all information?” but “How much useful information does this market incorporate, how quickly, at what cost, and relative to which alternative?” Some predictable discrepancy can be the payment that sustains research. Conversely, a market that appears nearly efficient after a major public poll may say little about its ability to discover obscure local information. The no-trade logic adds another tension. With common priors, fully rational Bayesian agents, and common knowledge of rationality, a willingness to trade can reveal that the counterparty knows something, potentially unraveling speculative trade. Actual prediction markets trade because assumptions fail in productive and unproductive ways: participants differ in priors, information, hedging needs, entertainment value, risk tolerance, and reasoning. Those differences generate liquidity, but they also weaken the clean interpretation of price as a pooled posterior. Conditions that improve aggregation No single checklist guarantees informational efficiency, but the evidence suggests several favorable conditions. Clearly specified and discriminating claims. Traders must know which state pays. Ambiguous resolution makes research about the political event compete with research about adjudication. A well-designed family of claims can separate hypotheses that one coarse contract confounds. [[Prediction-market resolution risk]] is therefore an information problem as well as a legal one. Two-sided, executable liquidity. Informed beliefs correct price only if traders can act at meaningful size in both directions. A cheap-looking yes contract is not fully contestable if skeptical traders cannot sell, obtain no shares, or efficiently buy “no.” Bid–ask spread, depth, position limits, fees, collateral, and access determine how much information can become price. Diverse, partially independent evidence. Demographic representativeness is not necessary for forecasting, as the Iowa evidence shows. Informational coverage is. A politically homogeneous group can forecast well if it contains diverse models and rewards correction; a demographically diverse crowd can fail if everyone consumes the same erroneous signal. Incentives large enough to correct, not so distorted that they dominate. Stakes should reward costly research and disagreement. Yet wealth concentration, hedging demand, entertainment trading, or publicity motives can disconnect order size from information quality. Market subsidies or automated market makers can keep trading possible, but their parameters affect how strongly orders move prices. Time for error correction. Manipulative or mistaken orders can create opportunity for informed counterparties, and experiments and Iowa episodes suggest that some distortions decay. That claim is conditional. Correction requires observability, capital, access, and time before settlement; a thin contract near expiry may not recover. A comparison architecture. Aggregation should be tested against preregistered alternatives: a polling average, statistical model, expert aggregate, or participants' pre-trade forecasts. Measuring only final accuracy cannot show whether trading added information. The strongest design elicits initial beliefs, records signal structure, follows trades, and measures how much the market forecast improves beyond a mechanically defined baseline. Alternatives and limits Markets are one aggregation technology among several. A simple average of independent forecasts often reduces idiosyncratic error and may outperform a thin market without requiring collateral or trading literacy. Properly weighted expert or superforecaster ensembles can preserve individual forecasts, expose disagreement, and avoid confusing risk appetite with confidence. Polling estimates what a target population currently says; statistical election models combine polls, fundamentals, and uncertainty under explicit assumptions. [[Proper scoring rules and market forecasts]] shows how a sponsor can elicit probabilities without operating a conventional exchange. Markets have a comparative advantage when information is dispersed, updates arrive continuously, and participants can profit from correcting a public number. They are less attractive when claims are hard to define, participation is restricted, inside information creates ethical or legal concerns, or the sponsor needs an auditable explanation rather than a price alone. A hybrid can be better: maintain independent forecasts and a market, compare both prospectively, and investigate divergences rather than declaring one mechanism universally superior. Several empirical hazards recur. Closing prices select one time and may benefit from late public information. Reusing many daily observations from a few elections exaggerates sample size. Contract selection can omit failures that never became popular. A market can appear prescient because its traders read the benchmark before trading. Prices can be accurate yet miscalibrated across probability bins, or calibrated yet no better than base rates. None of these objections nullifies aggregation; each specifies evidence needed to identify it. For current political venues, the safest stored object is therefore not “the crowd believes 63%.” It is a timestamped contract definition, executable bid and ask, available depth, fees, access conditions, and a labeled interpretation of what evidence the market may be combining. Information aggregation is a hypothesis about the process behind that object, to be tested rather than assumed. Why it matters Prediction markets are compelling because they promise a compact answer to a hard organizational problem: how to combine evidence that no analyst possesses in full. Laboratory experiments demonstrate that trading institutions can perform this function and that security design materially changes success. Political and corporate field studies show useful composite forecasts alongside bias, selection, and correlated information. The practical lesson is neither “trust the market” nor “markets are just gambling.” It is to treat a price as the output of an information-processing institution. That framing makes analysis more demanding and more useful. It directs attention to who can trade, which distinctions the contracts express, whether informed disagreement is executable, how independent the signals are, and what baseline the market beats. A prediction market earns epistemic weight when those conditions and comparative evidence support it. The label alone earns none. Sources Friedrich A. Hayek, “The Use of Knowledge in Society” , American Economic Review 35(4), 1945 — foundational account of dispersed knowledge and prices as communication; accessed July 9, 2026. Charles R. Plott and Shyam Sunder, “Efficiency of Experimental Security Markets with Insider Information: An Application of Rational-Expectations Models” , Journal of Political Economy 90(4), 1982 — controlled evidence on information integration in security markets; accessed July 9, 2026. Charles R. Plott and Shyam Sunder, “Rational Expectations and the Aggregation of Diverse Information in Laboratory Security Markets” , Econometrica 56(5), 1988 — experiments showing how preference heterogeneity and the available security set alter aggregation; accessed July 9, 2026. Robert Forsythe, Forrest Nelson, George R. Neumann, and Jack Wright, “Anatomy of an Experimental Political Stock Market” , American Economic Review 82(5), 1992 — trader-level and market-level evidence from the 1988 Iowa market; accessed July 9, 2026. Sanford J. Grossman and Joseph E. Stiglitz, “On the Impossibility of Informationally Efficient Markets” , American Economic Review 70(3), 1980 — theoretical limit on costless full revelation; accessed July 9, 2026. Joyce E. Berg, Forrest D. Nelson, and Thomas A. Rietz, “Prediction Market Accuracy in the Long Run” , International Journal of Forecasting 24(2), 2008 — comparison of Iowa vote-share market forecasts with 964 polls; accessed July 9, 2026. Joyce E. Berg and Thomas A. Rietz, “The Iowa Electronic Markets: Stylized Facts and Open Issues” , in Information Markets , 2006 — primary synthesis by IEM researchers of accuracy, trader behavior, and unresolved mechanisms; accessed July 9, 2026. Bo Cowgill, Justin Wolfers, and Eric Zitzewitz, “Using Prediction Markets to Track Information Flows: Evidence from Google” , 2009 manuscript, later published in Auctions, Market Mechanisms and Their Applications — field evidence on optimism, participation, and socially correlated trading in an internal market; accessed July 9, 2026. Open questions In field political markets, how much forecast improvement remains after controlling prospectively for the exact polls, models, and public news available to traders? What metric should estimate the effective number of independent information sources when traders share polls, social networks, or model code? When does adding a richer family of state-contingent political claims improve identification enough to offset the liquidity divided across contracts? How strongly do access restrictions, position limits, fees, and asymmetric shorting constrain informed correction on modern event-contract venues? Which hybrid design—market plus independent scored forecasts—best distinguishes genuine synthesis from synchronized copying?

title: Liquidity manipulation and insider incentives in prediction markets
deck: Manipulation and informed trading are not labels that can be read from a price chart: they are competing explanations for order flow whose effects depend on liquidity, trader incentives, contract design, and the observer's decision rule.
headings: Four mechanisms that must not be collapsed
The self-correction hypothesis and its limits
Insider incentives are productive and dangerous
A research design for identifying manipulation
text: Manipulation and informed trading are not labels that can be read from a price chart: they are competing explanations for order flow whose effects depend on liquidity, trader incentives, contract design, and the observer's decision rule. Up: [[Political prediction markets]] Prediction markets deliberately pay people for moving prices toward outcomes they believe are more likely. That creates a difficult boundary. A trader with private, lawfully acquired information may improve a forecast by trading aggressively. A partisan may make the same trade to create a favorable headline, even while expecting to lose money at settlement. A political actor may both know more about the outcome and possess some ability to change it. The visible data—an order, a price move, and perhaps a later profit—do not by themselves identify which motive operated. The durable research question is therefore not “was this large trade suspicious?” It is: what objective did the trader appear to optimize, what market mechanism transmitted the order into price, how long did the effect persist, and what evidence distinguishes information from price pressure or outcome influence? Answering that question requires the executable book and contract rules, not trader folklore or screenshots. Four mechanisms that must not be collapsed The word manipulation often bundles together four economically different processes. Informational trading occurs when a participant has a better estimate of the contract's settlement probability and trades for expected profit. If a binary Yes claim pays 1 when the event occurs, a risk-neutral trader who estimates probability q has an incentive to buy at an ask below q$ and sell or buy No above it, subject to fees, limits, collateral, and risk. The order may move the market sharply, especially when the book is thin. That movement is not evidence of manipulation; it is the mechanism by which private beliefs can enter price. Price-targeting manipulation occurs when a participant values the quoted price itself in addition to settlement profit. The motive could be publicity, fundraising, morale, an automated model that consumes the market quote, or a policy decision keyed to it. The trader may knowingly accept an expected trading loss to push the displayed probability in a desired direction. Robin Hanson and Ryan Oprea formalize this by adding a non-settlement preference over price to a Kyle-style microstructure model. Their surprising theoretical result is conditional: a manipulator can attract more informed countertrading and thereby improve average price accuracy. It is not a theorem that every attack self-corrects. Outcome influence occurs when a trader can change the probability of settlement through an action outside the market. A campaign can alter advertising, a candidate can withdraw, an official can accelerate or delay an administrative act, and a person covered by a contract may make a public statement relevant to its wording. Trading then coexists with moral hazard: the participant may be forecasting an intended action, hedging its consequences, or creating an incentive to take it. A final profit is compatible with superior information, causal influence, or both. Settlement or oracle influence occurs when a participant can affect which evidence the resolver recognizes, how ambiguous terms are interpreted, or the underlying benchmark used for settlement. This is distinct from changing the real-world event. It is primarily a contract-design and governance failure, discussed further in [[Prediction-market resolution risk]]. A trader may rationally buy a semantic interpretation rather than a political outcome. These mechanisms can coexist. An informed partisan may buy a genuinely underpriced candidate and also enjoy a favorable displayed quote. An official may possess private information about a forthcoming decision while having partial influence over its timing. Classification should therefore permit mixed motives rather than forcing every episode into “insider” or “manipulator.” Why liquidity changes the result Liquidity determines both the cost of moving a displayed price and the reward available to correct it. Suppose the best Yes ask is 55 cents, but only 100 contracts rest there, with the next offers at 60, 68, and 80 cents. A market buy can print a dramatic last trade without committing enough capital to sustain an 80% belief. If observers report only that print, a shallow book converts a modest order into a large apparent probability change. The relevant defense is not historical volume. It is contemporaneous two-sided contestability: spread, depth by price level, replenishment, position limits, fees, collateral, access, and the ability to express the opposite view. [[Bid-ask spreads as probability uncertainty]] explains why a quote interval measures transaction conditions rather than irreducible event uncertainty. [[Order-book microstructure of event contracts]] supplies the corresponding execution vocabulary. Liquidity has opposing effects: More resting depth raises the immediate capital required to move the book. More active informed capital increases the probability that a distorted quote is challenged. More noise or recreational flow can help informed traders conceal their information, as in Kyle-type models, but can also make order flow harder to interpret. Automated market makers guarantee a quoted path but not unlimited resistance. Their cost function determines exactly how much money buys a given price displacement. Subsidies and maker incentives can tighten quotes, yet displayed liquidity may vanish when adverse-selection risk rises or rewards change. Position limits reduce the power of one account but can also prevent a well-informed trader from fully correcting a distortion. Thus “thin markets are manipulable” is only a beginning. Thinness can make a transient print cheap, while the prospect of trading against an obvious subsidy can make correction profitable. Whether correction occurs depends on attention, access, capital, and time before the quote is consumed by observers. The self-correction hypothesis and its limits Hanson, Oprea, and David Porter's laboratory study gave traders information about a common-value asset and assigned some subjects an incentive to move price away from value. In those experimental markets, attempts to manipulate could increase trading opportunities for informed participants, and prices remained informative in important treatments. Later work by Oprea, Porter, Hibbert, Hanson, and Tila asked uninformed observers to infer asset values from market prices. Manipulators tried to influence those observers, but the study reported no evidence that their presence made observers' forecasts less accurate. These experiments identify a real mechanism: a predictable willingness to lose money is a subsidy offered to counterparties. If informed traders recognize the subsidy and can take sufficient opposite positions, the attacker transfers wealth to them and may accelerate revelation. Historical work by Paul Rhode and Koleman Strumpf similarly examined alleged and deliberately induced attacks in US political betting markets. Their field experiment placed substantial trades intended to move prices; the reported distortions were short-lived, while the historical record contained many accusations but limited evidence of durable successful attacks. The evidence does not establish universal immunity. Laboratory traders know the experimental structure, sessions are bounded, and the definition of fundamental value is cleaner than in politics. Historical price series often lack full order books, account linkages, exact fees, and synchronized public-information controls. A temporary price can still matter if a journalist, donor, model, or decision maker acts before correction. And a sufficiently funded, persistent attacker can consume counterparty capital or make the informational signal difficult to separate from pressure. Cary Deck, Shengle Lin, and David Porter's policy-feedback experiment is especially important because it changes the observer's incentives. In their setting, decision makers used market prices for forecasts and a single-minded, well-funded manipulator could damage information aggregation and mislead the decision process, even though outstanding bids and asks retained information that transaction prices obscured. The contrast with the robustness studies is not a simple contradiction. It shows that attack success depends on budget, persistence, the price statistic observed, and whether downstream decisions feed back into the value of manipulation. The strongest synthesis is therefore conditional: A manipulator who must trade against alert, unconstrained informed capital often pays for a temporary distortion. A distortion can nevertheless succeed when the target is a momentary print, an inattentive observer, a mechanically sampled index, or a decision taken before correction. Robustness of closing or average prices does not imply robustness of intraday maxima, last trades, screenshots, or causal narratives. Informative quotes remaining in the book can coexist with misleading executed trades; researchers must preserve both. Insider incentives are productive and dangerous Prediction markets are designed to reward informational advantage. Removing every participant who knows more than the public can defeat their aggregation purpose. Yet the phrase “insider information” hides distinctions relevant to ethics, law, and forecast quality. One category is distributed expertise : a local organizer understands turnout operations, a legislative specialist understands procedure, or a language expert reads a primary source sooner. Trading rewards costly research and attention. Another is confidential but non-causal information , such as advance knowledge of an internal poll or a decision already made but not announced. It can make price more accurate while creating fairness, duty, or public-integrity concerns. A third is decision-linked information , held by someone who can still influence whether or when the event occurs. Here the trade can alter incentives outside the market. Forecast value and social legitimacy are separate axes. An order can improve the quoted probability while violating a duty, exploiting protected information, or encouraging harmful conduct. Conversely, a partisan trade intended to mislead can accidentally improve accuracy by subsidizing informed opposition. Price accuracy alone cannot settle whether conduct is acceptable. The legal classification is also venue- and jurisdiction-specific. Event contracts may be offered under different regulatory structures, and platform rules may prohibit categories of conduct beyond—or different from—statutory prohibitions. This note therefore does not infer legality from economic labels. A claim that a trade was unlawful requires the governing contract, venue rulebook, jurisdiction, participant status, and law in force at the time. A research design for identifying manipulation Identification begins by defining the alleged target. Was the trader trying to change the last trade, midpoint, closing price, volume-weighted average, public chart, news coverage, or the underlying outcome? Without a target and time window, “manipulation” is unfalsifiable. Preserve the market state A research-grade episode file should contain: nanosecond- or finest-available timestamps for orders, cancellations, executions, and book snapshots; signed trade direction under a documented classification method; bid and ask depth across multiple levels, not merely the last price; fees, rebates, maker programs, position limits, collateral rules, and access restrictions; contract wording, resolution source, amendments, and dispute history; related contracts and comparison venues normalized for semantics and settlement time; public news timestamps from primary sources; and any downstream publication or decision that allegedly made the quote valuable. Wallet or account clustering can be uncertain and privacy-sensitive. Public research should avoid naming a trader from pattern matching alone. Multiple addresses may belong to one actor, one address may execute for several beneficial owners, and transfers can have innocent operational explanations. The safer unit is the documented order-flow episode unless identity is established by authoritative public evidence and is necessary to the question. Estimate price pressure, not intention An event study can estimate abnormal movement relative to related markets or a pre-specified forecast baseline. Let p_t be a normalized midpoint or executable interval summary and let \hat p_t be a counterfactual derived without using post-event information. The deviation d_t=p_t-\hat p_t can be traced before and after the order. Useful outcomes include peak displacement, time to half-reversion, cumulative signed volume, depth recovery, and cross-market propagation. Fast reversal without corroborating news is consistent with temporary price pressure, but it does not prove malicious intent. Persistence and later settlement in the trade's direction are consistent with information, but a manipulator can be lucky and an informed trader can be early. Profit is likewise non-identifying: it depends on exit timing, hedges, fees, and whether the trader influenced the event. Stronger designs exploit exogenous variation. Examples include a documented experimental attack; a venue outage that prevents correction on one market but not another; an announced change in position limits or maker subsidies; or a mechanical sampling cutoff whose timing was fixed in advance. Difference-in-differences or synthetic-control comparisons can help only if affected and comparison contracts have parallel information exposure and compatible semantics. Political contracts often violate that assumption during campaign news. Test rival implications Each hypothesis should make predictions beyond “price moved.” A pure price-targeting trader may accept worse execution as the measurement deadline approaches, concentrate trades in the venue observed by the target audience, and unwind after the target passes. An informed trader should normally prefer favorable execution, distribute orders to reduce impact, and retain exposure when expected value remains. An outcome influencer may trade before private actions or announcements and show returns correlated with controllable timing. These are tendencies, not identity tests; strategic traders can mimic them. Order-book response is particularly informative. If new opposing limit orders arrive rapidly and the midpoint barely moves while one extreme transaction prints, the episode demonstrates resilience of quotes but vulnerability of the last-trade display. If makers cancel, depth collapses, related markets follow, and the displacement persists, the event is compatible with information or a successful capital-intensive attack. Public-news and cross-venue evidence are needed to distinguish them. Reporting without amplifying an attack Prediction-market reporting can become part of the mechanism it studies. Repeating an extreme print, naming a supposedly omniscient account, or treating profit as proof of access rewards publicity-seeking trades and invites copycat inference. A disciplined report should publish the contract, timestamp, executable interval, depth at stated sizes, and alternative explanations. It should state whether the chart uses last trade, midpoint, or a venue-defined mark. Avoid real-time attribution of trades to unnamed “insiders.” If identity is not necessary, analyze the episode without it. If a public authority later establishes misconduct, link the primary finding rather than reconstructing identities from on-chain breadcrumbs. Do not publish tactics that materially lower the cost of exploiting a resolution or surveillance weakness before it is fixed. The central language should be calibrated: “a large order moved the last trade by 12 cents and half-reverted within six minutes” is evidence. “Someone knew” is an inference. “The market was manipulated” is a causal conclusion requiring a specified target, motive evidence, and excluded alternatives. Why it matters Political prediction markets increasingly function as public signals, not merely private wagers. Their prices can enter journalism, campaign narratives, fundraising, and forecast ensembles. That makes the relevant robustness standard stricter than eventual settlement accuracy. A venue can be accurate on average yet vulnerable at the exact timestamps outsiders sample. For Andrew's research, the practical rule is to distrust isolated prints and identity stories. Preserve executable liquidity, study the entire response path, and separate three judgments: whether the trade contained information, whether it distorted a chosen price statistic, and whether the conduct was socially or legally permissible. Those questions overlap, but no one answers the others. Sources Robin Hanson, Ryan Oprea, and David Porter, “Information Aggregation and Manipulation in an Experimental Market,” Journal of Economic Behavior & Organization 60, no. 4 (2006), 449–459, DOI landing page: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jebo.2005.08.004 Robin Hanson and Ryan Oprea, “A Manipulator Can Aid Prediction Market Accuracy,” Economica 76, no. 302 (2009), 304–314: https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1468-0335.2008.00734.x Ryan Oprea, David Porter, Chris Hibbert, Robin Hanson, and Dorina Tila, “Can Manipulators Mislead Prediction Market Observers?” Chapman Economic Science Institute Working Paper 08-01: https://digitalcommons.chapman.edu/esi_working_papers/148/ Cary Deck, Shengle Lin, and David Porter, “Affecting Policy by Manipulating Prediction Markets: Experimental Evidence,” Journal of Economic Behavior & Organization 85 (2013), 48–62: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jebo.2012.10.017 Paul W. Rhode and Koleman S. Strumpf, “Manipulating Political Stock Markets: A Field Experiment and a Century of Observational Data,” working paper (January 2007): https://users.wfu.edu/strumpks/papers/ManipNBER.pdf Albert S. Kyle, “Continuous Auctions and Insider Trading,” Econometrica 53, no. 6 (1985), 1315–1335, stable JSTOR record: https://www.jstor.org/stable/1913210 Justin Wolfers and Eric Zitzewitz, “Prediction Markets,” Journal of Economic Perspectives 18, no. 2 (2004), 107–126; NBER working-paper record and full text: https://www.nber.org/papers/w10504 Open questions Which public prediction-market archives preserve full order events, maker identities or stable pseudonyms, fees, and related-contract snapshots well enough for reproducible manipulation studies? How much price distortion occurs specifically at media sampling times, rather than in closing or time-averaged prices? When do position limits protect a market from an attacker, and when do they mainly constrain informed correction? How should venue surveillance distinguish confidential information that improves forecasts from decision-linked trading that creates moral hazard? Can a privacy-preserving audit establish concentrated control or coordinated trading without publicly identifying individual traders?

title: Logical coherence across prediction markets
deck: Logical coherence asks whether prices on related event contracts can all arise from one probability distribution over the states their rules actually define, after spreads, fees, and execution constraints are respected.
headings: Apparent incoherence is not executable arbitrage
Contract semantics are the event algebra
text: Logical coherence asks whether prices on related event contracts can all arise from one probability distribution over the states their rules actually define, after spreads, fees, and execution constraints are respected. Up: [[Political prediction markets]] A prediction market can look sensible one contract at a time and still contradict itself as a system. A venue might quote 55% for a party to win the House, 48% for it to win the Senate, and 30% for it to win both. Those numbers satisfy one necessary restriction—“both” is no more likely than either component—but many larger contract families fail subtler tests. Candidate outcomes may sum above 100%; a narrower event may cost more than an event that logically contains it; a conditional contract may conflict with its joint and marginal counterparts; or contracts on different venues may appear to price the same payoff differently. Logical coherence is the discipline for separating three possibilities. The first is a genuine inconsistency in the quoted contingent payoffs. The second is an apparent inconsistency created by using midpoints or last trades rather than executable prices. The third is a false comparison between contracts whose wording, resolution source, deadline, or exceptional-case rules make them different events. Only the first is a probability contradiction, and even then it is not automatically a realizable arbitrage. This distinction matters because “the market probability” is often constructed from several securities. Election dashboards sum candidates, infer conditionals, compare chamber-control contracts, or combine markets into scenarios. If the inputs cannot belong to one joint distribution, the dashboard is not merely noisy. It is mathematically inconsistent. But forcing every visible number to sum to one can be equally misleading when the numbers came from wide books or semantically mismatched contracts. Coherence is a diagnostic applied after [[From event-contract prices to probabilities]] and [[Prediction-market resolution risk]], not a substitute for either. Coherence begins with state-contingent payoffs Let the possible terminal states be \omega \in \Omega . A binary contract on event A pays 1_A(\omega) : one dollar when A occurs and zero otherwise. If a set of prices behaves like probabilities, there must exist some probability distribution q(\omega) \ge 0 , with \sum_{\omega}q(\omega)=1 , such that each contract price equals the expected payoff under that same distribution: p(A)=\sum_{\omega \in \Omega}q(\omega)1_A(\omega). This single representation produces the familiar probability laws. The sure event costs one and the impossible event costs zero. A complement satisfies p(A)+p(A^c)=1 . Mutually exclusive and exhaustive outcomes A_1,\ldots,A_n satisfy \sum_i p(A_i)=1 . If A\subseteq B , then p(A)\le p(B) . For any two events, \max(0,p(A)+p(B)-1)\le p(A\cap B)\le \min(p(A),p(B)). These Fréchet bounds require no independence assumption. They say only that “both” cannot happen more often than either event and cannot be so rare that the two marginals have nowhere to overlap. If a House win is priced at 0.55 and a Senate win at 0.48, a coherent price for winning both lies between 0.03 and 0.48. A 0.30 joint price is possible. A 0.60 price is not. The classical Dutch-book interpretation makes the connection to markets operational. Treat the assessor as willing to buy or sell arbitrary finite quantities of each unit-payoff bet at one quoted price. The assessment is coherent if no counterparty can choose a portfolio whose net payoff is strictly positive in every possible state—equivalently, one that forces a sure loss on the assessor. Modern finite-event statements of de Finetti's theorem express this geometrically: such a precise price assessment is coherent exactly when it extends to a probability distribution on the algebra generated by the events. Probability axioms are therefore not cosmetic formatting rules. The equivalence depends on the idealized symmetric price and unrestricted-stake setup; a real limit-order book with different bids and asks requires the interval and portfolio tests below. Real prediction markets differ from that ideal. A displayed price is rarely an unlimited two-sided commitment by one bookmaker. It may be a midpoint, a stale last trade, or a bid available for only a few contracts. Short sales, conversions, collateral, fees, and access can be asymmetric. The theorem supplies the logical benchmark; the order book determines whether anyone can implement the benchmark's portfolio. The basic families of constraints The easiest coherence test is complementarity. If “Yes” and “No” are claims on the same binary condition and together redeem for exactly one dollar, their frictionless values sum to one. Kalshi's official order-book documentation encodes this directly: a Yes bid at price x is equivalent to a No ask at 1-x , so its API can return bids on both sides without separate asks. An analyst who adds the displayed Yes and No asks , however, may obtain more than one simply because both include the spread. That is not a probability failure; it is the cost of demanding immediate execution on both legs. The next family is partition coherence. Suppose a presidential-nomination event has mutually exclusive, exhaustive outcomes for candidates C_1,\ldots,C_n . Their fair probabilities sum to one. At executable prices there are two distinct portfolio tests: If the sum of the asks is below one by more than all costs, buying one unit of every exhaustive outcome locks in a one-dollar terminal payout for less than one dollar. If the sum of the bids is above one and the venue permits the necessary selling, minting, or offsetting portfolio, selling the complete set can lock in proceeds above its liability. The words “exhaustive,” “permits,” and “all costs” do most of the work. A candidate list without an “Other” outcome may not cover every state. A platform may cap positions or require separate collateral for each leg. Available size is the minimum depth across the portfolio, not the largest order on any one candidate. Quotes may move while a multi-leg order is being assembled. Polymarket's official negative-risk documentation illustrates how venue design can make partition relationships economically real. In a negative-risk event, one No share in an outcome can be converted into one Yes share in every other outcome; the mechanism assumes only one outcome wins. Standard negative risk requires the full outcome set to be known at creation. Augmented negative risk allows placeholders and an explicit Other outcome, but the documentation warns that Other changes meaning as placeholders are named. That warning is a semantic coherence issue: the payoff partition itself can evolve, so a time series must preserve which outcome universe applied at each observation. Monotonicity supplies another strong test. If event A logically implies event B , then the payoff of A is never greater than the payoff of B in any state, so p(A)\le p(B) . “Candidate wins the presidency” should not exceed “candidate becomes the party nominee” when the first contract truly requires the second under matched rules. Yet ordinary-language implication can fail at the contract level. A replacement nominee, death, disqualification, faithless electors, a date cutoff, or different definitions of “wins” can create a state in which one contract pays and the other does not. Before flagging a monotonicity violation, construct an explicit state table from both rulebooks. Joint and conditional contracts create the most tempting derived quantities. The identity P(A\mid B)=\frac{P(A\cap B)}{P(B)} holds when P(B)>0 and all terms describe the same event algebra. It does not license dividing any contract labeled “A if B” by a separate contract labeled “B.” Some conditional markets void or refund if B does not occur; others resolve from a counterfactual rule; still others are ordinary joint events. Their prices can encode different collateral timing and payouts. A ratio of two midpoints also compounds two non-executable estimates and can become unstable when P(B) is small. [[Conditional political probabilities]] therefore requires contract-level payout algebra, not just labels. Coherence is a feasibility problem For a small family, inequalities can be checked by hand. For a large political market, the clean formulation is linear feasibility. Enumerate every logically possible terminal state, place a nonnegative probability q_\omega on each, require the probabilities to sum to one, and constrain every contract's expected payoff to its observed value. If the linear system has a solution, the point-price vector is coherent. If it has none, no joint distribution can generate all the inputs. Bid-ask data turn equalities into intervals. If contract i has an executable bid b_i and ask a_i , the analyst can ask whether there exists a state distribution with b_i\le \sum_{\omega}q_\omega x_i(\omega)\le a_i for every i . A feasible distribution means the books admit at least one common set of state prices. It does not establish that any particular midpoint is correct. An infeasible system suggests a possible executable inconsistency, but a portfolio optimizer must still include direction-specific prices, depth, fees, and trading constraints. The geometry is useful. Every terminal state produces a vector of contract payoffs. Coherent point prices lie in the convex hull of those payoff vectors. Checking coherence is checking membership in that polytope. Finding a separating hyperplane when a price vector lies outside it is equivalent to finding a portfolio whose payoff reveals the inconsistency. This is the bridge between probability logic and no-arbitrage. The computational problem can become hard because n binary questions can generate as many as 2^n assignments, and political clauses introduce dependencies. Work on combinatorial prediction markets addresses exactly this scale problem. Dudík, Lahaie, and Pennock propose a constraint-generation market maker that begins with a tractable subset of constraints and adds violated logical constraints as they are discovered. Their application to large sets of election predictions shows why independently pricing related securities wastes information: a coherent mechanism can propagate restrictions across the family without listing every joint state in advance. More general work on arbitrage-free combinatorial market making represents feasible outcomes with integer programs. The intellectual lesson for Rome is modest but important: a coherence scanner needs a formal event model. Text similarity between market titles is not enough. The system must know which outcome assignments are possible, which claims imply others, and how each security pays in each assignment. Apparent incoherence is not executable arbitrage An arbitrage claim should specify a portfolio, prices, sizes, cash flows, and terminal payoff in every rule-consistent state. Saying that probabilities “sum to 103%” does not meet that standard. Several frictions can consume or invalidate the apparent edge. First, use the correct side of the book. To buy an exhaustive set, sum asks at the intended size. To sell it, sum bids and verify that shorting or complete-set conversion exists. Midpoints cannot be executed, and last trades may have occurred at different times. A family can have midpoint prices summing to 0.97 while the executable asks sum to 1.08. Second, size every leg simultaneously. A ten-cent discrepancy visible for one share is not available for a thousand shares if one outcome has only one share at its best quote. Walking the book raises acquisition cost, and partial execution leaves directional exposure. A reproducible test stores the full depth used, a common timestamp, and a policy for quote changes during execution. Third, subtract all costs. Trading fees, conversion or redemption costs, blockchain transaction costs where relevant, withdrawal costs, collateral opportunity cost, taxes, and settlement delay can exceed a small gross gap. Fees can also depend on price, order type, or series. A correct scanner treats these as portfolio-level cash flows rather than applying one generic percentage. Fourth, respect access and balance-sheet constraints. A price difference between venues is not a single-venue Dutch book unless the same participant can legally and operationally trade both, move or pre-position collateral, and bear platform and settlement risk. Capital locked until certification has a cost. An apparent cross-venue arbitrage can be a basis trade with residual risk. Fifth, distinguish deterministic payout from adjudication risk. If two contracts name different resolution authorities, dates, fallbacks, or cancellation rules, there may be states in which they settle differently. The payoff difference is then real even if both titles say “wins the House.” [[Prediction-market resolution risk]] is not a nuisance adjustment to a logical test; it defines the propositions being tested. Research on prediction-market misalignment reinforces this separation. Rothschild and Pennock's field work argues that published books can understate available price support and that logical contradictions can persist, while also emphasizing design changes that move the burden of finding inconsistencies from traders to the exchange. That evidence supports studying incoherence as a market-design and information-aggregation problem. It does not authorize treating every static screen discrepancy as free money. Contract semantics are the event algebra The hardest part of a political coherence audit is not optimization. It is deciding what each event means. Consider three superficially nested claims: a party wins the most House seats, the party controls the House, and a member of the party is elected Speaker. Those events usually align, but vacancies, ties, independents, delayed races, coalitions, and organizing votes can separate them. A monotonicity constraint is valid only if the actual resolution rules establish implication in every admissible state. A useful audit begins with a semantic matrix: Field Coherence relevance Exact contract identifier and version Prevents joining a current rule to an old price. Resolution proposition Defines the contract's payoff indicator. Source hierarchy and adjudicator Determines which evidence creates settlement. Deadline and effective time Separates announcement, certification, seating, and control. Void, refund, and cancellation rule Adds terminal payoff states beyond Yes and No. Exhaustiveness and mutual exclusivity Determines whether a candidate set is a partition. Other or placeholder behavior Determines whether the outcome universe can change. Payout and conversion rights Determines which portfolios replicate one dollar. Void states are especially important. If every leg of a family refunds in the same void state, a complete-set identity may survive. If some legs void and others resolve, it may not. A binary model that forces every contract to zero or one can invent an arbitrage by deleting the venue's actual third settlement state. Semantics should be versioned. When a venue clarifies a placeholder, edits a rule, changes a source, or adds an outcome, the old and new instruments should not be spliced into one coherent time series without a break. The same title can denote a different payoff vector after the change. From detection to coherent summaries An analyst often wants one clean probability table even when raw quotes are inconsistent. Projection can help: find the coherent probability vector closest to the observed vector under a chosen loss function. Squared-error projection, likelihood-based methods, or spread-weighted optimization can produce a coherent summary. But projection is an analytical transformation, not a recovered market belief. Every projection makes choices. Equal weighting treats a deep one-cent market like a stale twenty-cent market. Liquidity weighting can over-reward volume that does not represent current depth. Midpoint projection discards direction-specific execution. A Euclidean objective spreads correction across contracts differently from a log-loss objective. If the events are not a genuine partition, normalization manufactures a relationship that the contracts do not possess. The best output is often an interval or a flagged contradiction rather than one repaired number. Report the raw bid and ask, the semantic constraints, whether the interval system is feasible, the smallest identified conflicting subset, and any projected table under an explicit method. Preserve raw observations so later work on [[Prediction-market calibration]] can score what the venue actually showed rather than a silently repaired series. Coherence and calibration answer different questions. A forecast can be coherent but badly calibrated: probabilities obey all logical laws yet systematically overstate favorites. A set can be individually calibrated in coarse bins but jointly incoherent because related questions were generated independently. Coherence is internal consistency at a timestamp; calibration is empirical agreement with outcomes over repeated observations. Serious forecast aggregation needs both. A research-grade coherence workflow For Rome's political desk, a defensible audit proceeds in this order: Freeze a synchronized snapshot of bids, asks, sizes, fee rules, and timestamps; do not start from rounded display probabilities. Retrieve and version the complete rules for every contract. Define terminal states, including Other, void, cancellation, postponement, replacement, tie, and source-unavailability states. Encode each contract's payoff in every state and document every claimed implication or partition. Test whether one state-price distribution fits all executable intervals. If infeasible, identify the smallest conflicting family and solve for a direction-specific portfolio using available depth. Apply fees, collateral, settlement timing, conversion constraints, access limits, and platform risk. Classify the result as coherent, point-estimate incoherent but not executable, executable within one venue, cross-venue basis with residual risk, or unresolved because semantics are ambiguous. This workflow produces useful findings even when no arbitrage remains. A wide but coherent family shows how little the books jointly identify. A semantic mismatch explains why two dashboards disagree. A persistent non-executable violation can reveal fragmented liquidity or weak market-maker incentives. A true executable contradiction can reveal a design failure, but public research should document it without placing trades or encouraging account activity. Place in the map Logical coherence sits between contract interpretation and forecast evaluation. It depends on [[From event-contract prices to probabilities]], [[Prediction-market resolution risk]], and [[Bid-ask spreads as probability uncertainty]]. It supplies the formal foundation for [[Conditional political probabilities]], [[Cross-market arbitrage and contract basis risk]], and any candidate, chamber-control, or policy dashboard that combines several markets. Its central rule is simple: do not ask whether numbers add up until the contracts' payoffs add up; do not call the remaining gap arbitrage until a complete portfolio is executable. Sources Kalshi, “Orderbook Responses” — official explanation of complementary Yes/No order-book quotes; accessed July 10, 2026. Polymarket, “Negative Risk Markets” — official documentation of multi-outcome conversion, placeholders, and Other; accessed July 10, 2026. Polymarket, “Orders Overview” — official tick-size and negative-risk order documentation; accessed July 10, 2026. Tommaso Flaminio, Lluís Godo, and Enrico Marchioni, “A logical characterization of coherence for imprecise probabilities” , International Journal of Approximate Reasoning 55(1), 2014 — accessible manuscript; includes a finite-event Dutch-book theorem. Miroslav Dudík, Sébastien Lahaie, and David M. Pennock, “A Tractable Combinatorial Market Maker Using Constraint Generation” , Proceedings of the 13th ACM Conference on Electronic Commerce , 2012, DOI 10.1145/2229012.2229047 . Christian Kroer, Miroslav Dudík, Sébastien Lahaie, and Sivaraman Balakrishnan, “Arbitrage-Free Combinatorial Market Making via Integer Programming” , 2016 — combinatorial no-arbitrage under outcome spaces specified by integer programs. David M. Rothschild and David M. Pennock, “The Extent of Price Misalignment in Prediction Markets” , 2014 — field evidence and market-design analysis of logical contradictions. David M. Pennock and Rahul Sami, “Computational Aspects of Prediction Markets” , in Algorithmic Game Theory , 2007 — survey of combinatorial securities, matching, and automated market making. Open questions What formal event language can represent political contract rules, including void and changing-placeholder states, without hiding human interpretive judgments? Which weighting and loss function should Rome use when projecting an incoherent quote vector onto the coherent polytope? What minimum synchronized depth and fee metadata should be required before a logical violation is labeled executable? How should a coherence ledger distinguish venue design failures from temporary quote latency and fragmented trader access?

title: Missing-data policy for political market backtests
deck: A political-market backtest needs a prospective missing-data policy because absent quotes, vanished contracts, voids, and ambiguous outcomes are different failures, often caused by the same liquidity and uncertainty the study is trying to measure.
headings: Voids, disputes, and nonbinary terminal states
Missing-data mechanisms are diagnoses, not labels
Choose the estimand before the remedy
text: A political-market backtest needs a prospective missing-data policy because absent quotes, vanished contracts, voids, and ambiguous outcomes are different failures, often caused by the same liquidity and uncertainty the study is trying to measure. Up: [[Political prediction markets]] Related: [[Backtesting political forecasts without leakage]] · [[Political prediction-market calibration ledger]] · [[Versioning political event-contract semantics]] · [[Voids cancellations and postponements in event contracts]] · [[Order-book microstructure of event contracts]] Missing is not one state Suppose a study asks for the probability of each eligible political event 30 days before its scheduled date. At one cutoff the collector times out. At another it retrieves a book with an ask but no bid. A third contract has disappeared from the public listing endpoint. A fourth traded normally but was later voided. A fifth has prices and a final payout, yet its archived rules are too incomplete to establish what proposition those prices represented. All five rows can become in a score table. They do not mean the same thing. The distinction matters because every repair embeds a claim about the missingness mechanism. Carrying forward a quote assumes the unobserved forecast is adequately represented by an older market state. Taking the next trade assumes later information did not matter. Replacing an empty bid with zero assumes nobody willing to quote is equivalent to an executable zero-cent valuation. Deleting a void assumes the forecast universe excludes questions that become operationally difficult. Treating a vanished market as never listed assumes the venue's later catalog preserves its historical opportunity set. None of those claims is automatic. The first rule is therefore architectural: keep a coverage ledger containing every event generated by the frozen universe rule, then derive score tables for explicitly named estimands. Do not let a database join decide the sample. A left join from the frozen event-horizon manifest to captured observations preserves absences; an inner join silently converts capture and venue failures into exclusions. A stage-based taxonomy Each eligible event-horizon row should receive one primary status at the earliest stage where it fails, plus secondary flags that preserve later facts. A useful decision order is: Universe and listing: Was the event eligible, and was a matching contract listed under the prospective rule? Lifecycle: Had the contract opened by the cutoff, and was it active, halted, delisted, closed, or replaced? Capture: Did the research system obtain the required point-in-time artifact? Quote admissibility: Did the artifact contain fresh, two-sided, sufficiently deep executable quotes under the registered size and fee rule? Semantic admissibility: Can the archived contract version be mapped to the target proposition without unresolved meaning changes? Outcome admissibility: Did the contract and substantive event reach the terminal state required by the estimand? This order prevents double counting. A collector can fail on a contract that later voids; can be the primary forecast-status code while remains a terminal-outcome flag. The complete record should preserve both. Capture failure means the observation should have been obtainable under the design, but the research pipeline did not preserve it. Causes include network failure, rate limiting, authentication or access changes, parser breakage, clock skew, corrupt storage, or a missed scheduler run. This is primarily a measurement-system failure, not evidence that the venue lacked a forecast. Record the request time, target endpoint and parameters, collector and parser versions, error class, response status when available, retry count, last successful observation, next successful observation, and whether an independent official endpoint was checked. Retries may occur only within the prospectively defined observation window. A successful request after the cutoff is provenance about recovery, not the forecast that existed at the cutoff. Capture failure can be plausibly unrelated to the unobserved price when caused by a random local outage, but it can also be informative. Traffic spikes around debates or surprise withdrawals may overload both the collector and venue precisely when prices move most. API schema changes can affect particular old or exceptional contracts. Rate limits may preferentially drop high-frequency markets. The coverage report should therefore tabulate failures by venue, time, political event type, observed volatility before failure, and lifecycle status rather than assuming a benign mechanism. One-sided or non-executable books An observed but one-sided book is not a missing raw record. It is an observed market state that may lack the point forecast required by the registered extractor. If only a Yes ask is present, the analyst knows an offered purchase price at a stated quantity, not the best executable sale price. Coding the missing bid as zero manufactures the interval [0,a] ; coding it as the complement of the same side can double-count a quote unless the venue's contract and order-book representation actually justify that transformation. [[Order-book microstructure of event contracts]] explains why Yes and No complementarity depends on payout and venue mechanics. Preserve each side, price level, quantity, exchange timestamp, quote age, tick size, status, and any venue-native empty-book indicator. Use , , , , or as analysis-relevant flags. A primary midpoint estimand should classify the point forecast as unavailable when either admissible side is absent. A distinct interval or partial-identification analysis may use valid observed bounds, but it must state what economic assumptions produce the unobserved bound. One-sidedness is often informative: market makers may withdraw under adverse-selection risk, contract ambiguity, inventory imbalance, technical stress, or imminent resolution. Deleting these rows can make remaining forecasts look more liquid, stable, and calibrated than the venue was as a usable forecasting instrument. Delisting, suspension, and replacement A delisted market must remain in the event manifest. Distinguish , , , , and . A current API that omits a contract does not establish that it never existed. Preserve initial listing artifacts, immutable venue identifiers, lifecycle-event history, the last observed rules, and the relationship to any replacement. Kalshi's official lifecycle documentation distinguishes active trading, close, determination, amendment, and settlement-related fields. Those states should not be collapsed into “available” versus “missing.” A market can be closed to new trading yet still await determination; an amendment can alter timing without erasing its prior history. Likewise, a relisted or replacement contract should not be spliced onto the original merely because its title is similar. Apply [[Versioning political event-contract semantics]] and record whether the replacement is semantically equivalent, economically continuous, both, or neither. Delisting is especially likely to be outcome- or difficulty-related. Venues may remove markets because of legal risk, ambiguous rules, event cancellation, low interest, or operational problems. Complete-case analysis then selects for contracts that remained easy to administer. Report delisting as an operational outcome even when no binary score is possible. Voids, disputes, and nonbinary terminal states A void is observed terminal information, not an unknown binary outcome. A pending dispute is a known procedural state with an unknown final payout. A split payout or refund is an economic outcome that may not correspond to y\in\{0,1\} . Use separate values such as , , , , , , , and . Preserve the venue settlement vector, the real-world fact under the named authoritative source, and the researcher's semantic mapping as distinct fields. Polymarket's documented resolution process includes proposal, a challenge period, repeated proposal or dispute, and potential escalation to UMA's Data Verification Mechanism. A proposal is therefore not a final outcome. Kalshi also documents determination and settlement as lifecycle stages rather than a single undifferentiated end timestamp. The backtest must use the state available at its declared analysis freeze and later append revisions; it must not overwrite a disputed history with the eventual final label. Ordinary binary Brier or log loss is undefined for a void unless the study prospectively defines a different target. Coding a refund as y=0.5 pretends the political event occurred halfway and changes the scoring problem. Coding every void as a loss measures an operational penalty but is no longer a proper score for the binary event. Both may be legitimate in a separately named economic-utility estimand; neither belongs silently in a binary forecast-accuracy table. Semantic uncertainty applies when prices were captured but the proposition cannot be reconstructed well enough to score. Missing rule text, an undated clarification, conflicting resolution sources, an unclear amendment boundary, or a questionable cross-venue match can create this state. It is not cured by the existence of a payout. The venue may have paid Yes while the researcher remains unable to show that the archived forecast question matched the target defined by the study. Store the rule artifacts available at the cutoff, content hashes, clarification times, named sources and fallbacks, reviewer judgment, alternative plausible interpretations, and a confidence or adjudication status. Do not allow a present-day page to retroactively supply historical semantics. When two interpretations would generate different labels or inclusion decisions, exclude the row from the confirmatory semantic estimand and show both mappings in sensitivity analysis if evidence supports them. Semantic uncertainty is predictably concentrated in politically unusual cases—withdrawals, vacancies, delayed certifications, procedural votes, court intervention, and disputed authority. Removing it can produce an evaluation of easy-to-word politics rather than political forecasting generally. Missing-data mechanisms are diagnoses, not labels Rubin's framework distinguishes missingness that is independent of observed and unobserved data, missingness explainable by observed data, and missingness that still depends on the unseen value after conditioning. The familiar shorthand is MCAR, MAR, and MNAR. These are assumptions about a probability distribution, not synonyms for administrative codes. Let R_i=1 when the forecast needed for event-horizon row i is admissibly observed, P_i be its latent or unavailable forecast, Y_i its outcome, and X_i recorded covariates. A missing-at-random claim has the form \Pr(R_i=1\mid P_i,Y_i,X_i)=\Pr(R_i=1\mid Y_i,X_i). For rows with a final observed binary outcome, it says that after conditioning on that outcome and the chosen observed covariates, observability no longer depends on the missing forecast. It is not validated merely because the dataset contains many covariates. If the outcome is also missing, MAR must instead be stated relative to whatever components of that row were actually observed; the displayed formula no longer applies unchanged. In prediction markets, a more realistic mechanism often links R_i to latent liquidity, volatility, ambiguity, surprise, trader attention, or venue intervention—variables also related to forecast extremity and error. Examples clarify the limits. A power failure at the researcher's machine may approximate MCAR over a short interval, unless it occurs during a storm or news spike that also affects markets. Missing depth may be MAR conditional on contract age, category, time of day, prior volume, and spread, but only if unobserved contemporaneous volatility adds no residual effect. One-sided books and delistings are often MNAR for the point-score problem because quote withdrawal or removal can respond to information and resolution difficulty not fully captured in X_i . Little's pattern-mixture perspective is useful here: compare the distribution of observed covariates and outcomes across missingness patterns rather than burying all failures in one indicator. A contract absent because it was never listed belongs to a different pattern from one captured until an ambiguous event caused suspension. Pattern tables do not identify the missing forecasts, but they reveal where complete-case claims cease to generalize. Choose the estimand before the remedy There is no universal “correct” way to handle missing political-market data because different questions target different populations. The available-forecast accuracy estimand asks: among eligible rows where the venue supplied an admissible forecast under the protocol, how accurate were those forecasts? Complete-case scoring can estimate this descriptive quantity. Its denominator must be visible, and the conclusion cannot be generalized to all eligible political events without additional assumptions. The forecast-service estimand asks: if a user relied on the venue at every registered cutoff, what accuracy and coverage would the service deliver? This requires two outcomes: score conditional on availability and availability itself. A service with excellent Brier loss on 40% coverage is not equivalent to one with slightly worse loss on 95% coverage. A composite utility can penalize absence, but the penalty is a user decision, not a proper scoring rule; publish results across plausible penalties. The listed-contract estimand asks about every contract in the frozen venue universe, including later delistings, voids, and unresolved cases. Report binary forecast performance on the eligible resolved subset plus operational failure rates on the full set. If a single number is demanded, define a decision problem with explicit costs for no quote, void, delayed settlement, and error. The substantive political-event estimand asks how well markets forecast a political target independent of venue settlement. It needs a prospectively defined authoritative outcome and semantic mapping. Venue voids do not necessarily erase the real-world outcome, but a missing or mismatched forecast remains missing. This estimand must not switch between venue payout and political fact case by case. The matched-comparator estimand asks which system performed better where both produced admissible forecasts. It should use identical event-horizon pairs and report paired loss differences. A separate coverage comparison is essential because matching may select the easiest shared cases. Imputing the market when only the model is present, or vice versa, changes the target and should be a registered sensitivity analysis. Primary policy and sensitivity analyses A defensible primary policy is conservative: Freeze the candidate universe and scheduled cutoffs before outcome inspection. Never substitute a later or earlier quote for a missing cutoff in the confirmatory analysis. Require the registered two-sided depth, freshness, spread, fee, and semantic rules for a point forecast. Score only final binary outcomes for the binary proper-score estimand. Retain every other row in the coverage ledger with a primary code, secondary flags, and lifecycle history. Report the flow from eligible events to listed, captured, quote-admissible, semantically admissible, binary-final, and comparator-matched rows. Compare observed characteristics and failure rates across missingness patterns, venue, horizon, event family, and election cycle. Sensitivity analysis should then test assumptions rather than conceal them. Useful analyses include: Tolerance grids: Repeat results over prospectively bounded quote-age, spread, and depth thresholds, showing both score and coverage. Interval scoring bounds: For partially observed or wide books, compute the range of Brier or log loss over defensible probability bounds rather than inventing a midpoint. Worst- and best-case bounds: Assign missing forecasts the loss-minimizing and loss-maximizing values permitted by an explicit range. These wide bounds honestly show what the observed data alone identify. Pattern-mixture shifts: For a sensitivity parameter \delta , posit that missing forecasts are shifted on a chosen scale relative to predictions from observed covariates, and plot conclusions over substantively plausible \delta . Do not present one untestable shift as recovered truth. Selection models: Model observability jointly with forecast error only when exclusion restrictions or strong domain assumptions can be defended. Report how conclusions depend on them. Void and dispute policies: Compare binary-final-at-freeze, eventually-final, and substantive-outcome analyses without overwriting the original terminal state. Leave-pattern-out results: Show whether venue rankings survive exclusion of delistings, semantic-review cases, particular cycles, and high-volatility capture windows. Service-penalty curves: Vary the utility penalty for an unavailable forecast, keeping conditional accuracy and coverage visible beside the composite. Multiple imputation is not a default cure. Standard imputation can propagate observed relationships under an MAR model, but it does not reconstruct an executable quote that never existed. For capture failure with rich adjacent book data, imputation may support a clearly labeled latent-price sensitivity analysis. For a one-sided market, delisting, or ambiguity-driven suspension, it risks replacing a venue failure with a model forecast and then crediting the venue for the model's answer. Imputed rows must never be described as observed market performance. Minimum audit fields The row-level audit record should make every exclusion reproducible. At minimum preserve: stable event, contract, semantic-version, venue, and dependence-cluster identifiers; target proposition, full rules artifact, resolution source, fallback, and content hash; scheduled cutoff, venue timestamp, ingestion timestamp, timezone, and permitted observation window; listing, open, halt, close, delist, amendment, determination, dispute, finalization, and settlement timestamps, each labeled scheduled, observed, inferred, or missing; raw request URL or endpoint and parameters, response status, raw artifact hash and storage pointer, collector/parser/schema versions, retries, and error class; bids, asks, quantities, depth levels, last trade and time, quote ages, spread, tick size, fees, order-book status, and the exact admissibility rule result; primary missingness code, secondary flags, decision rule version, decision time, automated reason, reviewer, review status, and superseded-record pointer; venue payout state and vector, substantive outcome and authority, evidence publication time, mapping rationale, dispute and revision history; estimand eligibility flags for each published analysis, imputation or bound method if any, sensitivity parameters, and parent artifact or code version. Use append-only corrections. If a late archive proves that a supposed capture failure was actually a suspended market, append a corrected classification linked to the original. Reproducibility requires knowing what the analysis believed at each freeze, not merely seeing the latest cleaned row. Why it matters Missingness is where a backtest's clean numerical claim meets the institution that generated the data. Political markets are most likely to become thin, ambiguous, suspended, disputed, or operationally stressed when politics becomes unusual. Those are not peripheral cases. They are the environments in which a forecasting system's availability and contract design matter most. A backtest that silently deletes failures can answer a narrow conditional question while sounding universal. A backtest that fills gaps with later prices introduces leakage. One that imputes venue outages from a statistical model may end up evaluating the imputation model. One that treats voids as ordinary outcomes confuses forecast accuracy with settlement utility. A good missing-data policy prevents these category errors by preserving the full opportunity set, naming the estimand, and showing how conclusions move under explicit assumptions. The goal is not to force every contract into a score. It is to distinguish what the data identify from what an analyst assumes. Sometimes the honest conclusion is that observed forecasts performed well conditional on two-sided availability, while the evidence is insufficient to claim performance over all eligible political events. That narrower result is more useful because another researcher can reproduce it, challenge its assumptions, and design a better capture system for the next cycle. Sources Donald B. Rubin, “Inference and Missing Data” , Biometrika 63(3), 1976, pp. 581–592 — foundational formalization of missing-data mechanisms and likelihood-based inference. Roderick J. A. Little, “Pattern-Mixture Models for Multivariate Incomplete Data” , Journal of the American Statistical Association 88(421), 1993, pp. 125–134 — original pattern-mixture formulation for studying distributions by missingness pattern. National Research Council, The Prevention and Treatment of Missing Data in Clinical Trials , National Academies Press, 2010 — authoritative treatment of estimands, sensitivity analysis, and the limits of unverifiable missingness assumptions. Kalshi, “Market Lifecycle” — official distinctions among trading, close, determination, amendment, and settlement lifecycle fields; accessed July 10, 2026. Kalshi, “Get Market Orderbook” — official order-book response structure and Yes/No bid representation; accessed July 10, 2026. Polymarket, “Resolution” — official proposal, challenge, dispute, and final-resolution process; accessed July 10, 2026. Polymarket, “Orderbook” — official CLOB book representation and market-data endpoint; accessed July 10, 2026. UMA, “Data Verification Mechanism” — official description of optimistic assertions, disputes, and DVM voting; accessed July 10, 2026. Open questions Which venue endpoints expose append-only delisting and suspension histories rather than only current catalog state? What adjacent-book variables are rich enough to make a capture-failure MAR analysis credible during political news spikes? How should a forecast-service utility score value an unavailable quote relative to a confidently wrong forecast without hiding the separate coverage and accuracy components? Can partial-identification bounds use cross-contract coherence without assuming the missing contract shared the same trader access, liquidity, and resolution basis? How frequently do missingness classifications change after independent semantic review, and which audit fields best predict those corrections?

title: Oracle and dispute mechanisms in political prediction markets
deck: Political prediction markets do not merely “look up” an answer: they run an adjudication pipeline whose evidence channels, challenge rights, financial incentives, escalation path, and finality rule determine what claim a contract actually pays on.
headings: The oracle is a procedure, not a source
Eight stages of an adjudication pipeline
text: Political prediction markets do not merely “look up” an answer: they run an adjudication pipeline whose evidence channels, challenge rights, financial incentives, escalation path, and finality rule determine what claim a contract actually pays on. Up: [[Political prediction markets]] Related: [[Political event-contract resolution designs]] · [[Prediction-market resolution risk]] · [[Voids cancellations and postponements in event contracts]] · [[Versioning political event-contract semantics]] The oracle is a procedure, not a source A market rule may name the Associated Press, a state election authority, Congress.gov, or another source. That does not make the source the whole oracle. A source publishes evidence; an adjudication mechanism decides whether the evidence is timely, authentic, applicable to the exact proposition, and sufficient under the contract. It also decides what happens when the source is silent, changes its report, conflicts with another authority, or becomes unavailable. That distinction is especially important in politics. “Candidate X wins” might refer to a media call, certified popular-vote totals, an electoral-vote milestone, congressional counting, or inauguration. Recounts, court orders, faithless electors, replacement nominees, vacancies, ties, and delayed certifications can separate those milestones. A contract’s [[Political event-contract resolution designs|resolution design]] defines the substantive event; its oracle and dispute mechanism defines the process for turning evidence about that event into a payout.
