Date or window Event Status as of 2026-07-10 1 April 2026 Presidential campaign-finance period began Officially confirmed by the CNCCFP and its 2027 guide 18 April 2027 First round Published by the Interior Ministry ; the election-specific convocation decree is still awaited 2 May 2027 Second round, if required Published by the Interior Ministry and also follows constitutionally from a first round on 18 April No later than 7 February 2027 Ordinary convocation decree must be published Derived legal deadline , assuming the first round remains 18 April 5 March 2027, 18:00 Presentations must reach the Conseil constitutionnel Derived legal deadline , subject to the law in force in 2027 and future instructions No later than 26 March 2027 Government publication of the candidate list Derived legal deadline , not a scheduled announcement date 5 April 2027 Official first-round campaign opens Derived legal date under the current implementing decree 17 April 2027, 00:00 Official first-round campaign ends Derived legal date : campaigning closes when Friday 16 April ends 18 April 2027 Ordinary Sunday vote in metropolitan France and most territories Published ballot date ; some overseas and Americas voting normally occurs the preceding Saturday No later than 21 April 2027, 20:00 Conseil makes first-round totals known if no one wins outright Derived outer deadline under the implementing decree 22 April 2027, midnight Deadline for possible withdrawals by runoff-eligible candidates Derived legal deadline 1 May 2027, 00:00 Official second-round campaign ends Derived legal date : campaigning closes when Friday 30 April ends 2 May 2027 Runoff Published ballot date No later than 12 May 2027 Final result must be proclaimed Derived outer deadline if the election is won on 2 May 2 July 2027, 18:00 Campaign accounts due Derived legal deadline , the eleventh Friday after the first round This table is not an election notice. A derived deadline is a transparent calculation from current law and the ministry's published first-round date. It can be useful for planning without being mistaken for a date that the Conseil constitutionnel, Arcom, or the Government has formally appointed. What is actually official now The Interior Ministry's presidential-election portal says the next first round will take place on 18 April 2027 and the second on 2 May 2027 . That is a current official government publication, stronger than a press estimate or a date inferred from past practice. The CNCCFP has independently moved from generic preparation to an election-specific 2027 finance regime: it states that the financing period began on 1 April 2026 , and it published a candidate-and-mandataire guide adopted on 26 March 2026 after an opinion from the Conseil constitutionnel. Those facts do not mean that every instrument for the election already exists. Article 7 of the Constitution says that voting opens on the Government's convocation. Article 1 bis of the 6 November 1962 law now requires the decree convoking electors for an ordinary end-of-term election to be published at least ten weeks before the first round. The decree is therefore not ceremonial. It is the election-specific legal act around which administrations, candidates, courts, broadcasters, and electors can organize. As of this note's cutoff, the ministry page supplies the ballot dates, but a search of the cited official election and legal sources did not identify the 2027 convocation decree, a 2027 Conseil constitutionnel presentation decision, a 2027 Arcom recommendation, or the final administrative circulars and orders. Their absence is expected this far from voting. It nevertheless matters: an article should not say that all 2027 deadlines are “officially announced” merely because they can be calculated. The constitutional skeleton Article 7 provides the durable sequence. In an ordinary election, the new president is elected between twenty and thirty-five days before the incumbent president's powers expire. The Government convokes the electorate. If nobody wins an absolute majority of valid votes in the first round, the second round occurs on the fourteenth day following the first. This makes the ministry's two published dates internally coherent: 2 May is exactly fourteen days after 18 April. It does not by itself explain why 18 April was selected inside the constitutional window. That choice depends on the end of the current presidential powers and the Government's calendar judgment. The future convocation decree should be treated as the definitive election-specific reference for the ordinary schedule. The Constitution also makes the calendar conditional in a deeper sense. Candidate death or incapacity, a vacancy in the presidency, definitive presidential incapacity, or force majeure can activate different clocks. The ordinary April–May calendar is therefore the baseline, not an unalterable natural fact. From the ballot date to candidate qualification Assuming the first round remains Sunday 18 April 2027, the ten-week convocation rule yields Sunday 7 February 2027 as the latest permissible publication date for the decree. “At least ten weeks” is an outer deadline: the Government may publish earlier. Describing 7 February as the decree date would be wrong until a decree actually carries that date. The current version of article 3 of the 1962 law establishes two further relative rules for an ordinary election. Presentations—the formal acts commonly called the 500 parrainages —must reach the Conseil constitutionnel by 18:00 on the sixth Friday preceding the first round . Counting backwards from 18 April gives 5 March 2027 at 18:00 . The Government must publish the list established by the Conseil no later than the fourth Friday preceding the first round, which gives 26 March 2027 . These dates need an explicit legal-version warning. The Légifrance consolidation viewed in 2026 displays article 3 in a version effective only through 31 December 2026, with enacted changes scheduled afterward. The correct operational rule is the version in force during the 2027 presentation window, plus the Conseil's election-specific decision and forms. The March dates are sound calculations from the currently displayed relative rules, but campaign teams should not substitute this note for the 2027 legal package. Publication “no later than” the fourth Friday also does not promise that the candidate list will appear precisely on 26 March. In 2022 the list appeared earlier than the outer limit. Once it appears in the Journal officiel , a person who was the subject of at least one presentation has only the specialized, very short challenge period described by the implementing decree. A party nomination, declaration, poll showing, or claimed tally of promised signatures does not start this clock and does not confer [[The 500 presentations in French presidential elections|ballot qualification]]. The official campaign clock The official campaign is much shorter than the political campaign. Under article 10 of the 8 March 2001 implementing decree, it opens on the second Monday preceding the first round . For an 18 April vote, that is 5 April 2027 . It ends on the eve of voting at zero hour, meaning 00:00 on Saturday 17 April —in ordinary language, at the end of Friday 16 April. The phrasing matters because “through Saturday” would add a day that the rule does not allow. If a runoff is required, its official campaign opens when the names of the two eligible candidates are published in the Journal officiel . Possible withdrawals must reach the Conseil constitutionnel by midnight on the Thursday after the first round: 22 April 2027 on the present assumptions. The second-round campaign closes at 00:00 on Saturday 1 May , when Friday 30 April ends. This official-campaign window governs a concentrated set of propaganda and equality rules. It should not be confused with campaign-finance accounting, which began a year earlier, or with audiovisual pluralism, which operates before the official campaign. During the official period, qualified candidates receive equality of speaking time and airtime in comparable programming conditions; before it, the presidential regime uses equity. [[Media pluralism and speaking time in French elections]] explains why those terms are not interchangeable. The exact 2027 media calendar remains partly unissued . Arcom will need an election-specific recommendation establishing its monitoring periods, reporting rhythm, services covered, attribution rules, and practical method. The 2022 recommendation began an anticipatory equity regime on 1 January 2022, but that precedent does not itself appoint 1 January 2027 or any other date for the coming contest. The legally derived April equality window is firmer than any attempt to copy Arcom's entire 2022 timetable forward by five years. Likewise, the official broadcasts made available on public-service radio and television depend on Arcom decisions after consultation with candidates. The implementing framework guarantees equal durations and minimum totals, but it does not yet provide a 2027 broadcast grid. Dates for clips, recordings, draws, submissions, and transmission are future operational facts. Voting, counting, and proclamation The national labels “18 April” and “2 May” conceal territory-specific voting times. The 1962 framework provides Saturday voting for specified overseas territories and for polling in the Americas so that local electors do not vote after metropolitan results have begun to circulate. If the ordinary scheme applies, affected electors would vote on 17 April and, if necessary, 1 May , local time. Election-specific instruments must still be checked for the exact 2027 territorial implementation; [[Overseas France in presidential elections]] should own the full territorial explanation. After each round, departmental or equivalent recensement must be completed by midnight on the Monday following the vote, and records are sent to the Conseil constitutionnel. If nobody wins in the first round, article 29 of the implementing decree requires the Conseil to make each candidate's totals known by 20:00 on Wednesday at the latest— 21 April 2027 under the ordinary calendar. This is an outer deadline, not a forecast of the exact announcement hour. The Conseil constitutionnel, not an election-night television projection, decides the authoritative totals. It also informs the Government of the two candidates eligible to remain after the withdrawal window, leading to immediate publication in the Journal officiel . After the round in which an absolute majority is obtained, the Conseil must proclaim the election's result within ten days. If the runoff on 2 May decides the election, the outer limit is therefore 12 May 2027 . The actual proclamation may come earlier, as past practice suggests; “by 12 May” is the legally derived claim. The handover date should not be guessed from the ballot date alone. The elected person's term and the incumbent's expiration of powers interact with the Conseil's proclamation and the constitutional continuity rules. The proclamation decision and later official announcements will establish the operational transition. Campaign finance is a different calendar The CNCCFP's 2027 guide makes the earliest major election-specific date unusually clear: the finance period opened on 1 April 2026 . From this period, funds collected and electoral expenses incurred for the campaign must be handled and recorded under the applicable rules. A prospective candidate may need a financial agent long before the Conseil constitutionnel decides whether that person appears on the ballot. The end point also differs from the media and propaganda clocks. Presidential candidates must deposit their accounts by 18:00 on the eleventh Friday following the first round . Starting with the first Friday after 18 April and counting eleven yields 2 July 2027 at 18:00 . This deadline applies to presidential candidates under the organic regime even though the winner may have been known for two months and even though eliminated candidates stopped competing after the first round. The CNCCFP then examines the accounts through an adversarial procedure and decides whether to approve, reform, or reject them and what reimbursement is due. The 1962 law gives the commission six months from deposit to decide. Publication of accounts and decisions follows statutory rules; those later dates depend on actual deposits, decisions, possible proceedings, and the precise law then in force. They should not be compressed into a single fictional “campaign ends” date. See [[French presidential campaign finance]]. Dates still awaiting election-specific instruments At least six operational layers remain open as of 10 July 2026: the Government's decree convoking electors and any associated territory-specific provisions; the Conseil constitutionnel's 2027 decision and instructions for presentations, electronic or paper transmission, validation, publication, and challenges; the final candidate list and its actual publication date; Arcom's presidential recommendation, its pre-campaign start date, measurement phases, and reporting deadlines; decisions for official public-service broadcasts and the campaign-control commission's practical calendar; and ministry circulars, polling-station arrangements, overseas and expatriate voting details, and administrative deadlines not fixed directly by the relative rules above. Future instruments can add detail without changing the constitutional skeleton. A legal amendment, however, could change a calculated deadline. Every live calendar should therefore store three fields: the source instrument, the date on which that source was checked, and whether the displayed date is quoted or derived. Vacancy, incapacity, and candidate contingencies An early presidential vacancy or definitive incapacity does not simply move every ordinary date forward by the same amount. Article 7 requires a new election between twenty and thirty-five days after the vacancy opens or incapacity is declared definitive, unless the Conseil constitutionnel finds force majeure. The Government convokes electors without delay. The candidacy timetable is compressed: under the current organic framework, presentations arrive by 18:00 on the third Tuesday before the first round, and the candidate list is published at least fifteen days before it. The Senate president normally performs interim presidential functions, but the point for the calendar is that the ten-week ordinary convocation rule no longer applies. Separate rules protect the integrity of an election already underway. In the seven days before the presentation deadline, the death or incapacity of a person who publicly announced a candidacy within the preceding thirty days permits the Conseil to postpone the election. Death or incapacity of a qualified candidate before the first round requires postponement. If one of the two best-placed first-round candidates is affected before possible withdrawals, or one of the two remaining candidates is affected before the runoff, the entire electoral operation begins again. The Conseil may extend constitutional deadlines in these cases, but article 7 caps the rescheduled vote at thirty-five days after its decision. If postponement carries voting beyond the normal expiration of the incumbent's powers, the incumbent remains until a successor is proclaimed. Thus “18 April and 2 May” describes the ordinary scheduled path, not every constitutionally possible 2027 path. Why it matters Calendar errors change political analysis. Calling someone an “official candidate” before the candidate list confuses aspiration with legal qualification. Treating the finance period as beginning with the official campaign erases a year of regulated fundraising and spending. Copying the 2022 Arcom dates into 2027 turns precedent into a nonexistent decision. Calling every calculated deadline “official” hides which authority can still change or implement it. The sequence also determines incentives. Presentation gathering must culminate a month and a half before voting; strict audiovisual equality arrives only during the final two weeks; and finance accountability continues after the result. A candidate can be politically prominent but legally unqualified, legally qualified but weakly covered during an equity phase, or eliminated while still owing a full campaign account. The calendar is therefore the connective tissue among [[2027 French presidential candidate field]], campaign finance, media rules, voting, adjudication, and succession. Sources Primary and official sources, all accessed 2026-07-10: French Interior Ministry, The presidential election and information for electors — published first- and second-round dates and basic constitutional framing. Légifrance, Constitution of 4 October 1958, article 7 — two-round interval, ordinary end-of-term window, convocation, vacancy, incapacity, postponement, and force-majeure rules. Légifrance, Law no. 62-1292 of 6 November 1962, consolidated text — ten-week convocation rule, presentations, candidate-list publication, campaign accounts, and special voting provisions; the version applicable in 2027 must be rechecked. Légifrance, Decree no. 2001-213 of 8 March 2001, consolidated text — campaign opening and closing, withdrawals, recensement, and proclamation deadlines. CNCCFP, 2027 presidential election resources and presidential-election category — official confirmation that the finance period began 1 April 2026 and links to the 2027 materials. Légifrance, CNCCFP decision of 26 March 2026 and 2026–2027 candidate guide — election-specific accounting guide, adopted after the Conseil constitutionnel's opinion. Légifrance, Decree no. 2026-273 of 15 April 2026 — recent changes to the presidential implementing decree, a reminder to use the current consolidation rather than a 2022 snapshot. Arcom, 2022 presidential recommendation — authoritative precedent for the distinction between anticipatory equity and official-campaign equality; not a 2027 appointment. Open questions On what date will the Government publish the convocation decree, and will it alter any operational assumption behind the derived table? What exact version of article 3 of the 1962 law will govern presentations in March 2027 after the scheduled consolidation changes? When will Arcom's election-specific monitoring begin, and how will its 2027 phases account for the broader pluralism doctrine adopted since 2022? Which dates will the Conseil constitutionnel choose for presentation forms, publication batches, candidate-list challenges, and result announcements inside the legal outer limits? What exact local dates and administrative arrangements will apply across overseas France and consular polling stations?

title: 2027 French presidential election
deck: France's 2027 presidential election is scheduled for April 18 and May 2, but its outcome will be filtered through ballot-access, campaign-finance, two-round, and parliamentary institutions that polling alone cannot capture.
text: France's 2027 presidential election is scheduled for April 18 and May 2, but its outcome will be filtered through ballot-access, campaign-finance, two-round, and parliamentary institutions that polling alone cannot capture. Up: [[Politics]] · Related: [[Political prediction markets]] Current state The Interior Ministry lists the first round for April 18, 2027 and the runoff for May 2. Candidate labels must distinguish discussed, exploring, declared, party-selected, and formally qualified people. The Commission des sondages expanded systematic scrutiny in April 2026 to surveys of political popularity and notoriety because they increasingly shape the pre-campaign. Its notice archive is the canonical source for field dates, sample, sponsor, tested slate, and adjustments. The archive added four presidential-tagged notices dated July 8: two political-image/barometer studies and two studies framed around Marine Le Pen's appeal conviction and possible candidacy. These notices establish what was tested, not that any candidacy status changed. Scenario comparison still requires extracting field dates, sample, mode, sponsor, wording, and tested slate. Institutional foundations [[How the French presidential election works]] explains eligibility, presentations, the two rounds, voting, results, disputes, and exceptional cases. [[The 500 presentations in French presidential elections]] explains the elected-official presentation system, territorial-spread rule, publication, verification, and its political effects. [[French presidential campaign finance]] explains the mandataire, accounting period, lawful resources, spending ceilings, reimbursement, CNCCFP review, and appeal. [[From the Élysée to a National Assembly majority]] explains why a presidential victory does not itself create a legislative majority and distinguishes cohabitation from a hung Assembly. Coverage map The institutional layer includes [[Media pluralism and speaking time in French elections]], [[Official campaign period in French presidential elections]], [[Official presidential election propaganda]], [[Cohabitation in the Fifth Republic]], [[French presidential nomination mechanisms]], [[Presidential powers in the Fifth Republic]], and [[Presidential vacancy and succession in the Fifth Republic]]. The [[2027 French presidential election calendar]] separates published ballot dates from derived deadlines and future instruments. Administrative coverage follows [[Administration of French presidential elections]], [[Mayors and communes in French presidential elections]], [[Voter registration for French presidential elections]], [[French citizens abroad in presidential elections]], [[Prison voting in French presidential elections]], [[Accessibility in French presidential elections]], [[Identity checks in French presidential elections]], [[Ballot secrecy and proxy voting in French presidential elections]], [[Polling hours in French presidential elections]], and [[French presidential polling-station operations]] through [[Vote counting in French presidential elections]]. [[Turnout reporting in French presidential elections]] explains the metropolitan noon and 5 p.m. checkpoints; [[Election-night results in French presidential elections]] separates estimates, provisional totals, and legal proclamation. [[Election observation in French presidential elections]], [[Electoral fraud controls in French presidential elections]], and [[Electoral offenses in French presidential elections]] map scrutiny, integrity safeguards, and the distinct criminal-law catalogue. [[Constitutional Council review of presidential elections]] and [[Presidential election complaints and annulments]] explain supervision, complaints, remedies, and final proclamation. The living-election layer uses one canonical [[2027 French presidential coalition map]], [[2027 French presidential candidate field]], and [[2027 French presidential polling tracker]] rather than repeated snapshots. [[How to read French presidential polls]] supplies the methods needed to compare those scenarios. Analytical notes separate [[2027 French presidential first-to-second-round transfers]], [[2027 French presidential territorial coalitions]], [[2027 French presidential issue agenda]], [[Abstention in French presidential elections]], [[Blank and invalid votes in French presidential elections]], and [[Overseas France in presidential elections]] so incompatible questions and electorates do not collapse into one forecast page. Why it matters French first-round polling depends strongly on the tested candidate slate. A durable tracker must compare like scenarios and preserve the institutional difference between declaration and qualification. Sources French Interior Ministry presidential-election portal — accessed July 9, 2026. Commission des sondages communiqués — April 15, 2026 methodological notice; accessed July 9, 2026. Commission des sondages 2027 notice index — accessed July 9, 2026. Commission des sondages 2027 notice index — notices 10220–10223 dated July 8, 2026; accessed July 9, 2026. Open questions Which tested candidate scenarios are genuinely comparable across institutes? When will direct declarations and party decisions justify a candidate-status ledger?

title: 2027 French presidential first-to-second-round transfers
deck: First-to-second-round “transfers” are conditional choices made after the presidential field collapses to two candidates; they are not votes owned by eliminated candidates, and abstention and blank or null ballots are part of the transfer matrix rather than statistical leftovers.
headings: Four mechanisms that produce a runoff choice
What 2022 demonstrates—and what it does not
How to read a 2027 transfer poll
text: First-to-second-round “transfers” are conditional choices made after the presidential field collapses to two candidates; they are not votes owned by eliminated candidates, and abstention and blank or null ballots are part of the transfer matrix rather than statistical leftovers. Up: [[2027 French presidential election]] · Related: [[2027 French presidential coalition map]] · [[How to read French presidential polls]] · [[How the French presidential election works]] The French phrase reports de voix invites a misleading picture: votes collected by an eliminated candidate in the first round appear to be poured into one of two runoff containers. No institution performs that operation. Each voter faces a new ballot, on a new day, after endorsements, conflict, campaign events, and information about the first-round result. Some choose finalist A, some finalist B, some abstain, and some cast a blank or null ballot. Others had already voted strategically in round one, so even the first-round label may imperfectly describe their political attachment. For 2027, transfer analysis should therefore answer a conditional question: given a specified pair of finalists, how might the electorates observed or measured in round one divide among the two names and non-expression? It should not answer “which party’s votes belong to whom?” No 2027 first-round electorate exists yet, the qualified field is not settled, and hypothetical runoff surveys remain scenario tests. Historical evidence can identify mechanisms and plausible constraints, but it cannot supply a fixed 2027 matrix. The transfer matrix For an electorate that chose candidate i in round one, a complete runoff accounting has at least four destinations: p_{iA}+p_{iB}+p_{i,\mathrm{abstain}}+p_{i,\mathrm{blank/null}}=1. Poll releases often combine the last two destinations with refusal or uncertainty into non exprimé . That is useful for showing how much of the first-round group has not selected a finalist, but it is not identical to eventual abstention. A respondent who declines to state a runoff choice may later vote; a respondent who currently says “blank” may abstain; and a late campaign event may move someone between the finalists. An election-night survey can separate reported abstention from blank/null voting more directly, but it remains a survey estimate rather than a count of linked individual ballots. The final runoff total can be represented as the sum of each first-round electorate multiplied by its destination rate, plus the behavior of people who did not cast an expressed first-round vote but participate in the runoff. That last term matters. Published “transfer” tables centered on named first-round candidates can omit first-round abstainers who mobilize in round two, while some first-round voters demobilize. Turnout is not a conserved quantity. Official results establish aggregate flows, not individual ones. France uses a secret ballot; the Ministry of the Interior and the Conseil constitutionnel publish totals by round and territory, but those totals do not reveal how the same person voted twice. A transfer matrix is consequently estimated from surveys, panel reinterviews, ecological patterns, or a combination. The method must be named because each supports a different claim. Four mechanisms that produce a runoff choice Proximity and program Some voters choose the finalist they regard as closer on ideology, program, social interests, or governing style. This is the most intuitive mechanism, but “distance” is multidimensional. A first-round voter may place economic redistribution, immigration, Europe, climate, institutional reform, or presidential temperament at different weights. Two voters who chose the same first-round candidate can therefore rank the finalists differently. Candidate identity matters independently of party family. The [[2027 French presidential coalition map]] is best read as a set of coalition projects rather than permanent blocs precisely because adjacent parties do not create identical electorates. A runoff featuring a conventional conservative, a post-Macron centrist, a left candidate, or an RN candidate would activate different dimensions and produce different transfer patterns. Substituting one figure for another inside the same broad family changes the counterfactual. Blocking and the republican front A voter may choose primarily to prevent the other finalist from winning. In France this is often discussed as a front républicain , a barrage , or a vote “against” rather than “for.” These expressions should not be treated as synonyms for an automatic anti-RN majority. The strength and direction of blocking depend on who the two finalists are, how each is perceived, the conduct of the inter-round campaign, and whether voters consider the recommended alternative acceptable. Elite endorsements can provide information and moral or strategic cues, but they do not bind voters. An eliminated candidate can recommend a vote for one finalist, say that not one vote should go to another, refuse to endorse, or consult supporters. Each message leaves multiple compliant behaviors. “Do not vote for B” can mean vote for A, abstain, or cast a blank ballot. Reporting the instruction as a guaranteed transfer erases that choice. The intensity of rejection matters as much as left–right placement. A voter can dislike both finalists but perceive one as uniquely dangerous; another can see them as different versions of an unacceptable system and opt out. Campaigns try to convert negative motivation into participation, yet harsh first-round attacks can make a later unity appeal less credible. Strategic first-round voting Transfer tables classify voters by what they did in round one, not necessarily by their preferred candidate. A vote utile can concentrate voters behind the contender thought most able to qualify. In that case the apparent first-round electorate is already a coalition of core supporters, late strategic voters, and people voting against exclusion. Its runoff behavior may be unusually heterogeneous. This creates a selection problem. Suppose voters from several left parties converge late on one candidate to try to reach the runoff. A table labeled with that candidate’s name may be read as the behavior of a coherent party electorate even though part of it arrived for strategic reasons. The same logic can operate among right, center, or nationalist contenders. Stable candidate labels do not guarantee stable electorate composition. Mobilization and non-expression The choice is not only between finalists. Participation responds to closeness, perceived stakes, campaign legitimacy, practical access, and whether either option feels tolerable. Blank voting communicates that the voter participated but selected neither finalist; a null ballot is invalid, whether intentionally or accidentally. Official statistics distinguish abstentions, blank ballots, null ballots, and expressed votes. A poll that collapses them should say so. Non-expression is often concentrated among the supporters of eliminated candidates whose preferences do not map neatly onto the runoff. It can decide the result without appearing as a “transfer” to either finalist. The proper question is not merely who wins a plurality within an eliminated electorate, but how much of that electorate supplies expressed votes at all. What 2022 demonstrates—and what it does not The 2022 Macron–Le Pen rematch offers an observed case, not a template for 2027. The Conseil constitutionnel proclaimed 18,768,639 votes for Emmanuel Macron and 13,288,686 for Marine Le Pen in the second round, or 58.55% and 41.45% of expressed votes. It also recorded 13,655,861 abstentions, 2,233,904 blank ballots, and 805,249 null ballots. The distinction is substantive: the winner’s percentage of expressed votes does not mean 58.55% of registered voters endorsed him, and millions participated without selecting either finalist. Ipsos and Sopra Steria’s election-weekend survey, fielded April 21–23 among 4,000 registered adults, estimated how first-round electorates divided. Among people identified as first-round Jean-Luc Mélenchon voters, 42% reported choosing Macron and 17% Le Pen; 24% abstained and 17% reported a blank or null ballot. Among Yannick Jadot voters, the estimated destinations were 65% Macron and 6% Le Pen, with 16% abstention and 13% blank/null. Among Valérie Pécresse voters, they were 53% Macron and 18% Le Pen, with 15% abstention and 14% blank/null. Among Éric Zemmour voters, 73% reported Le Pen. These estimates illustrate fragmentation within every eliminated electorate; they are not administrative counts or linked-ballot observations. Pre-election measures also moved. In the Ipsos daily barometer published through the Commission des sondages, estimated intentions among Mélenchon’s first-round voters varied during the inter-round period. On 15 April, the table showed 28% Macron, 16% Le Pen, and 56% non-expressed; by 22 April it showed 33%, 19%, and 48%. The election-weekend survey later estimated 42%, 17%, and 41% split between abstention and blank/null. Differences in timing, design, and the meaning of “non-expressed” prohibit a clean claim that nine percentage points mechanically “switched” to Macron. They do show why an early matrix is not a final allocation. The 2022 history supplies several durable lessons. The Mélenchon electorate was pivotal but not unitary. The Jadot and Pécresse electorates leaned toward Macron while retaining meaningful non-expression. The Zemmour electorate leaned strongly toward Le Pen, yet even a strongly aligned adjacent electorate did not transfer unanimously. Macron’s and Le Pen’s own first-round electorates also had different retention and participation rates. A runoff coalition is assembled through both expansion and core remobilization. The history does not establish stable coefficients such as “a left voter transfers to the center at 42%” or “a nationalist-right voter transfers to RN at 73%.” In 2027 the candidate identities, records, issue agenda, party endorsements, first-round strategic composition, and governing context will differ. Even a repeated Macron–Le Pen pairing would not be the same experiment; Macron cannot seek a third consecutive term, and the alternatives inherit neither his electorate nor his rejection profile automatically. How to read a 2027 transfer poll Start with the pairing. “Second-round voting intention” is meaningless without two names. A poll testing several alternative finalists contains several separate counterfactual elections, not interchangeable measurements of party blocs. A respondent can choose the center against one opponent and abstain against another. Next identify the base. Before the first round, a table may cross a hypothetical first-round intention with a hypothetical second-round intention in the same interview. That is a scenario matrix, not a transfer from an observed vote. After the first round, the base can be reported first-round vote, which is more concrete but still subject to recall and sample size. A late-campaign or election-weekend survey samples reported behavior close to voting; a panel can recontact the same people and observe within-person changes, but attrition and panel conditioning require attention. Then preserve the non-expressed category. A topline such as 52–48 is normally calculated among respondents who select a finalist. If 20% of the relevant base is non-expressed, the displayed gap describes the other 80%, not the full group. For a first-round electorate of 100 respondents, a 60–40 split among expressers could mean 48 for A, 32 for B, and 20 non-expressed. Reporting only 60–40 makes the transfer look more complete and certain than it is. Inspect sample sizes. Even a large national survey can contain small subgroups for minor first-round candidates. If 8% of a 1,500-person relevant sample supports a candidate, the unweighted subgroup is roughly 120 before further filters; weighted effective size may be smaller. A five-point change inside that subgroup can reflect few interviews. The notice should provide the total sample, relevant voting-intention base, quotas or recruitment, field dates, mode, adjustment criteria, and question wording. [[How to read French presidential polls]] gives the full audit routine. Finally, distinguish three products: Stated intention: what respondents say under a named pairing at a particular time. Estimated behavioral transfer: an inference about how first-round groups may divide, with sampling and modelling uncertainty. Forecast: a prediction of the actual runoff result, requiring assumptions about qualification, late change, turnout, and error. A poll directly observes only the first product. A transfer model and forecast add assumptions. They should be labeled rather than smuggled into a confident verb such as “will go.” A practical 2027 ledger A useful transfer tracker should keep one row per institute, fieldwork window, and named pairing. It should record: sponsor and exact notice URL; interview dates and publication date; mode, total sample, and subgroup bases where disclosed; whether the first-round category is a hypothetical intention, recalled vote, or observed panel response; shares for finalist A, finalist B, abstention, blank/null, undecided, and refusal, without silently redistributing missing categories; exact candidate slate and question wording; whether figures are among all eligible respondents or only expressed choices; endorsements or major events that occurred during fieldwork; revisions to weighting, turnout filters, or candidate configuration. Comparisons should remain within the same institute and design when possible. Cross-institute convergence can strengthen an inference, but averaging incompatible “non-expressed” definitions or candidate slates produces false precision. Territorial results can test whether a proposed story is plausible, yet aggregate departmental change cannot prove individual movement: different people may enter and leave the electorate, an error known as ecological inference. Uncertainty specific to 2027 The largest uncertainty comes before any transfer percentage: who qualifies for round two. As of 10 July 2026, no official 2027 candidate list exists. Prospective coalitions are still choosing candidates and selection methods. A hypothetical matrix can be informative about acceptability or rejection, but its political meaning is conditional on a first round that may never occur. The second uncertainty is compositional. A candidate who becomes the focal vote utile can absorb voters from adjacent first-round options. Their apparent electorate then changes just as analysts begin estimating its transfers. Poll-to-poll variation can reflect this changing mixture rather than persuasion between finalists. The third is turnout. Early surveys ask people to imagine abstention many months ahead. Expressed certainty at that horizon measures present engagement as much as eventual behavior. Runoff turnout also depends on the first-round outcome and the inter-round campaign, neither of which can be observed in advance. The fourth is coalition asymmetry. Formal party support may secure activists, elected officials, finance, and legitimacy while moving relatively few voters; an endorsement-free strategic convergence can move many voters without creating a governing coalition. The presidential transfer matrix therefore should not be used as a shortcut to predict the subsequent National Assembly majority. [[From the Élysée to a National Assembly majority]] is a separate question. Why it matters Qualification is only the first coordination test in a two-round election. A candidate can reach the runoff with a cohesive minority and then fail to expand; another can enter with a less enthusiastic base but become the acceptable blocking choice for several eliminated electorates. Analysts who add first-round party percentages miss abstention, blank voting, candidate-specific rejection, and the fact that strategic voters have already crossed party lines. Transfer evidence also shapes the first round. Claims that one contender has larger réserves de voix can influence endorsements and vote utile , thereby changing the electorate whose later transfer is being forecast. This feedback makes methodological restraint politically important. A noisy subgroup table can become a narrative of “electability,” while a large non-expressed share can be hidden behind a crisp two-candidate topline. For 2027, the defensible approach is conditional and plural: publish matrices for exact pairings, retain every non-expression category, identify whether the first-round base is observed or hypothetical, and treat endorsements as inputs rather than commands. Historical patterns establish possibilities, not entitlements. Voters transfer themselves. Sources Conseil constitutionnel, Decision proclaiming the results of the 2022 presidential second round , 27 April 2022, official votes, abstentions, blank ballots, null ballots, and expressed-vote shares, accessed 2026-07-10. Commission des sondages, Ipsos/Sopra Steria daily barometer notice, wave 33 , 22 April 2022, original questionnaire, bases, method, and inter-round transfer table, accessed 2026-07-10. Commission des sondages, Ipsos/Sopra Steria daily barometer notice, wave 27 , 15 April 2022, original inter-round transfer table, accessed 2026-07-10. Ipsos, Second tour: profil des abstentionnistes et sociologie des électorats , 24 April 2022, Ipsos/Sopra Steria election-weekend survey analysis and estimated first-round destinations, accessed 2026-07-10. Ipsos, L’Enquête Électorale 2022 , panel design, runoff question wording, and final pre-first-round wave, accessed 2026-07-10. Commission des sondages, Consultation database for polling notices , statutory notice archive, accessed 2026-07-10. Légifrance, Law no. 77-808 of 19 July 1977 on the publication and diffusion of certain opinion polls , consolidated legal framework for electoral-poll disclosure and oversight, accessed 2026-07-10. Open questions Which institutes will publish stable 2027 pairing series with subgroup bases large enough to interpret first-round electorates? Will notices distinguish abstention, blank/null voting, undecidedness, and refusal, or combine them as non exprimé ? How much will late vote utile change the composition of the leading first-round electorates before transfer estimates become politically salient? Can a high-quality recontact panel distinguish genuine individual movement from changing cross-sectional composition without excessive attrition? Which endorsements will affect expressed runoff choice, and which will mainly affect turnout or blank voting?

title: 2027 French presidential issue agenda
deck: France enters the 2027 presidential pre-campaign with a broad cost-of-living concern, sharply polarized security and immigration concerns, a newly salient crisis of political competence, and no settled hierarchy that can be read straight from one poll.
headings: Five quantities that must not be collapsed
Ownership: who is trusted or associated with an issue
Differentiation: what choice the candidates make visible
Intensity: how strongly the issue can move behavior
Uncertainty: what the measurement cannot yet tell us
Purchasing power, prices, and living standards
Political life, competence, and democratic control
Debt, social protection, and public services
Europe, defense, and the international environment
How issue competition may shape the blocs
What to watch through the campaign
text: France enters the 2027 presidential pre-campaign with a broad cost-of-living concern, sharply polarized security and immigration concerns, a newly salient crisis of political competence, and no settled hierarchy that can be read straight from one poll. Up: [[2027 French presidential election]] Related: [[2027 French presidential candidate field]] · [[2027 French presidential coalition map]] · [[How to read French presidential polls]] · [[2027 French presidential territorial coalitions]] The direct reading As of 10 July 2026, four conclusions are defensible. First, purchasing power and the cost of living form the widest common pressure . In a June 2026 YouGov forced-choice question, purchasing power led at 24%; an open-ended CEVIPOF–L'ObSoCo survey in January put inflation/cost of living at 27%, tied with security and political life. The European Parliament's spring 2026 Eurobarometer adds intensity: 44% of French respondents expected their living standard to fall, the highest national result reported in its release. Second, security and immigration are more politically owned than purchasing power . They are not synonymous: security can mean crime, narcotics, disorder, terrorism, policing, or justice, while immigration can mean borders, asylum, integration, nationality, or labor. Both are disproportionately mentioned on the right, especially the radical right. That gives candidates there a ready-made interpretive frame, but not necessarily exclusive electoral ownership. Third, political dysfunction is itself an issue rather than background noise. Open responses put “political life” among the three leading concerns in January 2026. CEVIPOF's February confidence barometer found only 22% trusted politics, 15% trusted parties, and 18% trusted the president; 80% said the government was “navigating by sight.” A presidential contender therefore competes not only over taxes, borders, schools, or climate, but over whether the state can decide and execute at all. Fourth, the agenda remains unusually available for reframing . Purchasing power is widely felt but weakly owned; environmental concern looks modest in single-choice national rankings but can become intense through energy, transport, food, housing, heat, or disaster; debt is salient enough to constrain promises but can be narrated as either fiscal responsibility or austerity. A campaign event, budget shock, security crisis, climate disaster, international conflict, or candidate breakthrough could reorder the hierarchy. These claims describe the pre-campaign, not the final 2027 ballot. They do not identify a nominee, predict a winner, or assume that a concern automatically produces a vote. Five quantities that must not be collapsed An “issue agenda” sounds like a ranked list. It is better understood as five related but distinct measurements. Salience: what comes to mind Salience is the prominence of a problem when respondents are asked what matters. It depends heavily on the question. An open prompt records what people retrieve without cues. A closed list makes every supplied category available. A single-choice question forces trade-offs; a multiple-choice question records breadth. “For you personally,” “for France,” “for the EU,” and “for your vote” are different objects. This explains why CEVIPOF–L'ObSoCo and YouGov should not be treated as a trend line. The former used open-ended responses and coded themes; the latter asked respondents to select one principal political concern from a list. January's three-way 27% tie and June's 24–15–13 ranking can both be true. They answer different questions with different instruments. Ownership: who is trusted or associated with an issue Ownership asks which party or candidate voters associate with handling a problem. High salience without ownership creates an opportunity; ownership without salience creates a niche. CEVIPOF–L'ObSoCo's January interpretation is revealing: security was mentioned by 49% of Reconquête sympathizers, 41% of LR sympathizers, and 34% of RN sympathizers, against 9% among LFI sympathizers. Immigration reached 65% among Reconquête and 44% among RN sympathizers. The survey therefore shows partisan association and constituency intensity—not proof that all voters trust those parties to govern well. Purchasing power is the opposite case. Respondents across camps use similar language—prices, wages, and daily life—but no single diagnosis dominates. The left can frame it through wages, benefits, rents, public services, and price regulation; the center through employment, investment, targeted relief, and European coordination; the right through taxes, energy, work incentives, and spending control; the radical right through tax cuts, protection, energy sovereignty, and immigration-linked distribution. Shared pain does not produce shared causation. Differentiation: what choice the candidates make visible An issue can be salient but electorally inert if every candidate offers indistinguishable language. Differentiation concerns the policy conflict voters can actually perceive. On purchasing power, useful dividing lines include universal versus targeted relief, wage-setting versus tax reduction, deficit-financed support versus fiscal consolidation, regulated prices versus market adjustment, and national discretion versus EU constraints. On security, the choices include police and prison capacity, prevention, judicial procedure, local policing, and civil-liberties safeguards. On immigration, they include asylum administration, legal migration, removal capacity, nationality law, integration, and France's relationship to European law. No complete official 2027 programs existed across the field by the as-of date. Existing party texts are directional evidence, not a substitute for future manifestos. LFI's evolving Avenir en commun , reopened to contributions in May 2026, retains social redistribution and ecological planning as organizing principles. Other party families continue to develop their offers and selection mechanisms. Candidate rhetoric should not be promoted into a settled program merely because a campaign has begun. Intensity: how strongly the issue can move behavior A respondent may mention an issue without changing vote choice over it. Intensity includes personal exposure, emotional force, perceived threat, willingness to trade off other goals, and capacity to mobilize or demobilize. Eurobarometer's June release helps distinguish intensity from ranking: 44% in France expected their living standard to decline, while financial circumstances were one of the two leading components of quality of life EU-wide. The 2025 CEVIPOF–Ipsos Fractures françaises survey likewise reported that more than half in France had difficulty making ends meet. Intensity is often uneven. Housing costs bite renters and young adults differently; fuel and car dependence divide territories; pension reform affects age cohorts differently; public-service closure has a spatial pattern; immigration and insecurity perceptions vary by ideology and local experience. See [[2027 French presidential territorial coalitions]]. National averages can conceal electorates for whom a lower-ranked issue is nearly dispositive. Uncertainty: what the measurement cannot yet tell us Uncertainty is substantive as well as statistical. The YouGov notice reports a sample of 1,002 and illustrates margins of error around percentages, but sampling error is only one limit. Category wording, mode, coding, field dates, nonresponse, news context, and the difference between sympathizers and prospective voters matter too. A two-point movement across differently worded polls is usually less meaningful than it looks. The largest uncertainty is temporal. Eleven months before the expected election, candidacies and coalitions are unsettled, and many voters are not processing detailed platforms. Issues become electoral through campaigns: contenders select dimensions, attach causes and villains, demonstrate competence, and link several concerns into a story. The eventual agenda will be co-produced by events, media, institutions, and candidate supply. The leading issue complexes Purchasing power, prices, and living standards Purchasing power is the safest candidate for the agenda's broad base. YouGov's June single-choice result put it first at 24%, ahead of insecurity at 15%, immigration at 13%, debt/public finance at 12%, and social protection at 9%. The European Parliament's winter 2025 survey found 56% in France wanted inflation, rising prices, and cost of living prioritized; its spring 2026 survey reported especially strong French pessimism about future living standards. But “purchasing power” is a container, not a policy. It can absorb food, energy, fuel, rent, mortgage rates, wages, pensions, benefits, taxes, and service charges. That breadth makes it resilient and politically difficult. A promise that benefits one group may be financed by another; short-term price relief can conflict with deficit reduction or climate investment; nominal wage gains may not address housing scarcity. The candidate who owns the issue will need a credible distributional account: who gains, who pays, through which institution, and on what timetable. Political life, competence, and democratic control The unusual feature of the 2026 agenda is that political life itself ranks beside material and security concerns in spontaneous responses. This category plausibly combines disgust with parties, instability, blocked governing, ethical complaints, institutional reform, and a desire for clearer authority. It should not be reduced to a generic anti-incumbent mood. CEVIPOF's February evidence indicates a competence and accountability crisis: 20% thought political leaders tried to keep promises, 80% believed the government improvised, and 88% believed failed elected officials did not accept responsibility. Yet 82% remained attached to democracy; 79% wanted more frequent referendums, and 77% supported citizens' conventions. The demand is therefore not simply withdrawal. It mixes rejection of national political performance with interest in direct participation, local proximity, and visible control. This issue is weakly owned because nearly every challenger can denounce the status quo. Differentiation requires specifying whether reform means a Sixth Republic, proportional representation, referendums, decentralization, stronger executive authority, parliamentary coalition-building, or merely a change of personnel. Institutional promises also interact with [[Presidential powers in the Fifth Republic]] and the possibility that the president lacks a compatible Assembly majority. Security, justice, and order Security has high spontaneous salience and strong right ownership. It also connects to unusually trusted institutions: CEVIPOF found 77% confidence in the gendarmerie and 73% in the police in February 2026. That combination—concern about safety alongside trust in coercive institutions—can favor offers emphasizing capacity and authority. Still, the category is unstable. A survey label may merge everyday crime with organized narcotics, public disorder, terrorism, or judicial delay. Policy ownership can also be contested: a candidate may agree that security matters while arguing that housing, schools, mental health, prevention, customs, or court resources are the missing mechanisms. The campaign's decisive question is less whether candidates say “security” than which diagnosis becomes dominant and whether voters believe the proposed instruments can be delivered. Immigration, borders, and national membership Immigration remains below purchasing power in the June single-choice national ranking but is much more intense among radical-right sympathizers. This gives RN and Reconquête a mobilizing axis and pressures LR and parts of the center to respond. It also means national salience can understate campaign impact: an issue concentrated among highly motivated voters may shape turnout, candidate selection, and agenda-setting beyond its average percentage. Ownership is not the same as agreement on implementation. Border control, asylum adjudication, expulsions, legal labor migration, family reunification, integration, secularism, and nationality raise different administrative and legal questions. Proposals may encounter constitutional, European, fiscal, or capacity constraints. A credible comparison must test concrete measures rather than code every reference to immigration as one position. Debt, social protection, and public services Debt and public finances reached 12% in YouGov's June redressed result, level with immigration within ordinary sampling uncertainty. Social protection followed at 9%, while education was 3% and health 1% under the forced single-choice design. It would be a mistake to conclude that schools and hospitals do not matter. Forced choice compresses service concerns into whichever immediate category respondents prioritize, while trust in hospitals remained 79% and in social security 68% in CEVIPOF's February barometer. Fiscal constraint can become the bridge connecting the whole agenda. Tax cuts, pension commitments, defense spending, ecological investment, police recruitment, and public-service restoration compete for resources. The campaign can frame debt as a threat to sovereignty and future generations, or frame consolidation as a threat to protection and demand. This is a differentiation engine: detailed financing may expose conflicts that broad valence language conceals. Climate, energy, housing, and adaptation Environment registered only 6% in YouGov's single-choice June list and 7% in the 2025 open-ended CEVIPOF–L'ObSoCo wave. That is evidence of low top-of-mind ranking under those instruments, not evidence that ecological policy is electorally irrelevant. Climate is often experienced through other categories: electricity and fuel prices, farm incomes, housing renovation, transport, insurance, water, heat, and industrial employment. The issue's campaign strength will depend on bundling. An abstract emissions target may lose a forced choice against prices; a proposal framed as cheaper energy, thermal comfort, resilience, or industrial sovereignty can enter through a higher-salience door. Conversely, opponents can link climate policy to taxes, restrictions, or territorial unfairness. This makes climate a prime example of differentiation exceeding measured salience. Europe, defense, and the international environment Foreign and European affairs scored 3% in YouGov's June single-choice result. Yet EU-level surveys show strong concern about war, irregular migration, security, and defense. National presidential power over diplomacy and defense also gives external shocks unusual agenda-setting potential. Low routine salience therefore carries high event risk. Candidates may connect international issues to domestic ones through energy prices, industrial policy, agricultural trade, migration, defense budgets, or European fiscal rules. The analytical rule is to preserve levels: an answer about what the EU should prioritize is not directly a forecast of a French presidential vote. How issue competition may shape the blocs The radical right benefits when immigration and insecurity dominate and when living costs can be integrated into a protectionist or national-preference story. Its challenge is to convert ownership of grievance into confidence about governing, financing, and legal execution. The conventional right has potential ownership of security and debt but faces differentiation pressure from the radical right and competition over economic competence. Its strategic problem is to make fiscal restraint compatible with public demand for protection. The left has strong programmatic differentiation on wages, redistribution, services, and ecological planning, but coalition divisions can blur ownership. Its opportunity is to connect material hardship to a coherent social-ecological diagnosis; its risk is that security and immigration split its electorate or displace its chosen terrain. The center and post-Macron space can claim administrative experience, Europe, and economic modernization, but the incumbent record makes competence a liability as well as an asset. With trust in the government and economic management low in June's YouGov barometer, a continuity-adjacent contender must explain both what was achieved and why a new governing method would work. These are strategic inferences, not voter-transfer estimates. They should be read alongside [[2027 French presidential first-to-second-round transfers]] and [[2027 French presidential candidate field]]. What to watch through the campaign A useful tracker should preserve the exact question and measure at least five series separately: open-ended national concern; forced single-choice concern; multiple-choice personal concern; party or candidate competence; and issue-specific vote importance. It should also record field dates, sponsor, mode, sample, population, response options, coding, and original notice. Substantively, watch whether purchasing power acquires a dominant explanation; whether political dissatisfaction attaches to a concrete institutional remedy; whether security and immigration remain distinct; whether debt rises when budgets become more specific; whether climate is activated by events or bundled into energy and prices; and whether international conflict shifts attention toward presidential competence. The key campaign signal will not be a one-point change in a generic ranking. It will be a durable alignment of high salience, strong intensity, recognizable ownership, and visible policy differentiation . That is when an issue becomes capable of reorganizing the race. Why it matters Candidate polls show who respondents select in hypothetical slates; the issue agenda helps explain why those coalitions might hold or move. It also guards against two recurring errors: assuming the most-mentioned problem determines every vote, and assuming the party most associated with a problem has already persuaded the electorate about its solution. For 2027, the central contest is not simply “economy versus immigration.” It is whether contenders can link material insecurity, public order, national membership, ecological transition, fiscal constraint, and democratic control into a credible account of state capacity. Because purchasing power and political dysfunction are broad but weakly owned, the agenda remains more open than a static ranking suggests. Sources CEVIPOF–L'ObSoCo, Priorités françaises , wave 2 (29 January 2026) — open-ended salience and partisan differences; accessed 2026-07-10. Commission des sondages, YouGov–HuffPost political barometer notice, June 2026 — questionnaire, method, sample, margins, and full concern results; accessed 2026-07-10. CEVIPOF, Political Confidence Barometer, wave 17 (9 February 2026) — institutional confidence, governing competence, and democratic-reform attitudes; accessed 2026-07-10. CEVIPOF, Fractures françaises , wave 13 (October 2025) — material strain, decline, anger, and issue context; accessed 2026-07-10. European Parliament, Spring 2026 Eurobarometer release (29 June 2026) — French living-standard expectations and EU-level priorities; accessed 2026-07-10. European Parliament, Winter 2025 Eurobarometer release (25 March 2025) — French cost-of-living priority and living-standard expectations; accessed 2026-07-10. CEVIPOF, “La démocratie à l’épreuve de la fracture cognitive” (18 June 2026) — information environment and orientation in the developing campaign; accessed 2026-07-10. La France insoumise, program consultation announcement (20 May 2026) and L'Avenir en commun program portal — directional program evidence, not a completed cross-party 2027 comparison; accessed 2026-07-10. Open questions Will a common 2027 survey measure open salience, issue competence, vote importance, and policy trade-offs in the same sample? Which contenders will publish sufficiently costed programs to distinguish symbolic ownership from deliverable policy? Does “political life” resolve into institutional reform, anti-incumbency, corruption, instability, or a broader demand for state competence? How much do issue intensities differ by age, income, education, territory, and likelihood of voting once identical questions are used? Which shock—budget, security, climate, war, or government collapse—is most likely to reorder the agenda before the official campaign?

title: 2027 French presidential polling tracker
deck: As of July 10, 2026, the defensible polling signal is that the tested Rassemblement national option leads every published first-round scenario, while the identity and number of center and center-left candidates materially change the contest behind it; no poll yet measures the eventual official ballot.
headings: A leading RN line, not a certified finalist
The center's candidate count changes its apparent strength
The left is plural, and stability can be deceptive
Runoff polls belong in a separate lane
What the tracker cannot tell us
text: As of July 10, 2026, the defensible polling signal is that the tested Rassemblement national option leads every published first-round scenario, while the identity and number of center and center-left candidates materially change the contest behind it; no poll yet measures the eventual official ballot. Up: [[2027 French presidential election]] · Related: [[How to read French presidential polls]] · [[2027 French presidential candidate field]] · [[2027 French presidential coalition map]] · [[2027 French presidential first-to-second-round transfers]] What this tracker does This is a scenario ledger, not a polling average. It records original institute releases only when the electorate, candidate slate, field dates, question, and published denominator can be recovered. A row represents a counterfactual ballot offered to respondents. It does not establish that everyone named will run, qualify, or appear together on the ballot established by the Conseil constitutionnel. The central finding is robust but narrower than a forecast. Across the original first-round intention surveys examined here from late May through July 8, the tested RN name received roughly the low-to-high thirties and led each tested configuration. The second-place ordering was much less settled. Édouard Philippe generally performed better when Gabriel Attal was absent; Attal likewise rose when Philippe was absent. Jean-Luc Mélenchon was comparatively stable across many slate changes. Raphaël Glucksmann polled above François Hollande when each was tested as the non-LFI center-left option in otherwise similar Ipsos configurations. These are conditional contrasts, not predictions of nominations or transfers. The tracker deliberately does not blend Marine Le Pen and Jordan Bardella. Nor does it average a poll containing Philippe and Attal with one containing only one of them. Those substitutions change the choice set. [[2027 French presidential candidate field]] separately records verified political status, which a poll cannot confer. Latest comparable first-round snapshots The table emphasizes scenarios that expose the most consequential slate choices. Percentages are shares of published expressed voting intentions, not shares of all registered respondents. A dash means the name was not tested in that scenario. The compact display is not permission to erase them analytically. Nathalie Arthaud, Fabien Roussel, Marine Tondelier, Nicolas Dupont-Aignan, and Éric Zemmour were present in the cited configurations, with exact slates preserved in the original reports. Omitting a smaller option in a future poll could redistribute measured support and would break comparability. What can be compared The cleanest within-study experiment is the substitution or removal of one candidate while the institute, fieldwork, sample construction, question, and most of the slate remain fixed. In Toluna Harris Interactive's July survey, Philippe moved from 14% when Attal was also offered to 20% when Philippe was the sole tested center option. Attal moved from 8% with Philippe present to 16% without him. The RN line stayed between 34% and 36%, while Mélenchon remained at 16%. This supports an inference about fragmentation in the tested center: offering two adjacent names divided expressed intentions much more than it changed the leading line. Ipsos showed the same mechanism in May, though its levels differed. With Glucksmann and Bardella held constant, Philippe measured 13% alongside Attal and 17.5% without him; Attal measured 8.5% alongside Philippe and 14.5% without him. Ipsos also showed Glucksmann moving from 11% with both center names present to 13–14% when only one was present. Choice-set effects therefore can cross bloc boundaries: removing a center candidate does not mechanically send every supporter to the remaining center candidate. The Glucksmann–Hollande comparison is also meaningful only within matched configurations. In the eight Ipsos scenarios, Glucksmann received 11–14%, whereas Hollande received 7–8%; Mélenchon stayed at 13–13.5%. In July Toluna Harris measured Glucksmann at 11% and Hollande at 8% in the corresponding one-center scenarios, with Mélenchon at 16% in both. This is evidence that respondents reacted differently to the two named center-left options under those survey conditions. It is not a primary, a forecast of a common-left selection process, or evidence that either has qualified. Cross-institute changes require greater caution. Ipsos screened registered respondents who said they were certain to vote and reported results among expressed choices, with scenario bases around 1,037–1,079 out of a 1,500-person registered sample. Toluna Harris began with 1,592 registered respondents from a broader 1,837-person adult sample and published expressed-vote shares while separately offering blank, null, and abstention responses. Ifop interviewed 984 registered respondents drawn from 1,095 adults and calculated published scores using its turnout and political adjustments; only about 624–625 certain voters expressed a first-round choice in the two scenarios. Differences of a few points across those designs may reflect screening, adjustment, timing, and slate—not opinion change alone. The strongest current signals A leading RN line, not a certified finalist The most persistent result is the RN's first-round lead. Ipsos measured Bardella at 33.5–36% across its six Bardella scenarios and Le Pen at 31–32% across two Le Pen scenarios in late May. Toluna Harris measured Le Pen at 34–36% across five July scenarios. Ifop measured Le Pen at 36% in both July scenarios. An OpinionWay survey fielded June 30–July 1 and published July 3 also placed Bardella at 36% in a broad slate, according to its original Commission-filed report. Persistence across different slates and institutes is more informative than any single decimal. Yet “leading the tested first round” is not “will reach the runoff.” The eventual candidate, legal eligibility, valid presentations, campaign, turnout, and official ballot remain unresolved. The distinction is especially important when institutes switch between Le Pen and Bardella around political or judicial events. Combining their lines would conceal the very contingency being tested. The center's candidate count changes its apparent strength The center is not measured as a fixed bloc. A Philippe-only scenario produces a different object from a Philippe-plus-Attal scenario. In July Toluna Harris, their combined score with both present was 22%, compared with Philippe's 20% alone or Attal's 16% alone. In May Ipsos, the pair combined for 21.5% in the matched Glucksmann/Bardella configuration, versus Philippe at 17.5% or Attal at 14.5% alone. Adding individual scores therefore overstates what a unified candidacy automatically inherits, while citing only the stronger one-center scenario understates the cost if both run. The within-survey recall tables explain the structure without proving future behavior. In July Toluna Harris's Glucksmann/Philippe-only scenario, 55% of respondents recalling a Macron first-round vote in 2022 chose Philippe among those expressing a 2027 choice; 12% chose Glucksmann, 12% Le Pen, and 10% Retailleau. When Philippe and Attal were both offered, those recalled Macron voters divided 40% Philippe and 21% Attal. Because vote recall is weighted and self-reported, these are modeled subgroup estimates, not a voter file. They nevertheless show why nomination structure is central to polling interpretation. The left is plural, and stability can be deceptive Mélenchon's 13–13.5% across the May Ipsos permutations and 16% across all five July Toluna Harris permutations looks stable. But stability under a limited set of substitutions does not mean his electorate, turnout, or transfer prospects are fixed. The surveys retained several left options, and the population expressing a choice can change between designs. Glucksmann's higher result than Hollande in matched tests is a named-candidate contrast, not the result of a shared selection mechanism. No first-round table should be converted into a single “left total” without defining the political proposition. Mélenchon, Glucksmann or Hollande, Roussel, Tondelier, and Arthaud represent distinct candidacies and organizations. Their voters may coordinate, fragment, abstain, or reconsider depending on the actual field. [[2027 French presidential coalition map]] owns those organizational questions. Runoff polls belong in a separate lane First-round support and second-round performance answer different questions. Ifop's July 7–8 survey tested Le Pen at 54% to Philippe's 46%, 55% to Attal's 45%, and 70% to Mélenchon's 30%, among expressed choices. Non-expression was substantial: 28.2%, 29.2%, and 38.9% of registered respondents respectively did not express a choice in those pairings. Toluna Harris separately offered abstention and blank/null responses; in its July survey, blank/null plus abstention amounted to 22% for a Philippe–Le Pen pairing, 25% for Attal–Le Pen, and 34% for Mélenchon–Le Pen before the reported expressed-vote normalization. Those figures are scenario stress tests. They do not show that Le Pen will qualify, that the named opponent will qualify, or that today's non-expression will persist through a real two-week runoff campaign. They also cannot be compared directly with a table that excludes abstention from the question or groups blank and null choices differently. [[2027 French presidential first-to-second-round transfers]] explains why subgroup transfer matrices are not administrative flows. Method and comparability ledger Series Sample and mode Published voting base Adjustment/comparability rule Toluna Harris Interactive for M6/RTL, Jul. 7–8 Online; 1,592 registered respondents within 1,837 adults; quotas and weighting by sex, age, occupation, region, and past electoral behavior Expressed votes; blank, null, and abstention separately offered Compare its April, May, and July reminders only where the full slate and procedure match; fieldwork began after the July 7 appeal verdict and Le Pen declaration Ifop for LCI/Le Figaro, Jul. 7–8 Online; 984 registered within 1,095 adults; quotas including education; political weighting using 2022 first-round recall Expressed choices after turnout/adjustment; about 624–625 certain voters expressed in each first-round scenario Keep Philippe and Attal scenarios separate; do not equate NSP with abstention Ipsos bva for CESI/Le Parisien, May 27–28 Online; 1,500 registered adults; quotas; 2022 first-round recall adjustment Certain-to-vote expressed choices; scenario bases 1,037–1,079 Eight scenarios permit strong within-study contrasts; Le Pen and Bardella rows remain separate OpinionWay for Le Figaro, Jun. 30–Jul. 1 Online; 1,000 metropolitan French adults, quota sample; original notice/report Published expressed first-round intentions Useful as a broad-slate snapshot, but geographic universe and slate must match before trend comparison Three rules govern future updates. First, preserve the exact slate. Second, record the denominator and non-expression categories. Third, treat repeated waves as comparable only when the institute confirms the same method and the underlying question has not changed. A chart should break—not bridge—when one of those conditions fails. What the tracker cannot tell us Polls do not observe qualification, campaign finance, media equality, tactical withdrawals, or a governing majority. They also do not eliminate ordinary survey uncertainty. The institutes' illustrative 95% intervals are roughly two to three points for many reported national shares, before adding design effects, turnout-model error, political weighting, and uncertainty created by a hypothetical slate. Subgroup estimates are less precise. Nor should publication timing be confused with causal identification. The July surveys were fielded immediately after a major legal and political event involving Le Pen. They measure opinion after that event, but without a clean experiment they cannot isolate how much any result was caused by the judgment, her declaration, news coverage, other contemporaneous events, or sampling variation. The right reading as of July 10 is therefore layered: the RN line leads persistently; the competition behind it is highly sensitive to who is offered; Philippe has generally been the strongest tested center option when only one center name is present; Mélenchon remains competitive for second place in some broad fields; and runoff resistance varies sharply by opponent and non-expression. Every clause remains conditional on a ballot France does not yet have.
