title: Ballot secrecy and proxy voting in French presidential elections
deck: French presidential voting combines a tightly staged secret-ballot procedure with a limited form of proxy voting: the proxy casts a physical ballot in the principal’s polling station, under the same secrecy rules, but the law cannot technologically verify that the proxy followed the principal’s private instruction.
headings: What protects secrecy—and what secrecy means
Limits on how many proxies one elector may hold
Cancelling, replacing, and arriving in person
How the proxy vote is executed
text: French presidential voting combines a tightly staged secret-ballot procedure with a limited form of proxy voting: the proxy casts a physical ballot in the principal’s polling station, under the same secrecy rules, but the law cannot technologically verify that the proxy followed the principal’s private instruction. Up: [[2027 French presidential election]] The distinction matters. France does not generally allow an ordinary presidential elector to send a ballot from home, vote online, or hand a completed ballot to another person. Voting is personal and takes place at the ballot box. A procuration changes who performs the physical act when an elector cannot attend: the absent elector is the mandant (principal), and the chosen elector is the mandataire (proxy). The mandate is recorded before polling day; the proxy then goes to the principal’s assigned polling station and votes there. This note describes the law and official procedure in force on 10 July 2026 . It is a baseline for the [[2027 French presidential election]], not a guarantee that every administrative or digital rule will remain unchanged by polling day. The ordinary physical voting sequence The legal architecture begins with a terse rule in article L59 of the Electoral Code: the ballot is secret. Article L62 and the Interior Ministry’s voter guidance turn that principle into a physical sequence designed to separate three facts: who is entitled to vote, whether only one ballot envelope enters the box, and which candidate the elector chose. The elector arrives at the assigned polling station. Registration on that station’s electoral roll is checked. Identity is controlled under the applicable rules. The electoral card is useful but is not itself always indispensable; in communes of 1,000 inhabitants or more, an accepted identity document is required, while in smaller communes the presiding officer must still be able to establish identity. The elector takes an official envelope and ballots. Interior Ministry guidance tells the elector to take several candidates’ ballots, because visibly taking only one could disclose the choice. An elector may instead use a ballot received with the official election materials at home, but the envelope used at the station remains the controlled vehicle placed in the box. The elector enters the voting booth alone. Passage through the isoloir is compulsory. Article L62 requires the elector, without leaving the polling room, to go alone to the screened area and place the chosen ballot in the envelope out of sight. The Code requires one booth per 300 registered electors or fraction thereof. Booths must protect the elector’s choice without concealing the voting operations themselves from public observation. Identity is confirmed at the ballot box. Official guidance describes the presiding officer or deputy reading the presented identity document or electoral card aloud. The point is to connect the eligible person to the next act without learning the content of the vote. The single-envelope rule is checked without contact. The elector shows that only one envelope is being carried. Article L62 expressly says the president observes this without touching the envelope. The elector personally inserts it into the transparent ballot box. The elector signs the roll. The signature on the liste d’émargement records that the voting entitlement has been used. It records participation, not choice. If the elector cannot sign, another elector chosen by that person may sign with the prescribed handwritten indication that the elector cannot sign personally. These steps deliberately create a chain of public controls around a private decision. Eligibility, identity, the single envelope, deposit in the box, and the signature are observable. The selection and enclosure of the ballot are not. The transparent box lets participants and observers see that envelopes enter the box while leaving their contents hidden. Public counting after the close of polls then converts anonymous envelopes into totals; the voter roll and ballots are never designed to be linkable voter by voter. What protects secrecy—and what secrecy means Secrecy is more than permission not to tell anyone one’s choice. The system tries to make a provable vote difficult. Taking several ballots and entering the booth interrupt visual inference. The standardized opaque envelope prevents observers from reading the ballot. The ban on the president touching the envelope limits discretionary handling at the decisive moment. Personal insertion prevents an official from substituting or withholding the envelope. Finally, the signature roll and the ballots are distinct records: one proves that a named elector voted; the other contributes anonymously to the count. This design protects both privacy and freedom. If a voter cannot reliably prove how they voted, a buyer, employer, family member, party organizer, or coercer has less ability to enforce a demanded choice. The booth therefore serves the collective integrity of the election even when an individual says they do not care about privacy. Accessibility rules qualify, rather than abandon, personal voting. Article L64 permits an elector with a disability that makes it impossible to introduce the ballot or operate a voting machine to be assisted by an elector of their choice; if the elector cannot sign, the chosen person may sign with the statutory notation. That helper is not a proxy exercising an absent person’s franchise. The voter is present and chooses assistance for the acts they cannot perform. Because assistance necessarily creates some knowledge or opportunity for influence, it is a carefully bounded exception and one reason the Code penalizes fraudulent attempts to circumvent both article L64 and the proxy rules. Creating a proxy Article L71 now states that any elector may, on request, vote by proxy. There is no longer a need to prove a work, health, travel, or similar reason. The essential legal and administrative controls instead concern the identities of the principal and proxy, the proxy’s electoral capacity, the duration and election covered, and formal validation. The principal chooses a proxy who enjoys electoral rights and is registered on an electoral roll. Since 1 January 2022, the proxy need not be registered in the same commune as the principal. This makes selection easier, but it does not move the vote: on polling day the proxy must travel to the principal’s polling station. Official guidance offers two principal routes: Through Maprocuration , the principal enters the request online and ordinarily validates identity in person at a police station, gendarmerie brigade, or consulate, presenting the registration reference and identity document. Through the paper Cerfa process , the principal completes and validates the form before an authorized authority, including specified police, gendarmerie, judicial, consular, or prefecturally designated public locations, with identity evidence. The principal must identify the proxy accurately. The online route accepts the proxy’s national elector number and date of birth, or the required civil-status details and voting commune. The official electoral-situation service can be used to check whether a proxy has been given or received. For electors unable to travel because of serious illness or disability, authorized police officers or agents may collect the request at home. The request for travel must be in writing and accompanied by a sworn statement describing the manifest inability to appear. This accommodation concerns creation of the proxy; it does not turn the home into a polling station. Fully digital creation and cancellation have been expanding. As of the 2026 official guidance, a completely dematerialized route is available in defined circumstances to users with a high-assurance France Identité identity whose certification involved an in-person municipal check. The 2024 European and legislative elections served as an experiment, and rules were expanded for the 2026 municipal elections. Because the exact eligibility and scope of this route have changed recently, a 2027 voter should check Maprocuration and Interior Ministry instructions rather than assume the 2026 implementation will carry over unchanged. Timing and duration A request can legally be made close to polling day, but there is an operational difference between submitting it and having it recorded in time. The Interior Ministry urges early action because validation, transmission, and municipal processing take time. If the polling station’s records have not been updated when the proxy appears, the proxy may be unable to cast the principal’s vote. A request received too late for the first round can still operate in the second round if its stated validity includes that round. The principal can establish a proxy for a particular election—both rounds or only one—or for a stated period, normally up to one year from creation. For French citizens resident abroad, a consularly established proxy may last up to three years. These duration options do not give the proxy an unlimited stock of ballots; use remains tied to elections for which the principal is eligible and to the statutory cap on mandates held on the day. Limits on how many proxies one elector may hold Article L73 provides the core rule: one proxy may hold no more than two mandates, only one of which may have been established in France. If the limits are exceeded, the earliest mandates remain valid and later ones are automatically void. In ordinary domestic terms, the practical message is simpler: on election day an elector may hold only one proxy established in France . That person may alternatively or additionally hold mandates established abroad within the legal combinations. Interior Ministry guidance lists: one French-established mandate; one foreign-established mandate; one of each; or two foreign-established mandates. There is a consular-list exception in current official guidance: an elector may hold as many as three mandates if at least one comes from an elector registered on a consular electoral roll, but only one of the three may have been established in France. This is relevant to a presidential electorate that includes French citizens abroad, yet it should not be generalized into a three-proxy domestic rule. The cap is an anti-concentration safeguard. It makes it harder for a party operative, employer, care provider, or local broker to aggregate many votes in one person’s hands. Article L72-1 adds specific protections for adults under legal protection: they vote personally and cannot appoint their court-appointed guardian or defined categories of owners, managers, staff, volunteers, and personal-service workers connected to institutions or services caring for them. Those exclusions target relationships where dependency can undermine free choice. Cancelling, replacing, and arriving in person Article L75 gives the principal a continuing right to revoke the mandate and to issue a new one. Official guidance says cancellation uses the same competent authorities and form framework as creation, and Maprocuration can also be used. Recent high-assurance digital procedures may permit fully online cancellation where eligibility conditions are met. Revocation should still be completed early enough to reach the electoral records. Merely telling the proxy privately not to vote is not the same as formally cancelling the recorded mandate. Likewise, appointing someone new must be regularized through the official process; personal messages do not change the polling station’s authorization record. There is also a polling-day priority rule. Under article L76, the principal may vote personally if they arrive before the proxy has used the mandate. If the principal votes first, the proxy cannot later use it. If the proxy has already voted for the principal, the principal cannot cast a second ballot. This is not a recall of an already cast vote: once the proxy’s envelope has entered the anonymous ballot box, secrecy makes it impossible to identify and retrieve. Death or loss of civic rights by the proxy automatically cancels the mandate under article L77. A change in the principal’s commune of registration does not, according to Interior Ministry guidance, itself invalidate an otherwise valid proxy, though the voter should verify current registration and polling-station information. How the proxy vote is executed The proxy goes to the principal’s polling station and presents only the proxy’s own identity document. The proxy does not need the principal’s electoral card or another document belonging to the principal. Poll workers check the recorded mandate. Article L74 then brings the act back inside article L62’s ordinary voting process. After the mandate is confirmed, the proxy takes an electoral envelope, uses the booth, presents the single envelope, and personally places it in the ballot box. The proxy signs the roll opposite the principal’s name , in ink, recording use of that principal’s entitlement. If the proxy also votes personally at the same station, that is a separate exercise of the proxy’s own entitlement and a separate signature. The proxy is expected to follow the principal’s instructions, but the secret ballot produces an unavoidable limit: neither the principal nor polling officials can observe the marked or selected ballot inside the booth, and the deposited envelope cannot later be linked to the proxy. The state verifies authorization and prevents double voting; it does not verify obedience to a candidate instruction. Proxy voting therefore rests on personal trust. The principal should choose someone reliable and communicate clearly, but no lawful receipt can prove performance. Fraud controls and residual risks Controls operate at several layers. Identity validation at creation reduces impersonation. The electoral register and national elector identifiers reduce mistaken attribution. Formal transmission to the municipality puts the mandate on the polling record. Capacity and number limits constrain accumulation. At the station, the proxy’s identity and recorded mandate are checked, and the signature opposite the principal’s name creates an auditable record that the authorization was used. The first-vote rule blocks a second ballot by the principal or proxy. Criminal law backs those controls. Article L111 punishes fraudulent maneuvers intended to violate the disability-assistance rule or articles L71–L77 on proxies by reference to the penalties in article L107. More broadly, article L116 reaches fraudulent maneuvers that violate or attempt to violate ballot secrecy, impair the sincerity of the poll, obstruct operations, or change results. These provisions do not make manipulation impossible, but they make proxy abuse an electoral offense rather than a private disagreement. The main residual risk lies before the booth: coercion or deception in choosing a proxy, pressure on a dependent principal, unauthorized creation using compromised identity credentials, or a trusted proxy deliberately voting differently. The system’s answer is not surveillance inside the booth, because that would destroy secrecy. It uses identity assurance, restricted proxy capacity, vulnerable-person exclusions, revocation, the principal’s right to vote first, auditable use of the mandate, and penalties. This is a deliberate tradeoff: a secret ballot can verify that an authorized proxy cast a ballot, not which ballot was cast. Why it matters for 2027 In a close two-round presidential election, proxy voting can preserve participation for travelers, ill or disabled voters, people with work or family constraints, and citizens whose trusted proxy lives in another commune. The reform removing the need to justify an absence and the growth of Maprocuration lower procedural barriers. But late processing, misunderstanding about where the proxy must vote, and misplaced trust can still disenfranchise an elector in practice. The subject is also fertile ground for misleading claims. A digital request is not an online presidential ballot. A proxy registered elsewhere cannot vote for the principal at the proxy’s own station. Holding a mandate does not allow the proxy to bypass the booth or carry in a completed envelope. And a proxy vote does not create two votes for the proxy: it uses the principal’s distinct entitlement and is signed against the principal’s name. For election-integrity analysis, secrecy and auditability should not be treated as opposites. France makes the use of an entitlement auditable through identity checks and signatures, while deliberately making the content of the choice unlinkable. Proxy voting preserves that same boundary. The hard policy question is whether identity and authorization controls remain strong and accessible as creation becomes more digital—without creating a trace that would reveal the vote itself. What final operational deadline will municipalities recommend for each 2027 round, especially for requests validated abroad? title: Blank and invalid votes in French presidential elections
deck: Blank and invalid ballots are acts of participation but not suffrages exprimés : since 2014 France reports them separately, yet neither enters the denominator that decides a presidential candidate's percentage or victory.
headings: What French law counts as blank
The 2014 change—and what it did not change
Blank and invalid votes are not abstention
Why second rounds often attract attention
How to interpret the numbers without overclaiming
text: Blank and invalid ballots are acts of participation but not suffrages exprimés : since 2014 France reports them separately, yet neither enters the denominator that decides a presidential candidate's percentage or victory. Up: [[2027 French presidential election]] Related: [[How the French presidential election works]] · [[Abstention in French presidential elections]] · [[2027 French presidential first-to-second-round transfers]] The distinction in one table Category What the elector does Counted among voters? Counted among suffrages exprimés ? Separately reported nationally since 2014? Blank ( blanc ) Returns an empty envelope or an envelope containing a blank ballot Yes No Yes Invalid ( nul ) Returns material that violates ballot-validity rules—for example, certain altered, annotated, non-regulatory, or contradictory ballots Yes No Yes Abstention Does not cast a ballot and does not sign the polling register No No Yes, as the difference between registered electors and voters Valid vote for a candidate Returns a valid official ballot for one candidate Yes Yes Yes These are administrative categories, not reliable opinion labels. A blank ballot is the clearest available way to participate without selecting a candidate, but the count does not disclose why it was cast. An invalid ballot may be accidental, expressive, or procedural. Abstention can reflect rejection, indifference, incapacity, absence, registration problems, or a strategic choice. Any political interpretation therefore begins with the count and must not pretend that the count is a survey. What French law counts as blank Article L65 of the Electoral Code governs the count. Its post-2014 rule says that blank ballots are counted separately and attached to the official report. They receive a special mention in the published result but do not enter the determination of suffrages exprimés . The article also treats an envelope containing no ballot as a blank ballot. This definition matters because France does not normally place an official “none of the above” paper on the table. The elector can create a legally blank vote by depositing an empty envelope or, subject to the applicable material rules, a blank paper. The secrecy of the ballot means officials observe the paper or empty envelope at the count, not the elector's motive. A blank vote is consequently a valid act of electoral participation but not a valid choice between candidates. In everyday English, “valid vote” can mean any properly cast ballot. French result tables use a narrower decisive category: exprimés are the votes attributed to candidates. That terminological difference is the source of many mistaken percentage calculations. What makes a ballot invalid Article L66 lists ballots that do not enter the result. It covers ballots without a sufficient designation, ballots through which voters identify themselves, papers found in the box without an envelope or in a non-regulatory envelope, ballots written on colored paper, ballots or envelopes bearing internal or external marks of recognition, and ballots or envelopes carrying insulting statements about candidates or third parties. Other presidential-election rules and official instructions govern such problems as non-official or altered candidate papers. The exact ground for rejection should therefore be checked against the rule applicable to that ballot, not inferred from a generic label. Article L65 also addresses envelopes with multiple papers. Multiple identical ballots for the same candidate count only once. If an envelope contains ballots for different candidates, the vote is invalid. Rejected ballots and non-regulatory envelopes are attached to the polling-station record, countersigned, and marked with the reason for rejection. This documentary trail allows later electoral review. The legal difference is therefore not “protest” versus “mistake.” It is a difference in ballot form. Blank describes a recognized absence of candidate choice; invalid describes a ballot that cannot be credited under the rules. A voter who writes a political message across a ballot may intend a protest, but the resulting paper is classified by its legal characteristics, not by a poll worker's theory of intent. The 2014 change—and what it did not change Law no. 2014-172 of 21 February 2014, effective 1 April 2014, changed the reporting architecture. It amended Article L65 to require blank ballots to be counted separately, annexed to the polling record, and specially mentioned in results. It removed “blanks” from the opening wording of Article L66, which had grouped blank and invalid ballots together among ballots excluded from the count. The reform recognized the blank vote statistically. It did not make blank ballots suffrages exprimés . It did not add a “blank” competitor to the presidential ballot, establish a threshold at which an election must be rerun, or reduce the winning candidate's share of expressed votes. The candidate percentage remains: \text{candidate share among expressed votes} =\frac{\text{candidate votes}}{\text{votes for all candidates}}. The law's first nationwide use was the 2014 European election, not a presidential election. The 2017 presidential election was therefore the first presidential contest conducted under the separate-count rule. That date creates a genuine series break. Before the reform, national tables commonly combined the two categories as blancs et nuls . A pre-2014 combined total cannot generally be decomposed into a blank series and an invalid series from the published national result alone. Researchers should either compare the combined category consistently across time, restrict separate-category comparisons to elections held under the new regime, or locate sufficiently granular archival records whose definitions and coverage are documented. Relabelling an old blancs et nuls number as “blank votes” overstates what the source knows. The denominator ladder French election tables can place several legitimate percentages beside the same count. They answer different questions. Let: R = registered electors ( inscrits ); A = abstentions; V = voters ( votants ); B = blank ballots; N = invalid ballots; E = expressed votes credited to candidates. Ignoring small reconciliation issues caused by scope or later adjudication, the accounting identities are: V=R-A and E=V-B-N. From these come three different rates: Turnout is V/R . It includes people who cast blank and invalid ballots. Blank share of voters is B/V ; invalid share of voters is N/V . These show the composition of deposited ballots. Blank share of registered electors is B/R , while candidate support among registered electors is candidate votes divided by R . These rates incorporate abstention into the baseline. There is no ordinary “blank share of expressed votes” because blank ballots are excluded from E . Some commentators nevertheless divide B by E as an analytical ratio. That can be calculated, but it should be labelled explicitly rather than presented as an official vote share. The Ministry of the Interior's national 2022 second-round table illustrates the ladder. It reports 48,752,339 registered electors, 35,096,478 voters, 2,233,904 blank ballots, 805,249 invalid ballots, and 32,057,325 expressed votes. Thus blank ballots were 4.58% of registered electors and 6.37% of voters; invalid ballots were 1.65% of registered electors and 2.29% of voters. The two candidates' official shares—58.55% for Emmanuel Macron and 41.45% for Marine Le Pen—sum to 100% because their denominator is the 32,057,325 expressed votes, not all voters. This is not statistical sleight of hand. It follows the legal question the runoff decides: which candidate received a majority of votes validly attributed to candidates? But a complete account of the electorate should also report turnout and non-candidate ballots. Candidate share among expressed votes measures the division of valid candidate choices; it does not measure endorsement by all registered citizens or even by everyone who visited a polling station. Blank and invalid votes are not abstention In administrative data, the separation is exact. A voter who deposits a blank or invalid ballot has attended, been checked against the electoral register, voted in secret, and signed the register. The person is therefore a votant . An abstainer is not recorded as having voted. The distinction is analytically important. Turnout studies—including Insee's participation studies—treat a blank or invalid ballot as participation because there is an electoral-register signature. This lets researchers study the decision to attend separately from the decision to support a candidate. A citizen may cross the first threshold but refuse or fail to cross the second. The separation also affects political rhetoric. Saying that blank voters “abstained between the candidates” may be a useful metaphor, but it is not the official category. Combining blank ballots with abstentions produces a broad “no candidate choice” measure, yet it joins behaviors with different observable costs and institutional meanings. Anyone using that composite should publish the formula. Why second rounds often attract attention The second round compresses choice to two candidates. Voters whose first-round preference has been eliminated can support one finalist, vote blank, cast an invalid ballot, or abstain. Blank and invalid totals can therefore illuminate the limits of finalist coalition-building, especially alongside geographic results and survey evidence on [[2027 French presidential first-to-second-round transfers]]. They cannot, by themselves, allocate discontent to a party or ideology. In 2017, when Emmanuel Macron faced Marine Le Pen, the Interior Ministry reported 31,381,603 expressed votes and a 74.56% turnout at the second round. The finalized election is notable for the very large volume of non-candidate ballots under the new separate reporting regime. Comparisons with 2022 are meaningful only if the source perimeter and result stage are aligned—for example, provisional Interior totals should not be silently mixed with the Conseil constitutionnel's definitive proclamation after it has annulled irregular polling-station returns. The Conseil constitutionnel is the constitutional judge of the presidential election and proclaims the definitive result. Its decisions can remove ballots from particular polling stations where irregularities are serious. The Interior archive is indispensable for accessible national and territorial tables; the Council's proclamation is the final legal authority. Small numerical differences between an election-night table and a definitive decision may reflect timing and adjudication, not arithmetic failure. How to interpret the numbers without overclaiming Blank voting is often described as rejection of the available offer. That is plausible at an aggregate level, particularly in a two-candidate runoff, but the category has no recorded reason. It may include principled refusal, equal dislike, indecision, civic attachment to attendance, or a belief that blank voting should itself be recognized. Invalid voting is even less interpretable because intentional spoiling and accidental noncompliance are observationally mixed. Four disciplines improve analysis: First, report counts and denominators together. “Blank voting rose to 6.37%” is incomplete unless it says “of voters.” The same 2022 total is 4.58% of registered electors. Second, preserve the 2014 break. The reform changed classification and publication, so apparent long-run changes can reflect measurement as well as behavior. Separate blank and invalid series begin cleanly only after implementation. Third, distinguish fact from inference. Official returns establish how many ballots entered each category. They do not establish that those voters belonged to the left, the right, or the center, nor whom they would have chosen under another matchup. Transfer surveys can estimate motives and prior votes, but sampling and question wording add uncertainty. Fourth, match geographic and temporal scope. “France entière” may include overseas territories and French citizens abroad, while an Insee study may cover registered French citizens resident in metropolitan France or the overseas departments. Final Council figures and Interior archive figures can refer to different stages. A comparison is only as sound as its common perimeter. Why it matters for 2027 For the [[2027 French presidential election]], blank and invalid votes are best treated as a diagnostic layer between turnout and candidate choice. A high-turnout election can still contain a substantial group that selects no candidate. Conversely, a low blank-ballot share does not prove enthusiasm if abstention is high or if voters choose a finalist defensively. The metric will matter most in three arguments. The first concerns mandate: a winner's constitutional victory is determined among expressed votes, while political claims about social breadth should also examine shares of voters and registered electors. The second concerns coalition transfer: changes between rounds should be decomposed among finalist votes, blank ballots, invalid ballots, and abstention rather than forcing every first-round bloc into a candidate column. The third concerns institutional reform: proposals to count blank ballots as expressed votes, offer an official “none” option, or trigger a new election are not descriptions of current law. They are proposals that would change the rule. A responsible 2027 results note should therefore display, for each round, registered electors, abstentions, voters, blank ballots, invalid ballots, expressed votes, and candidate totals. That full accounting makes candidate percentages intelligible without confusing a legally decisive majority with universal approval. Open questions What definitive blank and invalid totals will the Conseil constitutionnel report for each 2027 round, and which Interior publication stage will provide the closest like-for-like territorial data? Which 2027 post-election surveys will distinguish intentional blank voting from accidental invalid voting with adequate sample sizes? How much of any change from 2022 will remain after controlling for matchup, turnout, electorate perimeter, and result stage?

title: Cohabitation in the Fifth Republic
deck: Cohabitation is the Fifth Republic's constitutional stress test: when the president and a durable National Assembly majority belong to opposing camps, the government answers to that majority and controls most policy, while the president retains the powers the Constitution gives personally to the head of state.
headings: The government, not the president, “determines and conducts” policy
Appointment is constrained by parliamentary survival
Countersignature separates personal from shared powers
Foreign affairs and defence are shared, not a textual presidential reservation
1993–1995: a broad opposition majority and a weakened presidency
text: Cohabitation is the Fifth Republic's constitutional stress test: when the president and a durable National Assembly majority belong to opposing camps, the government answers to that majority and controls most policy, while the president retains the powers the Constitution gives personally to the head of state. Up: [[2027 French presidential election]] · Related: [[From the Élysée to a National Assembly majority]] · [[How the French presidential election works]] What cohabitation is—and is not France does not elect a single executive ticket. Voters elect the president directly, but the government must remain compatible with the separately elected National Assembly. Cohabitation names the situation in which those two electoral mandates point in opposite partisan directions: the sitting president faces an Assembly majority able to sustain a prime minister and government from the opposing camp. The term describes a political configuration, not a special constitutional regime. No article of the 1958 Constitution declares that cohabitation has begun, reallocates a list of ministries, or suspends presidential powers. The same text applies before and after the legislative election. What changes is the political condition under which its powers operate. A president supported by the Assembly majority can usually secure compliance through partisan leadership. A president opposed by a coherent Assembly majority cannot make that majority's government politically dependent on the Élysée. This is why cohabitation must be distinguished from two nearby situations. First, an unpopular president governing with a friendly parliamentary majority is not cohabitation. Political weakness does not itself reverse the partisan alignment. Second, a hung or fragmented Assembly is not automatically cohabitation. Classic cohabitation presupposes an alternative majority capable of supporting a government. If no bloc can assemble or tolerate 289 deputies, the central problem is not a disciplined opposition government confronting the president but the absence of any stable governing coalition. France after the 2024 dissolution illustrated that different problem: divided government without the clear majority structure that existed in 1986, 1993, and 1997. The constitutional mechanism The mechanism begins with four parts of the constitutional text that are sometimes obscured during periods of unified partisan control. The government, not the president, “determines and conducts” policy Article 20 says that the government “determines and conducts the policy of the Nation” and is responsible to Parliament under Articles 49 and 50. Article 21 says that the prime minister directs the action of the government, is responsible for national defence, ensures execution of statutes, and exercises regulatory power subject to the president's specified powers. These clauses give the parliamentary majority a governing instrument of its own. The government can be removed by the National Assembly. Under Article 49(2), a motion of no confidence must meet procedural requirements and win an absolute majority of the Assembly's members; Article 50 then requires the prime minister to tender the government's resignation. The president, by contrast, is not politically responsible to the Assembly. Cohabitation therefore does not make the president a parliamentary opposition leader inside government. It creates a divided executive in which the cabinet's survival turns on Parliament rather than presidential preference. Appointment is constrained by parliamentary survival Article 8 gives the president the formal power to appoint the prime minister. It does not say that the Assembly elects the premier, and it does not expressly command the president to choose the leader of the largest group. Yet the appointment cannot be understood apart from Articles 20, 49, and 50. A president who appointed someone unacceptable to a cohesive opposition majority would invite the government's defeat or make governing impossible. In all three completed cohabitations, the president appointed a prime minister drawn from the victorious opposing majority: Jacques Chirac in 1986, Édouard Balladur in 1993, and Lionel Jospin in 1997. Article 8 also matters in the other direction. The president ends a prime minister's functions only when the prime minister presents the government's resignation. During ordinary aligned government, presidents have often been able politically to induce that resignation. Under cohabitation, the president cannot simply dismiss a prime minister who retains Assembly support. The words of the article become a real constraint once presidential party discipline disappears. Countersignature separates personal from shared powers Article 19 supplies a practical map. Most presidential acts require the countersignature of the prime minister and, where appropriate, responsible ministers. A limited set does not: the first paragraph of Article 8, the referendum power in Article 11, dissolution under Article 12, exceptional powers under Article 16, messages to Parliament under Article 18, and specified referrals or appointments involving the Constitutional Council under Articles 54, 56, and 61. This distinction prevents either simple slogan—“the president still rules” or “the president becomes ceremonial”—from being accurate. The president retains meaningful autonomous levers, including appointment of the prime minister, dissolution subject to Article 12's conditions, and Constitutional Council referrals. But broad administrative and legislative action normally moves through a government that controls ministries, prepares most bills, executes statutes, and holds regulatory authority. Where countersignature is required, the president cannot treat a hostile government as a staff subordinate. The 1986 dispute over ordinances made the point concrete. The Chirac government sought authority under Article 38 to legislate by ordinance on privatisation and other reforms. President François Mitterrand declined to sign several ordinances, forcing the government to pursue ordinary legislation. That episode showed both presidential resistance and its limits: refusal could alter the route and timing, but it did not give the president a general veto over a parliamentary majority's programme. Foreign affairs and defence are shared, not a textual presidential reservation Commentary often speaks of a presidential domaine réservé in foreign affairs and defence. The phrase describes political practice, not a constitutional article assigning those fields exclusively to the president. Article 5 makes the president guarantor of national independence, territorial integrity, treaties, and regular institutional functioning. Article 15 makes the president commander-in-chief and chair of higher defence councils. Article 52 says the president negotiates and ratifies treaties. But Articles 20 and 21 still apply: the government determines national policy, and the prime minister is responsible for national defence. Ministers and the administrative apparatus answer through the government. Cohabitation thus produces negotiation and coordination between two constitutionally armed poles. Presidents maintained a prominent international and defence role in all three cases, but the prime minister did not lose constitutional competence. Where the two agreed, France could present continuity; where they differed, institutional practice required compromise, careful representation, or visible duality. The three historical cohabitations 1986–1988: the precedent is made The first cohabitation followed the March 1986 legislative election. François Mitterrand, a Socialist elected president in 1981 for a seven-year term, remained at the Élysée while the right won the Assembly election. He appointed Jacques Chirac as prime minister. The novelty mattered: before this result, constitutional argument had not been converted into a full operating precedent. The arrangement quickly established enduring rules. Chirac's government pursued a right-wing domestic programme, including privatisation and changes in economic and security policy. Mitterrand used the presidency's textual resources, public speech, and refusal to sign some ordinances to resist parts of that programme. Yet he did not claim a power to remove Chirac while the government possessed parliamentary support. In foreign affairs, both executives remained active, demonstrating that cohabitation would mean shared state representation rather than the president's disappearance. The arrangement ended through elections, not institutional breakdown. Mitterrand defeated Chirac in the 1988 presidential election. He then dissolved the Assembly under Article 12, and the subsequent legislative election produced a relative left majority. The first case therefore proved that opposing executives could complete the interval until the scheduled presidential contest and submit their rivalry back to voters. 1993–1995: a broad opposition majority and a weakened presidency The second cohabitation followed the right's overwhelming victory in the March 1993 legislative election. Mitterrand was again president, nearing the end of his second term, and appointed Édouard Balladur as prime minister. The configuration was less openly combative than the first. Balladur had an exceptionally large parliamentary base, while Mitterrand's political authority was diminished by his camp's electoral defeat and his declining health. The constitutional allocation, however, was not a new model. The government directed domestic policy and possessed the legislative majority; the president retained his office, personal powers, and international role. The difference in atmosphere shows that cohabitation is not a fixed level of conflict. Its operation depends on electoral arithmetic, personalities, the president's remaining time and legitimacy, and whether the prime minister is already competing for the next presidency. This cohabitation ended when Jacques Chirac won the 1995 presidential election. Because the elected president and the existing Assembly majority were then aligned on the right, no immediate legislative election was needed to restore congruence. 1997–2002: dissolution creates the longest case The third cohabitation began differently. President Jacques Chirac already had a supportive right-wing Assembly majority, but in April 1997 he dissolved the Assembly early. The left won the resulting election, and Chirac appointed Socialist leader Lionel Jospin as prime minister. The president's own use of Article 12 had produced the adverse majority. Unlike the two Mitterrand cases, which occupied the final two years of seven-year presidential terms, this cohabitation lasted a full five-year legislature. The Jospin government enacted a substantial domestic agenda, including the statutory 35-hour workweek, universal health coverage, the civil solidarity pact, and further decentralising or social measures. The duration and policy output refute the idea that cohabitation necessarily means paralysis. It can instead generate a clear domestic governing centre—provided the Assembly majority is cohesive—while forcing coordination at the top of the state. The long experience also strengthened the political case for reducing the presidential term from seven years to five. Voters approved the quinquennat in the 2000 referendum. An organic law then placed the 2002 legislative election after the presidential election. Chirac was reelected and his supporters won the Assembly contest. Since then, the paired calendar has tended to align the two majorities, although it does not legally guarantee alignment. What the historical cases establish Three cases are enough to establish constitutional possibility, but not a mechanical script for every future divided Assembly. They establish, first, that the Fifth Republic can operate without presidential–parliamentary partisan unity. The institutions did not collapse in 1986, 1993, or 1997. Governments legislated, budgets passed, and France continued to act internationally. Cohabitation is therefore neither an unconstitutional anomaly nor necessarily a caretaker interlude. Second, they reveal that presidential primacy is partly political rather than purely textual. In aligned periods, the president usually chooses the prime minister politically, sets broad direction, and can expect government compliance. Under cohabitation, Articles 20 and 21 become much more visible. The shift is sometimes called a “parliamentary reading” of the Constitution, but the president does not cease to be directly elected or surrender personal constitutional powers. Third, the cases show that institutions channel conflict without eliminating it. Disputes can arise over senior appointments, ordinance signatures, diplomatic representation, defence choices, European negotiations, and credit for policy. The Constitution contains both separate competences and interlocking procedures. Outcomes therefore depend on law, convention, electoral legitimacy, and bargaining. Finally, cohabitation changes political accountability. The prime minister has the administrative machinery and Assembly programme but may be blamed for day-to-day outcomes. The president can criticise domestic policy while remaining head of state, yet still shares responsibility in fields where presidential action is visible. Voters must judge two competing executives, each able to claim a national mandate of a different date. Implications for 2027 The 2027 presidential election cannot by itself decide whether France will be governed through presidential primacy, cohabitation, minority government, or coalition bargaining. The National Assembly elected after the 2024 dissolution normally remains in office beyond the presidential election; absent another dissolution or legal change, no legislative election follows automatically in spring 2027. The decisive question is therefore the majority the new president confronts—either in that existing Assembly or in a later Assembly if Article 12 is used. A new president could win the Élysée but fail to secure an aligned Assembly. Conversely, a president whose camp holds only a plurality may face fragmentation rather than classic cohabitation. Three distinctions should discipline analysis of 2027. A presidential win is not a legislative mandate. The two-round presidential contest rewards a person who can assemble a runoff majority, sometimes through defensive voting against the opponent. Legislative elections operate constituency by constituency and can produce a differently composed Assembly. Calling them merely the presidential election's “third round” captures campaign sequencing but understates their independent constitutional function. The largest bloc is not necessarily a cohabitation majority. Article 8 does not mechanically assign the premiership to the head of the largest group. The relevant question is whether an appointee can lead a government that the Assembly will tolerate and that can pass budgets and legislation. A plurality opposed by several mutually incompatible blocs may lack that capacity. A cross-party agreement or narrower cabinet with negotiated support would not reproduce the disciplined left–right cohabitations of 1986, 1993, and 1997. The usual calendar reduces risk but does not abolish it—and the 2024 dissolution disrupted that sequence. Since 2002, legislative elections held soon after the presidency have usually created momentum for the new president. They cannot compel voters to confirm the presidential result, prevent mid-term dissolution, stop coalition fracture, or guarantee a majority. Because the 2024 dissolution started a new Assembly term, a president elected in 2027 would need to use Article 12 to seek an immediate electoral reset rather than receiving one automatically. Article 12 requires consultations and bars another dissolution within the year following an election caused by dissolution. The failed 1997 dissolution and the fragmented result after the 2024 dissolution are reminders that the president chooses whether to return to voters but not what voters decide. For forecasting, the most useful questions are institutional rather than theatrical: Which candidate's coalition can nominate viable legislative candidates nationwide? Can it reach an absolute majority, or only a plurality? Is there a coherent opposing majority capable of sustaining one prime minister? Which parties would support, join, or merely refrain from censuring a government? Without answers to those questions, declaring “cohabitation” after a presidential poll or even after a first legislative round is premature. Why it matters Cohabitation explains why the 2027 race is not a contest for unlimited control of the French state. The president's office carries exceptional visibility, direct electoral legitimacy, autonomous constitutional tools, and central roles in defence and diplomacy. Yet the government possesses the ordinary machinery of national policy and must survive in the Assembly. The actual balance depends on the relationship between two electoral mandates. That relationship also changes how campaign promises should be read. A presidential candidate can credibly describe how they would use personal powers, nominate a prime minister, or seek a legislative majority. They cannot guarantee enactment of a domestic programme without parliamentary support. If an opposing majority emerges, its government—not the defeated presidential platform—will usually control taxation, spending, social legislation, and most regulatory policy, while the president retains the capacity to shape, delay, refer, represent, and sometimes force a new electoral confrontation within constitutional limits. The deeper lesson is that cohabitation is not a strange import from another presidential system. It grows from the Fifth Republic's own mixed architecture: a directly elected president alongside a government responsible to Parliament. Understanding it on French terms prevents two opposite errors—treating the president as all-powerful, or treating cohabitation as if it instantly converted the presidency into a ceremonial office. Sources Constitution of 4 October 1958, consolidated text (Conseil constitutionnel, QPC360) — Articles 5, 8, 9, 12, 15, 19–21, 38, 49–52, 54, 56, and 61; accessed July 9, 2026. Constitution of 4 October 1958, English translation (Conseil constitutionnel, QPC360) — official institutional translation used to check English renderings; accessed July 9, 2026. Les cohabitations (Vie-publique) — French government public-information account of the three periods, their different origins and durations, and their institutional effects; published June 19, 2019; accessed July 9, 2026. Calendrier politique depuis 1958 (Assemblée nationale) — official chronology of presidencies, legislatures, dissolutions, electoral systems, prime ministers, and the three cohabitations; accessed July 9, 2026. Decision no. 2011-192 QPC of 10 November 2011 (Conseil constitutionnel, QPC360) — confirms, in a defence-secrecy case, both Article 5's presidential guarantee and Article 20's governmental responsibility, while applying separation of powers to president and government; accessed July 9, 2026. Constitution of 4 October 1958 (Assemblée nationale, 17th legislature) — National Assembly publication used to cross-check the current wording of the appointment, countersignature, governmental-responsibility, dissolution, ordinance, and censure provisions; accessed July 9, 2026. The reduction of the presidential term to five years (Vie-publique) — institutional history of the quinquennat , the 2000 referendum, and electoral-calendar alignment; accessed July 9, 2026. Open questions If 2027 produces no absolute majority, what observable threshold would justify describing the arrangement as cohabitation rather than minority or coalition government? How would a future cohabitation divide representation in European Council meetings when president and prime minister disagree on a live policy question? Which senior civil and military appointments would become the most consequential sites of countersignature bargaining? Would a president elected in 2027 accept an opposition prime minister immediately after a clear legislative defeat, or test whether a narrower government could survive censure? How much has post-2002 presidentialisation changed political expectations even though the underlying Articles 8, 20, 21, and 49 remain in force?

title: Constitutional Council review of presidential elections
deck: The French Constitutional Council does not merely bless an election-night result: it supervises the presidential vote, receives complaints, removes or corrects legally defective returns, fixes the national totals, and proclaims the winner, while campaign-account disputes arrive later through a separate appeal track.
headings: One constitutional mandate, several different functions
Supervision begins before a complaint exists
Complaints travel through the official record
Local annulment and correction are remedial tools
From local records to authoritative national totals
Campaign accounts are a later, separate jurisdiction
text: The French Constitutional Council does not merely bless an election-night result: it supervises the presidential vote, receives complaints, removes or corrects legally defective returns, fixes the national totals, and proclaims the winner, while campaign-account disputes arrive later through a separate appeal track. Up: [[2027 French presidential election]] · Related: [[How the French presidential election works]] · [[French presidential campaign finance]] One constitutional mandate, several different functions Article 58 of the Constitution gives the Conseil constitutionnel three compact duties. It “shall ensure the proper conduct” of the presidential election, examine complaints, and proclaim the result. Those words make the Council the ultimate election authority for the presidency, but they do not describe a single proceeding. In practice, the institution changes roles as the election moves from preparation to polling, tabulation, judgment, and proclamation. The legal framework is layered. Article 58 supplies the constitutional assignment. Article 3 of the organic provisions contained in the Law of 6 November 1962 supplies important machinery, including on candidacies, Council delegates, campaign accounts, and appeals. Decree no. 2001-213 of 8 March 2001 and the Electoral Code specify polling, minutes, departmental or equivalent canvasses, complaint channels, and deadlines. Election-specific Council decisions and official instructions then operationalize that framework. This division matters because “the Council reviews the election” can conceal six distinct propositions: it supervises the conduct of voting through preparation, information flows, and delegates in the field; it examines complaints recorded through legally recognized channels; it may annul polling-station votes or correct tabulation errors when the record cannot lawfully stand; it conducts or supervises the national aggregation that produces authoritative totals; it proclaims the result in a constitutional decision; months later, it may hear campaign-account appeals from CNCCFP decisions under a different grant of jurisdiction. These functions interact, but they should not be collapsed. A local annulment is not necessarily an annulment of the national election. A preliminary Interior Ministry total is not the proclamation. A campaign-account ruling does not reopen the vote count merely because both kinds of decision carry the label PDR in the Council's case law. Supervision begins before a complaint exists The Council's first election-judge function is preventive and observational. Article 3, III of the 1962 organic framework authorizes it to designate delegates to follow electoral operations on site. The implementing decree links those delegates to local machinery. Delegates have access to polling stations and may place observations in polling-station minutes. The heads of canvassing commissions must remain in contact with any delegate assigned to follow operations and provide information or documents the delegate considers useful. The scale is national rather than symbolic. The Council's report on the 2017 election described roughly 2,200 delegates, drawn from judicial and administrative magistrates, deployed to monitor polling. Their presence creates an evidentiary network between tens of thousands of polling stations and the Council in Paris. They do not replace mayors, polling-station officers, scrutineers, prefectural services, diplomatic posts, or canvassing commissions. They observe within a decentralized election administration and help ensure that irregularities enter an official record capable of review. That is why supervision should be distinguished from ordinary election administration. The Interior Ministry organizes much of the nationwide administrative operation and publishes rapidly updated results. Municipal officers run polling stations; local commissions conduct intermediate canvasses. [[Media pluralism and speaking time in French elections|Arcom]] supervises audiovisual pluralism under its own statutory authority. The CNCCFP audits campaign accounts. Article 58 nevertheless places ultimate responsibility for the regularity and result of the presidential vote in the Constitutional Council. Supervision is also broader than reacting to fraud. Delegates can record failures to follow formal safeguards even when nobody alleges a partisan scheme: an inadequately constituted polling board, an inaccessible record, improper handling of an urn, premature closure, defective identity checks, voting or counting conducted outside the prescribed public conditions, or refusal to follow a delegate's warning. Electoral formalities protect secrecy, equality, public verification, and the reliability of the count. A violation may therefore be serious without proof that anyone fabricated ballots. Complaints travel through the official record Article 58 requires the Council to examine complaints, but presidential-election complaints do not simply mirror the post-election petition used in a parliamentary constituency. The implementing framework builds challenges into the voting and canvassing record. Article 30 of the 2001 decree gives every elector access to the polling-station minutes while voting is under way and permits an elector to contest the regularity of the operations by having the complaint recorded in those minutes. Candidates and their authorized representatives also possess Electoral Code rights to demand that observations, protests, or challenges be entered. The first copy of the later canvassing record transmitted to the Council includes the relevant polling-station records and attachments, including those bearing elector complaints. A Council delegate's observations and the findings of canvassing commissions provide additional routes by which a problem reaches the national judge. The procedural lesson is concrete: a social-media post, press interview, or campaign allegation is not itself the equivalent of a complaint entered in the official electoral file. Public evidence can prompt attention, and the Council can examine the records before it under its constitutional duty, but an elector who witnesses a defect should use the polling-station process rather than assume that publicity preserves a legal claim. The minutes identify the place, time, people involved, votes affected, immediate response, and supporting documents while the evidence is fresh. There is a separate complaint concerning the official candidate list. Under article 8 of the 2001 decree, the right to challenge establishment of that list belongs to a person who was presented as a prospective candidate; the claim must reach the Council by the end of the day after publication in the Journal officiel , and the Council decides without delay. That accelerated pre-poll procedure concerns ballot access, not irregularities during voting. [[The 500 presentations in French presidential elections]] explains the preceding presentation process. This narrowness of channels should not be mistaken for passivity. In its proclamation decisions the Council considers complaints, polling-station records, canvassing materials, and reports of its delegates together. Its review is integrated into the national canvass rather than postponed until a losing candidate brings a single nationwide lawsuit. Local annulment and correction are remedial tools When a defect is established, the Council must decide what to do with the affected return. The central value is the freedom and sincérité —the genuineness or integrity—of the vote. Not every procedural error requires removing ballots. The question is whether the irregularity, its persistence, scale, circumstances, and effect leave the votes reliably attributable to a free and lawful process. The proclamation decision often states the facts polling station by polling station and either maintains the return, corrects it, or annuls all votes cast there. An annulment at this stage normally means that the affected polling station's votes are excluded from the certified national figures. It does not mean that the voters are treated as having cast blank ballots, that the poll is rerun locally, or that the whole presidential election is automatically void. Because the presidency is one nationwide constituency, removal of a local return flows directly into the nationwide aggregation. Whether irregularities could justify a still broader remedy would depend on their nature and capacity to compromise the national result; routine proclamation decisions usually resolve discrete defects by excluding the affected votes. The Council's 27 April 2022 second-round proclamation illustrates the range. It annulled votes where magistrate delegates reported polling stations improperly constituted despite warnings; where premature closure could prevent voting; where identity was not checked as required; where voters signed the register before placing ballots in the urn; and where counting safeguards made the result impossible to verify. It also annulled the 90 votes at Lourdios-Ichère after former candidate Jean Lassalle staged and broadcast a political statement of abstention inside the polling station on election day, treating it as prohibited electoral propaganda capable of impairing the sincerity of the vote. In Cizancourt, voting took place in a church with a confessional used as the booth; the Council found the setting capable of impairing freedom and sincerity and excluded the commune's 25 votes. These examples show that the remedy protects more than arithmetic. Public counting, neutral premises, an orderly ballot path, secrecy, and the absence of election-day propaganda are conditions under which citizens can trust the number. The Council need not identify which candidate gained from every defect before excluding a return whose integrity cannot be verified. Correction is analytically different from annulment. Canvassing commissions and the Council can rectify transcription, addition, classification, or treatment of ballots when the lawful figure can be recovered from the record. If an error can be corrected reliably, discarding every ballot would be unnecessarily destructive. If the safeguards needed to reconstruct the result have failed, annulment may be the only defensible option. News coverage should therefore say whether the Council corrected totals , annulled votes in named polling stations , or confronted an allegation but found no basis to alter the return . The same precision applies to magnitude. “Thousands of votes annulled” can sound as if the result were close to being overturned, yet the legal and electoral significance depends on the national margin and the distribution of the defects. The 2022 second-round decision excluded roughly twenty thousand votes while Emmanuel Macron's certified lead over Marine Le Pen exceeded five million. That fact does not make the violations harmless: exclusion preserves the integrity of the official totals. It does mean the local remedies did not place the identity of the winner in doubt. From local records to authoritative national totals Polling-station officers first count votes publicly and prepare minutes. Results then pass to departmental or equivalent canvassing commissions. Under article 28 of the 2001 decree, that canvass must be completed by midnight on the Monday following the vote. Records are prepared in duplicate and signed; the first copy goes immediately to the Constitutional Council, accompanied by polling-station records carrying elector complaints and their annexes. Article 29 provides that the general canvass is conducted under the Council's supervision at its seat and recorded in minutes. The Council is therefore not merely choosing between two totals published by others. It receives the territorial records, resolves complaints and irregularities, applies corrections or annulments, and aggregates the lawful figures. This produces the official national denominator for registered voters, voters, blank ballots, null ballots, votes cast for candidates, and expressed votes. The first round has a distinctive intermediate endpoint. If no candidate obtains an absolute majority of expressed votes, the Council must make known each candidate's total by 20:00 on the following Wednesday at the latest. It also identifies the two candidates eligible for the second round, subject to the constitutional and regulatory rules on withdrawal and succession. That declaration determines who may continue; it is not just a delayed media call. Election-night figures from the Interior Ministry remain extremely useful. They are based on official local transmissions, become nearly complete quickly, and are the appropriate source for real-time public information. Media estimates and projections answer a different question still. But all remain provisional relative to the Council's completed review. The gap will usually be small, yet its legal meaning is large: the Council's total includes the adjudication that turns reported ballots into the constitutionally authoritative result. This distinction is especially important for turnout and vote-share claims. A candidate's percentage is calculated from expressed votes after blank and null ballots are separated and after corrections or annulments. [[Blank and invalid votes in French presidential elections]] explains why participation, valid candidate votes, and the winner's share are different denominators. A researcher reproducing the definitive result should cite the proclamation decision, not freeze an election-night dashboard and call it final. Proclamation is the legal endpoint Article 58 says the Council proclaims the result. Article 29 of the decree requires proclamation of the result of the election within ten days after the round in which a candidate obtains the absolute majority of expressed votes. The proclamation decision combines adjudication and certification: it identifies the irregularities affecting the count, fixes national totals, records the votes for each remaining candidate, calculates the relevant shares, and declares the elected President of the Republic. The word “proclaims” should be used narrowly. A television network can project a winner; a rival can concede; the Interior Ministry can publish a near-complete count; political leaders can congratulate the apparent victor. None performs the constitutional act. The Council's proclamation is the authoritative decision from which official accounts of the result should work. The decision is also the point at which local review becomes publicly inspectable as a national judgment. Readers can see that a reported total changed not because officials quietly “adjusted” it but because specified votes were excluded or corrected for stated legal reasons. That transparency connects the decentralized poll to a single nationwide outcome. Under article 62 of the Constitution, Constitutional Council decisions are not subject to appeal and bind public authorities and administrative and judicial authorities. That finality makes verification before proclamation especially important. It also means that disagreement with the Council's handling of a polling station is not followed by an ordinary domestic appeal to the Conseil d'État or Cour de cassation. Campaign accounts are a later, separate jurisdiction The Council's involvement does not end with proclamation, but its later campaign-finance role must be kept separate from review of voting operations. Article 3, II of the 1962 organic framework applies campaign-account rules to presidential candidates. Each candidate files a compte de campagne ; the CNCCFP audits it and may approve, reform, or reject it, determine public reimbursement, and impose the statutory financial consequences of overspending or disallowed items. The candidate concerned may bring a full-jurisdiction appeal against the CNCCFP decision to the Constitutional Council within one month of notification. In that appeal the Council can examine the account and alter the Commission's decision. Rapporteurs and investigative powers support that review. This is judicial control of a specialist regulator's accounting decision, not a second national recount. The timelines make the distinction visible. Proclamation follows within days of the decisive round. Accounts are filed later, the CNCCFP investigates them over months, and appeals follow its notifications. A candidate can therefore be validly included in the proclaimed vote totals while later losing part or all of a reimbursement, having an account reformed or rejected, or facing other legal consequences. Conversely, a campaign-account allegation during the campaign is not an adjudicated fact merely because it may eventually reach the Council. The Council's 1995 handling of presidential accounts has generated sustained criticism and historical scrutiny, reinforcing the importance of not treating institutional finality as a substitute for analytical transparency. The contemporary system places initial audit with the CNCCFP and gives the Council a defined appeal jurisdiction. For current coverage, the reliable sequence is: candidate filing, CNCCFP decision, possible Council appeal, and final outcome. [[French presidential campaign finance]] owns the detailed accounting rules and reimbursement mechanics. Why it matters for 2027 The institutional chain prevents four common reporting errors about the [[2027 French presidential election]]. First, it prevents provisional election-night numbers from being labeled certified. Second, it prevents every reported polling-station incident from being called an annulment before the Council acts. Third, it prevents local exclusions from being described as though the nationwide election were rerun. Fourth, it prevents campaign-finance allegations or CNCCFP decisions from being confused with adjudication of the vote itself. For the scheduled 18 April and 2 May 2027 rounds, the useful evidence hierarchy will change over time. During voting, polling-station minutes and official delegate or authority statements establish incidents more reliably than viral clips alone. During the canvass, Interior Ministry figures describe the developing administrative count but remain subject to Council review. The first-round decision fixes candidate totals and the second-round field. The final proclamation decision supplies the certified national result and reasons for exclusions. Months later, CNCCFP and Council account decisions answer financial questions. The Council's role is consequently both practical and constitutional. Practical supervision creates records from a dispersed national poll; adjudication separates remediable errors from returns that cannot be trusted; aggregation turns local counts into a coherent national total; proclamation gives that total final legal force. The process does not promise a vote without mistakes. It supplies an identifiable institution, evidentiary path, remedial vocabulary, and public decision for converting an enormous administrative event into a legitimate presidential result. Légifrance, Decree no. 2001-213 of 8 March 2001, consolidated text — articles 22–31 on voting, delegates, canvassing, complaints, totals, and proclamation; accessed 2026-07-10. Conseil constitutionnel, Decision no. 2022-197 PDR of 27 April 2022 — second-round irregularities, corrected national totals, and proclamation; accessed 2026-07-10. Conseil constitutionnel, 2017 activity report — official evidence on the deployment of roughly 2,200 magistrate delegates and election review; accessed 2026-07-10.
