Open questions How will institutes define and disclose their likely-voter models once the official 2027 calendar and candidate field are settled? Which 2027 series will publish enough detail to distinguish demographic weighting from vote-recall adjustment and other model choices? How should an aggregator handle mutually exclusive candidate scenarios before nominations and sponsorships are final? Will the Commission issue election-specific recommendations that alter or clarify the practical disclosure and embargo rules for 2027? Can repeated-panel designs provide credible evidence about individual switching without introducing panel-conditioning effects?

title: Identity checks in French presidential elections
deck: Identity at a French presidential polling station is established through the voter list, a public name check, and—mandatorily in communes of at least 1,000 inhabitants—an approved identity document; the electoral card helps locate the record but is neither compulsory nor proof of identity.
headings: The check answers two different questions
The electoral card is useful but not an identity document
Identity is one layer of election security
Special voting channels do not erase authentication
text: Identity at a French presidential polling station is established through the voter list, a public name check, and—mandatorily in communes of at least 1,000 inhabitants—an approved identity document; the electoral card helps locate the record but is neither compulsory nor proof of identity. Up: [[2027 French presidential election]] · Related: [[Voter registration for French presidential elections]] · [[French presidential polling-station operations]] · [[Ballot secrecy and proxy voting in French presidential elections]] The check answers two different questions An identity control at a polling station is easy to describe as “showing ID,” but French election law separates two propositions. First, is this person entered on the electoral list used by this bureau de vote ? Second, is the person standing before the officials the elector whose name appears there? Registration answers the first question; the polling-station identity process answers the second. Neither alone is sufficient. Article L.62 of the Electoral Code makes the sequence visible. On entering the room, the elector’s identity or right to vote is verified. The elector then takes an envelope and at least two different ballots, goes alone through the voting booth, presents at the table, has identity checked, places the envelope in the transparent ballot box, and signs the liste d’émargement . The public declaration of the elector’s name and the signature are not substitutes for secrecy: they document participation, while the booth and envelope hide the choice. The distinction matters for 2027 analysis. An expired electoral card does not extinguish a valid registration, and the absence of the card is not itself disfranchisement. Conversely, possessing a card does not establish a current right to vote if the person is not on the polling station’s list. A registration dispute belongs to the procedures described in [[Voter registration for French presidential elections]], not to ad hoc discretion over an otherwise valid identity document. The electoral card is useful but not an identity document The carte électorale records practical information: the elector, commune, polling station, and national electoral number. It helps officials find the correct list entry and helps voters arrive at the correct bureau. It is not a national identity card, and official guidance says it is not mandatory in order to vote. This produces three common cases: An elector brings both the electoral card and an approved identity title. In a commune of at least 1,000 inhabitants, this is the ordinary and fastest route. An elector has no electoral card but appears on the bureau’s list. The missing card does not bar the ballot. Where Article R.60 applies, the elector still must present an approved identity title. A person presents an electoral card but is not on the relevant list. The card does not override the list. Officials must determine whether the person is at the wrong bureau, has been removed, is covered by a judicial or administrative correction, or lacks a current registration. This is why “ID requirement” is an incomplete description. The legal object is not a free-standing photographic-ID test. It is the authentication of a listed elector at a specified polling station, followed by an auditable signature. The 1,000-inhabitant threshold Article R.60 establishes a bright administrative distinction. In communes with 1,000 inhabitants or more , electors must present to the polling-station president, at the time of voting, an identity title alongside the electoral card or an attestation that replaces it. The permissible titles are set by an Interior Ministry order. Assessors may participate in the identity control if they ask to do so. In communes with fewer than 1,000 inhabitants , official Interior Ministry and Service-Public guidance says that no particular identity document is compulsory. This is not an exemption from identity verification. The president of the bureau must still be able to verify who the elector is and, where doubt persists, may require identity to be established by any means. Familiarity in a small commune can therefore perform an evidentiary role that the prescribed-document list performs in a larger one, but it does not authorize voting under an unverified name. The threshold attaches to the commune, not to the size of an individual polling station or to whether local officials personally recognize the voter. A small bureau inside a large commune remains subject to Article R.60. The rule should also not be confused with municipal-election voting systems; it is an administrative identity rule incorporated into national elections, including the presidential election. The asymmetry embodies a tradeoff. A uniform documentary rule is easier to administer and audit in more populous places where officials cannot be expected to know electors personally. A flexible rule in very small communes reduces exclusion when local knowledge can establish identity. Yet flexibility also makes the quality of the bureau president’s judgment important, which is why the public nature of the operation, assessors, signatures, minutes, and later review remain part of the safeguard. Which documents count The controlling list is regulatory, not a matter of what seems persuasive to an individual official. The Interior Ministry’s order of November 16, 2018 lists documents usable to prove identity when voting in a commune of at least 1,000 inhabitants. Official public guidance includes, among others, a national identity card, passport, health-insurance card with photograph, driving licence, military identity or circulation card with photograph, state civil-servant identity card with photograph, disability or mobility-inclusion card with photograph, combatant’s card with photograph, and hunting permit with photograph issued by the competent public body. The order itself, rather than a campaign’s checklist or a polling-place improvisation, is authoritative. French nationals may use a national identity card or passport that is current or that expired less than five years earlier, according to Service-Public’s voting guidance. Most other listed documents must be current. This limited acceptance of recently expired national documents should not be generalized to every title on the list. The voter must present the original . A photocopy or a photograph displayed on a telephone is not accepted as the document. This is an authentication rule: a recognisable image of a document lacks the physical and administrative characteristics on which the prescribed control relies. The name on a document and the electoral list may require ordinary reconciliation—for example, after a change in civil status—but officials should not invent an extra eligibility condition. The material question is whether the prescribed evidence establishes that the person present is the listed elector. Difficult cases should be recorded rather than resolved by partisan intuition. What happens at the bureau The polling-station president has responsibility for order and regularity, assisted by assessors and the secretary. Identity is checked publicly enough for the bureau and representatives to observe the operation, but personal data should not be turned into campaign material. Article R.60 expressly allows assessors to join the control on request, distributing scrutiny beyond a single official. Once identity and list entry are established, the ordinary sequence continues. The elector votes personally, even when another elector has appointed that person as proxy for a separate ballot. The official says the person’s name aloud; after the envelope is placed in the box, the elector signs beside the list entry. If the elector cannot sign, the Electoral Code provides a notation and assistance procedure rather than making handwriting ability a condition of suffrage. [[Accessibility in French presidential elections]] treats assistance and accessible voting more fully. For a proxy vote, the proxy voter proves their own identity at the polling station assigned to the principal and states the principal’s name. Officials verify the valid proxy notation and the applicable proxy limits. The principal’s electoral card is not required. Identity checking therefore authenticates the person physically casting the ballot, while the proxy register supplies legal authority to cast it for someone else. The proxy never gains a right to reveal or replace the principal’s political choice. Officials cannot cure a missing registration simply because a person’s identity is obvious, nor refuse a registered elector merely because the electoral card is absent. These opposite errors—letting identity substitute for enrolment and letting the card substitute for identity—are the core conceptual traps. Disputes, refusals, and documentation If a voter is directed to the wrong bureau, the first response should be to identify the correct registration location through the electoral list and official lookup tools. If the dispute concerns a recent omission or removal, statutory administrative and judicial remedies may allow correction, sometimes through a court order presented at the bureau. The polling station is not free to rewrite the list on oral assurance. If an elector in a commune of at least 1,000 inhabitants cannot present an approved title, the bureau cannot waive Article R.60 because the person is locally known or because turnout is high. In a smaller commune, by contrast, the president evaluates proof by any means. The different rules make the commune’s population category a fact that election administrators must establish before polling day. A disagreement should be entered in the procès-verbal when it bears on the regularity of voting. Candidate delegates and electors may make observations through the legally available channels. The record permits later review by recensement bodies and ultimately the Constitutional Council, whose Article 58 function is explained in [[Constitutional Council review of presidential elections]] and [[Presidential election complaints and annulments]]. A court assessing an irregularity will care not only that a rule was breached but also about scale, circumstances, corrective action, and whether the integrity or result could have been affected. Identity controls should therefore be strict in content and neutral in application. Selectively demanding extra evidence from some electors, accepting non-listed substitutes for allies, or using the process to intimidate would undermine equality even if the underlying document rule is valid. The best protection is a rehearsed, published rule applied consistently, with edge cases documented. Identity is one layer of election security Documentary control is sometimes presented as the entire answer to impersonation. In the French system it is one linked layer. Registration assigns each elector to a list and bureau. Identity control authenticates the person. The public call of the name allows observation. The signature records that the vote was cast. The ballot-box counter, reconciliation of envelopes and signatures, count, minutes, and higher-level recensement expose discrepancies. Complaints and constitutional review provide remedies. No single layer proves that the whole election is sound. A perfectly checked document cannot correct an erroneous list; a correct list cannot prevent someone from voting twice without signature and reconciliation controls; a numerical reconciliation cannot protect secrecy without the booth. The architecture works because checks answer different questions. For journalists and campaigns, this means reports of an “ID problem” should specify the precise failure: absent electoral-card convenience, absent list entry, missing prescribed identity title, doubt in a sub-1,000 commune, proxy-record problem, civil-status mismatch, unequal treatment, or a wrongly located bureau. These have different legal consequences and different remedies. Special voting channels do not erase authentication The ordinary commune rule should not be projected mechanically onto every French presidential elector. Citizens voting at consular polling stations abroad are registered on a consular electoral list and follow the identification rules administered through the diplomatic network. Electors in overseas territories may be governed by locally applicable adaptations. Detained electors using the presidential postal-voting mechanism are authenticated and reconciled through a different custodial and electoral chain, described in [[Prison voting in French presidential elections]]. These are adaptations of the control environment, not identity-free voting. Proxy voting is likewise a change in who appears at the bureau, not a suspension of verification. The principal has established the proxy through an authorized procedure, the administration transmits or records that authority, and the proxy appears in person and proves their own identity. Officials then connect three records: the person present, the valid proxy, and the principal's list entry. Treating a proxy ballot as though the principal had simply lent an electoral card would miss the legal chain. The French framework also distinguishes identity at registration from identity at voting . An applicant registering online or at a mairie supplies identity and nationality evidence under registration rules. That earlier check does not eliminate polling-day authentication because circumstances and records can change and because the bureau must establish who is physically casting this particular ballot. Conversely, a strong identity document at the bureau cannot repair failure to register by the legal deadline. The two controls occur at different times and guard against different errors. These distinctions matter when comparing turnout channels. A consular voter, detained postal voter, proxy principal, and ordinary in-person voter should not be placed in a single “showed ID” count unless the underlying authentication events are defined. For public evaluation, the better question is whether each channel established eligibility, identity, authorization, uniqueness, secrecy, and an auditable record under its applicable law. Why it matters for 2027 The presidential electorate will encounter a nationally important ballot through locally operated polling stations. Small variations in training or communication can generate dramatic anecdotes without establishing systematic fraud or exclusion. The proper denominator is essential: how many electors were affected, in which commune category, under which document rule, whether they were registered, whether they returned with valid proof, and whether the incident was entered in the minutes. Election-specific instructions issued before April 2027 may update operational details, and the Interior Ministry may amend the approved-document order. The durable structure is nonetheless clear under current law: enrolment and identity are distinct; the electoral card is useful but optional; prescribed identity evidence is mandatory at the 1,000-inhabitant threshold; and smaller communes still must establish identity. That structure also limits premature political claims. A queue caused by slow document checks is not itself disenfranchisement. An elector turned away for lack of registration is not evidence of an identity-document rule. A documented refusal of an approved title, however, is a concrete administrative failure worthy of immediate correction and possible complaint. Precise classification is more informative than importing a generic international argument over “voter ID.” Sources Electoral Code, Article L.62 — voting sequence, identity verification, ballot box, and signature; accessed July 10, 2026. Open questions Will the Interior Ministry amend the 2018 approved-document order before the 2027 presidential election? What election-specific instructions will standardize handling of civil-status mismatches and digital identity tools? How often do identity disputes appear in presidential polling-station minutes, and how many lead to a formal correction or complaint?

title: Mayors and communes in French presidential elections
deck: France's presidential election is national in its choice and result but municipal in much of its physical execution: mayors and communes turn uniform law into registration decisions, polling places, staffed bureaux, counts, records, and—through eligible officeholders' presentations—access to the ballot itself.
headings: A national election built from communes
From buildings to bureaux de vote
Municipal scale changes the practical problem
text: France's presidential election is national in its choice and result but municipal in much of its physical execution: mayors and communes turn uniform law into registration decisions, polling places, staffed bureaux, counts, records, and—through eligible officeholders' presentations—access to the ballot itself. Up: [[2027 French presidential election]] Related: [[Administration of French presidential elections]] · [[French presidential polling-station operations]] · [[The 500 presentations in French presidential elections]] · [[2027 French presidential territorial coalitions]] A national election built from communes The president is elected in one national constituency. A ballot cast in Lille and one cast in a village in the Creuse enter the same nationwide calculation; a commune does not award presidential electors or a territorial block of votes. Yet the voter normally experiences the election through a commune: registration is attached to a communal electoral list, the voter is assigned to a local bureau de vote , the mayor designates polling premises, municipal personnel and local electors help operate them, and a communal result is recorded before results travel upward. That combination is not a contradiction. France separates political decision from administrative production. The state and the organic law establish the presidential rules; the Constitutional Council supervises the regularity of the election, examines claims, conducts the national canvass, and proclaims the result. Prefects transmit instructions and supervise implementation territorially. Communes supply the last-mile institution. The election is therefore neither simply centralized nor a federation of local elections. It is a nationally governed operation executed through a highly dispersed municipal network. France had 34,875 communes on 1 January 2026 according to the official geographic code. Their scale varies radically, from Paris and other large cities to communes with only a few dozen residents. The common legal framework must work across that range. This makes the commune both an administrative strength and a recurrent source of operational asymmetry: the same duties are easier to staff, specialize, and audit in a large city than in a tiny rural municipality, while small communes may possess local knowledge and dense civic ties that large administrations cannot reproduce. The mayor's role also needs careful definition. A mayor is an elected municipal executive, but certain election tasks are performed as an agent of the state. The General Code of Local Authorities places the mayor under the administrative authority of the prefect when exercising state functions, including functions assigned by electoral law. A mayor organizing a presidential polling operation is therefore not free to redesign it according to a local political mandate. Municipal autonomy supplies premises, personnel, and practical judgment within nationally prescribed rules; prefectural and judicial supervision constrain that judgment. The electoral register begins locally The modern registration system joins a national database to local decisions. INSEE maintains the répertoire électoral unique (REU), while mayors decide ordinary applications for entry and certain removals from their commune's list. Consular authorities perform corresponding functions abroad. The national register helps prevent fragmented local lists from quietly retaining duplicate registrations, but it does not eliminate municipal responsibility. An applicant's connection to the commune—residence, domicile, or another statutory basis—still has to be assessed, and decisions can be contested through the statutory commission and courts. Each commune has a control commission for its electoral list. Its composition depends partly on municipal size and political configuration, but its broad purpose is stable: review the regularity of mayoral registration and removal decisions, decide specified administrative appeals, and ensure publication of the list. This distributes checking rather than leaving a politically interested mayor as the final local judge of who votes. Judicial remedies add another layer. The REU, commission review, public-list procedures, and court access should be understood as a system; none alone guarantees a flawless roll. Registration illustrates why “the mayor runs the election” is too loose. The mayor makes legally defined decisions, INSEE manages the national infrastructure, a commission controls the list, and judges can correct errors. Before the 2027 contest, official election-specific instructions will specify deadlines and operations. Analysts should cite the then-current guidance rather than infer every detail from the 2022 cycle. From buildings to bureaux de vote The prefect fixes the number and perimeter of polling stations on the mayor's proposal, under Article R.40 of the Electoral Code. The mayor then assigns polling places. The premises must permit regular, accessible, and secret voting. In practice, town halls, schools, community rooms, and other municipal buildings are common. A polling place is not merely a room with a ballot box: it needs voter-list materials, an identity-control position, ballot papers and envelopes, booths, a signature register, public circulation, counting tables, posted legal information, and a route usable by disabled voters. Municipal preparation begins well before polling day. Communes receive and sort election material, prepare voter lists and signature registers, notify voters, arrange equipment, recruit or schedule staff, and coordinate with prefectural services. They must anticipate shortages and incidents without altering the equal rules of the contest. A missing ballot pile, inaccessible booth, late-opening station, or improperly composed bureau is a local fact with national constitutional significance because it can affect equal suffrage. The mayor, deputy mayors, and municipal councillors are central to constituting bureaux. Under the Electoral Code, each bureau has a president, at least two assessors, and a secretary. Candidates may appoint assessors and alternates; when those appointments do not fill the statutory places, municipal mechanisms supply members. The president has authority to maintain order inside the polling station, but that authority is procedural, not partisan. Candidate delegates may monitor operations and require observations to be entered in the minutes. Voting and counting are public, allowing electors to observe subject to order and space. The municipal institution thus performs two roles that must remain distinct. It supplies the organization, but it does not own the process. Competing candidates receive representation rights; electors can watch; commissions may inspect; prefectural services receive records; and the Constitutional Council can annul votes or take incidents into account. A well-run commune makes these controls possible rather than treating them as interference. Municipal scale changes the practical problem Uniform legal rights do not imply identical local conditions. In a very small commune, officials and voters may know one another, a single polling station may cover the whole electorate, and recruiting a full team for a long Sunday can be difficult. In a major city, there are many bureaux, more professional administrative capacity, more candidate delegates, and greater logistical complexity. Neither setting is inherently more reliable. Familiarity can help establish identity in a small commune, but it can also make social pressure more visible; scale can support specialization in a city, but it multiplies handoffs and coordination points. The law sometimes recognizes scale expressly. In communes of at least 1,000 inhabitants, voters must present an approved identity document; in smaller communes, no particular listed document is categorically compulsory, although the polling president must still be able to establish identity. In communes with more than 20,000 inhabitants, a commission controlling voting operations monitors the regular composition and conduct of polling bureaux. These thresholds solve different problems and should not be conflated. They do not create a general division between “secure” large communes and informal small ones. Accessibility duties apply everywhere. Article L.62-2 requires polling places and voting techniques to be accessible to disabled people, whatever the disability. A commune may use temporary adaptations, but formal availability is not enough: the route, booth, writing surface, ballot box, and signature table must work in normal conditions. Small municipal budgets may make adaptation harder, yet the legal right does not shrink with the tax base. Prefectures and national guidance matter because local implementation capacity is unequal. Polling hours similarly join national baseline and territorial adjustment. Presidential voting ordinarily runs from 8:00 to 19:00, with authorized local extensions no later than 20:00. The prefectural order, not a mayor's convenience, determines an extension. Communes then bear its staffing consequences. Researchers comparing turnout should remember that differently timed communes have unequal opportunity windows and different social profiles. Counting locally, deciding nationally After the last admitted elector votes, the bureau establishes signatures, opens the ballot box, and organizes the count. Scrutineers work at public counting tables. Envelopes and ballots are reconciled, doubtful ballots are treated under legal categories, and results are announced and entered in the official minutes. The commune aggregates its bureaux where necessary and transmits records through the prefectural chain. Municipal results are therefore provisional components, not autonomous declarations of the presidential outcome. Departmental canvassing commissions review and total them; records and complaints go onward; the Constitutional Council has the authoritative final role. This distinction matters during election-night reporting. A commune's published number may be accurate and politically revealing, but media aggregation does not replace legal canvassing, and a mayor cannot certify the national winner. The minutes are a crucial bridge between local incident and national review. Bureau members, candidate representatives, or electors can preserve observations. Numerical discrepancies, improper ballots, disruptions, or failures to follow procedure then become reviewable evidence rather than anecdote. The Constitutional Council may cancel votes from a bureau or commune when irregularities warrant it, taking account of their nature and potential effect. Local administration is consequently part of constitutional adjudication: the quality of the paper trail determines what can later be established. Commune-level returns are also an important public dataset. They allow territorial comparison below departments and reveal differences between central cities, suburbs, small towns, tourist areas, industrial basins, and rural territories. But a commune is not a voter type. Its result aggregates people with different occupations, incomes, ages, and motivations. In tiny communes, a handful of votes can produce dramatic percentage changes; in large communes, an average can conceal sharp neighbourhood divisions. Commune returns are evidence about places, not proof of individual behavior. Mayors as presenters of candidates Mayors connect local government to the presidential field before election day through the system commonly called the 500 parrainages . The legal act is a présentation . Mayors, delegated mayors, certain arrondissement mayors, and specified intercommunal and other officeholders belong to the eligible body. Each eligible official can present only one prospective candidate. The Constitutional Council receives, validates, and publishes presentations under the organic rules. Mayors matter numerically because the communal map creates a very large body of eligible officeholders, many from small municipalities and many without a strong national party label. Campaigns lacking a dense parliamentary or regional network therefore devote substantial effort to contacting them. Yet a presentation must not automatically be reported as an ideological endorsement. An official may present a candidate to support pluralism or ballot access while intending to vote differently. Conversely, a public political endorsement is not necessarily a valid presentation received by the Council. The rule's territorial design prevents qualification through a single fortress. A candidate needs at least 500 valid presentations from at least thirty departments or equivalent territories, with no more than one tenth of the required total—effectively fifty—coming from any one territory. This turns municipal reach into a test of organizational breadth. For 2027, claims that a campaign “has its signatures” remain claims until the Council's published validation. Publicity is contested. Since the 2016 reform, the Council publishes all valid presentations rather than only a selected 500. Transparency makes official responsibility visible and permits auditing. Critics argue that publication can expose small-commune mayors to party, voter, or social pressure and deter presentations made only to broaden debate. Official reports document the concern, but public lists alone cannot establish its size or causal effect. Reporting should separate established rules, officials' testimony, and inference. Mayors as political intermediaries Beyond formal duties, mayors are political actors. Their endorsements can signal local legitimacy, provide venues and networks, and help national candidates demonstrate territorial breadth. Associations of mayors articulate municipal priorities such as local finance, public services, housing, ecological transition, security, and decentralization. Presidential contenders use mayoral congresses and local visits to frame themselves as attentive to “the territories.” The phrase can obscure more than it explains. France's mayors do not form a single rural bloc. They govern dense suburbs, wealthy metropolitan communes, shrinking villages, overseas municipalities, industrial towns, and fast-growing peri-urban areas. Party labels are unevenly meaningful, particularly in small communes. A list categorized sans étiquette or divers is not politically empty, but neither can it safely be assigned to a national camp without evidence. Municipal elections also create organizational capital. Parties and movements with councillors, mayors, and intercommunal executives possess experienced officeholders, local voter knowledge, venues, volunteer networks, and eligible presenters. But municipal implantation does not translate mechanically into presidential votes. A popular mayor can endorse a candidate whom residents reject nationally; local coalitions often combine actors who divide in presidential politics; and the two-round national contest activates different issues and strategic choices. For the 2027 election, mayoral support should therefore be measured in multiple columns: valid presentations, explicit endorsements, campaign committee participation, municipal-party control, and actual commune results. Combining them into one “mayor support” number invites false precision. The most defensible claim is functional: communes administer the vote, while mayors also supply one important network through which candidates qualify and seek territorial credibility. Accountability and failure modes Because mayors are political figures administering a contest, neutrality safeguards matter. Municipal premises and communications cannot lawfully be converted into unequal campaign resources. Polling-station composition, candidate representation, public counting, written minutes, control commissions, prefectural oversight, and Constitutional Council review distribute authority. The point is not to assume mayoral bad faith; it is to make regularity demonstrable even when local political interests are strong. Operational fragility can arise without fraud. Volunteer shortages, storms, inaccessible buildings, mistaken registers, material-delivery failures, cybersecurity or transmission problems, and inconsistent training can interrupt an otherwise honest operation. The response should distinguish remediation from accusation. A late opening documented and corrected is an incident; evidence that it selectively prevented voting is a more consequential claim. The Council evaluates concrete circumstances and effect rather than treating every procedural defect as proof of manipulation. Mayoral nonperformance is not the end of the chain. The mayor's state functions are performed under prefectural authority, and election law supplies substitution and supervision mechanisms. The exact remedy depends on the duty and circumstances. Before 2027, prefectures will issue detailed instructions, and communes will update plans, staffing, accessible premises, and transmission procedures. Those documents will be better evidence of readiness than general assurances. Why this matters for 2027 The 2027 field will be narrated through leaders, polls, parties, and national television. The communal layer determines whether those national choices become an accessible and auditable vote. It also shapes the candidate field through presentations and supplies the finest official geography for interpreting the result. Ignoring communes means missing both the administrative mechanism and a major source of political organization. Three distinctions should guide coverage. First, administration is not endorsement: a mayor who flawlessly operates a bureau may campaign for one candidate, oppose all of them, or remain publicly neutral. Second, presentation is not necessarily support: only the Council certifies the legal act, and the official's motive cannot be read from the list. Third, territory is not demography: a commune result describes an aggregate place, not the reasons each resident voted. The best 2027 reporting will test preparedness locally while keeping the national legal chain in view. It will check prefectural orders, accessible premises, staffing, candidate representation, incidents recorded in minutes, validated presentations, and official results. It will avoid romanticizing village familiarity or assuming metropolitan professionalism. France's commune system works through redundancy: local knowledge and labor, standardized state rules, partisan scrutiny, public observation, documentary records, and judicial review reinforce one another. Open questions Which 2027 prefectural instructions will materially change communal staffing, accessibility, cybersecurity, or result-transmission practice from 2022? How many communes will report difficulty recruiting bureau members and scrutineers, and will comparable national data exist? Can the effect of publishing every valid presentation on small-commune mayors be estimated separately from party-network strength and candidate strategy? Which measures best compare administrative capacity across communes without treating population size as a proxy for quality? How should commune-level 2027 returns be joined to functional urban-area and socioeconomic data without committing an ecological fallacy?

title: Media pluralism and speaking time in French elections
deck: French audiovisual law applies a permanent pluralism regime to political expression, then overlays special presidential-election rules that move from equity to strict equality as polling day approaches.
headings: Four concepts that should not be collapsed
The routine regime outside the presidential sequence
2. Equity after the official candidate list
3. Equality during the official first-round campaign
A practical checklist for reading 2027 coverage
text: French audiovisual law applies a permanent pluralism regime to political expression, then overlays special presidential-election rules that move from equity to strict equality as polling day approaches. Up: [[2027 French presidential election]] The short version “Speaking time” is not one rule. France uses several related controls, principally for radio and television: Outside an election-specific period , Arcom supervises political pluralism continuously. Government, parliamentary majority, opposition, and other political forces do not receive identical shares; exposure is assessed against institutional position and political representativeness. Since a 2024 Conseil d’État judgment and Arcom’s July 2024 deliberation, the regulator’s broader pluralism review also considers the range of viewpoints expressed by all on-air participants, not only politicians whose seconds can be counted. During the early presidential-election period , likely candidates and then declared candidates receive equitable , not equal, speaking time and airtime. Equity permits different quantities, but the differences must be justified by measurable political weight and participation in the campaign. From the start of the official campaign , every candidate receives equal speaking time and equal airtime, in comparable scheduling conditions. The same strict equality governs the two finalists from the Monday after the first round through the Friday before the second. The decisive distinction is therefore not “regulated” versus “unregulated.” Political broadcasting is regulated throughout. What changes is the unit being measured, the people being compared, the permissible justification for differences, and eventually the governing principle: pluralism, then electoral equity, then electoral equality. Four concepts that should not be collapsed Pluralism Pluralism is the durable constitutional and statutory objective. The Constitutional Council has treated pluralism of sociocultural currents of expression as a constitutional objective and a condition of democracy. The 30 September 1986 freedom-of-communication law charges Arcom with guaranteeing pluralism of information and ensuring pluralistic expression of currents of thought and opinion in audiovisual programming, especially political and general information. This is an internal pluralism obligation: within a regulated radio or television service, the range and balance of political expression must not become manifestly and durably one-sided. It is different from external pluralism , meaning diversity among separately owned media outlets. Ownership concentration matters to democratic debate, but it is not what a speaking-time table directly measures. Arcom’s 17 July 2024 deliberation broadened the operational lens after the Conseil d’État held on 13 February 2024 that the regulator could not assess pluralism solely from airtime granted to political personalities. Arcom must also consider the currents of thought and opinion expressed by presenters, journalists, columnists, experts, and other participants. The deliberation calls for a holistic assessment of the diversity of participants, the variety of subjects, and the plurality of viewpoints, looking for a manifest and lasting imbalance . It does not require mechanically labeling every journalist’s ideology or imposing second-for-second balance among commentators. Speaking time Temps de parole is the duration for which a candidate, political figure, or qualifying supporter is actually heard speaking. A candidate’s interview answers count; so may a supporter’s advocacy. A journalist describing the candidate normally does not become the candidate’s speaking time. The category matters because access to direct speech gives a politician control over wording, emphasis, and emotional presentation. But speaking time alone can mislead. A candidate might speak briefly while a channel devotes hours of favorable or hostile discussion to that person. Airtime Temps d’antenne is broader. In a presidential campaign it includes speaking time plus editorial material devoted to a candidate and their supporters: reports, commentary, presentation, images, and other treatment of the candidacy. This is why the presidential rules demand equity or equality in both speaking time and airtime. A broadcaster cannot satisfy equality by giving every candidate the same interview duration while surrounding some with dramatically more campaign coverage. The distinction also explains why tone cannot be reduced to a stopwatch. Equal airtime can include critical reporting; the rules do not create a right to favorable journalism. Separate duties of honesty, independence, and rigor continue to apply. Comparable programming conditions Equality at 3 a.m. is not equivalent to equality in prime time. The organic presidential-election law therefore requires equity and equality in comparable programming conditions , which Arcom specifies in its election recommendation. In 2022 it divided the day into morning (6–9), daytime (9–18), evening (18–24), and night (0–6) bands. Broadcasters had to balance exposure within meaningful scheduling contexts, not merely reach an aggregate total across the entire day. Comparable conditions also concern the nature and audience of programs. Exact arrangements for 2027 will depend on Arcom’s future recommendation, so the 2022 bands are a strong precedent rather than a legally fixed 2027 calendar. The routine regime outside the presidential sequence The permanent framework rests mainly on articles 1, 3-1, and 13 of the 1986 law and Arcom’s general pluralism deliberations. It applies whether or not an official campaign has begun. Broadcasters themselves make editorial choices, keep relevant records, and transmit political speaking-time statements where required; Arcom examines the results and can seek corrections or use its enforcement powers. Routine political speaking-time accounting has historically distinguished the executive from other political forces. The governing framework does not promise each party an identical fraction. Instead, it seeks a politically intelligible distribution that recognizes the government’s institutional role while preserving meaningful access for the parliamentary majority, opposition, and non-parliamentary currents. Representativeness can be inferred from election results, numbers of elected officials, polling, and contribution to political debate. This ordinary regime remains important before the presidential recommendation starts. A person may behave like a candidate long before becoming legally nominated, but not every appearance is automatically counted under a presidential-candidate ledger. Arcom must decide when an election-specific framework should begin and whom it covers; meanwhile ordinary pluralism still constrains the channel. The 2024 expansion adds a second analytic layer. Quantified political speaking times remain a central tool, but Arcom also assesses whether the overall information service persistently excludes or overwhelms certain currents through its choice of guests, themes, and opinions. This qualitative review is deliberately longer-horizon: isolated programs or individual statements do not alone establish a manifest and durable imbalance. Nor does the broader test replace the precise presidential stopwatch once election rules apply. Both can operate together. Print newspapers are not subject to Arcom’s radio-and-television speaking-time allocation. Online political debate is also not generally converted into candidate time ledgers merely because it is influential. The relevant election recommendation defines which audiovisual services and programs fall within its scope. Digital platforms may face other transparency, systemic-risk, or electoral-integrity duties, but those are not the same as French broadcast equality. The presidential clock The exact dates for 2027 are not yet available as of 9 July 2026. They will depend on the election calendar, the Constitutional Council’s candidate-list publication, the statutory start of the official campaign, and Arcom’s election-specific recommendation. The 2022 sequence shows how the legal machinery works. 1. An anticipatory equity period For 2022, the CSA—the predecessor whose recommendation Arcom administered from January 2022—made its presidential recommendation effective on 1 January 2022 . From 1 January through 7 March, before publication of the official candidate list, broadcasters had to provide prospective candidates and their supporters equitable speaking time and airtime. Equity was assessed using two families of indicators: Representativeness , including results obtained by the candidate or supporting political formations in the most recent elections, indications from opinion polls, and the political weight of supporters. Contribution to the animation of the electoral debate , including campaign activity, meetings, field visits, public exposure of the person or program—including through social networks—and participation in debates. The second criterion prevents equity from becoming a frozen entitlement based only on past results. A new candidacy that demonstrably structures the current contest may deserve substantial exposure. Conversely, declaring an intention to run does not by itself compel a broadcaster to provide the same time as a nationally established and active campaign. 2. Equity after the official candidate list Article 3, I bis of the 1962 organic-law framework creates a statutory phase from publication of the Constitutional Council’s list of candidates until the eve of the official campaign. In 2022 this ran from 8 March through 27 March . The same principle—equity—continued, but now the comparison was among legally established candidates. This phase matters because obtaining 500 valid presentations and appearing on the Constitutional Council’s list does not immediately produce equal broadcast time. The 2016 reform replaced the former longer equality phase with equity until the official campaign. Its practical purpose was to reduce the programming burden created by strict equality among numerous candidates while preserving justified access for all. Equity is not editorial discretion without reasons. Arcom examines quantitative discrepancies against representativeness and campaign activity, across speaking time, airtime, and comparable schedule bands. In March 2022 it publicly identified overexposure on particular channels and demanded correction. Broadcasters therefore must monitor balances while there is still time to repair them; a mathematically improved final week may not erase prolonged earlier distortion in every context. 3. Equality during the official first-round campaign For 2022 the official campaign began on 28 March and ended on 8 April , the Friday before the Sunday vote, because campaigning and electoral propaganda stop before polling day. From the campaign’s start, article 3, I bis requires equality in the reproduction and commentary of candidates’ declarations and writings and in presentation of their person. Arcom operationalizes this as equality of both speaking time and airtime in comparable programming conditions. Equality means each legally qualified candidate is owed the same quantity, irrespective of polls, previous results, campaign budget, or perceived newsworthiness. A broadcaster may choose formats and retain journalistic freedom, but its overall allocation must satisfy the rule. This is the sharpest departure from routine pluralism and early equity. Separately, official campaign broadcasts on national public-service channels are allocated under article 15 of the 8 March 2001 decree. Each first-round candidate receives an equal duration, fixed by Arcom after consultation and no less than fifteen minutes. These candidate-produced official broadcasts are not the whole media-equality regime; they sit alongside equality across ordinary audiovisual coverage. 4. Equality between the two rounds If no candidate wins an absolute majority on the first ballot, equality resumes for the finalists from the Monday after the first round through the Friday before the second . In 2022 Arcom applied equality from 11 through 22 April. The two finalists and their supporters had to receive equal speaking time and airtime in comparable conditions. Public-service official broadcasts are again separately guaranteed. Under the 2001 decree each finalist is allocated at least one hour, unless both agree to a shorter duration. The televised debate is politically pivotal but not itself the complete legal balance sheet; other interviews, reports, and commentary throughout the inter-round period count as well. Who and what gets counted The candidate’s own political expression is straightforward. Supporters are harder. A minister, party official, elected representative, celebrity, or civil-society figure may be attributed to a candidate when their intervention supports that candidacy. Broadcasters must classify context, not merely identity: the same person can speak in an institutional capacity at one moment and campaign at another. The incumbent president poses the most visible classification problem. Arcom distinguishes speech arising from presidential duties from speech belonging to political debate or the campaign. In 2022, interventions linked to constitutional or diplomatic functions were not automatically charged to the president-candidate, while statements entering partisan debate were. The label attached by the broadcaster is not conclusive; substance and context govern. This boundary is inevitably contestable because incumbency itself produces newsworthy images and authority that rivals cannot reproduce. Editorial comments about a candidate enter airtime even when the candidate is silent. Ordinary factual news may therefore affect the ledger. However, the system does not demand identical tone, identical questions, or identical sequences of favorable and unfavorable treatment. It regulates access and exposure while leaving room for journalism, subject to honesty and pluralism obligations. Broadcasters do much of the first-line measurement. Services designated by Arcom submit statements at specified intervals, and Arcom publishes or audits relevant totals, contacts editors about imbalances, and can require corrective action. The regulator’s leverage is partly preventive: frequent reporting makes it possible to rebalance before a phase closes. Formal enforcement can include notices and sanctions under the 1986 law, but public scrutiny and rapid compliance are especially important during a short campaign. Why it matters for 2027 First, the rule change alters campaign strategy. During equity, campaigns have incentives to demonstrate activity, polling relevance, elected support, and contribution to debate because those facts can justify more exposure. Once equality begins, marginal and leading candidates receive the same quantitative entitlement. Candidates who qualify late therefore acquire a scarce public resource that money alone cannot buy. Second, dates shape the information voters receive. A large portion of opinion formation occurs before strict equality. The later equality phase cannot fully reverse months of agenda setting under ordinary pluralism or equity. For analysis of [[2027 French presidential election]], every claim that a candidate was “excluded” or “favored” should identify the applicable period and compare speaking time, airtime, and schedule placement—not cite a single aggregate number. Third, the 2024 broadened pluralism doctrine may matter more in 2027 than it did in 2022. A channel could distribute candidates’ seconds correctly yet surround election coverage with a stable set of hosts and commentators expressing a narrow range of views. The quantitative presidential rules and qualitative general-pluralism assessment address different pathways to imbalance. How Arcom combines them in a high-intensity presidential campaign will be an important regulatory test. Fourth, equality can conflict with ordinary news judgment. A breakthrough, scandal, war, or incumbent presidential act may objectively make one candidate more newsworthy. The French system accepts that tension to protect the voter’s opportunity to encounter every qualified candidacy during the short official campaign. “Equal” does not mean a broadcaster endorses equivalence among programs; it means that editorial gatekeeping temporarily yields to a democratic allocation rule. Finally, television and radio no longer monopolize political attention. Candidates can build enormous audiences on platforms outside the traditional time-counting regime. Broadcast equality therefore protects access to regulated mass media but cannot equalize total visibility across the information environment. A rigorous 2027 assessment should place Arcom’s ledgers beside platform reach, paid and organic digital campaigning, and media-ownership patterns without pretending those are governed by the same rule. A practical checklist for reading 2027 coverage When a speaking-time controversy arises, ask: What exact dates does the claim cover? Was the governing rule routine pluralism, presidential equity, or presidential equality? Is the number speaking time or the broader airtime? Does it include supporters, and how were ambiguous interventions classified? Were comparable morning, daytime, evening, and night conditions respected? Is the comparison made service by service and phase by phase, or is it an aggregate that hides imbalance? Is the complaint about candidate allocation, or about the broader mix of hosts, guests, themes, and viewpoints under the 2024 pluralism doctrine? Is the medium actually within Arcom’s election recommendation? Without those answers, “equal time” is usually rhetoric rather than a legal diagnosis. Sources Primary sources, all accessed 2026-07-09: Arcom, Recommendation no. 2021-03 of 6 October 2021 for the presidential election — scope, 2022 periods, equity criteria, equality, airtime, and comparable schedule bands. Légifrance, Law no. 62-1292 of 6 November 1962, article 3 — organic rules for the candidate list and equity/equality phases. Légifrance, Law no. 86-1067 of 30 September 1986 — statutory basis for freedom of communication, Arcom, pluralism, monitoring, and enforcement. Légifrance, Decree no. 2001-213 of 8 March 2001, article 15 — equal official public-service campaign broadcasts and minimum durations. Légifrance, Conseil d’État, 13 February 2024, no. 463162 — requirement to consider currents expressed by all program participants, not politicians alone. Légifrance, Arcom deliberation no. 2024-15 of 17 July 2024 — current broader method for assessing manifest and lasting pluralism imbalance. Légifrance, Constitutional Council decision no. 86-217 DC of 18 September 1986 — constitutional basis and mandatory character of pluralism supervision. Arcom, Presidential election 2022: speaking-time rules between the rounds — applied dates, finalist equality, comparable scheduling, and treatment of the president-candidate. Arcom, Decision on equity for 1 January–7 March 2022 — concrete regulatory findings of overexposure and demands for correction. Open questions What dates, reporting intervals, services, and dayparts will Arcom specify in its 2027 presidential recommendation? Will the legal text governing the election be amended before candidate-list publication, especially after the April 2026 update to the implementing decree? How will Arcom combine strict candidate equality with its post-2024 qualitative review of presenters, columnists, guests, topics, and viewpoints? What classification guidance will apply to an incumbent or acting president’s institutional interventions if that person is a candidate or active supporter? Will Arcom publish data in a form that permits service-by-service comparison of speaking time, airtime, tone, and schedule placement without relying on broadcaster summaries? How should researchers compare regulated broadcast exposure with platform audiences that sit outside the traditional time-ledger system?

title: Official campaign period in French presidential elections
deck: France's campagne électorale officielle is a short, equality-centered legal phase immediately before each presidential ballot; it must not be confused with the much longer campaign-finance period, Arcom's pre-campaign media monitoring, or ordinary political campaigning.
headings: The phrase “the campaign” hides several clocks
The national control commission and equal state facilities
Arcom's media phases are broader than the formal campaign
The silence period and prohibited last-minute acts
Campaign finance runs on a different logic
What is known—and not yet known—for 2027
text: France's campagne électorale officielle is a short, equality-centered legal phase immediately before each presidential ballot; it must not be confused with the much longer campaign-finance period, Arcom's pre-campaign media monitoring, or ordinary political campaigning. Up: [[2027 French presidential election]] Related: [[2027 French presidential election calendar]] · [[French presidential campaign finance]] · [[Media pluralism and speaking time in French elections]] · [[French presidential nomination mechanisms]] The phrase “the campaign” hides several clocks In ordinary political speech, a French presidential campaign can last for months or years. A prospective contender tours the country, publishes a book, seeks a party nomination, recruits staff, raises money, and pursues the 500 presentations well before the official candidate list exists. None of that is made unreal by the fact that the official campaign has not opened. It simply belongs to a different legal phase. For legal and journalistic purposes, at least five clocks should be kept separate: Clock What it regulates 2027 position as of 10 July 2026 Political campaigning Declarations, meetings, party selection, organization, persuasion Already occurring as a political fact; no single statutory opening day Campaign-finance accounting Election-directed receipts and expenses, the financial agent, account and ceilings Opened 1 April 2026 , according to the 2027 CNCCFP guide Pre-official audiovisual phases Equitable access and exposure under an election-specific Arcom recommendation 2027 recommendation and exact phases not yet issued Official electoral campaign Strict equality, official broadcasts, state facilities and the final regulated phase before each ballot First-round opening is legally derivable as 5 April 2027 ; operational instruments remain future State propaganda operation Approved posters, candidate statements, audio versions, printing and delivery Detailed 2027 timetable, specifications, draws and submission deadlines not yet issued This separation prevents a common false binary. It is wrong both to say that candidates cannot campaign before April 2027 and to treat every activity since 2026 as part of the formal campaign. The law attaches different consequences to different periods. The formal campaign's legal boundaries Article 10 of Decree no. 2001-213, the presidential implementing decree, says that the campaign for the first round opens on the second Monday preceding the ballot and closes at zero hours on the eve of the ballot . Article L. 47 A of the Electoral Code supplies the general statutory formulation. For a first round scheduled on Sunday 18 April 2027, the opening is therefore Monday 5 April 2027 . Closure at zero hours on Saturday 17 April means the campaign activity governed by the closing rule stops as Friday turns into Saturday; it does not continue through Saturday daytime. The between-round rule needs more care. The Electoral Code generally says that a second-round campaign opens the day after the first round. The presidential implementing decree states more specifically that it opens upon publication in the Journal officiel of the names of the two candidates authorized to stand. The Conseil constitutionnel establishes the first-round result and the two-person field. For 2027, the exact publication event cannot be supplied in advance. Coverage should identify the actual Council decision and Journal officiel publication rather than inventing a date from the 2022 sequence. The second-round campaign closes at zero hours on the eve of the second ballot. With the second round scheduled for Sunday 2 May 2027, that closing point is Saturday 1 May at 00:00 . Again, the practical silence period occupies the Saturday before Sunday voting. The formal period is short because it is not intended to contain the whole democratic contest. Its distinctive purpose is to place the officially qualified candidates within a final common framework: equal state facilities, controlled official materials, equal audiovisual treatment, and a common cessation point before voting. Qualification comes before official equality The formal campaign is built around a settled candidate list. Under Article 3 of the 1962 law, the Government publishes the list no later than the fourth Friday before the first round, after the [[Conseil constitutionnel]] has handled presentations and the relevant eligibility process. The list is therefore a legal gateway: equality during the official phase applies to the people who have actually qualified, not to every declared, party-selected, or widely polled contender. That does not mean media pluralism begins only after qualification. It means the regulator must use different principles at different stages. Before a final field exists, mechanically equal treatment of every possible contender would be both difficult and potentially distortive. Once the field is fixed and the official campaign opens, strict equality becomes administrable and legally required. The [[French presidential nomination mechanisms|qualification system]] and the official campaign consequently answer different questions. Presentations and consent establish who may appear on the ballot. The official campaign establishes the common facilities and treatment available to those qualified candidates in the final days. The national control commission and equal state facilities The 1962 law requires all candidates to receive the same facilities from the state for the presidential campaign. Decree no. 2001-213 creates the Commission nationale de contrôle de la campagne électorale en vue de l'élection présidentielle to help enforce that equality and oversee the campaign's proper conduct. The commission is an election-specific body, not a continuously operating campaign regulator. The decree provides for it to be installed around the election and gives it a high-level institutional composition. Its work sits alongside, rather than replaces, other authorities. Arcom supervises the audiovisual rules. The CNCCFP later examines campaign accounts. The Conseil constitutionnel supervises the regularity of the presidential election and proclaims results. Interior and local administrations carry out logistics. Treating “the commission” as a single all-purpose electoral authority obscures this divided architecture. The national control commission's practical center is official candidate communication. It verifies that state-provided facilities are equal and examines official materials under the decree. Past commission reports are valuable because they show how rules are operationalized—format reviews, deadlines, printing problems, distribution, online accessibility, disputes and coordination—but a prior report is precedent and evidence, not the 2027 instruction sheet. This distinction also clarifies the meaning of “official propaganda.” In French election administration, propagande électorale is a neutral legal term for campaign communication. It does not necessarily imply deception. The official operation covers specified materials and facilities; it does not certify every political claim as true or convert the state into the author of a candidate's program. Posters, candidate statements, and delivery Articles 16–18 of the presidential decree organize the principal official physical materials. Authorities provide reserved poster locations. During the campaign before each round, each candidate may use the assigned space for a poster presenting declarations and another announcing electoral meetings; the decree permits specified additional information such as the time of official broadcasts and campaign internet or social-media identifiers. Each candidate may also have a text of declarations sent to voters. This is commonly called the profession de foi or electoral statement. The presidential system is national: the statement is a common candidate document rather than a patchwork of locally tailored leaflets. The commission examines conformity with the governing rules. An audio recording accompanies the accessibility system. The Interior Ministry has also made candidate statements available through its official online program portal in recent elections. State involvement should be described precisely. The candidate writes and politically owns the message. The control and administrative bodies set formats, examine compliance, coordinate production or receipt, and arrange equal distribution under the applicable instructions. Delivery to a household is not a governmental endorsement. Nor does failure of a particular envelope to arrive erase the election; distribution quality is an administrative issue whose legal consequence depends on scale, cause, unequal effect and the competent authority's findings. The controlled mailing is only one channel. Candidates and supporters may communicate through meetings, leaflets, websites, social platforms, interviews and other lawful means outside the official packet. Those channels remain subject to applicable propaganda, finance, advertising, data-protection, defamation and silence-period rules. “Official material” therefore means a state-facilitated category, not the universe of legitimate campaign speech. For 2027, the exact paper dimensions, grammage, electronic-file requirements, accessibility specifications, quantities, delivery addresses and deadlines should be taken from the future commission, ministry and prefectural instruments. Copying a 2022 technical deadline into a 2027 calendar would turn a precedent into a false fact. Official radio and television broadcasts Article 15 of Decree no. 2001-213 guarantees each candidate equal duration in official radio and television broadcasts carried by the national public-service program companies. Arcom fixes the duration after consulting all candidates. The decree sets a floor of 15 minutes per candidate for the first round . For the second round, the floor is one hour per candidate , unless both finalists agree to a shorter duration. These candidate broadcasts are a distinct object from news coverage. They are designated campaign programs produced and transmitted within rules set by Arcom. Equality of their allocated duration does not itself describe how every news bulletin, interview or debate is counted. Conversely, a candidate's appearance in editorial programming is not automatically part of that candidate's official broadcast allotment. The distinction matters operationally. Arcom normally issues one or more decisions dealing with duration, sequence, production conditions, use of archives or third-party material, technical delivery, draws, recordings, accessibility and schedules. None of the detailed 2027 broadcast grid existed in the official materials reviewed as of 10 July 2026. The statutory and decree-based guarantee is already knowable; the actual slots are future facts. Arcom's media phases are broader than the formal campaign [[Media pluralism and speaking time in French elections]] begins before the official campaign. For 2022, Arcom's election-specific recommendation created three periods. From 1 January until the eve of publication of the candidate list, broadcasters had to provide equitable speaking and airtime to candidates and supporters. From publication of the official list until the eve of the formal campaign, equity continued in comparable programming conditions. During the official campaign, equality replaced equity for speaking time and airtime, again in comparable programming conditions. Equity is not a euphemism for arbitrary favoritism. Arcom considers indicators such as political representativeness and demonstrated involvement in the campaign. Equality is the stricter presidential rule once the official campaign is underway. Arcom distinguishes temps de parole —candidate and supporter speech—from temps d'antenne , which additionally captures editorial sequences devoted to a candidate when they are not explicitly unfavorable. Equal raw minutes at 3 a.m. and prime time would not necessarily satisfy comparable programming conditions, so the regulator also examines scheduling bands. The 2022 chronology illustrates the mechanism but does not fix the 2027 calendar. The statutory equality requirement during the official campaign is durable. The date on which Arcom begins a pre-campaign equity count, the services covered, reporting intervals, attribution conventions and treatment of new audiovisual formats depend on a future 2027 recommendation. Until that text is issued, an analyst may use 2022 as a labeled precedent but should not announce “1 January 2027” as an appointed regulatory opening. Between rounds, the relationship between the Council's result process, formal campaign language and Arcom's equality count also deserves exact sourcing. In 2022, Arcom applied equality to the two finalists from the Monday after the first round. The eventual 2027 recommendation will govern the regulator's counting practice; the presidential decree governs the formal campaign opening tied to publication of the authorized names. These rules can be coordinated without being identical in wording. The silence period and prohibited last-minute acts The close of the formal campaign activates concrete restrictions. Article L. 49 of the Electoral Code prohibits, from zero hours on the eve of the ballot, distribution of ballots, circulars and other documents; electronic dissemination of messages constituting electoral propaganda; automated mass telephone appeals; and meetings of an electoral character. Article L. 48-2 bars candidates from bringing a new polemical electoral argument to public attention so late that opponents cannot usefully answer before the campaign ends. The rule is broader than a ban on purchasing new advertisements and narrower than a command to erase the internet. The key questions are who disseminated what, when, through which channel, and whether the act had the character of electoral propaganda. A pre-existing webpage remaining accessible is not analytically identical to a new campaign post pushed during the silence period. News organizations also retain their own legal and editorial responsibilities; the campaign-closing rules should not be paraphrased as a total news blackout. Separate rules restrict premature communication of election results and estimates before the legal closing time, while polling publication has its own statutory framework. Those subjects should not be collapsed into the official-campaign definition merely because they become especially salient on election weekend. Longer restrictions begin still earlier. Article L. 52-1 prohibits electoral use of commercial advertising through the press or audiovisual communication during the six months preceding the first day of the election month and through the decisive ballot. Article L. 51 restricts election posters outside authorized locations during the same general period. These rules demonstrate again why the formal two-week campaign is not the only regulated interval. Campaign finance runs on a different logic The [[French presidential campaign finance|campaign account]] exists to trace resources and election-directed expenditure, not to declare when public persuasion becomes politically legitimate. For 2027, the CNCCFP says the financing period began on 1 April 2026 —more than a year before the first ballot and a full year before the formal campaign. During that accounting period, the financial agent receives campaign funds and pays election expenses under the statutory framework. A cost can be relevant to the future account even though it was incurred before qualification and before the official campaign. Conversely, opening day on 5 April 2027 does not make every expense automatically reimbursable; purpose, payment route, documentation, timing and the substantive finance rules still matter. The CNCCFP does not pre-approve campaign rhetoric or run the official broadcast schedule. It reviews the filed financial record after the election and can approve, reform or reject an account and determine reimbursement. Arcom's equality finding and the CNCCFP's accounting classification are therefore different legal determinations. The national control commission's approval of the format of a profession de foi likewise does not settle whether every related invoice is properly included or reimbursable. What is known—and not yet known—for 2027 Given the officially published ballot dates, current law supports several firm statements: the finance-accounting period opened on 1 April 2026 ; the first-round formal campaign is scheduled by law to open 5 April 2027 ; it closes 17 April 2027 at 00:00 ; the second-round formal campaign opens through the legally required post-first-round publication process, whose exact 2027 timestamp is not yet known; the second-round campaign closes 1 May 2027 at 00:00 ; qualified candidates receive equal state facilities and equal treatment in the official audiovisual phase. But current law does not by itself provide every operational fact. Future 2027 instruments must establish or confirm the candidate list, the two finalists, the Arcom pre-campaign periods, monitoring and reporting method, official-broadcast durations above the minimum if any, production schedule, order, commission instructions, poster and statement specifications, delivery timetable, overseas adjustments and administrative contacts. The election could also be affected by later legislation, litigation or emergency constitutional circumstances. Any 2027 calendar should therefore label a date as statutory, derived, officially appointed, or still pending. That vocabulary is more informative than calling the entire year either “the campaign” or “pre-campaign.” Why it matters The clocks determine what claims are legally meaningful. Saying that the “official campaign began” implies strict equality and access to state facilities. Saying that the “financial campaign began” implies accounting and intermediary obligations, not equal broadcast time. Saying that Arcom is monitoring equity implies a regulator-defined audiovisual phase, not ballot qualification. Saying that propaganda was “official” identifies a controlled distribution channel, not official agreement with its content. For reporting on [[2027 French presidential election]], these distinctions prevent four recurring errors: calling a politically active person an official candidate; treating equity as equality; assuming the state mailing covers all campaign speech; and using the formal opening date as the start of financial accountability. They also identify the evidence needed to verify each claim: the Conseil constitutionnel and Journal officiel for the field, Legifrance for the legal window, Arcom for media phases and broadcasts, the control commission and Interior Ministry for official materials, and the CNCCFP for money.
