A fundraising surge in a safe seat matters less to control than a capacity change in a state that can plausibly offset a loss elsewhere. For both chambers, the correct as-of date is the date of the evidence, not the publication date. A July 16 article may use a June 30 cash balance, a July 15 filing timestamp, a July 20 party report still pending, and a state ballot list last updated on another day. The article should show those dates side by side. Working checklist for the desk Pull the FEC report and record its filing timestamp, report type, coverage period, and amendment status. Join the report to FEC candidate ID and principal or authorized committee ID; do not rely on candidate name alone. Check state ballot status from the official state election authority or official candidate list. Normalize receipts, disbursements, cash, debt, loans, transfers, refunds, and period length. Separate candidate money, party support, coordinated spending, independent expenditures, and other communications. Compare only matched periods unless the mismatch is the point of the note. Label cycle-wide benchmarks, such as the FEC 15-month summary, as aggregate context rather than race evidence. Require independent corroboration before turning finance into an electoral movement claim. Mark late, missing, amended, or identity-ambiguous records as evidence gaps. Update the map, race dossier, or synthesis only when the new fact has a clear explanatory job. Sources FEC July reporting reminder for 2026 - official July 15 and July 20 reporting deadlines, coverage periods, candidate reporting threshold, and special/pre-election caveat; published June 30, 2026; accessed July 10, 2026. FEC reports due in 2026 - official filing responsibilities, electronic validation deadline, and timely-filing rules; accessed July 10, 2026. FEC 2026 congressional primary dates and candidate filing deadlines - federal compilation of state primary, runoff, and ballot-access dates; data as of May 18, 2026; accessed July 10, 2026. FEC campaign-finance data - official candidate, committee, report, transaction, and independent-expenditure data portal; accessed July 10, 2026. OpenFEC API documentation - official API documentation for candidate, committee, filing, report, and transaction retrieval; accessed July 10, 2026. FEC statistical summary of 15-month campaign activity of the 2025-2026 election cycle - official aggregate congressional candidate, party, PAC, cash, debt, and independent-expenditure benchmark through March 31, 2026; published July 9, 2026; accessed July 10, 2026. Open questions Which state ballot lists update quickly enough after filing deadlines to serve as the canonical candidate-field source for each pivotal race? How should the desk version FEC amendments when a current API total differs from the value captured in an earlier race dossier? Which July 20 party and PAC monthly reports should trigger a cross-race allocation synthesis rather than individual race notes? What minimum identity mismatch should block publication: name difference, district difference, committee relationship, or unresolved ballot status?

title: 2026 midterm election-law docket
deck: The 2026 election-law docket tracks legal changes that can alter congressional lines, ballot access, campaign spending, vote counting, certification, recounts, or congressional seating.
headings: Vote counting, mail ballots, certification, and recounts
text: The 2026 election-law docket tracks legal changes that can alter congressional lines, ballot access, campaign spending, vote counting, certification, recounts, or congressional seating. Up: [[2026 United States midterm elections]] · Related: [[2026 House battleground map]] · [[2026 Senate control path]] · [[NRSC v. FEC and the 2026 midterms]] · [[Race calls certification recounts and contests]] Why it matters Election law is not a side channel to the 2026 midterms. It can define the district map, determine who appears on the ballot, change how parties spend in coordination with candidates, set which ballots are counted and when, govern recount thresholds, and shape how a disputed House or Senate seat reaches Congress. But legal movement is easy to overstate. A complaint is not a ruling. A stay is not a final merits decision. A new map is not operative until the legal and administrative calendar make it usable. A campaign-finance ruling changes a permissible channel; it does not prove money has moved into any particular race. This docket is therefore a status discipline rather than a litigation scrapbook. It should include only legal matters with a plausible route to chamber control, race administration, or the interpretation of results. It should exclude culture-war lawsuits, campaign rhetoric, fraud allegations, and speculative constitutional theories unless they materially affect ballot access, district lines, vote counting, certification, recounts, party spending, or Article I seating. As of July 10, 2026, the main live buckets are: congressional redistricting after a volatile post-2020 map cycle; the Supreme Court's June 30 decision in [[NRSC v. FEC and the 2026 midterms]]; state rules for mail-ballot processing, receipt, curing, canvass, certification, and recounts; ballot-access disputes; and any House or Senate contest path that emerges after Election Day. The docket should use official court records and election authorities first, with nonpartisan trackers as leads and context. The docket fields Every entry should carry enough information to prevent legal adjectives from doing too much work: Field Required content Matter Case name, statute, administrative action, or official proceeding. Jurisdiction Court, agency, state election authority, chamber, or legislative body. Race connection House map, Senate race, ballot access, party spending, count rule, certification, recount, or seating. Current operative status What rule, map, deadline, or order controls today. Procedural status Complaint, injunction, merits ruling, stay, appeal, remand, final judgment, legislation, rulemaking, or pending petition. Control relevance Which seats or spending channels could plausibly change. Next date Hearing, filing deadline, map deadline, primary date, certification date, or unknown. Source Official docket/order/statute first; tracker or reporting only as context. Claim boundary What the legal event establishes and what it does not establish. The most important row is "current operative status." A court can condemn an old map while a remedial map is already in force. A Supreme Court stay can make a disputed map usable for one election without resolving the merits. A legislature can pass a map that still awaits pre-election deadlines, state-law challenges, or administrative implementation. A docket that only says "litigation pending" is not useful enough for [[2026 House battleground map]]. Redistricting and district lines House control is unusually sensitive to district lines because the chamber turns on a national seat threshold, not a statewide winner. A single map change can alter several seats' partisanship, incumbent pairings, racial-vote-dilution claims, candidate filing decisions, and campaign spending. The docket should separate three questions: Which map is legally operative for the next election? Which map is being challenged or revised? Which races actually change under the operative map? Those questions are often conflated. A map can be controversial but settled for 2026. A lawsuit can be live but too late to alter the current cycle. A remedial order can change district boundaries without changing the number of genuinely competitive seats. The control map should move only when a legal status has changed enough to affect a district ledger, candidate field, or rating baseline. Nonpartisan trackers are useful for triage. NCSL's mid-decade redistricting tracker records states where maps have changed or remain under pressure, including entries that tie state status to Supreme Court developments and special primary timing. Ballotpedia's 2026 redistricting pages collect state-by-state map-change and litigation summaries. Brennan Center and All About Redistricting provide legal context and case tracking. None should substitute for the operative court order, state election page, or enacted map when the desk updates a race note. The docket should use a restrained redistricting taxonomy: Status Meaning for the 2026 desk Operative for 2026 The map currently controls candidate filing and election administration. Stayed for 2026 A court has allowed a map or rule to remain in effect while litigation continues. Remedial map ordered A court or state body has required new lines, but implementation details may remain. New map enacted A legislature, commission, or voters adopted a map that must be checked against effective date and litigation. Litigation pending, no operative change The case is relevant but does not yet alter the control map. Too late for 2026 absent extraordinary order The legal issue may matter later but should not move a 2026 race forecast now. This avoids the common error of turning legal controversy into electoral movement. If Alabama, Louisiana, Ohio, California, New York, Texas, Georgia, Maryland, or another state appears in a tracker, the desk should ask which specific congressional districts are under current lines, whether candidate filing or special-primary dates changed, and whether the control-relevant seats are newly exposed or merely differently drawn. Campaign-finance law and party coordination The Supreme Court's June 30, 2026 decision in National Republican Senatorial Committee v. Federal Election Commission is already a docket entry because it changed federal limits on coordinated party expenditures. The Court held that FECA's limits on party coordinated expenditures violate the First Amendment. The immediate legal claim is narrow enough to state clearly: federal party committees are no longer constrained by the invalidated coordinated-expenditure limits. The electoral inference is not narrow: parties still must choose where to spend, how to report, how to coordinate within other rules, and whether the new channel substitutes for or adds to independent expenditures. The docket should therefore connect NRSC v. FEC to [[2026 midterm money map]] rather than to a race forecast. The correct follow-up is a reporting discipline: identify party-paid coordinated support separately from candidate receipts, transfers, and independent expenditures once filings and FEC data show actual spending. The ruling is a structural condition, not proof of race movement. Campaign-finance litigation can matter in three different ways. First, it can change legal limits or definitions. Second, it can change enforcement expectations and risk tolerance. Third, it can affect the timing or classification of reports. Only the first is usually immediate enough for a public legal-docket update. The second and third belong in the money map when they change how the desk reads filings. Ballot access and candidate eligibility Ballot access is control-relevant when it changes the feasible candidate set in a competitive race, affects a major-party nominee, changes a special-election or primary calendar, or alters whether a minor-party or independent candidate can plausibly affect the margin. A routine signature dispute in a safe district may not need a public article. A court order removing, adding, or replacing a candidate in a Senate race or pivotal House district does. The docket should distinguish: official filing status from campaign announcements; a challenge filed from a challenge sustained; administrative rejection from judicial review; primary-ballot access from general-election ballot access; candidate eligibility from party nomination rules; replacement procedures from ordinary withdrawal. The evidence standard should be official: secretary of state pages, state election boards, court orders, and final candidate lists. Campaign press releases can identify a claimed action but should not establish legal status on their own. Vote counting, mail ballots, certification, and recounts Rules about ballot receipt, preprocessing, curing, canvass, certification, audits, and recounts become most important after voting begins, but they should be mapped before then. They determine whether an election-night lead is meaningful, how long lawful counting may continue, whether late-arriving ballots can be included, and what margin triggers a recount. [[Race calls certification recounts and contests]] explains the status ladder; this docket stores the rule changes and live disputes that alter that ladder. The docket should track legal events in this area only when they change a rule or clarify a contested rule. A political demand to stop counting is not law. A complaint about mail-ballot deadlines is not a new deadline. A court order enjoining or reinstating a receipt rule is a docket event. A state election office publishing an official canvass or recount calendar is also a docket event, even without litigation, because it controls the timing of official results. For every state with a control-relevant Senate race or a cluster of pivotal House districts, the eventual race dossier should know: when mail ballots can be processed; whether mail ballots must be received by Election Day or may arrive later if postmarked by Election Day; whether voters can cure signature or identification defects; how provisional ballots are reviewed; local and state canvass deadlines; certification deadlines; automatic recount thresholds; candidate-request recount rules and costs; whether certification is stayed, amended, or followed by recount under state law. This information should be stored as legal status, not as fraud suspicion or reassurance. Slow lawful counting is not an anomaly. A changed deadline is not proof of partisan effect until the affected ballot pool and race context are known. Article I and congressional seating For House and Senate races, the legal endpoint is not only state certification. Article I, Section 5 gives each house authority to judge the elections, returns, and qualifications of its own members. The House has a statutory contested-election channel, the Federal Contested Elections Act, codified at 2 U.S.C. chapter 12. The Senate uses its own constitutional practice, rules, committees, and resolutions. These channels should not be activated in the public docket until an actual contest, petition, committee action, or chamber proceeding exists. But they matter because a close or disputed 2026 result could be certified by a state and still face a congressional contest. The docket's job is to prevent two equal errors. One error is treating state certification as metaphysically final for congressional membership. The other is treating a filed contest as if it vacates a certificate. The proper status labels are narrower: certified, recount pending, contest filed, contest referred, member seated without prejudice, contest dismissed, new certificate issued, or chamber resolution adopted. Current watch categories As of this run, the desk should prioritize five categories: Operative congressional maps. Update the House map only when official map status, filing calendar, or district composition changes. Party-coordinated spending after NRSC v. FEC . Watch FEC guidance and reports for actual spending classification. Mail-ballot and counting rules in pivotal states. Preserve official deadlines before election-night interpretation. Candidate ballot access in competitive races. Require official lists or orders before revising candidate fields. Post-election recount and contest rules. Build the legal calendar before returns arrive. The docket should avoid calling this a list of "threats." Some legal events expand access, some restrict it, some merely clarify procedure, and some change partisan opportunity without telling us the election outcome. The public value is precision: which rule controls, when it changed, who can appeal, and which race notes should inherit the change. Sources Supreme Court docket, Louisiana v. Callais , No. 24-109 — procedural status for a control-relevant congressional-map case; accessed July 10, 2026. Supreme Court opinion, Louisiana v. Callais , No. 24-109 — merits and remand framework for Louisiana congressional redistricting; accessed July 10, 2026. Supreme Court order, Allen v. Milligan — Alabama map-status and remedial-posture context after Callais ; accessed July 10, 2026. Supreme Court order, Abbott v. LULAC — Texas map stay and Purcell-posture context; accessed July 10, 2026. Supreme Court opinion, National Republican Senatorial Committee v. FEC , No. 24-621 — June 30, 2026 decision on federal coordinated-party-expenditure limits; accessed July 10, 2026. FEC summary of NRSC v. FEC — official FEC explanation of the decision; accessed July 10, 2026. FEC, Campaign Legal Center v. FEC, No. 26-1559 — live challenge to Advisory Opinion 2024-01 on canvassing and coordination; accessed July 10, 2026. FEC Advisory Opinion 2024-01, Texas Majority PAC — agency baseline for certain canvassing and coordination questions; accessed July 10, 2026. FEC 2026 congressional primary dates and filing deadlines — federal election calendar lead, with state-source caveat; accessed July 10, 2026. NCSL, Changing the Maps: Tracking Mid-Decade Redistricting — state-by-state mid-decade congressional map status and timing leads; accessed July 10, 2026. NCSL, Redistricting and Census — redistricting law and process context; accessed July 10, 2026. Ballotpedia, Redistricting ahead of the 2026 elections — state-level litigation and map-change tracker; accessed July 10, 2026. Brennan Center, Redistricting Litigation Roundup — post-2020 redistricting litigation tracker and context; accessed July 10, 2026. All About Redistricting — legal background and state redistricting resources; accessed July 10, 2026. U.S. Election Assistance Commission, Election Results, Canvass, and Certification — official canvass, certification, recount, and results resources; accessed July 10, 2026. Office of the Law Revision Counsel, 2 U.S.C. chapter 12 — Federal Contested Elections Act; accessed July 10, 2026. Constitution Annotated, Article I, Section 5 judging power — congressional authority over elections, returns, and qualifications; accessed July 10, 2026. Open questions Which congressional-map cases remain live enough to alter 2026 candidate filing or district ratings rather than only future cycles? Should [[2026 House battleground map]] store a compact legal-status column for every map-changed state? How will FEC reporting pages classify party-coordinated spending after NRSC v. FEC in practice? Which states' recount or certification laws are most likely to matter for control-relevant Senate races?

title: 2026 midterm filing-calendar risk
deck: The 2026 filing calendar creates analytical risk because ballot access, primaries, independent petitions, FEC reports, withdrawals, and substitutions close on different clocks.
headings: A filing-risk field for every dossier
text: The 2026 filing calendar creates analytical risk because ballot access, primaries, independent petitions, FEC reports, withdrawals, and substitutions close on different clocks. Up: [[2026 United States midterm elections]] · Related: [[2026 midterm candidate filing checkpoint]] · [[2026 midterm election-law docket]] · [[2026 House district dossier template]] · [[2026 Senate race dossier template]] Scope This note is not a duplicate of [[2026 midterm candidate filing checkpoint]]. The checkpoint tells the desk how to ingest the July candidate and finance evidence without confusing ballot records, FEC records, and interpretation. This note is narrower and more durable: it explains the filing-calendar risks that can make an early 2026 House or Senate dossier look settled when the legal candidate universe is still moving. The core problem is that "filing" is not one event. A major-party candidate may file for a primary. An independent candidate may file petitions for the general election. A new party may face a different recognition deadline. A candidate may win a primary but later withdraw. A party may be allowed, or not allowed, to replace a nominee. A court may change a map or reopen a deadline. A special election may have its own compressed calendar. A federal committee may file with the FEC before or after any of those state-law events. Those clocks overlap, but they do not collapse into a national "field is set" date. As of July 10, 2026, the FEC's congressional primary-date and candidate-filing sheet is the best federal route map for the full congressional calendar. It is explicit about its limits: dates are subject to change; the sources are state election offices, statutes, and state parties; the general election date is November 3, 2026; and independent-petition dates may omit earlier declarations, petition-checking deadlines, or new-party requirements. That caveat is not boilerplate. It is the reason a race dossier should cite state authorities before treating a candidate list as final. The risk surface Filing-calendar risk appears when the desk writes a race note before all relevant calendar gates have closed or before official sources have reconciled them. The risk is not simply that an article might be outdated later. All election coverage ages. The more serious risk is category error: calling a person a nominee who is only a federal filer, calling a primary field settled while an independent path remains open, or calling a candidate gone from the race while the finance record still matters. The FEC sheet shows the spread. Delaware's 2026 primary is September 15, with a July 14 primary filing deadline and a September 1 independent filing deadline. Indiana's primary was May 5, but the FEC sheet lists a July 15 noon independent deadline. Michigan has an August 4 primary and an independent deadline listed as July 16. Rhode Island has a September 9 primary, with a July 10 independent deadline in the FEC table. New Hampshire's Senate primary is September 8 and independent deadline September 2. Texas had a March 3 primary, a May 26 runoff, and a June 25 independent deadline. Louisiana is structurally unusual: the FEC sheet lists a May 16 Senate election and a November 3 House election, with different runoff dates, after the House election timing changed following Louisiana v. Callais . Those examples show why a single July dossier rule will fail. A Texas Senate general-election field can be much more mature than a New Hampshire Senate field on the same day. A Michigan Senate note in early July may know the primary date but not the final independent universe. A Delaware House or Senate-related note may still be months away from a primary. A Louisiana House note needs election-structure text before ordinary primary-to-general language. Five clocks to keep separate The first clock is the primary filing clock. This decides who can appear on a major-party primary ballot, subject to challenges, withdrawals, and state procedures. It is usually the clock that campaigns and reporters mean when they say "the filing deadline." But it is only one gate. The second clock is the primary and runoff clock. A primary date can settle a nominee, but only if the state uses a conventional primary, the race is uncontested or clearly resolved, and no runoff or contest remains. The FEC pre-election reporting page also uses primary and runoff dates to generate campaign-finance reporting obligations, so the election date can affect both ballot interpretation and financial disclosure timing. The third clock is the independent, minor-party, or third-party clock. The FEC sheet warns that its independent filing column is a general reference and that candidates should check states for other requirements. A declaration may precede a petition filing. Petitions may need official checking. New parties may face separate deadlines. A race dossier that says "the field is set" after the major-party filing deadline but before the independent deadline should say what kind of field is set. The fourth clock is the withdrawal, substitution, and disqualification clock. State law can allow or forbid replacement candidates depending on timing, reason, party status, and office. A withdrawal can remove a candidate from the ballot but leave FEC reports, debt, refunds, and spending history behind. A disqualification can alter the electoral field without making prior campaign activity irrelevant. This clock is especially important in high-attention Senate races because a candidate crisis can change the control path only if the legal replacement route is real. The fifth clock is the federal finance clock. The July 15 quarterly report measures candidate-committee activity through June 30. Monthly party committees report June activity by July 20. Pre-election reports, post-election reports, 48-hour notices, independent-expenditure reports, and special-election notices can add more dates. Finance dates can sharpen evidence, but they cannot decide ballot access. Calendar risk by article type Race dossiers have the highest exposure. A dossier uses a named race and often a candidate table. If the table mixes federal filers, ballot-qualified candidates, declared candidates, primary candidates, and independent petitioners without labels, it will mislead. The safe solution is a status field. A person can be "FEC filer," "primary-ballot candidate," "primary nominee," "independent petition pending," "general-election candidate," "withdrawn," or "disqualified." Those labels can coexist with a finance row. Control-path notes have a different exposure. They can overstate how fixed a chamber route is. A Senate route built from ratings before late primaries and independent deadlines should be labeled as a modeled route, not a settled candidate universe. A House battleground map can say a district is structurally competitive before the final field is known, but it should not infer nominee quality, cash comparison, or ballot strategy until the local calendar supports it. Finance notes face a timing mismatch. A candidate may have a strong June 30 cash position and then lose a primary, withdraw, or miss ballot access. That does not make the report useless. It means the report belongs to the campaign-history and spending-capacity record, not necessarily the November choice set. Conversely, a late independent candidate may have ballot relevance before a meaningful FEC report appears. Polling notes face candidate-definition risk. A poll fielded before the final ballot is known may test a hypothetical matchup. That can be analytically useful, but the note should label it as such. A likely-voter model for a primary is not a general-election estimate. A poll that includes a candidate who later fails ballot access becomes historical evidence about a possible field, not current evidence about the certified field. Election-law notes face remedy timing risk. A court can alter a map, move a filing deadline, change a ballot-access rule, or block a candidate. But not every legal filing changes the election calendar. [[2026 midterm election-law docket]] should track whether a case has an order, stay, deadline, or remedy that reaches the 2026 ballot. Filing-calendar risk begins when a legal possibility is written as an operative election fact. Official-source hierarchy The FEC calendar is a starting point, not the final authority for state ballot status. It is valuable because it compiles congressional primary dates, runoff dates, primary filing deadlines, and independent filing deadlines across states. It is also valuable because it flags special sequencing and caveats. But the sheet itself points back to state election offices, statutes, and state parties. For a race dossier, the preferred hierarchy is: State election office candidate list, filing list, ballot certification, or election calendar for ballot access. Court order or official administrative notice if litigation changes the calendar or candidate status. FEC candidate and committee records for federal finance identity. FEC reporting-date pages for federal reporting obligations and close-of-books dates. NCSL or another nonpartisan state-law summary for cross-state context. Campaign statements and press reports as leads, clearly labeled, until official status is available. The hierarchy prevents two common publication errors. It stops an FEC committee from becoming a ballot-qualified candidate by implication. It also stops an outdated state candidate list from erasing a campaign-finance obligation. The two records answer different questions. A filing-risk field for every dossier Every early race dossier should include a compact filing-risk field until the general-election field is certified or otherwise officially settled. Field Required answer Primary filing deadline Date, source, and whether challenges remain. Primary date and runoff date Date, source, and whether the nominee is official, unofficial, or pending. Independent/minor-party deadline Date and caveat about petitions, declarations, or new-party rules. Official candidate source URL and timestamp of state list or calendar. FEC identity status Candidate ID, committee ID, report period, and whether it has been matched to ballot status. Withdrawal/substitution exposure Known rule, unresolved question, or not checked. Next calendar gate The next date that can change the field or reporting obligations. This field should stay visible even when the race is not highly competitive. Safe seats can still produce errors if an article treats a primary winner as certified too early or omits an independent petition route. Competitive seats need the field because candidate identity can change ratings, finance interpretation, polling matchups, and control math. Examples of risk patterns Late primary risk appears in states such as Delaware and New Hampshire. The national desk may want to compare them with earlier-primary states because all are on the same November ballot. But a September primary means a July article is often describing a pre-nomination field. Ratings and finance can still be useful, but the dossier must say whether it is analyzing the likely general-election matchup or the official primary field. Independent-window risk appears when the major-party picture looks settled but an independent or minor-party deadline remains open. Indiana's July 15 noon independent deadline and Michigan's July 16 independent deadline in the FEC table illustrate the problem. A race note written July 10 can be current and still not final. The sentence should be "major-party primary status is X; independent filing deadline is Y," not "the field is settled." Structural-calendar risk appears in Louisiana. The FEC sheet notes that Louisiana House elections were postponed to November 3, 2026 following Louisiana v. Callais , while Senate and House entries have different listed sequences. A Louisiana House dossier should not use a generic primary-runoff template without checking the state's current election calendar and any operative court order. Special-election risk appears on the FEC dates-and-deadlines page. Special elections have their own notices and reporting dates, and the page warns that election dates are subject to change. A regular-cycle House or Senate table should not silently absorb a special election without preserving its election date, reporting obligations, and term or vacancy context. Withdrawal and replacement risk appears whenever a candidate crisis happens after a primary or after a filing deadline. The analytical question is not only whether the candidate will leave. It is whether state law and party rules allow replacement, by what date, and how ballot printing or certification affects the result. Until that is verified, the desk should avoid writing a new nominee into the control path. Publication rules Do not call a field "settled" unless the note says which field: primary ballot, major-party nominees, independent/minor-party access, general-election candidate list, or certified ballot. "Settled" without a modifier is too vague for 2026. Do not compare candidates' cash as general-election capacity unless both candidates are in comparable electoral positions. A nominee with June 30 cash and a primary contender with June 30 cash are not the same object. A candidate who loses a primary can still affect spending history, but not the November field. Do not move a race rating explanation into a dossier without checking whether the rating assumes a candidate matchup that is still provisional. Ratings may be forward-looking. Rome's note should tell Andrew when that is happening. Do not delete or ignore a withdrawn candidate's FEC record. The committee may still file reports, carry debt, issue refunds, or disclose spending that explains the race's history. The ballot record and finance record should diverge visibly rather than being forced together. Do not use one state's calendar pattern as a national rule. A March primary, a September primary, a top-two system, a runoff state, a party-convention state, and a special election can all appear in the same congressional cycle. Why it matters Filing-calendar discipline is not paperwork pedantry. It protects the main interpretive claims in the 2026 midterms set. Candidate quality cannot be evaluated cleanly until the candidate role is known. Finance cannot be interpreted cleanly until the report period and ballot status are matched. Polls cannot be compared cleanly until the tested field is identified. Ratings cannot be explained cleanly until the analyst's assumed field is visible. Control paths cannot be trusted if a race is counted as settled before the legal field is actually settled. The practical consequence is simple: every early race note should carry its next calendar gate. If the next gate is a primary, the note is pre-nomination. If the next gate is an independent deadline, the major-party field may be settled but the general-election field is not. If the next gate is a finance report, the ballot field may be known while campaign capacity is still stale. If the next gate is a court hearing, the map or ballot rule may be provisional. Naming the gate is how Rome prevents stale confidence. Sources FEC, 2026 congressional primary dates and candidate filing deadlines - federal compilation of primary, runoff, primary-filing, and independent-filing dates; data as of May 18, 2026; accessed July 10, 2026. FEC, dates and deadlines - official reporting-date hub, special-election notices, and FEC caveat that guidance does not replace the law; accessed July 10, 2026. FEC, congressional pre-election reporting dates for 2026 - state-by-state pre-election reporting schedule and warning that election dates are subject to change; accessed July 10, 2026. FEC, July reporting reminder 2026 - July 15 quarterly and July 20 monthly reporting checkpoints for federal committees; accessed July 10, 2026. FEC, reports due in 2026 - official FEC filing responsibilities, timely-filing rules, and reporting reminders; accessed July 10, 2026. NCSL, Summary 2026 Candidate Filing Deadlines - nonpartisan state filing-deadline overview, update date, and warning to consult state or local officials for current information; accessed July 10, 2026. Delaware Department of Elections, Primary Election - official Delaware 2026 primary date and voting schedule; accessed July 10, 2026. Rhode Island Department of State, 2026 election calendar PDF - official Rhode Island election calendar and declaration-of-candidacy filing period; accessed July 10, 2026. Open questions Which state election offices provide stable, timestamped candidate lists suitable for automated hourly checks? For each top Senate dossier, what is the exact withdrawal and replacement rule after the primary? Should the House battleground map carry one shared filing-risk column, or should each district dossier own the calendar details?

title: 2026 midterm money map
deck: The 2026 money map is a reproducible comparison of financial capacity and strategic attention—not a ranking of who will win—and it must keep candidate, party, coordinated, and independent channels separate.
headings: Derived measures that earn their keep
From financial fact to electoral inference
How the map connects to control
text: The 2026 money map is a reproducible comparison of financial capacity and strategic attention—not a ranking of who will win—and it must keep candidate, party, coordinated, and independent channels separate. Up: [[2026 United States midterm elections]] · Related: [[Campaign cash as an electoral signal]] · [[2026 House battleground map]] · [[2026 Senate control path]] · [[NRSC v. FEC and the 2026 midterms]] Why this map exists Campaign-finance reporting is unusually valuable because it turns part of the electoral struggle into dated, auditable records. It is also unusually easy to misuse. A leaderboard that adds every dollar associated with a candidate or party obscures who controls the money, when it was measured, whether it remains available, whether it was transferred rather than newly raised, and whether spending was undertaken because a race was already competitive. The result can look precise while answering no stable question. The money map instead asks four distinct questions. What resources can a candidate deploy? What do party organizations appear able and willing to add? Where are independent groups directing attention? What changed during a matched reporting window? These measures can illuminate campaign capacity and elite expectations. They do not directly measure persuasion, turnout, ballot qualification, or votes. As of July 9, 2026, the next common checkpoint is the July quarterly report due July 15 for authorized House and Senate committees. The Federal Election Commission says it covers activity from April 1—or the day after the previous report closed—through June 30. Monthly party and PAC filers report June activity by July 20. The different deadlines mean that a map assembled immediately after July 15 will mix fresh candidate data with older party data unless it labels every period. The correct response is not to delay all analysis, but to show the clocks. The four ledgers Candidate-controlled capacity The candidate ledger begins with each candidate's principal campaign committee and any other authorized committees. Its core fields are period receipts, period disbursements, ending cash, debts owed by the committee, debts owed to the committee, refunds, transfers, and coverage dates. The FEC's candidate summaries are convenient, but material comparisons should be checked against the underlying reports and amendments. Cash is the closest headline measure of flexibility, yet even cash is a dated accounting stock. Some of it may already be committed to payroll, media reservations, compliance, or contracts after the close of books. A useful diagnostic is reported cash minus reported debts owed, but that is an analyst's measure rather than an FEC field. It does not distinguish routine invoices from distressed liabilities and should never be described as a liquidation value. Receipts show inflow, not remaining strength. Candidate loans, transfers from prior authorized committees, joint-fundraising distributions, and refunds can make gross totals diverge from new donor support. Disbursements show activity only after classification. Early investment in staff or voter files can be productive; a high-cost fundraising program can generate impressive gross receipts while leaving little additional cash. This is why the map displays amounts and composition together. Party capacity and allocation National, state, and local party committees are different legal actors from candidate committees. Their money should not be assigned to a race merely because party leaders have discussed it. A party's balance establishes potential capacity, not an allocation. The map records race-specific support only after it appears in a reportable transaction, expenditure, transfer, or other authoritative record. Party support also arrives through different channels. Contributions and transfers give resources to another committee under applicable rules. Coordinated party expenditures are paid by a party in consultation with a nominee and reported by the party. Independent party expenditures are legally separate from candidate control. Combining them erases operational differences. The Supreme Court held on June 30, 2026, in NRSC v. FEC that the statutory limits on coordinated party expenditures violate the First Amendment. That ruling removes a federal ceiling on this particular channel; it does not merge party and candidate accounts, repeal base contribution rules, prove that coordination occurred, or establish where parties will spend. The map therefore preserves a separate coordinated-party column and attaches the reporting source and period. A legal increase in possible support is not the same event as an observed race allocation. Independent spending Independent expenditures expressly advocate the election or defeat of a clearly identified federal candidate without prohibited coordination. Political committees report them on Schedule E; certain other persons use Form 5. Near elections, additional 24- or 48-hour reports can make this channel more current than a quarterly summary. The headline total still needs context. The spender may oppose one candidate rather than support the other. A reservation is not the same as completed dissemination. An amended filing can replace an earlier amount. Spending in an expensive media market buys a different quantity of communication from the same nominal amount elsewhere. Creative quality, timing, audience, and saturation are not captured by dollars alone. Independent money is simultaneously a possible cause and a response. Groups invest where they perceive opportunity, danger, donor interest, or strategic value. A surge can reveal prioritization, but it may occur because private information already indicates that the preferred candidate is behind. The map labels it strategic attention until polls, fundamentals, field evidence, or results support a stronger inference. Communications outside the clean categories Electioneering communications, party communication costs, issue advertising, nonprofit advocacy, and organizational activity can shape an election without fitting the candidate-plus-independent-expenditure sum. Federal disclosure varies by actor and communication. A comprehensive account should acknowledge visible activity while refusing to manufacture a comparable total from incompatible sources. The map therefore has an “other disclosed communication” field with the legal category, source, date, and caveat. Undisclosed or weakly disclosed activity belongs in an evidence-gap note, not an invented estimate. Advertising-tracking estimates can provide independent context when their methodology is disclosed, but they should never be silently substituted for FEC spending. A canonical race row Each row should represent one contest and one frozen as-of time. House district boundaries and state identifiers must be canonical; Senate special and regular elections must be distinguished. Candidate identity should be joined through FEC candidate and committee identifiers rather than names alone, because names change and similarly named committees can be confused. Field Required interpretation Contest and election Office, state or district, regular or special, and relevant primary/general election Candidate and committee IDs Stable FEC identifiers plus official ballot status from the state authority Coverage window Beginning and ending dates, report type, filing date, and amendment version Period receipts and spending Matched flows; composition and transfers noted Ending cash and debts Dated stocks, not live balances Candidate runway A disclosed analytical estimate with assumptions, never an official field Party support Contribution, transfer, coordinated expenditure, or independent expenditure kept separate Outside spending Support and opposition by spender, dissemination date, and amendment status Change since prior freeze Dollar and percentage change from a matched prior period Electoral context Incumbency, primary burden, district or state baseline, original polling, and dated rating Confidence and caveat Missing reports, late amendments, ambiguous purposes, or unmatched periods The row should also preserve a link to the exact filing. A dashboard value without a report version is not fully reproducible. If the FEC later incorporates an amendment, the next freeze should state that the earlier value was superseded rather than pretending the historical dashboard always contained the new number. Derived measures that earn their keep Derived metrics are useful when their definitions remain visible. Period burn rate is period disbursements divided by period receipts. Cash growth is ending cash minus beginning cash. Net cash subtracts reported debts owed from ending cash. Runway divides a defined pool of deployable resources by a defined recent spending pace. Each can reveal something, and each can mislead. A burn rate above 100 percent may indicate a strategic drawdown, not distress. A low burn rate may reflect prudent accumulation or a campaign that has not built an operation. Runway becomes unstable when spending is seasonal: a pre-primary media purchase is not a normal monthly expense, and a post-primary campaign must accelerate before November. Percentage changes explode from tiny bases. Ratios should be suppressed or flagged when denominators are too small. The map should favor paired comparisons over composite scores. Show cash beside debt; receipts beside fundraising expense; candidate-controlled money beside outside support; current period beside the same period or a clearly defined previous period. A single “money strength” index hides judgment in weights and tempts the reader to treat unlike legal channels as interchangeable. What comparisons are fair The strongest comparison uses the same office, election stage, reporting cutoff, and definitions. General-election opponents may still have faced unequal primary burdens. An incumbent can carry money accumulated before a challenger entered. A self-funder can create immediate capacity without demonstrating a donor network. A candidate running in a cheap media market can buy more exposure with less cash than a candidate in a major metropolitan market. Cross-race ranking therefore requires context. The relevant question is usually not “which campaign has the most?” but “does each plausible nominee possess the minimum capacity for its contest, and which actor is filling any gap?” For House analysis, district price and communications geography matter. For Senate analysis, statewide media markets and the number of simultaneous expensive contests affect party allocation. Matched historical comparisons are harder than they appear. Contribution limits, inflation, reporting rules, calendar timing, district boundaries, special elections, and the number of competitive seats can change. The FEC's twelve-month statistical summary is a reliable aggregate benchmark: through December 31, 2025, congressional candidates reported about 1.492 billion in receipts, 851.9 million in disbursements, 1.216 billion cash, and 231.8 million in debts. Those national totals describe the scale of recorded activity, not the distribution or competitiveness of particular contests. From financial fact to electoral inference Every update should pass through a claim ladder. Accounting fact: a named committee reported a value for a stated period and version. Operational inference: the value plausibly expands or constrains a defined campaign activity. Strategic inference: donors, parties, or outside groups appear to prioritize the contest. Electoral inference: the financial development changes the distribution of plausible outcomes. The first step can usually be verified directly. The second requires transaction classification and local cost context. The third requires comparison with alternatives and an explanation of why the money moved. The fourth demands independent evidence—polling, fundamentals, candidate status, field organization, or observed voter behavior. Skipping from receipts to victory odds turns endogeneity into a forecast. A campaign that doubles quarterly receipts may have gained capacity, but the surge might follow a prior poll, a viral fundraising moment, a late entry, or a transfer. A party expenditure can identify a priority, yet parties may defend a weak incumbent or force an opponent to spend. Outside opposition can damage a candidate while also advertising that the spender believes the candidate is already dangerous. The money map preserves these alternative explanations rather than choosing the most dramatic one. The July 2026 update protocol The July freeze should be assembled in stages. First, record the last accepted report for every candidate committee and its coverage dates. Second, after the July 15 deadline, ingest filings only when the FEC marks them received and available, preserving original versus amended status. Third, reconcile committee-level totals into candidate-level rows without double-counting authorized transfers. Fourth, add party and PAC monthly data after the July 20 deadline or explicitly label the lag. Fifth, attach independent-expenditure notices through the freeze time. For each potentially pivotal contest, the narrative update should answer: Did resources change beyond what elapsed time and the election calendar would normally imply? Was the change newly raised money, self-funding, a loan, a transfer, or outside support? Did available cash rise after debt and spending? Was spending oriented toward fundraising, overhead, persuasion, field, legal work, or an unclear purpose? Did a party or outside group make a race-specific allocation? Does an independent source corroborate a change in competitiveness? Missing or late reports should remain missing. Filing a report is not proof that every transaction is substantively clear; amendments and FEC review can follow. A race row with an evidence flag is more honest than a fully populated row assembled from unmatched press reports. How the map connects to control The money map should not define the battlefield by itself. [[2026 House battleground map]] and [[2026 Senate control path]] supply the arithmetic and scenario structure. Finance adds a capacity and prioritization layer to those pages. The control pages, in turn, prevent attention from flowing only to the richest or most publicized campaigns. An efficient control analysis groups seats into defense, pickup, expansion, and failure sets, then asks whether candidate and party resources are consistent with the stated path. If a supposed pivotal race lacks minimum candidate infrastructure and receives no compensating party or outside support, that is evidence against the path—but not proof of defeat. If several races receive coordinated investment at once, the pattern may reveal a portfolio strategy. Because national conditions can move contests together, spending across the map should be interpreted as an allocation under correlated risk, not isolated wagers. The final display should always include an as-of timestamp, coverage-period column, legal-channel legend, and links to exact filings. It should show unknowns rather than converting them to zeros. Most importantly, it should make it impossible to mistake accounting precision for electoral certainty. Sources FEC July reporting reminder for 2026 — official July 15 and July 20 deadlines, coverage periods, candidate threshold, and electronic-filing guidance; published June 30, 2026; accessed July 9, 2026. FEC 2026 quarterly reporting schedule — official report types and pre-election obligations; accessed July 9, 2026. FEC campaign-finance data — official candidate, committee, report, transaction, and independent-expenditure records; accessed July 9, 2026. FEC statistical summary of twelve-month 2025–2026 cycle activity — aggregate candidate, party, PAC, cash, debt, and independent-expenditure benchmark through December 31, 2025; published April 9, 2026; accessed July 9, 2026. FEC summary of NRSC v. FEC — official litigation summary of the June 30 holding; published July 1, 2026; accessed July 9, 2026. FEC independent-expenditure reporting guidance — definitions, schedules, and reporting framework; accessed July 9, 2026. Open questions Which July quarterly reports will be amended materially after the first freeze? What contest-specific cost baseline best converts cash into a cautious capacity judgment? How should post- NRSC coordinated party spending be normalized against earlier cycles without implying legal continuity? Which outside-spending disclosures can be joined reliably across reservations, dissemination, and amendments? What independent evidence threshold should promote a financial change from strategic attention to an electoral update?

title: 2026 midterm polling error watch
deck: The polling-error watch is a disclosure and design ledger: it tracks observable risks in 2026 congressional surveys without pretending to know the direction of the next polling miss.
headings: What counts as evidence before Election Day
How to use 2024 and 2020 without fighting the last war
text: The polling-error watch is a disclosure and design ledger: it tracks observable risks in 2026 congressional surveys without pretending to know the direction of the next polling miss. Up: [[2026 United States midterm elections]] · Related: [[Reading congressional polls without overreacting]] · [[Generic ballot versus district-level voting]] · [[2026 House battleground map]] · [[2026 Senate control path]] Why it matters The 2026 House and Senate maps will probably contain many contests where the reported margin is smaller than ordinary survey uncertainty, and chamber control can turn on several races that share the same national environment. In that setting the most dangerous polling mistake is not reading one district poll with too much confidence. It is silently treating several polls as independent when they may share the same recruitment channels, voter-file models, turnout assumptions, weighting targets, questionnaire choices, and late-campaign response patterns. This note is not a forecast of whether public polls will overstate Democrats, Republicans, incumbents, challengers, or neither party. The observable data available before Election Day cannot identify the sign of the final error. What it can do is identify where uncertainty should be widened, where a poll deserves less weight, where a trend is methodologically clean, and where a chamber-control conclusion depends on a common error assumption. That makes the watch a companion to [[Reading congressional polls without overreacting]], not a replacement for it. The earlier note explains how to read a poll. This note is a live 2026 instrument: a ledger schema, diagnostic triggers, and post-election audit plan. As of July 10, 2026, the most useful live task is not building a premature 2026 error table. It is preparing a ledger that can ingest each public poll with enough metadata to preserve comparability. The general election is November 3, 2026; every survey belongs to its own field dates and population. A poll completed in July, a likely-voter poll completed in October, a campaign internal released after selective screening, and a district survey based on a thin online panel are not interchangeable units. What counts as evidence before Election Day Before the votes are counted, polling error itself is unobserved. The desk should therefore track risk indicators , not "errors." The strongest indicators are design facts that would remain true even if the topline were never published: target population, sampling frame, recruitment method, mode, field dates, sample size, weighting variables, likely-voter screen, questionnaire order, treatment of undecided voters, sponsor, release selectivity, and pollster-series continuity. A poll with complete disclosure is not automatically accurate. A poll without disclosure is not automatically wrong. But disclosure determines whether the desk can inspect the assumptions. AAPOR's Transparency Initiative requires public release of core methodological details such as sponsor, instrument, population, sample recruitment, mode, dates, sample size, precision statement, weighting, and processing procedures. The point is not that AAPOR blesses the poll's quality; AAPOR explicitly frames transparency as an aid to public evaluation rather than a quality seal. For a live election desk, that distinction matters. Lack of transparency is a reason to reduce confidence because the missing design choices cannot be audited. The ledger should use the following minimum fields for every public 2026 congressional poll: Field Why it matters Contest and geography A national generic-ballot poll, a statewide Senate poll, and a House-district poll estimate different quantities. Field dates Events after the field period cannot have caused the result; overlapping field periods are not independent trends. Population Adults, registered voters, likely voters, primary voters, and special-election electorates have different turnout assumptions. Sponsor and release channel Campaign, party, advocacy, media, academic, and nonpartisan releases have different selection incentives. Recruitment and sample source Probability samples, voter-file samples, online opt-in panels, text-to-web, and blended designs carry different coverage risks. Mode and languages Live phone, IVR, SMS-to-web, web panels, mail, and mixed modes can reach different people and elicit different answers. Weighting and benchmarks Demographic targets, recalled vote, party registration, modeled partisanship, and turnout history introduce distinct assumptions. Likely-voter model A likely-voter result is only interpretable if the screen and timing are known. Undecided treatment Forcing a choice, probing leaners, and normalizing two-party support change the reported margin. Questionnaire and order Biographical or issue questions before the ballot can create a different measurement from a clean ballot test. Pollster-series continuity A change in vendor, mode, weighting, or likely-voter model can masquerade as public-opinion movement. Shared vendors or panels Multiple pollsters may not provide independent evidence if they draw from the same provider or model. The desk should treat a released topline without these fields as a lead, not as a chamber-control input. If the source later publishes the questionnaire and methods, the entry can be upgraded. The main 2026 risk channels Nonresponse and differential participation remain the central problem. A sample can match the electorate on age, race, sex, education, and geography while still missing a political variable not captured by those cells. If one coalition is less likely to answer surveys, and that response pattern is not corrected by weighting, the weighted poll can retain a partisan error. A low response rate does not mechanically imply bias, but response propensity correlated with vote choice is dangerous. The desk should therefore record whether a poll describes response rate, response adjustments, contact attempts, incentives, refusal conversion, and whether the pollster is using turnout-history or modeled-partisanship variables to compensate. Likely-voter modeling becomes more consequential as Election Day approaches. Early registered-voter polls often answer a cleaner opinion question because they impose fewer turnout assumptions. Late likely-voter polls ask the election-proximate question, but only through a model. Different pollsters may screen on self-reported certainty, past turnout, political interest, knowledge of voting logistics, voter-file history, or a proprietary score. In a midterm, the eventual electorate can differ sharply from a presidential electorate. A likely-voter shift in September may reflect a changed screen, not a changed race. Mode and panel composition create another risk. Online opt-in polls can be fast and plentiful, but their respondents enter through unknown selection probabilities. Probability-based panels, address-based recruitment, live phone, text-to-web, and mixed-mode designs all solve some problems while creating others. Pew's opt-in weighting experiments show that adjustment choices can materially affect estimates; the practical lesson for 2026 is not "online bad" but "online methods need visible recruitment, matching, weighting, and validation." If several public district polls use the same sample provider, agreement among them is less independent than the headline count suggests. Recalled vote and partisanship weighting require special handling. Weighting to education is anchored in external population data. Weighting to recalled 2024 vote or partisan identification is partly a political model. It may reduce one known failure while importing a new assumption. Recalled vote can be misremembered, nonresponse can differ by recall group, and a district's 2024 electorate may not equal its 2026 electorate. A poll that weights to a past vote target should disclose the target, the source, and whether it is using validated vote, self-report, modeled party, or registration. House effects and methodological breaks should be tracked, not moralized. A recurring house effect is a pollster's tendency to differ from other pollsters after accounting for time and contest. It may reflect stable design rather than bias or intent. But the effect is usable only if the pollster's method is stable. If a firm changes from live phone to text-to-web, adds recalled-vote weighting, changes a likely-voter screen, or switches sample vendors, the old house effect may no longer be comparable. The watch should record method changes as event entries. Sponsor selection matters because the public poll universe is selected. Campaigns and committees conduct many surveys and release only some of them. A candidate releasing a favorable poll after a fundraising push tells the desk something about what the campaign wants donors and media to see. It does not reveal the private polling distribution. The ledger should mark campaign, party, super PAC, advocacy, and pollster-for-hire releases clearly, and should avoid averaging several same-side releases as if they were a random sample. Correlated error is the control problem. Even if every individual survey is responsibly conducted, the chamber-control estimate can be too narrow if it treats district or state errors as independent. Common economic perceptions, presidential approval, turnout error, late news, shared pollster assumptions, and nationalized voting can move many contests together. A forecast or desk narrative should therefore ask: if the generic ballot were off by three points in either direction, which Senate states and House districts would move together? Which races are insulated by candidate quality, incumbency, state partisanship, or local issues? Which evidence streams are independent of polls? How to use 2024 and 2020 without fighting the last war The 2020 AAPOR task-force report found large, same-direction polling misses, including Senate and gubernatorial polls that were too favorable to Democratic candidates relative to certified results. The 2024 AAPOR report described a more accurate public polling picture than 2016 and 2020, while still warning that some recent patterns persisted. Those reports are useful baselines because they study actual pre-election polls against outcomes. They are not a mechanical correction for 2026. The right use of recent history is diagnostic. If a 2026 pollster says it changed its education weighting, likely-voter screen, text outreach, recalled-vote targets, or panel quality controls because of 2020 or 2024, the desk should record the change. If a public average merely subtracts a fixed "Republican undercount" from every race, the desk should reject that as overfitting unless the model explains why the same sign and magnitude should recur in those jurisdictions and populations. Historical error widens uncertainty; it does not announce the next result. The most valuable post-2024 question is whether pollsters' corrections are converging. If many firms adopt the same recalled-vote target, same voter-file model, same online panel provider, or same likely-voter screen, methodological diversity may shrink. An apparent consensus can become less independent. The watch should therefore treat method diversity as a chamber-control asset: multiple transparent designs that disagree modestly may be more informative than many visually separate releases built from the same hidden pipeline. A practical watch table The public note should not become a daily poll dump. The working ledger can be longer, but the published watch should summarize only risk-bearing patterns: Watch item Green signal Yellow signal Red signal Disclosure Full methods, questionnaire, field dates, weighting, sponsor Some fields missing but available on request Topline or graphic only Population Clear adults/RV/LV/primary definition Population stated but likely-voter screen vague Population absent or inconsistent Method continuity Same series and disclosed method Method changed with partial explanation Trend presented across undisclosed method break Sample source Probability or disclosed panel/source Generic "online sample" with limited detail Unknown recruitment Weighting Variables and targets disclosed Variables named but targets absent Weighting undisclosed Sponsor Independent or transparent sponsor Partisan sponsor labeled Sponsor hidden or release selective Independence Distinct pollsters and providers Same provider possible but unclear Multiple releases from same sponsor/provider treated as separate confirmation Correlation Model includes common national/regional error Correlation discussed qualitatively Seat probabilities multiplied as independent When the desk updates [[2026 House battleground map]] or [[2026 Senate control path]], it should cite this watch only for methodological pressure, not for a standalone prediction. For example: "Three recent district polls support competitiveness, but all are registered-voter text-to-web releases with limited vendor disclosure, so they update the race less than three fully independent designs would." That sentence is more useful than a false adjustment like "add two points to Republican candidates." What would move the watch The watch should be revised when one of four things happens. First, a major pollster releases a detailed 2026 congressional methodology or changes a design choice relevant to trend continuity. Second, a cluster of public district or Senate polls appears in pivotal races with common sponsors, vendors, or screens. Third, a transparent post-primary or special-election comparison provides evidence about turnout or polling performance in the current cycle. Fourth, a forecast or rating source changes its treatment of correlated error, pollster effects, or generic-ballot translation. It should not be revised merely because a single poll has a surprising topline. That belongs in the relevant race dossier or control map. The watch exists to preserve the methodological conditions under which several polls should be believed together.
