How should a control model represent an independent candidate who has not made a binding caucus commitment? Which July 15 quarterly reports change genuine campaign capacity rather than merely confirm national donor attention? How much correlated national error should link the principal defensive and pickup states? Which state vacancy and certification rules could affect the interval between November 3 and the organization of the 120th Congress?

title: 2026 Senate dossier source hierarchy
deck: Senate race dossiers should rank state ballot authority, Senate roster facts, FEC records, disclosed polls, ratings, and reporting by what each source can actually prove.
headings: Tier 2: official Senate and constitutional facts
Tier 3: FEC records and finance law
Tier 4: original polls and methodological disclosure
Tier 7: campaign, party, and market claims
text: Senate race dossiers should rank state ballot authority, Senate roster facts, FEC records, disclosed polls, ratings, and reporting by what each source can actually prove. Up: [[2026 Senate control path]] · Related: [[2026 Senate race dossier template]] · [[2026 Senate race prioritization]] · [[2026 midterm candidate filing checkpoint]] · [[Campaign cash as an electoral signal]] Why a hierarchy is necessary A 2026 Senate race page can go wrong even when every source it cites is real. The most common error is not fabrication; it is source overreach. A candidate website proves what a campaign says. An FEC Form 2 proves federal campaign-finance candidacy activity. A state candidate list proves ballot-process status at that state authority's as-of moment. A poll estimates a defined population under a defined method. A race rating is an analyst judgment. A news story can verify a campaign event, quote, endorsement, withdrawal, or allegation, but it does not become the legal record of ballot access unless the state authority says so. The 2026 Senate map makes these distinctions more important than usual. It has 33 regular Class II elections plus special elections in Florida and Ohio. It has open Democratic defenses in states such as Michigan, Minnesota, Illinois, and New Hampshire, Republican-held targets in states such as North Carolina and Maine, and special-election mechanics that can be miscounted if all Senate races are flattened into one category. The committee also has a near-term finance cliff: July 15 quarterly filings for House and Senate authorized committees and July 20 monthly-filer reports. A dossier written before those reports can describe the legal field and last available finance, but it should not claim a current cash hierarchy unless the current records exist. The hierarchy below is a rule for what each source is allowed to establish. It is not a rule that lower-tier evidence is useless. Campaign reporting, analyst ratings, and high-quality journalism are essential. They become unsafe when they are promoted to prove facts that only official sources can prove, or when they are allowed to erase uncertainty that remains unresolved. Tier 1: official election authority For candidate qualification, ballot access, withdrawals, disqualifications, substitution, recounts, canvass, certification, and state election calendar, the responsible state election authority is the controlling public source. In a Senate dossier, that usually means a secretary of state, state elections division, state board of elections, or equivalent office. The page may be a candidate listing, official ballot, election calendar, sample ballot, directive, canvass manual, recount procedure, or certified result. This tier answers narrow questions: Is the race on the state ballot calendar? Which office label and term does the state use? Which candidates are listed, qualified, disqualified, withdrawn, substituted, or write-in eligible? What are the primary, runoff, independent, minor-party, and general-election deadlines? Who canvasses and certifies results? What recount or contest procedures apply? It does not answer whether a listed candidate is active, viable, well-funded, electable, or likely to win. A candidate may appear on a state primary listing after suspending campaign activity. A candidate may have campaign activity before ballot qualification. A disqualified candidate may remain visible in an official table because the table preserves status history. The dossier should preserve that status rather than compress it into "running" or "not running." Michigan illustrates the point. The Michigan Bureau of Elections' official 2026 August Primary Candidate Listing shows Abdul El-Sayed, Mallory McMorrow, Haley Stevens, and Mike Rogers in the U.S. Senate row, and marks Republican Bernadette Smith as disqualified. AP reporting says McMorrow suspended her campaign after ballots had already gone out. The correct source hierarchy records both facts: state-listed on the primary ballot, campaign-suspended in public reporting. The news event does not silently rewrite the state table. Tier 2: official Senate and constitutional facts The U.S. Senate's official roster and class pages establish the chamber-side identity of regular seats. The Class II page says Class II terms run from January 3, 2021, to January 3, 2027, and lists the senators whose terms expire at the end of the 119th Congress. For regular 2026 races, that fixes why the seat is up and which term is expiring. This tier answers: Is the regular seat Class II? Who currently holds the seat? What party is listed for the incumbent? What term is expiring? Is the dossier dealing with a regular term or a vacancy/special-election complication? It does not prove the state ballot, nominee, campaign activity, or rating. A Senate roster is not a candidate filing list. A senator can retire, lose a primary, be appointed, or leave office, but the race's class identity remains a separate legal fact. A dossier should state "Class II term ending January 3, 2027" before discussing whether the incumbent is seeking another term or whether an open-seat field has formed. Special elections need additional official state and Senate evidence because they may fill unexpired terms outside the Class II cycle. Ohio and Florida should not be treated as ordinary Class II races merely because they appear on the 2026 control map. A special-election dossier should identify the vacancy chain, temporary appointment, term end, state election authority, certification timetable, and seating implication before discussing ratings or polling. The constitutional layer matters for control arithmetic. Article I, the Seventeenth Amendment, Senate classes, and the vice president's tie-breaking role define how seats and vacancies become organizational control. They do not forecast who wins any state. That distinction is why [[2026 Senate control path]] separates mathematical routes from modeled routes. Tier 3: FEC records and finance law FEC records are authoritative for federal campaign-finance activity. They are not authoritative for state ballot qualification. A candidate's FEC record can show a Statement of Candidacy, office sought, state, party, candidate ID, principal campaign committee, authorized committees, reports filed, receipts, disbursements, cash on hand, debts, loans, independent expenditures, and reporting periods. Those are valuable facts. They should be joined by IDs, not by loose name matching. The FEC layer answers: Has a person filed as a federal candidate for this office and cycle? What candidate ID and committee IDs are associated with the campaign? Which reports exist, when were they filed, and what period do they cover? What receipts, disbursements, cash on hand, debts, loans, transfers, and refunds are reported? What independent expenditures, communication costs, or electioneering communications are reported? Which deadlines govern the next update? It does not answer whether the candidate is qualified for the state ballot. It also does not by itself establish electoral strength. A high receipt total may signal donor enthusiasm, national attention, self-funding, or a real organizational edge; cash on hand, burn rate, debt, and outside spending have to be separated. A candidate can raise money and still fail to qualify for a ballot. A candidate can qualify and still have weak federal finance activity. For July 2026, finance timing is especially important. The FEC July reporting reminder sets July 15 as the quarterly deadline for House and Senate authorized committees covering activity through June 30, and July 20 for monthly filers. A race dossier accessed July 10 should not pretend to know the post-June-30 cash picture. It can say the next report is imminent and mark finance as provisional. The FEC's 2026 primary-date PDF is useful but should be classified carefully. It is an official federal compilation sourced from state offices, statutes, and state parties. It lists primary dates, runoffs, filing deadlines, independent deadlines, and the federal general-election date. But the PDF itself warns that dates are subject to change and that candidates should consult states for other deadlines and requirements. Use it for national comparison and as a checkpoint against state pages, not as the final word on state qualification. Tier 4: original polls and methodological disclosure Polling can be powerful evidence only when its target and method are visible. A Senate dossier should not cite a topline without sponsor, pollster, field dates, sample size, target population, mode, geography, weighting, question wording, candidate list, undecided handling, and access to the original release or crosstabs when possible. The standard from [[Reading congressional polls without overreacting]] is that polls estimate a defined population; they do not become a direct measurement of an eventual electorate unless the design supports that inference. This tier answers: Which population was sampled: adults, registered voters, likely voters, primary voters, or another defined group? Which candidates were tested and in what order? Was the poll conducted before or after a major candidate event? Is the sponsor partisan, campaign-connected, independent, or undisclosed? What is the uncertainty, including sampling and design uncertainty? Are crosstabs or questionnaires available? It does not answer ballot qualification, actual turnout, or certification. A Democratic primary poll in Michigan before Mallory McMorrow suspended her campaign does not estimate the same choice as a post-suspension poll. A general-election poll testing Haley Stevens versus Mike Rogers does not answer Abdul El-Sayed versus Rogers. A registered-voter poll in June should not be mixed with an August likely-voter poll without labeling the population change. Internal polls and memos require special handling. They can reveal campaign behavior and strategic claims, but without full methods they should be quarantined as campaign evidence. A partisan sponsor does not automatically invalidate a poll; hidden methods and selective release are the problem. The dossier can include a campaign memo in a "claims and leads" paragraph while refusing to treat it as the main polling evidence. Tier 5: race ratings and models Race ratings from Cook Political Report, Inside Elections, Sabato's Crystal Ball, and similar analysts are disciplined synthesis. They are valuable because they compress state fundamentals, candidate quality, national environment, polls, money, and reporting into a category. But the category is an analyst judgment, not an official status, poll result, or legal fact. This tier answers: How does a named analyst classify the race as of a date? Did the source move the race since a prior rating? Does the source explain whether the movement reflects candidate field, polling, finance, national environment, or another factor? Do multiple raters converge or diverge? It does not answer whether a candidate is on the ballot, how much cash a campaign has, or what a poll's topline says. It also should not be converted into a probability unless the source publishes a model probability and method. "Toss Up" means the rater's category, not 50.0%. Rating pages can also have date ambiguity. A live table may display a category while the page header carries an older publication date. A third-party ratings aggregator may preserve a dated representation of a rating, but it is not the primary source. The safe dossier practice is to cite the original rating page when accessible, preserve the access date, and describe any ambiguity. If a rating source is inaccessible or unclear, write "not cleanly verified" rather than fabricating a category. Ratings are most useful after official and FEC facts are pinned. They can tell the reader whether the outside analytical community sees Michigan as a defensive risk, North Carolina as a pickup opportunity, or Texas as an expansion race. They should not decide whether those races exist or who is actually qualified to run. Tier 6: high-quality reporting AP, Reuters, major local outlets, specialist campaign reporters, and transparent beat reporting are necessary for campaign events that official pages may not explain promptly. Reporting can verify suspensions, endorsements, debate moments, strategic spending, party pressure, replacement processes, candidate statements, and litigation developments. It can also supply context about why an official event matters. This tier answers: Did a candidate suspend a campaign, concede, endorse, or change strategy? Are parties planning a replacement process or convention? What do named sources and public records say about outside spending or strategic concern? How are candidates framing the race? Which official source should be checked next? It does not replace state ballot authority, FEC records, court dockets, or official certification. Reporting about an allegation should be handled with particular care: it can establish that an allegation was made and that the campaign or party responded, not necessarily that the underlying allegation is true. Reporting based on anonymous sources should be labeled and corroborated before it changes a durable dossier claim. In a fast-moving Senate race, reporting often leads the committee to a better official source. If AP says a candidate suspended, check whether the state listing changed. If a local outlet reports a court order, find the docket or order. If a campaign story cites an ad buy, search FEC independent-expenditure data and ad-library records where available. Reporting is an evidence path, not a stopping point. Tier 7: campaign, party, and market claims Campaign websites, press releases, emails, social posts, party memos, endorsements, and prediction-market prices are low in the proof hierarchy but still useful. They show what actors are saying and doing. They can identify candidate positions, endorsements, fundraising claims, strategic emphasis, and expectations. They become dangerous when used as independent proof of opponent behavior, ballot status, vote totals, fraud, or control probabilities. This tier answers: What does a candidate claim to support? Which endorsements or campaign messages are being promoted? How are parties trying to frame the race? What are traders pricing under a specific contract's wording, liquidity, and rules? It does not answer whether the claim is true, whether the candidate is qualified, or whether the price is an objective probability. A campaign's issue page is authoritative for that campaign's stated position. It is not authoritative for claims about an opponent. A market price is evidence about market behavior under a contract. It is not an election result, a poll, or a rating. Use this tier as a lead generator. If a campaign says it filed signatures, find the state filing list. If a party says a race is moving, find ratings, polls, finance, or field evidence. If a prediction market moves, check whether there was a source event, liquidity change, or contract ambiguity. If no higher-tier evidence appears, keep the claim out of the public race assessment or mark it explicitly as unverified actor behavior. A practical dossier build order Every Senate race note should be built in this order: Establish race identity with the Senate class page or special-election authority. Establish state ballot and calendar status from the responsible state authority. Add FEC candidate, committee, filing, and reporting-period data without treating it as ballot status. Add ratings as dated analyst judgments. Add polls only when disclosure is sufficient. Add reporting to explain campaign events and unresolved changes. Add campaign, party, and market claims only as actor behavior or leads. Write the control-role section last, after evidence type is separated. This order prevents the most expensive mistakes. It keeps a suspended campaign from being erased from a state ballot prematurely. It keeps an FEC candidate ID from becoming ballot qualification. It keeps an analyst rating from becoming an official fact. It keeps an internal poll from becoming a forecast. It keeps market price from becoming a result. Why it matters Senate control is a small-number problem. A single race can change whether Democrats need four Republican-held pickups, five, or more. A single special-election misclassification can distort the ledger. A single premature finance claim can make a campaign look stronger or weaker than the official reporting period supports. The hierarchy gives each source a job and a limit. State authorities govern ballot status. The Senate roster governs class identity. FEC records govern federal campaign finance. Polls estimate defined electorates. Ratings synthesize. Reporting contextualizes. Campaigns advocate. Markets price contracts. A dossier that respects those limits will be easier to update after July 15 filings, August primaries, November returns, canvasses, certifications, recounts, and seating. Sources U.S. Senate, Class II senators whose terms expire in 2027 — official Class II roster and term dates; accessed July 10, 2026. FEC, 2026 congressional primary dates and candidate filing deadlines — federal compilation of primary, runoff, filing, independent-filing, and general-election dates; data as of May 18, 2026; accessed July 10, 2026. FEC, dates and deadlines — official reporting-date and compliance hub; accessed July 10, 2026. FEC, July reporting reminder 2026 — July 15 quarterly and July 20 monthly filing deadlines; accessed July 10, 2026. FEC, browse campaign finance data — official candidate, committee, filing, receipts, disbursements, loans, debts, and independent-expenditure portal; accessed July 10, 2026. Michigan Department of State, Elections — example of state election authority, candidate listings, and voter calendar; accessed July 10, 2026. Michigan Bureau of Elections, 2026 August Primary Candidate Listing — example of official candidate status evidence; accessed July 10, 2026. AP, Democrat Mallory McMorrow suspends her Michigan Senate campaign — example of campaign-status reporting that must be reconciled with state ballot evidence; published July 6, 2026; accessed July 10, 2026. Cook Political Report, 2026 Senate race ratings — example of ratings as analyst judgment; accessed July 10, 2026. Inside Elections, Senate ratings — example of ratings as analyst judgment; accessed July 10, 2026. Sabato's Crystal Ball, 2026 Senate ratings — example of ratings as analyst judgment; accessed July 10, 2026. Open questions Which state authority pages should be snapshotted first for North Carolina, Maine, Georgia, Ohio, Texas, and Alaska dossiers? Should each race page carry a small source-status table showing which tiers have been verified and which remain pending? How should the committee preserve dated race ratings when a source updates a live table without a clear historical page? Which poll disclosure threshold should be mandatory for including internal primary polls in race pages? After July 15 and July 20 filings, which finance fields should become required in every control-relevant Senate dossier?

title: 2026 Senate race dossier template
deck: Every 2026 Senate race dossier should separate official race existence, ballot status, FEC activity, ratings, polls, finance, and uncertainty before turning those signals into a control claim.
headings: Class II seats need class discipline
Vacancies and special elections need their own block
text: Every 2026 Senate race dossier should separate official race existence, ballot status, FEC activity, ratings, polls, finance, and uncertainty before turning those signals into a control claim. Up: [[2026 Senate control path]] - Related: [[2026 United States midterm elections]] - [[Campaign cash as an electoral signal]] - [[Reading congressional polls without overreacting]] - [[2026 midterm money map]] - [[Race calls certification recounts and contests]] The template's job A Senate race dossier is not a campaign blog, a prediction market note, or a place to paste every story about a candidate. It is the canonical, auditable record for one contest: . Its first job is to tell Andrew what the race legally is, who is eligible or plausibly seeking to appear on the ballot, what evidence exists, what does not exist yet, and how the race fits into [[2026 Senate control path]]. That requires a stricter structure than ordinary political coverage. The 2026 Senate map contains 33 regular Class II elections plus special elections in Florida and Ohio. The regular Class II seats have terms ending January 3, 2027; the special elections are vacancy races attached to different original terms. Both kinds of contests count toward Senate control, but they do not have identical legal histories, term ends, certification questions, or candidate-status evidence. A dossier that flattens them into one undifferentiated "Senate race" category loses the very facts that can matter in a close-control scenario. The minimum dossier should therefore answer five questions before it offers analysis: What office and term is being filled? Which state authority confirms the election, calendar, candidates, ballot status, and result? Which FEC candidate and committee records exist, and what do they prove or not prove? What rating, polling, finance, and campaign evidence exists as of a dated scan? What uncertainty remains unresolved, and what evidence would resolve it? The dossier may be short when evidence is thin, but it should not be vague. "No public poll located as of July 10, 2026" is useful. "Race is quiet" is not. "Candidate has filed an FEC Form 2 but state ballot qualification is not yet confirmed" is useful. "Candidate is running" may be wrong if it silently turns federal campaign-finance activity into official ballot access. Frontmatter and opening block Use the standard Rome frontmatter plus date-sensitive committee fields: The first sentence should state the race's control relevance without pretending certainty. A good opening looks like this: Immediately below that, include: Then add related links only when they do work: [[Campaign cash as an electoral signal]] for finance, [[Reading congressional polls without overreacting]] for polls, [[Race calls certification recounts and contests]] for post-election status, and state or candidate notes only if they already carry durable evidence. Do not create empty candidate biography shells merely because the race has many names. Minimum facts table Every Senate dossier should begin with a compact table. It keeps the official facts separate from interpretation and makes stale evidence visible. Field Required content Evidence rule Contest ; regular Class II or special election. U.S. Senate class roster for regular Class II; state election authority and vacancy record for specials. Seat and term Incumbent, party/caucus, class, term start/end, and whether the winner fills a full term or unexpired term. Senate roster, state writ/directive, sample ballot, candidate list, or official election calendar. Control role Democratic defense, Republican defense, or special vacancy defense; link to control arithmetic. Derived from [[2026 Senate control path]], not from ratings alone. State authority Exact secretary of state or election-board page used for calendar, candidates, ballot, results, recounts, and certification. State authority beats FEC, campaign sites, and news for ballot status. Calendar Primary, runoff if any, independent/minor-party filing, general election, canvass/certification window if available. State authority first; FEC calendar is a federal compilation and should be cross-checked. Candidate field Officially qualified candidates; filed-but-not-qualified candidates; declared/no official confirmation; withdrawn/did not qualify. Do not merge these statuses. FEC records Candidate ID, Form 2, principal campaign committee ID, authorized committees, Form 1, Form 3 reporting status. FEC proves federal campaign-finance activity, not state ballot qualification. Ratings Cook, Inside Elections, Sabato, or another transparent rater; category and as-of date. Rating is analyst judgment; keep separate from official facts. Polling Pollster, sponsor, field dates, mode, sample size, population, topline, undecideds, questionnaire/crosstabs link. Original release preferred; require AAPOR-style disclosure before treating as evidence. Finance Receipts, disbursements, cash on hand, debt, outside spending, party/coordinated spending, reporting period. Compare matched periods; label missing July 15 or July 20 data. Uncertainty What is unresolved and what evidence would change the dossier. Must be concrete, dated, and revisited. This table is a guardrail against two common errors. The first is source collapse: a campaign announcement, an FEC filing, a state qualified-candidate list, and a poll all become "candidate is in." The second is time collapse: a rating from June, a filing from March, a finance number through March 31, and a candidate list accessed July 10 are treated as one current snapshot. The dossier should preserve the as-of date and coverage period for each evidence type. Class II seats need class discipline The regular 2026 Senate map is Class II. The official Senate page says Class II terms run from January 3, 2021 to January 3, 2027, and lists the Democratic and Republican senators whose terms expire then. A regular race dossier should state that class fact near the top because it fixes the legal reason the seat is on the ballot. It also prevents two avoidable mistakes. First, do not confuse the incumbent's current service path with the election class. A senator may have entered through appointment or a prior special election but still occupy a Class II seat with the term ending January 3, 2027. The dossier should record both: "Class II term ending January 3, 2027" and "incumbent entered office by <election/appointment>, if relevant." Second, do not treat retirements or primary losses as proof of competitiveness. The Senate Daily Press Gallery's Senate Facts page provides a useful official-like roster and marks several Class II retirements and primary losses as of the access date. Those labels are status evidence. The forecast consequence belongs in a separate section that considers state partisanship, candidates, money, polls, ratings, and the national environment. An open seat in a strongly aligned state may still be low-risk; an incumbent seat in a marginal state may be high-risk. The minimum Class II block should include: : Class II regular election. : January 3, 2027 to January 3, 2033 for the next full term, unless an official source shows a different seating detail. : name, party, caucus if relevant, and official source. : seeking reelection, retiring, lost primary, appointed, unknown, or not yet officially confirmed. : one of the 13 Democratic-held regular defenses or 20 Republican-held regular defenses from the control-path ledger. If any of these are uncertain, say so. "Incumbent status not independently confirmed from official or campaign source as of <date> " is better than laundering a stale political database into a fact. Vacancies and special elections need their own block Special elections are full control events but different dossier objects. The Seventeenth Amendment requires writs of election for Senate vacancies and permits state legislatures to empower governors to make temporary appointments until voters fill the vacancy as state law directs. That means a special-election dossier must preserve the vacancy chain: original elected senator and class; vacancy cause and date; temporary appointee, appointing authority, and appointment date; official writ, directive, statute, or state election page calling the special election; term being filled and term end; whether the winner serves immediately after certification, at the start of the next Congress, or under another state/Senate timing rule. Florida and Ohio illustrate why this matters. Florida's Division of Elections candidate list is a state source for the 2026 general-election United States Senator candidate field and qualification status. Ohio's Secretary of State directives page identifies the May 5, 2026 primary/special-election ballot materials and candidate-certification materials for a U.S. Senate unexpired term ending January 3, 2029. Those are not interchangeable with a generic Class II roster. They show state-administered ballot mechanics for vacancy contests. The dossier should also distinguish "special election on the 2026 general-election ballot" from "regular Class II race." Both can determine control of the Senate organized in January 2027. Only one is filling the normal 2027-2033 Class II term. If a race note does not track term end and seating status, later control analysis may count the seat correctly for the wrong reason. State authority confirmation For ballot status, the responsible state election authority is the controlling public source. The FEC's congressional primary-date sheet is useful because it compiles primary dates and candidate filing deadlines from state election offices, state law, and state parties, but it is not a substitute for the state authority on final qualification, withdrawal, disqualification, recounts, or certification. The FEC's own pre-election reporting page warns that election dates are subject to change. The minimum state-authority block should include: The candidate table should be status-aware: Candidate Party/ballot label State status FEC candidate ID Principal committee Evidence note Name Party Qualified / filed / declared / withdrawn / unknown ID or none located Committee ID or none located Exact source and access date Do not mix state and federal statuses in one cell. A candidate can have an FEC candidate ID and no ballot qualification. A candidate can appear on a state candidate list before a complete finance snapshot is available. A candidate can withdraw from the state process while old FEC records remain searchable. Names alone are weak identifiers; use state status plus FEC IDs where possible. FEC candidate and committee records The FEC layer should answer a narrow question: what campaign-finance records exist for people and committees connected to this race? It should not answer ballot access by itself. At minimum, record: candidate name as filed; FEC candidate ID; office, state, party, and election year on Form 2; principal campaign committee name and committee ID; any other authorized committees, including joint fundraising representatives when listed; Form 1 statement of organization for the committee; Form 3 receipts-and-disbursements reports for House and Senate authorized committees; filing receipt dates and coverage periods; requests for additional information if material to a finance claim; whether the committee has crossed reporting thresholds or whether only voluntary/early registration exists. The FEC explains that Form 2 is the Statement of Candidacy and Form 1 registers a candidate's authorized campaign committee; Form 3 reports receipts and disbursements for House and Senate authorized committees. The FEC data portal also separates candidates, committees, filings, receipts, disbursements, independent expenditures, loans, and debts. A serious dossier should join through candidate and committee IDs rather than relying on name matches. Timing matters. The July 15, 2026 quarterly deadline covers House and Senate authorized committees' financial activity from April 1, or the day after the prior report closed, through June 30. July 20 matters for national party committees and monthly filers. Before those filings are processed, a race dossier should not pretend to know the current cash hierarchy. It can say what the last available report showed, what period it covered, and what upcoming filing should update the picture. Use comparable finance units: candidate receipts, disbursements, cash on hand, debt, and burn rate; candidate self-funding and loans, with repayments separated; party coordinated spending and party transfers; independent expenditures supporting or opposing named candidates; outside spending by committee, not merely by partisan side; reporting period and filing date for every number. Never compare one candidate's current cash-on-hand figure with another candidate's older pre-primary receipt total. Never add outside spending to candidate cash as if the campaigns control the same resource. See [[Campaign cash as an electoral signal]] and [[2026 midterm money map]] for the broader finance logic. Ratings and polls Ratings belong in the dossier because they are disciplined outside synthesis. They should not become the dossier's spine. Cook, Inside Elections, Sabato's Crystal Ball, and similar sources are useful because they publish categories and update dates, but a rating is not a legal status, a poll, or a probability unless the source explicitly provides a model probability. The ratings section should be a dated ledger: Source Rating As-of date Prior rating Change note Link Inside Elections <category> <date> <prior> <if changed> URL Sabato's Crystal Ball <category> <date> <prior> <if changed> URL Cook Political Report <category> <date> <prior> <if changed> URL If one rating source is paywalled, inaccessible, or has a page-date ambiguity, say so instead of forcing a false comparison. If the rating changed, preserve the old rating in a compact ledger; do not overwrite history. Polling gets stricter treatment. A poll should enter the evidence table only with its metadata intact: sponsor, pollster, field dates, mode, sample size, population, weighting, geography, question wording, candidate list, undecided treatment, and link to the original release or crosstabs. The AAPOR disclosure checklist is a useful baseline because it asks for sponsor/conductor, measurement tools, population, sampling and recruiting method, mode, field dates, sample sizes, weighting, processing, and limitations. The dossier should reject or quarantine weak poll evidence: "internal poll, memo only" becomes a campaign claim unless full methods are available; primary polls do not substitute for general-election polls; registered-voter, likely-voter, and adult samples estimate different populations; a partisan sponsor does not make a poll unusable, but it makes sponsor and release context mandatory; a single poll should not erase fundamentals or ratings without corroboration. If no public poll meets the disclosure threshold, write: That sentence is more valuable than padding the page with commentary. Analysis sections After the official, FEC, rating, poll, and finance blocks, the dossier can analyze. A standard race page should include these sections only when evidence supports them: should cover recent presidential and statewide results, incumbent history, turnout geography, and state party structure. It should not turn past results into destiny. A Senate electorate can differ from a presidential electorate, and a midterm can differ from both. should explain the meaningful candidate options after separating state-qualified candidates from merely declared or FEC-filed candidates. Candidate quality claims need evidence: prior office, electoral record, endorsements, fundraising capacity, known coalition, legal or ballot constraints, and material controversies with reliable sourcing. should summarize campaign and outside finance by matched periods. It should state when the next FEC filing is expected and whether current evidence is incomplete. should compare public polls with ratings and fundamentals without averaging incompatible samples. If polls conflict with ratings, the text should ask why: field date, sample, nominee uncertainty, sponsor, house effect, or genuine movement. should link the race back to the Senate path. A Republican-held race can be a Democratic pickup target, a Republican defensive firewall, or merely part of the mathematical universe. A Democratic-held race can be a must-hold defense or an expansion opportunity for Republicans. The dossier should specify which layer it is describing: mathematical route, modeled route, or campaign-spending route. should be explicit. Examples: official nominee certification; a major candidate withdrawal; July 15 FEC reports; a disclosed likely-voter poll after both nominees are known; a court order affecting ballot access; a rating change from multiple independent analysts; or a national swing large enough to make the race part of a correlated map. Why it matters Senate control is discrete, but the evidence that feeds a control call is messy. The 2026 map gives Democrats a 34-seat off-ballot base and Republicans a 31-seat off-ballot base; with the current vice presidency, Democrats need 17 of the 35 contests for 51 seats while Republicans need 19 for a 50-seat organizing majority. A race dossier is the unit that keeps that arithmetic honest. The danger is premature completeness. Before state filing deadlines, the candidate field may be incomplete. Before July 15 reports are filed and processed, candidate finance can be stale. Before party and outside-spending reports are available, the visible money map may miss the real general-election channels. Before nominees are known, many polls are hypothetical. Before state certification, even a projected winner is not the same thing as a certified result. A good dossier does not eliminate uncertainty. It makes uncertainty usable. It tells the reader which claims are official, which are FEC-record facts, which are analyst judgments, which are campaign claims, which are polling estimates, and which are still unknown. That lets later committee runs update one layer without rewriting the whole race story. Place in the map This template is infrastructure for the Senate side of the [[2026 United States midterm elections]] graph. Each state race note should link upward to [[2026 Senate control path]] and sideways to methods notes when relevant. National control notes should not need to re-litigate every candidate filing, committee ID, poll disclosure, or state qualification page. They should be able to cite race dossiers that preserve those facts. The template also prevents clone pages. Not every Senate race needs a long narrative before evidence exists. A safe early dossier can be mostly tables and uncertainty. It becomes a substantial analytical page only when the race has official candidate definition, finance evidence, polling, ratings movement, litigation, or genuine control relevance. Thin races should still be accurate; pivotal races should be deep. Sources U.S. Senate, Class II senators whose terms expire in 2027 - official Class II term dates and roster; accessed July 10, 2026. title: 2026 Senate race prioritization
deck: The first full 2026 Senate dossiers should go to races that can change the control path and clarify uncertain evidence, not simply to races that attract the most noise.
headings: What each early dossier must prove
text: The first full 2026 Senate dossiers should go to races that can change the control path and clarify uncertain evidence, not simply to races that attract the most noise. Up: [[2026 Senate control path]] · Related: [[2026 Senate race dossier template]] · [[2026 United States midterm elections]] · [[Campaign cash as an electoral signal]] · [[Reading congressional polls without overreacting]] · [[2026 midterm money map]] The prioritization rule The committee should build the first full Senate race dossiers in this order: North Carolina, Maine, Georgia, Michigan, Ohio, Iowa, Texas, Alaska, New Hampshire, Minnesota, Florida, Montana, then the rest of the Class II and special-election map as official candidate and finance evidence matures. This is a research queue, not a prediction. It says where a full dossier will produce the most control-relevant understanding first. The queue starts from [[2026 Senate control path]]. The official Senate Class II roster gives 33 regular seats whose terms expire January 3, 2027. The 2026 ballot also includes special elections in Florida and Ohio. That makes 35 Senate contests. The continuing seats create a 34-seat Democratic-caucus and 31-seat Republican off-ballot base in the current two-bloc simplification. Democrats need 17 of the 35 winners to reach 51 seats; Republicans need 19 winners to reach 50 seats, which is enough to organize the Senate while the current Republican vice president holds the tie-breaking vote. That arithmetic is the first filter. A race deserves early dossier work when it changes one of four things: It is a plausible Democratic pickup in a map where Democrats need at least four Republican-held seats. It is a plausible Democratic defense whose loss forces Democrats to find a fifth pickup. It is a special election, vacancy contest, open seat, or calendar outlier whose official status could be miscounted. It has enough conflicting evidence that a dossier would prevent the committee from confusing attention with leverage. The last point is the reason this note exists. Attention is visibility: media volume, market volume, national fundraising, candidate celebrity, scandal, ideological stakes, or activist interest. Leverage is marginal control value: how much resolving the race changes the set of feasible Senate majorities. Attention can reveal leverage, but it can also distract from it. A safe-state open seat can dominate headlines without being the next decisive control unit. A quieter defensive seat can matter more if losing it lengthens every route to a majority. First full dossiers Priority Race Control role Why it should come first 1 [[2026 North Carolina Senate election]] Republican-held regular Class II defense A core pickup path if Democrats are trying to reach four Republican-held seats; open-seat status and early analyst attention make official candidate, calendar, polling, and finance evidence worth separating immediately. 2 [[2026 Maine Senate election]] Republican-held regular Class II defense A small-state, incumbent-centered contest that can be pivotal without being demographically typical; candidate replacement, qualification, finance, and rating evidence need discipline because the race attracts high narrative attention. 3 [[2026 Georgia Senate election]] Democratic-held regular Class II defense The main early Democratic defensive stress test. A loss here forces Democrats to add another pickup, so the dossier matters even though it is not a Democratic target. 4 [[2026 Michigan Senate election]] Democratic-held regular Class II open-seat defense Open Democratic defense in a presidential battleground. It is a control-path risk even when the headline frame focuses on Republican pickup opportunities elsewhere. 5 [[2026 Ohio Senate special election]] Republican-held special vacancy defense A special election for an unexpired term, not a regular Class II race. It needs early legal-status, term, certification, and seating discipline before any forecast layer. 6 [[2026 Iowa Senate election]] Republican-held regular Class II defense Republican-held open-seat/competitive-path candidate evidence can affect whether Democrats have more than the obvious pickup route. It is especially useful after the July 15 FEC checkpoint. 7 [[2026 Texas Senate election]] Republican-held regular Class II defense High attention and genuine potential upside, but not automatically higher leverage than North Carolina, Maine, or Ohio. The dossier should decide whether the attention is evidence of a moved race or mostly strategic/narrative heat. 8 [[2026 Alaska Senate election]] Republican-held regular Class II defense Small electorate, unusual coalition structure, and candidate-specific pathways can make a race more important than national shorthand suggests. It needs a full dossier once candidate and ballot evidence is clean. 9 [[2026 New Hampshire Senate election]] Democratic-held regular Class II open-seat defense Democratic defense with open-seat status and late primary timing. It may be safer than the top tier, but a defensive failure would be expensive in the net-four arithmetic. 10 [[2026 Minnesota Senate election]] Democratic-held regular Class II open-seat defense Open Democratic defense that can attract attention because of the vacancy, but early leverage depends on whether official candidate, finance, and rating evidence show real control risk. 11 [[2026 Florida Senate special election]] Republican-held special vacancy defense Special status alone makes it worth earlier-than-safe-state documentation, but present control leverage appears lower than Ohio unless ratings, polls, or candidate evidence change. 12 [[2026 Montana Senate election]] Republican-held regular Class II defense Open-seat and state-specific evidence deserve monitoring, but a dossier should test whether the race is a true expansion path or mostly an attention sink. The ordering is deliberately asymmetrical. Democratic pickups and Democratic defenses both appear near the top because control is net arithmetic. If Democrats hold all 13 Democratic-held contests, they still need four Republican-held seats. If they lose Georgia or Michigan, they need five. That makes a Democratic-held defense as control-relevant as a Republican-held target when it is close enough to threaten the base. North Carolina belongs first because it sits at the intersection of all the relevant filters: Republican-held, regular Class II, plausible pickup path, and a state where national and state-level signals can plausibly diverge. It is also the sort of race where a later dossier would have to reconstruct too much: official candidate status, primary history, state filing calendar, finance through the July 15 reporting window, public polling, and analyst ratings. Building it first gives the committee a reusable model for a high-leverage Republican defense. Maine belongs second for the opposite reason. It is not a generic battleground state. Its incumbent, candidate field, small electorate, and independent-minded voting history make it easy to overfit anecdotes. That is exactly why it needs a dossier early. If the race remains one of the shortest Democratic pickup routes, it has obvious leverage. If candidate or ballot volatility damages the Democratic path, the dossier should show that mechanism explicitly rather than laundering it into a vague "Maine chaos" narrative. Georgia and Michigan are the first defensive dossiers because they protect the denominator of the Democratic route. Georgia is an incumbent Democratic defense in a state that remains central to national coalition analysis. Michigan is an open Democratic seat. The right question is not whether either race gets the same amount of attention as Texas; it is whether a loss would force Democrats to find an additional Republican-held pickup. The answer is yes. That makes both races early dossier material even if a ratings table at some moment treats them differently. Ohio ranks above some regular Class II races because it is a special election. The official FEC primary-date compilation and state election materials treat Ohio as a Senate election on the 2026 calendar, but the race is filling an unexpired term rather than the regular Class II term. A full dossier should preserve the vacancy chain, term end, candidate status, certification, and seating implications. It is not enough to write "Ohio Senate" and move on. Iowa, Texas, Alaska, New Hampshire, Minnesota, Florida, and Montana form the next ring. Each can matter, but for different reasons. Iowa and Texas can expand the Democratic pickup set; Alaska can behave differently from a simple red-state model; New Hampshire and Minnesota are defenses whose open-seat status must be tested; Florida is a special election that must not be lost in a regular-seat table; Montana may become real if candidate, polling, or money evidence improves. The dossier queue should not flatten those reasons into one "competitive" label. Why attention is not leverage The cleanest mistake is to sort races by how often they are discussed. That feels empirical because it counts something visible. But visibility is not the same as control value. A race can receive attention because a candidate is famous, because a primary is ugly, because donors like a symbolic fight, because a market contract is liquid, because national reporters are nearby, because a scandal is legible, or because a party wants the other side to spend defensively. None of those facts by itself tells the committee how the race changes the 35-seat Senate equation. Control leverage has a narrower definition. A race has high leverage when changing its expected winner materially changes the feasible majority paths. In 2026, a Republican-held race becomes high leverage when it is part of a plausible Democratic set of four pickups or when it can offset a Democratic loss. A Democratic-held race becomes high leverage when losing it pushes Democrats from four required pickups to five, six, or more. A special election has extra leverage when misclassifying it could distort the control ledger, seating timeline, or term being filled. This distinction also protects against fundraising overinterpretation. July 15 reports will be useful because they put House and Senate authorized committees on a matched reporting deadline for activity through June 30. But money can be cause, effect, signal, or decoy. A fundraising surge in Texas may mean a real race is developing; it may also mean national donors are emotionally invested in a high-profile contest. A smaller finance change in North Carolina or Maine may have more chamber-control value if the race is already in the decisive set. Ratings should be handled the same way. Cook, Inside Elections, and Sabato's Crystal Ball are useful because they publish nonpartisan or explicitly analytical race ratings, dates, and categories. They are not official records. A rating tells the committee how an outside analyst synthesizes fundamentals, candidates, and environment at a point in time. It does not prove ballot status, nominee identity, cash on hand, polling quality, or a chamber-control path. The dossier should record ratings as one evidence layer, then explain what would make the race more or less decisive. Prediction markets and campaign spending are even more dangerous if they are treated as leverage. A liquid contract can measure trader expectations under the contract's wording; it can also reflect fees, eligibility, hedging, attention, or thin information. A party expenditure can reveal strategy; it can also try to shape strategy. Both belong in a dossier when documented, but neither replaces official status, rating context, original polls, and the control ledger. What each early dossier must prove Each first-wave dossier should start with the [[2026 Senate race dossier template]] and then answer the race-specific leverage question. For North Carolina, Maine, Iowa, Texas, Alaska, Florida, Ohio, and Montana, the key question is pickup value: does the race belong in the core Democratic pickup set, an offset layer, or only an expansion layer? The answer should cite official race status, state calendar, FEC candidate and committee records, ratings, polling if any, and finance evidence by reporting period. It should not cite national attention as a substitute for those inputs. For Georgia, Michigan, New Hampshire, and Minnesota, the key question is defensive fragility: how much evidence shows that a Democratic-held seat could fall, and what would that do to the net-four route? These dossiers need the same official and finance blocks as Republican-held races, but their control section should be written from the loss-offset table. "Democrats must hold it" is too blunt. The correct sentence is: "If Democrats lose this seat, the required Republican-held pickup count increases by one." For Ohio and Florida, the key question is legal identity before competitiveness. A special-election dossier should state the original vacancy, appointee, term being filled, state authority, primary and general calendar, certification process, and seating implication. Only after that should it analyze polling, ratings, money, and candidate quality. A special election can be decisive even if it is not a regular Class II seat; it can also be over-discussed because the word "special" makes it sound exceptional. The dossier's job is to separate those effects. For Texas, Alaska, and Montana, the committee should apply an attention discount. That does not mean ignoring them. It means asking what independent evidence would move them ahead of a core race. Examples: multiple transparent ratings moving the race into a more competitive category; public general-election polling with usable disclosure; July 15 finance evidence showing not merely enthusiasm but capacity against a defined opponent; a confirmed candidate or ballot event; or a state-specific issue that plausibly changes turnout or persuasion. Without that evidence, these races remain important monitoring targets but should not consume the first dossier slots. The practical build sequence The first pass should create complete but not bloated race files. A good order is: North Carolina and Maine as Republican-held core pickup tests. Georgia and Michigan as Democratic defensive tests. Ohio as the special-election template. Iowa and Texas as the first expansion-versus-attention comparison. Alaska, New Hampshire, Minnesota, Florida, and Montana as second-wave dossiers after official candidate and finance evidence is easier to compare. The July 15 FEC reporting deadline is the next major checkpoint. The committee should not freeze a finance hierarchy before those filings are processed. It can still build official-status and calendar blocks now, but candidate cash, party support, independent expenditures, debt, burn rate, and post- NRSC v. FEC party behavior need reporting-period discipline. The July 20 monthly-filer deadline matters for national party committees and other monthly filers, so a race dossier completed before both windows should carry a visible review-after date. Late-primary states require special caution. The FEC calendar lists different primary, runoff, independent, and minor-party filing dates by state, with dates subject to change. New Hampshire's September primary and Delaware's September primary are not on the same evidence timeline as states with March, May, or June primaries. A dossier should state whether it is describing a settled general-election field, a primary field, or a provisional candidate universe. The committee should also resist building all 35 dossiers at identical depth immediately. Every race eventually needs a canonical page, but the first full dossiers should be the pages that reduce the most analytical uncertainty. Safe-state pages can begin as official-status records. Competitive and confusing races need full explanatory treatment first. Why it matters A Senate control model can be mathematically correct and still narratively wrong. It can know that Democrats need 17 winners from the 35 contests while still spending too much time on races that do not change the feasible route. It can know that Republicans can retain control with 19 wins while underweighting the defensive seats that make the Democratic route longer. The remedy is a dossier queue that is explicit about its theory of value. First build the races that answer: what are the four most plausible Democratic pickups, which Democratic defenses could force a fifth, which special elections can be miscounted, and which high-attention races need evidence discipline? Then update the order whenever official status, transparent ratings, disclosed polls, finance reports, or legal events change the answer. That keeps Rome's 2026 Senate coverage useful. It treats attention as a lead, ratings as judgments, money as capacity evidence, polls as estimates, and official sources as the legal skeleton. Chamber control depends on how those layers combine, not on which race is loudest on a given day.
