Open questions How quickly will the FEC update help pages, forms, and reporting examples to match the Supreme Court's June 30 holding? Which 2026 party committee reports first show large post- NRSC coordinated party expenditures by race? Will parties mostly substitute coordinated buys for independent expenditures, or will the ruling produce additive spending? How will local station political files identify and price candidate-party coordinated buys during the 60-day general-election lowest-unit-charge window? Will later litigation use NRSC to challenge party contribution limits, outside-group coordination limits, or state-law analogues? Which race-analysis notes need a post- NRSC spending-channel field after July 15 and subsequent reporting windows?

title: Race calls certification recounts and contests
deck: Election results pass through distinct evidentiary and legal stages: media calls interpret incomplete returns, canvass and certification make the administrative result official, recounts re-tabulate under state law, contests adjudicate legal claims, and each house of Congress retains constitutional authority over its own membership.
headings: Unofficial returns are real data, not final data
A media call is an analytical judgment
Certification creates the official administrative result
Audits and recounts answer different questions
An election contest is an adversarial legal claim
House contests have a federal statutory channel
Senate contests follow Senate constitutional practice
text: Election results pass through distinct evidentiary and legal stages: media calls interpret incomplete returns, canvass and certification make the administrative result official, recounts re-tabulate under state law, contests adjudicate legal claims, and each house of Congress retains constitutional authority over its own membership. Up: [[2026 United States midterm elections]] · Related: [[How control of the House is won in 2026]] · [[How control of the Senate is won in 2026]] Why it matters On election night, several sentences may all be true at once: one candidate leads the reported count; a news organization has called the race; many ballots remain unprocessed; no official has certified a winner; and the trailing candidate retains legal options. Collapsing those sentences into “the result” produces either false certainty or false doubt. The stages serve different purposes. Unofficial returns give the public timely information. A decision desk asks whether the trailing candidate still has a realistic mathematical path. The canvass reconciles the election records. Certification formally attests the result under state law. A recount checks tabulation. A contest asks a tribunal to resolve alleged legal defects. For a congressional seat, Article I ultimately makes the House or Senate the judge of its members' elections, returns, and qualifications. These distinctions matter to chamber-control reporting. A projected winner can make control apparent without making it certified. A narrow uncertified race can leave the arithmetic unresolved without implying misconduct. A recount can be legally required without making the first count suspect. And filing a contest establishes that a claim exists—not that the claim is meritorious or that the certified result has been displaced. The status ladder A reliable race ledger should use explicit statuses rather than one “winner” field: Status What it establishes What it does not establish Reported unofficial returns Votes currently tabulated and reported by election offices or a data collector Complete count or legal finality Media race call An organization's analytical conclusion that no opponent can overtake the leader Government certification Local canvass complete Reconciliation and official aggregation at the local level under governing procedures Necessarily the final statewide certificate Certified result The designated official or board has attested the official result Immunity from recount, contest, or congressional review Recount complete Ballots were re-tabulated under the applicable recount law Resolution of every claim about eligibility or election conduct Contest resolved The authorized court, tribunal, or legislative chamber disposed of pleaded claims A general audit of every aspect of the election Member seated The chamber accepted the credentials and administered the oath, subject to its rules and constitutional authority That no later internal proceeding is possible Not every state uses identical labels or orders. A recount may occur before certification, after certification, or both in different forms. A court order can alter a canvass. A certificate can be amended. The ledger must follow the statute and official process for the state and office rather than assume a universal national sequence. Unofficial returns are real data, not final data Election-night totals generally originate with local election officials. They can change as jurisdictions add mail ballots, provisional ballots, cured ballots, late-arriving ballots permitted by law, and corrected uploads. A precinct-reporting percentage is not necessarily a ballot-completion percentage: precincts differ in size, and some ballot categories are not naturally represented as election-day precincts. “Outstanding vote” is itself an estimate until officials know how many submitted ballots satisfy legal requirements. A mail ballot may await signature review; a provisional ballot may depend on eligibility research; a voter may have a statutory cure period. These ballots are not surprise votes merely because their adjudication occurs after election night. They are part of the ordinary process defined before the election. Updates can move in a partisan direction because ballot methods and geography are not random. If one county reports election-day voting before mail voting, its early margin may not resemble its final margin. A raw lead should therefore be paired with what remains: jurisdiction, ballot type, approximate quantity, applicable receipt or cure deadlines, and how much of that vote the trailing candidate would need. The phrase unofficial result describes legal status, not data quality. Election officials often publish careful, accurate preliminary totals. The label signals that reconciliation, canvass, and certification are unfinished and that lawful additions or corrections remain possible. A media call is an analytical judgment The United States has no single national election authority that announces winners in every congressional race on election night. News organizations collect official local returns and operate decision desks. The Associated Press says it declares a winner when its decision team concludes that trailing candidates no longer have a path to victory; it considers reported votes, remaining ballot types and locations, historical patterns, and other election data. Organizations differ in terminology. Some say “call,” “project,” or “declare.” AP explicitly avoids the word “projection” for its own calls, but all such decisions remain nongovernmental analytical judgments. A call can be highly reliable and socially consequential without being a certificate. A candidate's victory declaration or concession is also political speech, not the legal act that completes the canvass. The decision problem is asymmetric. Calling too early risks naming the wrong winner; waiting until certification would withhold a conclusion long after the remaining vote could no longer alter the outcome. A sound call asks whether any plausible composition of outstanding eligible ballots could erase the margin. It does not require every vote to be counted. A landslide can be called with a small reported fraction; a near tie can remain uncalled after almost all ballots are tabulated. Race-call disagreement is possible because organizations use different data feeds, turnout estimates, thresholds, and review rules. Report which organization made the call and when. Do not turn “AP called” into “officials certified,” or “not yet called” into “the count is tied.” AP also distinguishes too early to call from too close to call . It calls a race too early while regular ballot tabulation remains active, even if counting will take days. It reserves too close for a tabulation that has reached what AP calls its primary conclusion—apart from categories such as provisional and late-arriving absentee ballots—without a clear winner. These are AP editorial classifications, not state-law statuses. Quoting the precise term prevents an ordinary unfinished count from being misreported as a near tie. Canvass reconciles the election record The canvass is the administrative process that turns precinct and ballot records into the jurisdiction's official vote statement. The Election Assistance Commission describes canvass as the stage in which officials compile and review returns, confirm that required materials are present, reconcile quantities, investigate discrepancies, and aggregate results according to law. Exact tasks vary, but a canvass may compare ballots cast with voter-credit or check-in records, review precinct tapes and memory devices, incorporate accepted provisional and cured ballots, correct transcription errors, and obtain explanations for discrepancies. This is not simply waiting for a computer to finish counting. It is a controlled reconciliation across records produced by decentralized election administration. Local canvassing bodies often certify local returns and transmit them to a state canvassing authority. Statewide and multi-county contests are then aggregated at the state level. The National Association of Secretaries of State's state-law survey shows substantial variation in canvassing deadlines, responsible officials, automatic-recount thresholds, candidate-request rules, and payment provisions. Normal canvass changes should be described precisely. “County added 2,400 valid mail ballots” is more informative than “vote total mysteriously changed.” Conversely, a reconciliation discrepancy deserves documentation rather than reflexive reassurance. The proper questions are what record differed, which rule governed the correction, who authorized it, and whether the updated official report explains the change. Certification creates the official administrative result Certification is the formal act by which the legally designated official or board attests the results. It ordinarily follows completion of the required canvass. The certificate supplies governments and legislative chambers with the official return and credentials on which they initially act. Certification is not a prediction and is not performed by a news organization. Nor is it a declaration that no error is imaginable. It means the responsible authority completed the duties state law assigns at that stage. Whether the certifying official has discretion, and what happens if an official refuses, are questions of the particular statute and any controlling court order—not a generic power to revisit the electorate's choice. Deadlines differ across states and offices. House races contained within one state follow that state's canvass and certification calendar; Senate races are statewide. A national chamber table that labels every projected winner “certified” on one date will be wrong. Store the certificate date and source for every contest. Certification can coexist with later proceedings. Some recounts occur after it. A court can order corrections or a new certificate where authorized. Congress can examine credentials and contests. Thus certified is a strong official status, but not the same proposition as incapable of legal challenge . Audits and recounts answer different questions A post-election audit evaluates some aspect of election equipment, records, or tabulation under a prescribed procedure, often by manually examining a sample of voter-verifiable records. A risk-limiting audit is designed to provide statistical evidence that the reported outcome is correct, escalating toward a fuller hand count when the evidence is insufficient. Audit design and legal consequence vary by state. A recount re-tabulates ballots in a specified contest. It may be automatic when the margin falls within a statutory threshold, requested by a candidate or voter, or ordered by a court. State law controls timing, eligible requestors, deposits or costs, scope, counting method, standards for ballot review, observers, and whether the recount changes the certified return. Neither procedure inherently alleges fraud. An automatic recount is triggered by arithmetic. A candidate-requested recount may be a statutory right exercised because the margin is small. Most recounts make small changes because the same ballots are being counted under established standards; “small” cannot be assumed in advance, and the legally completed recount controls where the law says it does. Recount coverage must name the trigger and denominator. “Within 0.5 percent” can mean a percentage of votes cast for certain candidates, total contest votes, or another statutory measure. The same numerical margin may qualify in one state and not another. Report who requested it, who pays initially, which ballots are reviewed, and whether certification is stayed or amended. A recount ordinarily answers “What is the correct tabulation of the ballots within scope?” It does not necessarily answer whether a candidate was eligible, whether unlawful conduct invalidated votes, or whether an election should be annulled. Those are potential contest questions. An election contest is an adversarial legal claim An election contest invokes a statutory or constitutional procedure to challenge the right to office or the validity of a result. Grounds, deadlines, pleading requirements, evidence, burden of proof, remedies, and tribunal all depend on the office and governing law. Possible allegations include candidate ineligibility, erroneous inclusion or exclusion of ballots, misconduct, or irregularities alleged to have affected the result. A contest is not a synonym for recount. It may use recount evidence, seek inspection of ballots, or request correction, exclusion, inclusion, or a new election. A court does not normally treat every administrative imperfection as outcome-changing. The claimant must meet the relevant legal standard and connect proved facts to an authorized remedy. Reporting should separate three levels: Allegation: what the pleading asserts. Evidence and ruling: what admissible evidence the tribunal credited and what legal conclusions it reached. Remedy and status: whether totals, certification, seating, or the election itself changed, and whether review remains. “Candidate files challenge” establishes only level one. Repeating allegations in declarative prose launders a party's claim into a fact. Conversely, dismissing a case merely because it is partisan ignores that election-contest systems exist to resolve genuine disputes. The pleading, docket, orders, and final judgment are the primary sources. House contests have a federal statutory channel Article I, Section 5 says each house is the judge of the elections, returns, and qualifications of its own members. For House elections, the Federal Contested Elections Act supplies the principal modern procedure for a candidate to bring a contest to the House. The statute, codified at 2 U.S.C. §§ 381–396, defines contestant and contestee, sets notice and answer procedures, permits depositions and evidence gathering, and leads to a record for House consideration. The Act is not a federal court trial and does not transfer the House's final constitutional judgment to an agency. It applies to official general or special elections for Representative, Delegate, or Resident Commissioner—not party primaries. CRS explains that a House contest can also arise through other parliamentary routes, but the Act is the principal candidate-initiated channel in modern practice. State recounts and House authority can coexist. Constitution Annotated's discussion of Roudebush v. Hartke explains that a state recount does not prevent the Senate from independently judging an election because the recount does not bind the chamber. The same structural point matters for Congress generally: state processes develop the official return and evidentiary record; Article I preserves the relevant house's final judgment over membership. Senate contests follow Senate constitutional practice The Federal Contested Elections Act is a House statute. The Senate instead relies on Article I, its rules, committees, precedents, and resolutions. The Senate's official history says it has developed its own procedures for settling contested elections and guards the power to judge qualifications and returns. A Senate dispute may be referred to the Committee on Rules and Administration or handled under a resolution tailored to the case. The Senate can examine ballots and evidence, authorize an investigation or recount, decide whom to seat, or determine that no candidate is entitled to the seat. Historical procedures are instructive, but they do not create one automatic modern timetable equivalent to the House Act. This difference must appear in reporting. “Congressional contest” is not one uniform federal lawsuit. A House candidate invoking 2 U.S.C. chapter 12 and a Senate claimant petitioning the Senate operate through different channels, even though both ultimately implicate Article I. Seating, exclusion, and qualifications Credentials based on state certification ordinarily support initial seating, but the chamber's constitutional judgment remains. Article I identifies age, citizenship, and inhabitancy qualifications for representatives and senators, while Section 5 assigns judging authority to each house. Congress cannot casually invent additional constitutional qualifications; it can judge whether the fixed qualifications and election requirements are met. The distinction between excluding a member-elect who lacks qualifications and expelling a seated member matters. Expulsion requires a two-thirds vote under Article I, Section 5. A contested-election resolution concerns entitlement to the seat, not punishment by expulsion. These doctrines can become legally complex, so a live case should cite the chamber's resolution, committee report, and controlling judicial precedent rather than rely on slogans. Administration of the oath is an important status marker, but a chamber may preserve a contest after seating a member. Seating can allow representation while an investigation continues; it need not predetermine the final merits. The exact resolution and reservations control. How to report chamber control Chamber-control claims inherit the status of their decisive seats. A useful ledger reports counts in parallel: certified or otherwise legally final winners ; projected winners not yet certified ; leaders in uncalled races ; races in recount or contest , with certification status; seated members once the new Congress convenes. If one party has enough called winners to cross the control threshold, it is reasonable to report that a named decision desk projects control. It is inaccurate to say all those wins are certified. If the threshold depends on an uncalled race, say control remains uncalled even if one party leads. If a recount is pending in a race whose outcome cannot change which bloc crosses the threshold, explain that the proceeding matters to the seat but not the present control projection. AP's own balance-of-power rule is seat based: it says a party controls the House only after AP has declared 218 winners for that party, and controls the Senate after 51 winners—or 50 when the vice president is of that party. AP says it does not use a national statistical model to project eventual chamber control. Other decision desks may use different terminology or thresholds, so attribute the control call as carefully as the underlying race calls. Do not subtract every contested seat from a certified count as if filing automatically vacated the certificate. Do not add every concession as if it were certification. And do not call control “official” without defining whether that means certified state returns, no outcome-determinative litigation, or chamber organization. Those are different milestones. A verification workflow Record the state election authority, local sources, and governing calendar before voting. Preserve unofficial totals with timestamps rather than silently overwriting them. Track outstanding ballot categories, deadlines, and estimated quantities. Attribute every race call to the organization and time that issued it. Obtain canvass reports and the actual certification, not a campaign statement. Read the recount statute before describing a trigger, threshold, scope, or payer. Treat a contest filing as an allegation packet; follow the docket and orders. For House contests, distinguish state litigation from the Federal Contested Elections Act record. For Senate contests, follow Senate committee and floor action rather than importing House procedure. State chamber control at the weakest status of the decisive seat and update the label when that status changes. This produces a record that can survive both speed and scrutiny. It gives timely projections their proper value, official administration its proper authority, and legal challenges their proper burden without confusing any one stage for all the others. Sources U.S. Election Assistance Commission, Election Results, Canvass, and Certification — official overview and resources on unofficial returns, canvass, certification, and recounts; accessed July 9, 2026. EAC Election Management Guidelines — official canvass and certification guidance; accessed July 9, 2026. Constitution Annotated, Article I — election rules, fixed qualifications, each house's judging power, and the expulsion clause; accessed July 9, 2026. Constitution Annotated, Judging Elections, Returns, and Qualifications of Members — congressional authority and Roudebush v. Hartke ; accessed July 9, 2026. Office of the Law Revision Counsel, 2 U.S.C. chapter 12 — current Federal Contested Elections Act, 2 U.S.C. §§ 381–396; accessed July 9, 2026. Congressional Research Service, The Federal Contested Election Act — statutory overview and recent House practice; accessed July 9, 2026. Congressional Research Service, Procedures for Contested Election Cases in the House — detailed House procedure and comparison with Senate practice; accessed July 9, 2026. U.S. Senate Historical Office, Contested Senate Elections — official overview of Article I authority, petitions, investigation, and seating without prejudice; accessed July 9, 2026. U.S. Senate Historical Office, Senate Procedures in Contested Elections — official precedents and distinction between exclusion and expulsion; accessed July 9, 2026. Senate Committee on Rules and Administration, Jurisdiction — current committee jurisdiction over credentials, qualifications, and contested Senate elections; accessed July 9, 2026. National Association of Secretaries of State, State Election Canvassing Timeframes and Recount Thresholds — state-law survey; accessed July 9, 2026. Associated Press, How we declare winners — AP's race-call standard, “too early” and “too close” terminology, recount approach, and seat-based chamber-control rule; accessed July 9, 2026. Associated Press, How AP counts the vote — AP's independent collection and verification of unofficial returns; accessed July 9, 2026. Bipartisan Policy Center, How Media Outlets Call Races from Unofficial Election Results — independent context on decision desks, unofficial returns, and certification; accessed July 9, 2026. Open questions Which 2026 states place recounts before certification, after certification, or on both sides of it? Which official data feeds report estimated ballots remaining by type rather than only precinct percentages? How should the control ledger label a certified winner whose contest remains pending but whose certificate is not stayed? What evidentiary threshold should trigger a public correction note rather than an ordinary status update? Which House and Senate precedents are most relevant if a 2026 contest reaches a chamber after state proceedings? How should the desk distinguish a chamber's initial seating decision from its final disposition of a contest?

title: Reading congressional polls without overreacting
deck: A congressional poll is a noisy, model-dependent estimate of opinion among a defined population during stated field dates—not a vote count, a forecast, or proof that a race has moved.
headings: Begin with the estimand, not the margin
Sampling asks who had a path into the poll
Weighting repairs representation by making assumptions
Mode can change whom a poll reaches and how people answer
Sponsor, questionnaire, and field dates are part of the result
What the margin of error does—and does not—mean
House effects are recurring differences, not automatic corrections
Correlated error is the central congressional danger
Aggregation reduces noise but cannot average away shared bias
text: A congressional poll is a noisy, model-dependent estimate of opinion among a defined population during stated field dates—not a vote count, a forecast, or proof that a race has moved. Up: [[2026 United States midterm elections]] · Related: [[How control of the House is won in 2026]] · [[How control of the Senate is won in 2026]] · [[Polling error and election uncertainty]] · [[Poll aggregation]] · [[Election forecasting]] Why it matters Congressional polling affects fundraising, news coverage, party spending, volunteer attention, race ratings, forecasts, and [[Political prediction markets|prediction-market prices]]. Yet the familiar topline—one candidate at 47 percent and another at 45 percent—compresses a chain of choices about whom to contact, who responded, how respondents were weighted, which voters were treated as likely, how the question was asked, and what happened to people who had not chosen a candidate. Those choices do not make polls useless. A carefully documented poll can reveal the plausible state of a race, identify which coalitions are uncertain, and update what district fundamentals alone would imply. The mistake is to treat the topline as a direct reading of Election Day. The general election is November 3, 2026; a survey completed weeks or months earlier measures responses during its own field period. Opinion may change afterward, and turnout may differ from stated intention. The right response to a new poll is therefore neither belief nor dismissal. It is structured updating: identify exactly what was measured, assess the main sources of error, compare like with like, and move the prior view only as far as the evidence warrants. This note is methodological and current as of July 9, 2026; it deliberately does not use a live 2026 poll as an example. Begin with the estimand, not the margin Before reading the result, ask what quantity the poll is trying to estimate. A survey of U.S. adults about congressional approval, a national survey of registered voters about the generic ballot, a likely-voter survey in one Senate contest, and a poll of registered voters in one House district answer different questions. Their toplines should not be placed on one trend line merely because all concern Congress. The target population is the group about which the poll claims to speak. Common election-poll populations include: adults , useful for broad public opinion but including people who cannot or will not vote; citizens or voting-eligible adults , closer to the legal electorate but still not a turnout forecast; registered voters , excluding unregistered adults while including registrants unlikely to participate; likely voters , a modeled subset whose definition varies by pollster; primary voters , whose eligibility, party-registration rules, and expected turnout must match the state and contest. A likely-voter poll is not automatically superior to a registered-voter poll. It asks the more election-proximate question by imposing a stronger model. Pollsters may use self-reported intention, past voting records, interest, knowledge of polling place, demographic patterns, or combinations of these signals. Early in a campaign, the eventual electorate is especially uncertain. A tight likely-voter result can therefore look more precise while depending heavily on assumptions about who will participate. The sample must also match the jurisdiction. A statewide sample cannot estimate one congressional district without a defensible district subsample or model, and a national generic-ballot sample does not directly estimate any particular district. District boundary changes make old geographic labels dangerous: results collected or tabulated on superseded lines do not automatically describe the current constituency. Sampling asks who had a path into the poll In a probability sample , researchers use a sampling frame and a design that gives covered units a known, nonzero selection probability. Random-digit-dial telephone samples and address-based samples are familiar examples, though actual designs can be complex. If the design assumptions hold, sampling variability can be estimated from the selection process. In a nonprobability sample , respondents' selection probabilities are unknown. Online opt-in panels are the most familiar case: people join a panel or encounter a survey rather than being randomly selected from a frame covering the target population. Researchers can match and weight these respondents to population benchmarks, and well-designed nonprobability polls can perform well. But their uncertainty cannot be justified by the classical probability-sampling formula alone. AAPOR distinguishes a model-based credibility interval from a margin of sampling error and warns against treating them as interchangeable. The recruitment label is only a beginning. A probability sample with severe differential nonresponse can be biased; a rigorously adjusted nonprobability sample can be informative. Ask instead: What was the sampling or recruitment frame? Who was covered and who had no route into the sample? How were people contacted and selected within households? What proportion participated, where meaningful and disclosed? Did response propensity relate to vote choice after adjustment? That last question is decisive. A low response rate does not mechanically imply a large bias, and a higher response rate does not guarantee accuracy. Bias arises when participation is related to the quantity being estimated after the survey's corrections. If supporters of one candidate are systematically less reachable or less willing to answer even within weighting cells, a demographically balanced sample may still misstate the race. Weighting repairs representation by making assumptions Raw respondents rarely resemble the target electorate in exactly the right proportions. A survey therefore assigns each case a weight , determining how much that response contributes to the estimate. In a probability survey, a base weight often begins as the inverse of selection probability. Pollsters may then adjust for nonresponse and align the weighted sample with external population totals through poststratification, raking, calibration, matching, or related procedures. Typical targets include geography, age, sex, race and ethnicity, and education. Election polls may also use party registration, past vote, recalled vote, partisan identification, modeled partisanship, or turnout-history variables. The exact targets matter. Census benchmarks can describe demographic composition, but there is no official census of current partisan identity. Weighting to a partisan target therefore adds an estimate or model rather than a neutral fact. Weighting can correct observed imbalances only through variables measured in both the sample and a credible benchmark, or through justified modeling. It cannot guarantee correction for an unobserved difference between respondents and nonrespondents. Two respondents who share age, education, race, and geography may still differ politically in a way related to answering surveys. Weights also affect precision. If a hard-to-reach respondent receives a large weight while many easy-to-reach respondents are downweighted, the survey's effective sample size can be much smaller than its nominal number of interviews. A reported margin of sampling error should account for the design effect from unequal weighting, clustering, or other features when appropriate. “1,000 respondents” is not by itself a complete statement of information. The useful questions are concrete: Which variables were used? What external sources set their targets? Were extreme weights trimmed? Was the likely electorate imposed before or after demographic weighting? Does the stated error calculation incorporate the design effect? Methodological transparency does not prove that every choice is right, but it makes the choices inspectable. Mode can change whom a poll reaches and how people answer Mode means the way participants are contacted or interviewed: live telephone, interactive voice response, text-to-web, mail, online panel, in-person interviewing, or a mixed design. Mode operates through at least two channels. First, modes cover and recruit different people. A telephone design that omits cell phones has a different coverage problem from an address-based web survey that provides no offline option. Online opt-in panels depend on who joins and remains active. Mixed-mode designs may improve reach, but the respondents arriving through each mode can differ. Second, the presence and interface of the interviewer can affect answers. People may respond differently to a human interviewer than to a private web form, especially for socially sensitive questions. Visual surveys can randomize or display options differently from an audio interview. A long list that is easy to scan on screen may be harder to retain by phone. Mode changes can therefore create an apparent trend even when underlying opinion is stable. This does not justify a universal ranking such as “live caller good, internet bad.” Design and execution matter more than a slogan. Compare repeated polls from the same organization when possible, and flag any shift in recruitment, interview mode, languages, questionnaire, or weighting. A mode break can be real methodological improvement while still making pre-break and post-break numbers imperfectly comparable. Sponsor, questionnaire, and field dates are part of the result The sponsor paid for or commissioned the research; the pollster conducted it. Sometimes the same organization fills both roles. A campaign, party committee, advocacy organization, news outlet, university, or independent research firm may sponsor a poll. Sponsorship is not proof of manipulation. It is relevant context because sponsors choose questions, timing, populations, and whether to release results. Selective publication creates an additional problem. The public sees released polls, not every private poll that was conducted. A sponsor may publish a favorable result and withhold an unfavorable one. Several public polls from aligned sponsors do not necessarily represent several independent views of the evidence. Read the full questionnaire and methodology rather than assigning or withholding credibility solely from the sponsor's name. Question order and wording can matter. Asking about a salient issue, candidate biography, or attack immediately before the vote question may prime respondents. A ballot test should make clear which candidates and labels were presented, whether names were rotated, whether leaners were probed, and whether the contest was hypothetical or reflected a settled ballot. Push polls, whose purpose is persuasion rather than measurement, should not be treated as ordinary surveys. Field dates tell when interviews occurred. Use the final interview date—not the press-release date—as the endpoint when judging recency. A five-day survey spanning a major event mixes responses from before and after it. Overlapping polls may not be independent time points, and a new release can be based on older interviews than a release already in the average. Events after the field period cannot have caused the poll's result. Undecided voters and reported margins Candidate support does not always sum to 100 percent. Respondents may be undecided, prefer another candidate, refuse, or say they will not vote. A poll may report all respondents, reallocate leaners after a follow-up, or present a two-party-normalized result that excludes other answers. These are different quantities. Suppose, as a purely hypothetical illustration, Candidate A has 45 percent, Candidate B 43 percent, and 12 percent are elsewhere or undecided. A leads by two points among all respondents. Renormalizing only A and B produces roughly 51.1 to 48.9, but that arithmetic does not reveal how the uncommitted group will vote or whether it will vote. An analyst must not silently convert one presentation into the other. Undecideds are not a party-owned reserve. Their eventual behavior may reflect late persuasion, habitual partisanship, turnout, third-party support, or continued nonchoice. Compare the level of support as well as the margin: 49–47 and 45–43 share a two-point margin but imply different amounts of unresolved preference. Also inspect whether the poll forces a choice and whether its leaner procedure changed over time. What the margin of error does—and does not—mean For a simple random probability sample, a percentage estimate has standard error approximately SE(\hat p)=\sqrt{\frac{\hat p(1-\hat p)}{n}}, and a conventional 95 percent margin of sampling error is about 1.96SE . The familiar maximum near 50 percent produces roughly three percentage points for a simple random sample of about 1,000. Real surveys may require a larger error because of weighting, clustering, and design. The uncertainty of a difference between candidates is not interpreted by mechanically comparing the lead with the reported error for one percentage. If \hat p_A and \hat p_B come from the same survey, then \operatorname{Var}(\hat p_A-\hat p_B)=\operatorname{Var}(\hat p_A)+\operatorname{Var}(\hat p_B)-2\operatorname{Cov}(\hat p_A,\hat p_B). The two shares are dependent because respondents cannot simultaneously choose both candidates in an ordinary single-choice ballot test. For a simple multinomial sample, the covariance is negative, so the standard error of the lead is generally larger than the standard error of either share alone. The poll's documentation or underlying microdata are preferable to a shortcut; design effects and weighting can further change the calculation. More important, this interval addresses sampling variability under specified assumptions. It does not automatically include coverage error, nonresponse bias, question effects, inaccurate likely-voter models, data processing mistakes, late opinion change, or turnout error. These forms of nonsampling error can be as important as sampling error and may push many polls in the same direction. “Within the margin of error” is therefore not a binary truth test. Nor does a one-point lead establish that the leading candidate is more likely than not to win without a model connecting the survey, other evidence, future opinion, and turnout to the election. A poll estimates support during its field dates; an election forecast estimates a future event. House effects are recurring differences, not automatic corrections A house effect is a persistent tendency for a pollster's results to differ from other pollsters' estimates after accounting for time and the contests being measured. It can arise from sampling frame, mode, questionnaire, weighting targets, likely-voter screen, treatment of leaners, or other stable design choices. It need not imply partisan intent or poor quality. House effects are estimated relative to a comparison model or the broader polling consensus, not observed as an objective constant. If all pollsters share a bias, the outlying firm might be closer to the truth. If a firm's methods change, its historical house effect may no longer apply. Small numbers of polls and selective contest coverage make estimates noisy. Use house effects to avoid mistaking a return to a pollster's typical level for movement in the electorate. The cleanest short-term comparison is often within the same pollster, population, mode, and questionnaire. Even then, ordinary sampling and nonsampling noise remains. Across firms, an aggregator may estimate and partially adjust house effects, but the adjustment should be documented rather than treated as a revealed partisan truth. Correlated error is the central congressional danger Poll errors are not independent coins. Pollsters may share population benchmarks, turnout assumptions, vendor data, mode limitations, or difficulty reaching the same political groups. Districts can share national or regional political forces. A bad assumption about participation among one coalition can therefore push Senate, House, and generic-ballot estimates in the same direction. This matters most for chamber control. If ten pivotal House districts each look like a narrow independent contest, multiplying ten separate probabilities understates the chance of a common miss. One national polling error can move several seats together. Agreement among many polls is less reassuring when those polls share methods or respondents; a large number of correlated observations does not create the information of the same number of independent observations. Correlated error also explains why a chamber forecast can have a wide seat distribution even when individual district averages look stable. Models should include common national, regional, and pollster components rather than treating every survey error as isolated. A reader need not reconstruct the model, but should ask whether its uncertainty widens for shared error and whether generic-ballot and district evidence are being double-counted. Aggregation reduces noise but cannot average away shared bias An average is usually better than choosing the most dramatic poll. Aggregation can reduce random sampling noise, pool information across dates and pollsters, and expose an outlier. Sophisticated averages may weight recency, sample size, population, pollster history, and design; adjust house effects; estimate an underlying trend; and prevent one pollster with many releases from dominating. But the word average hides choices. Inspect: which polls and sponsors qualify; whether adults, registered voters, and likely voters are separated; whether internal and partisan polls are labeled or adjusted; how overlapping samples and repeated pollsters are handled; how quickly old polls decay; whether house effects and methodological changes are modeled; whether the output is a polling estimate or a forecast using fundamentals; whether uncertainty includes historical nonsampling and correlated error. A simple mean of incompatible polls can be less meaningful than a careful reading of fewer comparable surveys. Conversely, an opaque complex average can create false confidence. Aggregation narrows idiosyncratic noise; it does not rescue a common coverage failure, a mistaken turnout model, or an electorate that changes after the polls. A disciplined reading workflow For each new congressional poll: Freeze the metadata: sponsor, pollster, exact contest, target population, sample size, field dates, recruitment, mode, weighting, likely-voter definition, questionnaire, leaner and undecided treatment, and reported uncertainty. Find the original release: use the methodology and crosstabs, not a headline, screenshot, social post, or campaign paraphrase. Check comparability: compare with the same pollster's earlier wave and with other polls of the same population. Do not call a difference between registered-voter and likely-voter surveys a trend without qualification. Separate level from change: a poll can improve knowledge of a close race without showing that the race recently moved. Use a prior: district partisanship, incumbency, candidate status, finance, and national conditions provide context. A sparse district poll should update this baseline, not erase it. Look for independent confirmation: another poll with genuinely different methods, credible administrative or turnout evidence, fundraising, or a documented event can strengthen the inference. Repackaged versions of the same evidence do not. State the residual uncertainty: sampling error, nonsampling error, future opinion change, turnout, and correlated error remain after averaging. Move the conclusion proportionally: one poll may justify “the race is plausibly competitive,” not “the candidate will win” or “the chamber has flipped.” The durable question is not whether a poll was eventually “right.” Chance can make a weak method land near the result, while a strong poll can miss because it measured opinion before a late change. Evaluate design prospectively and performance over many contests. Election results are the outcome to explain, not permission to reverse-engineer a story that crowns whichever poll happened to be closest. Limits Even complete disclosure cannot reveal every operational decision, and crosstabs often have small effective samples that make subgroup stories especially unstable. Pollster-performance ratings inherit choices about which contests, dates, error metrics, and corrections to use. Historical accuracy may not transfer after changes in candidates, technology, turnout, or method. Public polling is also an incomplete sample of all polling. Campaigns and parties possess private research, and publication decisions can distort the visible record. Districts with little public polling are not necessarily safe; they may simply be expensive or unattractive to poll. Polling volume is partly an outcome of perceived competitiveness, producing a selection problem when analysts compare well-polled and poorly polled races. Finally, measuring intention is not the same as causing or forecasting a vote. A poll does not incorporate future events, and a forecast adds assumptions that deserve their own audit. The sound conclusion is calibrated uncertainty: polls are among the best direct measurements of expressed electoral preference, but their precision is bounded by the full survey process and the future separating fieldwork from Election Day. Sources AAPOR, Transparency Initiative disclosure standards — sponsor, population, sampling, mode, dates, weighting, questionnaire, and error-disclosure expectations; accessed July 9, 2026. AAPOR, Sampling Methods for Political Polling — probability and nonprobability sampling, coverage, nonresponse, and election-poll design; accessed July 9, 2026. AAPOR, Margin of Sampling Error — interpretation and limits of sampling error; accessed July 9, 2026. AAPOR, credibility intervals versus margins of sampling error — why nonprobability model intervals are not classical margins of sampling error; accessed July 9, 2026. AAPOR, 2020 Pre-Election Polling Task Force report — empirical post-election analysis of weighting, likely-voter methods, and unresolved sources of error; accessed July 9, 2026. Pew Research Center, U.S. Survey Methodology — total survey error framework and probability-based online-panel design; accessed July 9, 2026. Pew Research Center, Methods 101: What are nonprobability surveys? — recruitment, selection probabilities, adjustment, and limits; accessed July 9, 2026. Pew Research Center, For Weighting Online Opt-In Samples, What Matters Most? — experimental comparison of weighting and matching approaches; accessed July 9, 2026. U.S. Census Bureau, Current Population Survey weighting — base weights, noninterview adjustment, and population controls; accessed July 9, 2026. U.S. Census Bureau, nonsampling-error quality standard — coverage, nonresponse, measurement, and processing error framework; accessed July 9, 2026. Jennings and Wlezien, “Election polling errors across time and space,” Nature Human Behaviour (2018) — comparative evidence on election-poll error and political context. Shirani-Mehr et al., “Polls and Elections: Measurement and prediction,” Annual Review of Statistics and Its Application (2018) — scholarly review of election-poll error and information quality. Heidemanns, Gelman, and Morris, “Grappling With Uncertainty in Forecasting the 2024 U.S. Presidential Election,” Harvard Data Science Review (2024) — transparent discussion of hierarchical forecasting, nonsampling error, and correlation across jurisdictions. Open questions Which 2026 pollsters disclose enough detail to estimate design effects and distinguish true probability intervals from model-based credibility intervals? How should a House polling average estimate common national, regional, and vendor-level error when many districts have only one or two public polls? Which apparently independent congressional polls share sample providers, voter-file models, weighting targets, or respondents? How should the desk preserve methodological breaks within a pollster's series without discarding useful older evidence? What evidence can distinguish late opinion change from a stable nonresponse or turnout error after the election?

title: Autonomous research committees
deck: Rome now expands through nineteen independent subject committees that launch together every hour, followed by a dedicated half-hour publisher.
text: Rome now expands through nineteen independent subject committees that launch together every hour, followed by a dedicated half-hour publisher. Up: [[Rome Wiki]] The hourly wave At the top of every hour, all nineteen topics begin separate research runs: the 2026 US midterms; the 2027 French presidential election; applied PDEs; exometeorology; the NBA and Dallas Mavericks; Duke men's basketball; Duke football; Tottenham; the Colts; the Mets; fantasy basketball; US markets and commodities; top-100 crypto; political prediction markets; frontier AI; Korean history; European history from 500 to 1914; Romantic piano through 1945; and Romantic violin through 1945. Each lane owns a separate article route and persistent state. It uses the coordinator and up to three delegated workers when Codex exposes them, then refills available slots through research, long-form writing, verification, and editing. Triggering all nineteen together maximizes parallel opportunity, though the runtime may still queue or resource-manage actual execution. Collision-free publishing Research lanes do not append to the same registry, run log, root MOCs, homepage ledger, or generated site files. They write topic-local work plus unique publisher receipts. At half past the hour, the twentieth committee serially integrates completed receipts, applies shared links, updates the editorial records, synchronizes the public snapshot, validates it, and publishes the new edition to GitHub Pages when every gate passes. Work that finishes after the cutoff appears in the next edition. Production ambition The individual bands sum to roughly 63–145 substantial completions per ideal hourly wave, or 1,512–3,480 across twenty-four ideal waves, with no ceiling. These figures describe ambition rather than guaranteed throughput. Evidence, depth, runtime capacity, deduplication, privacy, and safety decide what is actually published. Standard explanatory articles require 2,000–4,000 useful body words; major dossiers may require 4,000–8,000. Two-paragraph pages, padded prose, source dumps, and lightly expanded notices do not count. Ledgers, timelines, source maps, and MOC edits remain valuable but are reported separately. Priorities and safeguards Dallas Mavericks/NBA leaguewide, Duke men's basketball, and Duke football retain the largest sports allocations. Tottenham keeps a higher evidence threshold. Markets emphasizes US equities, rates, credit, FX transmission, derivatives, and commodity chains. Crypto tracks a provider-ranked top 100 with identity controls. Piano and violin coverage follows Romantic and post-Romantic traditions through 1945. Current claims carry as-of dates; official or primary evidence leads; forecasts, market prices, rumors, model outputs, and inference stay labeled. Committees do not trade, spend money, change fantasy rosters, contact people, access private accounts, or rewrite Andrew's prose. The publisher can commit and deploy only the approved public website repository after privacy and build gates pass. Operating requirements The computer must remain on, the Codex desktop app must be running, and the Rome and website projects must remain available. Codex can resource-manage concurrency even when every schedule shares the same start time. Open questions Which lanes most often arrive after the half-hour cutoff? How should the site surface hourly editions without overwhelming readers? When should graph and search generation become incremental?

title: Rome Wiki
deck: The Rome Wiki turns Andrew Park's external brain into a static, searchable encyclopedia while keeping Markdown and wikilinks as the source of truth.
text: The Rome Wiki turns Andrew Park's external brain into a static, searchable encyclopedia while keeping Markdown and wikilinks as the source of truth. Public edition: chronicaria.github.io/rome-wiki · Source: github.com/chronicaria/rome-wiki Up: [[Build My Brain (Rome)]] · [[Home]] Related: [[Wiki editorial and corpus pass 2026-07-09]] · [[Autonomous research committees]] Current edition The front-end lives in the separate project and uses a restrained old-newspaper design: warm paper, editorial serif type, fine rules, dense navigation, and no faux aging. Its article template now borrows Wikipedia's information hierarchy without imitating Wikipedia's visual branding. The validated snapshot publishes the human-facing corpus across its reading rooms; article, link, word, and research-seed counts are recalculated on every sync as the continuous committee loop expands it. The universe map arranges articles into separated, proportionally sized, labeled topic galaxies. Their boundaries remain invisible: local topic gravity creates readable neighborhoods, nearby documents repel, links and shared tags shape each galaxy, and cross-topic links remain visible as bridges. Map labels now use the same editorial serif as the site, with a larger vertical topic-and-color legend on the left. Article pages use a wide 100-character reading measure, a compact contents rail, smaller display type, flatter heading hierarchy, subtle title rules, and lightweight source/status metadata. The String Theory reading room is a six-part, 27-chapter course table of contents built from the module folders and notes. The homepage research ledger records additions, revisions, retirements, relocations, topics, and contributing agents. Search covers titles, tags, headings, summaries, and body text; full vault paths keep repeated titles distinct. The renderer supports backlinks, related notes, Obsidian wikilinks, unwritten research seeds, callouts, math, code, tables, tasks, and local media. Rome is explicitly identified as Andrew Park's brain; article-level provenance remains visible separately. Publishing loop All nineteen standalone subject committees launch together at the top of every hour and write only their exclusive routes, state, and unique receipts. copies only the publishable vault into a frozen repository snapshot and rebuilds the graph. The public audit, route/graph tests, lint, type checking, and GitHub Pages build must all pass. The publisher stages only the approved content paths, pushes non-destructively, dispatches the Pages workflow, and verifies the deployment. The continuous committees can expand Rome without requiring the front-end to know which agent produced a note: the vault and ledger remain the contract. [[Autonomous research committees]] describes the parallel hourly wave, collision-free receipts, dynamic worker-refill model, half-hour publisher, and unlimited expansion mandate. Publication boundary The wiki publishes the durable human knowledge layer, not every operational file. A shared publication policy excludes agent instructions, prompts, runbooks, Claude/Codex memory and skill files, selected AI status reports, internal String Theory plans and review reports, and any note marked before the snapshot is copied. Private wikilink targets render as plain text rather than public pages or false “unwritten article” assignments. Andrew approved public publication after a path-level review on July 9, 2026; individualized health and training notes, personal balances and wealth plans, broker-workflow notes, and capital-action memos remain explicitly excluded. The dispatch-only Pages workflow runs only after each half-hour edition passes every gate. Editorial organization The 30 NBA team research briefings now live together under [[Basketball/NBA team briefings 2026-27/00_INDEX|2026-27 NBA team briefing index]]; the obsolete branch is gone. Individual team roster audits were retired, while the two aggregate audit records remain. [[Crypto]] now researches the dynamic top 100 by market capitalization; JUP, PENDLE, SYRUP, AERO, and PUMP remain a conviction subset rather than a universe ceiling. [[BealeSurfaceSolver research (MOC)]] brings Andrew's surface-PDE solver, level-set geometry, equilibration, shallow-water verification, and exometeorology research into the public knowledge graph. [[RAPM]] connects Andrew's six-factor RAPM decomposition, regularization, cross-league translation, player/team forward models, evaluation, implementation, and public model site to the basketball corpus. Operational AI, agent, skill, memory, and internal course-report material stays in Rome for tools to use but outside the public edition. Open questions Which subject committees most often run past the half-hour publication cutoff? Should the publisher eventually open audited pull requests instead of pushing validated content editions directly? Which graph metrics should trigger deduplication and consolidation alongside unlimited expansion? Which additional reading rooms deserve purpose-built course or atlas pages? Should agent-authored notes eventually declare or explicitly at creation time? When the corpus reaches tens of thousands of pages, should galaxy coordinates be precomputed during the publication build rather than settled in the browser?
