Open questions Will Pierce receive an official camp availability designation, and when will he resume unrestricted team work after ankle surgery? How often will Downs align outside, and does that experiment preserve his best slot and pressure-answer work? Which receiver and tight end inherit Pittman's third-down, red-zone, contested-target, and blocking responsibilities? Does Westbrook-Ikhine establish a regular outside role, or does Indianapolis distribute those snaps across several players and formations? Which secondary tight end makes the multi-tight-end package most flexible rather than merely heavier? Can Burks turn verified speed into route, return, and coverage-unit value sufficient for a game-day role? Which reserve pass catchers supply true functional redundancy if Pierce, Downs, or Warren is unavailable?

title: Indianapolis Colts practice-squad construction 2026
deck: The Colts should build their 2026 practice squad as a balanced developmental portfolio—not a list of the last 16 or 17 players cut—combining scarce-position insurance, weekly elevation utility, succession bets, and players whose growth can be measured in the current systems.
headings: Construction starts with jobs, not rankings
Quarterback: operation and development are separate values
Offensive line should receive disproportionate attention
The defensive front requires different kinds of patience
Linebacker and defensive back are the special-teams engine
Weekly elevations should be planned, not improvised
Evidence gates for the final squad
text: The Colts should build their 2026 practice squad as a balanced developmental portfolio—not a list of the last 16 or 17 players cut—combining scarce-position insurance, weekly elevation utility, succession bets, and players whose growth can be measured in the current systems. Up: [[Indianapolis Colts 2026]] Related: [[Indianapolis Colts 2026 roster map]] · [[Indianapolis Colts 2026 roster cut mechanics]] · [[Indianapolis Colts special teams 2026]] · [[Indianapolis Colts 2026 availability ledger]] Direct answer A useful Indianapolis practice squad would cover four different needs at once. It would preserve players who can fill an urgent game-week job; develop young players at positions where technique requires time; supply enough bodies to run representative practices; and hold a few longer-range bets whose eventual value could exceed their immediate readiness. Those purposes overlap, but they are not identical. A veteran quarterback may be valuable because he can operate the offense on short notice. A rookie tackle may be valuable because tackles are difficult to find and develop. A receiver or defensive back may be valuable because he can reproduce an opponent's speed and also play on coverage units. A converted edge defender may need a season of technical work even if he is not yet trustworthy on Sunday. That is why the squad should not simply mirror the bottom of a projected 53. The active roster is selected under game-day constraints; the practice squad extends the organization's capacity to learn and respond. The best portfolio preserves functions the 53 cannot redundantly carry while avoiding 16 versions of the same low-probability prospect. No July roster list can identify the final members. Indianapolis has not completed training camp, preseason evaluation, the August 30 reduction, the August 31 waiver period, or the outside-player market that follows. The names in this article are candidate pools , not projections. Official membership, transactions, practice assignments, preseason film, waiver outcomes, and player choice must replace the hypotheses below. Construction starts with jobs, not rankings The [[Indianapolis Colts 2026 roster map]] contains far more players than the regular-season roster can hold. Practice-squad construction begins by asking what the active roster cannot afford to duplicate. A 53-player roster may carry only two quarterbacks, eight or nine offensive linemen, a compressed set of pass-catchers, and defensive reserves selected partly for special teams. That leaves credible players outside the 53 even when their development remains valuable. Indianapolis should map every practice-squad place to at least one of five jobs: Emergency replacement. The player can learn a defined regular-season assignment and become usable after an injury. Weekly elevation option. The player has a narrow function—line depth, coverage, return, blocking, or a package role—that may be needed for a particular opponent. Developmental investment. The player has traits or scarce-position value worth carrying through a longer teaching cycle. Practice function. The player can reproduce an upcoming opponent's personnel or style without making that the sole reason for retention. Succession option. The player could compete for a larger role in 2027 after a year inside Indianapolis's terminology, conditioning, and technique program. One player may cover several categories. That multiplicity is more valuable than a rigid quota. A young defensive back who learns outside and slot responsibilities, plays on multiple special-teams units, and has enough speed for scout-team work supplies more portfolio value than a one-position reserve with no plausible path to Sunday. The same principle applies to an interior lineman who can snap, a tight end who can block from several alignments, or a linebacker who can cover kicks while learning the defense. The practice squad is not, however, protected storage. As [[Indianapolis Colts 2026 roster cut mechanics]] explains, Indianapolis cannot reserve a waived player before waivers run, and players who clear can weigh other offers. Practice-squad players can also leave for eligible active-roster opportunities elsewhere. A plan that assumes every preferred cut returns is not a plan; it is one possible outcome. A portfolio allocation for Indianapolis The exact count should change with the final 53, health, and outside acquisitions. A reasonable planning range is more useful than a fixed 16-name forecast: Portfolio lane Planning range Primary value Quarterback and offensive operation 1–2 Emergency operation, developmental continuity, scout-team execution Offensive line 3–4 Scarce-position insurance, cross-training, eight-lineman game-day contingency Running back, receiver, and tight end 3–5 Skill and blocking variety, return/coverage utility, opponent reproduction Defensive front and edge 2–4 Rotation insurance, technical development, opponent run/pass-rush looks Linebacker and secondary 4–6 Coverage depth, communication development, multi-phase special teams International pathway or specialist contingency 0–1 additional or embedded Long-horizon development or a specific emergency function These ranges intentionally overlap and exceed total capacity. They are decision lanes, not quotas. If Indianapolis keeps only eight offensive linemen on the 53, the squad should probably hold more line insurance. If the active roster carries a deep defensive front but a thin secondary, the final places should shift toward defensive backs. Injuries and reserve designations can change the balance again before Week 1. The important constraint is diversification. Four developmental receivers may all look appealing, but retaining them together has an opportunity cost if the organization then lacks a usable center, tackle, corner, or linebacker. Conversely, filling the squad only with one-rep-away veterans can eliminate the upside that makes a developmental roster worthwhile. The portfolio needs both immediacy and time horizon. Quarterback: operation and development are separate values The current official roster lists Daniel Jones, Anthony Richardson Sr., Riley Leonard, and Easton Stick. Those four names create several possible active-roster structures, none official in July. If the Colts carry two quarterbacks on the 53, a third quarterback on the practice squad could preserve terminology, meeting continuity, and emergency depth. If they carry three, a fourth may be difficult to justify unless his developmental trajectory or practice value clearly exceeds candidates at scarcer positions. The right evaluation is not simply preseason passer rating. Coaches need to judge whether the player can call the offense, set protections, handle cadence, deliver the correct concept on schedule, and prepare as though he could be elevated with limited repetitions. Scout-team work adds a different demand: can he approximate mobile, movement-heavy, or quick-game opponents well enough to prepare the defense without corrupting Indianapolis's own development? Stick's June signing and Leonard's returning membership establish candidates, not destinations. Experience can make a quarterback a better short-notice operator; youth and team control can make another a better developmental hold. The final active-roster count and waiver or contract status will determine whether either question is relevant. The Colts' January 2026 transaction history supplies a useful mechanism example: Seth Henigan and Sean McKeon were elevated from the practice squad for the January 4 game and reverted afterward. It shows how a retained player can bridge a specific weekly need; it does not prove the same positions will receive priority in 2026. Offensive line should receive disproportionate attention Indianapolis's line is the strongest case for multiple developmental places. The current roster includes established players, a right-tackle transition, several young tackles, and overlapping center/guard candidates. The likely practice-squad pool can emerge from players such as Bayron Matos, Nolan Rucci, Jimmy Morrissey, Josh Sills, Josh Kreutz, Geno VanDeMark, and other linemen who do not make the 53. That list is illustrative only: some may win active places, fail to clear waivers, sign elsewhere, or be replaced by outside cuts. Line development is slow because the work is relational. A guard's value depends on passing off movement with the center and tackle. A center must identify fronts and make calls. A reserve tackle must survive enough one-on-one space that the offense does not abandon its route structure. Classroom knowledge matters, but padded repetitions and live rushes reveal whether footwork, hand timing, anchor, and recognition hold under force. The squad should therefore favor credible cross-training , not nominal versatility. A roster page can list a player at center or guard without establishing that he can enter an NFL game at both. Indianapolis should chart where each player actually practices, whether communication remains clean after combinations change, and whether preseason snaps show a repeatable floor. A center/guard with reliable exchanges and protection recognition may be a better emergency option than a more spectacular athlete at one spot. A developmental tackle may deserve patience because the league-wide replacement market is thin, even if he is not yet the ninth-best lineman in camp. Matos requires exact administrative treatment. The Colts' transaction ledger designated him exempt/international on April 20. NFL Football Operations says a practice squad can hold a 17th player when that additional player is a qualifying International Player Pathway participant. That does not establish in advance that Matos will occupy an extra place, nor does one designation explain every restriction attached to it. The Colts and league transaction notice must confirm his final status before analysts count a seventeenth slot. Skill positions need complementary functions The current roster contains many reserve candidates at running back, receiver, and tight end. At receiver alone, Deion Burks joins returning or veteran players and younger candidates including Coleman Owen, Eli Pancol, Sahmir Hagans, E.J. Horton, and Raylen Sharpe. Running back includes several competitors behind Jonathan Taylor, while six tight ends appear on the roster map. The wrong construction would retain the most productive preseason stat lines without asking what those players add together. The squad should preserve a complementary menu: a receiver who can handle outside releases, a player who can work inside or motion, a secure return option, a back who can protect and catch, or a tight end capable of reproducing attached and move alignments. One player covering multiple functions creates space for a longer-term bet elsewhere. Special teams are the bridge from development to activation. A reserve receiver, back, or tight end who can cover kicks, block in space, and handle an emergency offensive assignment has a credible weekly elevation path. A player who needs offensive volume but provides no fourth-down role may still be worth developing, but his retention should be justified by upside rather than a fictional immediate contribution. Preseason evaluation should separate production from mechanism. A long reception against a coverage bust is evidence of finishing a play, not a complete receiver evaluation. Route depth, releases, blocking effort and legality, assignment accuracy, ball security, and special-teams execution are more portable. For backs, pass protection and checkdown spacing can be more important to emergency usability than rushing average. For tight ends, attached blocking, movement, route detail, and coverage-unit value should be graded independently. The defensive front requires different kinds of patience Indianapolis has broad interior and edge groups. The 2026 draft added George Gumbs Jr. and Caden Curry, while undrafted additions included Cameron Ball and Mitchell Melton. Returning and veteran players make the active-roster competition deeper than a four-name developmental list suggests. The practice-squad question is which traits can improve inside the Colts' program. Gumbs's conversion from wide receiver to defense creates an unusually visible long-horizon story, but draft status does not predetermine his roster tier. A developing edge must learn run fits, hand usage, rush-lane integrity, counters, and how to contribute on special teams. An interior defender must show pad level, block recognition, gap discipline, and enough pass-rush value to avoid becoming a single-down practice body. These are not interchangeable projects. A heavy interior defender may supply emergency early-down depth. A lighter penetrator may reproduce a movement front in practice or develop into a sub-package option. An edge with coverage-unit ability may have a shorter activation path than a more polished pass rusher who cannot defend the run or play teams. The portfolio should retain complementary archetypes rather than merely the next names in a single depth order. Linebacker and defensive back are the special-teams engine The Colts' linebacker and secondary rooms contain major 2026 turnover and many young candidates. Linebackers Tahj Chambers and West Weeks and safety Austin Brown joined as undrafted rookies; the broader roster also includes returning developmental players and a large cornerback group. Those pools are natural practice-squad sources, but camp must establish which players can perform distinct jobs. For linebackers, the evaluation should combine run fits, coverage spacing, tackling, communication, and kick coverage. A player who can align correctly on defense and contribute on all four primary special-teams units may become an early elevation option. A more instinctive defender who is not ready for coverage units may be a longer developmental bet. Neither profile is automatically superior; the squad needs a controlled mix. For defensive backs, outside corner, slot, deep safety, box safety, and special teams are separate competencies. Indianapolis should favor players who demonstrate real multi-role capacity, but it should not confuse a July position label with proven flexibility. Communication is especially important in a remade defense. A young safety who reduces assignment errors and can organize a scout-team secondary may have developmental value even before he becomes an NFL coverage answer. Coverage and return units also determine weekly readiness. The [[Indianapolis Colts special teams 2026]] framework emphasizes releases, block fits, lane integrity, tackling leverage, ball security, and penalties rather than isolated highlights. Those are the exact details that can turn a practice-squad defensive back or linebacker into a trustworthy elevation when the active roster loses a core special-teamer. Weekly elevations should be planned, not improvised NFL Football Operations describes a standard-elevation process through which one or two practice-squad players can join the active/inactive list for a game and revert afterward. It also says a player can receive up to three regular-season elevations before a further use requires a promotion and corresponding roster transaction. That mechanism makes the squad a weekly resource, but repeated elevations can expose a structural weakness. Indianapolis should maintain a readiness board by function. The board might identify the first emergency tackle, interior lineman, coverage linebacker, outside corner, returner, blocking tight end, or quarterback. Every entry should record actual practice position, assignment grade, special-teams units, health status, and elevation count. A player should not be called “next up” because he shares a roster-page position with an injured Colt. Elevations also need a time horizon. Using the same player three times can sensibly bridge a short injury. If the need persists, the club must decide whether to create a 53-player place, use a different eligible player, or accept that its original roster allocation was too thin. Rotating elevations simply to avoid a permanent decision can weaken continuity and does not make the underlying need disappear. Evidence gates for the final squad Before assigning a player to the projected practice squad, require evidence in this order: Official current membership and status. Reconcile the Colts roster and transaction ledger; do not rely on an old signing announcement. Demonstrated role. Identify the positions, packages, and special-teams units the player actually performs. Mechanism-level execution. Grade assignment accuracy, communication, technique, ball security, penalties, and repeatability. Preseason translation. Check whether those functions survive live pace and representative competition. Final transaction and waiver result. A release does not equal a return, and a preferred player may be claimed or choose another club. Official practice-squad signing. Only the transaction establishes membership; eligibility should not be inferred from age or experience shorthand. This ladder prevents three common errors. It avoids treating every undrafted rookie as a practice-squad lock, every veteran cut as ineligible, and every final-53 omission as organizational rejection. It also keeps practice-squad analysis distinct from [[Indianapolis Colts 2026 roster cut mechanics]]: the mechanics describe how players move; this portfolio explains what Indianapolis should try to retain and why. Why it matters The practice squad is where roster construction acquires time. The 53 must solve Week 1; the developmental group can preserve Week 6 insurance and 2027 possibilities. For Indianapolis, that matters most at offensive line, in a defense with turnover at linebacker and safety, and among young front-seven players whose traits require technical refinement. A strong squad does not guarantee successful replacements. It improves the quality of the available options. Players already know the terminology, practice against the Colts' starters, receive position-specific coaching, and can be evaluated over months rather than one preseason. That continuity can make a short-notice elevation more functional and can reveal which long-range bets deserve future contracts. The durable standard is portfolio value. The Colts should emerge from August with more than recognizable leftover names: they should have emergency answers, special-teams call-ups, scarce-position development, and several asymmetric upside bets without concentrating every place in one room. The final list will be evidence of those choices only after waivers and official signings are complete. Sources NFL Football Operations, Contract language and roster sizes — official 2026 practice-squad size and eligibility categories, 53- and 47/48-player roster structure, and standard-elevation rules; accessed July 10, 2026. NFL Football Operations, NFL Important Dates — official 2026 final-reduction deadline, waiver window, and practice-squad establishment sequence; accessed July 10, 2026. Indianapolis Colts, Official roster — current membership, listed positions, experience, and reserve display; accessed July 10, 2026. Indianapolis Colts, 2026 transactions — official dated signings, releases, waivers, reserve/future actions, elevations and reversions, and Bayron Matos's international designation; accessed July 10, 2026. Indianapolis Colts, Colts sign six draft picks, 12 undrafted free agents — official 2026 rookie intake and biographical information; accessed July 10, 2026. Open questions Which Colts fall into each 2026 practice-squad eligibility category after accrued-season and game-count rules are applied exactly? Will Bayron Matos qualify for and occupy an additional International Player Pathway practice-squad place, and what restrictions will accompany it? Which offensive linemen demonstrate real multi-position readiness rather than roster-page versatility? Which reserve linebackers, defensive backs, receivers, backs, and tight ends win multi-phase special-teams assignments? Does Indianapolis keep two or three quarterbacks on the 53, and what kind of quarterback value remains for the practice squad? Which preferred cuts clear waivers and choose to return, and which outside releases improve the portfolio? After three or four regular-season weeks, which repeated elevation need reveals a weakness in the original 53-player allocation?

title: Indianapolis Colts preseason evaluation framework 2026
deck: The Colts' three 2026 preseason games should be read as controlled but imperfect tests of assignments, combinations, and roster utility—not as miniature regular-season forecasts or a scoreboard referendum.
headings: Defense: grade the chain, not only the finish
Special teams: roster evidence in four phases
What preseason can and cannot establish
text: The Colts' three 2026 preseason games should be read as controlled but imperfect tests of assignments, combinations, and roster utility—not as miniature regular-season forecasts or a scoreboard referendum. Up: [[Indianapolis Colts 2026]] The evaluation problem Indianapolis has three preseason games before the roster reduction: at New England on Thursday, August 13; home against Atlanta on Saturday, August 22; and home against Detroit on Saturday, August 29. The NFL's calendar requires clubs to reduce to a maximum of 53 players on the Active/Inactive List by 6 p.m. New York time on August 30. The last game therefore ends only about 29 hours before the transaction deadline, making the series both an evaluation window and a compressed decision process. The scoreboard is real, but it is a poor organizing variable for this work. Coaches can restrict a scheme, protect established starters, rotate combinations, emphasize a particular installation, or leave a player in the game because they need more evidence. An opponent can make the opposite choices. A backup quarterback succeeding against a defense made largely of developmental players is not automatically ready for regular-season first-team work; a reserve tackle losing one rep to an established rusher is not automatically out of the competition. The useful unit of evidence is the assignment in context . This framework connects preseason observations to the unresolved questions in the [[Indianapolis Colts 2026 roster map]], [[Indianapolis Colts quarterback structure 2026]], and [[Indianapolis Colts 2026 roster cut mechanics]]. It does not project the final 53 or prescribe how many snaps a medically managed player should receive. Those are club decisions informed by private medical, practice, and meeting-room evidence that an outside observer does not possess. The known calendar Checkpoint Date Evidence it can add Important limit Camp opens to public practice July 29 Participation, combinations, installation, and repeated opportunity A public practice is not a live game and may omit situational work Preseason Week 1 at New England August 13, 7:30 p.m. ET First live operation against an unfamiliar opponent Early personnel plans and scheme menus may be intentionally narrow Joint practices with Atlanta August 19–20 Repeated matchup work, situational periods, and responses between reps Reports may lack full assignment and play-call context Preseason Week 2 vs. Atlanta August 22, 1 p.m. ET Whether joint-practice corrections transfer into a game Familiarity from two joint sessions changes the matchup context Preseason Week 3 vs. Detroit August 29, 1 p.m. ET Final live roster-edge and contingency evidence One late performance cannot erase the larger body of work Roster reduction August 30, before 6 p.m. ET Official initial 53-player decisions The initial 53 is not the permanent Week 1 roster The two Atlanta practices distinguish the middle week. Repetition against the same opponent can create an unusually useful correction loop: identify a protection, leverage, release, or communication failure; adjust it; then see whether the correction survives another practice and the game. That is stronger process evidence than one highlight. It still does not make Atlanta a regular-season simulation. Teams control access, tempo, contact, personnel, and the portion of the playbook exposed. The Detroit game presents the opposite problem. Its proximity to the deadline raises the salience of every snap but does not necessarily raise its informational quality. Decision-makers will already possess weeks of practice film, meeting performance, medical information, and two earlier games. A late explosive play can be relevant without becoming dispositive. An analyst should ask what the rep adds to the accumulated file, not whether it supplies a dramatic final verdict. A claim ladder Every observation should be labeled at the strongest level the evidence permits: Event: what visibly happened. A player aligned at right tackle, handled the first punt return, communicated a protection change, missed a tackle, or played on two coverage units. Assignment reading: the most defensible account of the player's apparent responsibility, with uncertainty when the call is unavailable. Repeated tendency: the same role or execution quality appearing across multiple snaps, periods, or games. Roster inference: what the repeated tendency may mean for functional value, stated as an inference rather than club fact. Official outcome: a transaction, designation, published roster, or actual regular-season assignment. This ladder prevents common overclaims. “Anthony Gould took the first punt return” is an event. “Gould is the primary punt returner” requires repeated ordering and relevant availability context. “Gould won the job” requires an official or operational outcome. Likewise, a quarterback entering second does not alone identify the regular-season backup: the order may reflect a planned snap distribution, different protection groups, or the need to evaluate another quarterback later in the game. Negative claims require special restraint. Television does not always show the secondary, line calls, route conversions, or the point where responsibility passed between defenders. When the assignment is unknowable, chart the outcome and the uncertainty. Do not assign blame to the nearest player merely because he appears on screen. Quarterbacks: evaluate decisions before totals The quarterback questions are structurally different. Daniel Jones is the intended starter while returning from a torn Achilles; Anthony Richardson Sr. and Riley Leonard enter the club's stated backup competition; Easton Stick supplies a fourth rostered quarterback. Preseason playing time should therefore be interpreted through health, role, and supporting personnel rather than combined into one passer-rating leaderboard. For Jones, the first question is participation. If he plays, chart whether Indianapolis uses normal dropback, movement, and under-center actions or a constrained menu. Then chart operational details: getting the offense aligned, cadence, protection identification, time from snap to decision, pocket response, and willingness to finish throws when space compresses. A clean statistical line on screens and quick throws would not establish that every movement or downfield function has returned. Conversely, one pressured incompletion would not establish a rehabilitation failure. For Richardson and Leonard, chart equivalent situations where possible. Separate first-read throws from full-field progression work; designed runs from scrambles; accurate decisions from fortunate outcomes; and pressure created by the quarterback from pressure allowed immediately by protection. A completion can still be a poor process if the throw is late and exposes a receiver. An incompletion can be good process if the quarterback recognizes a covered concept and safely discards the ball. Stick's presence matters because four quarterbacks create allocation constraints. A low snap count may reflect limited possessions rather than an evaluation conclusion. Report who played with which line, receivers, backs, and opponent personnel. The most useful comparison is not raw yards but repeated execution of the same functional tasks: third down, backed-up offense, red zone, two-minute work, pressure answers, and ball security. Useful quarterback fields include drop type, personnel grouping, pressure state, first-open-window decision, throw location, turnover-worthy action, scramble trigger, and down-and-distance result. Avoid pretending that a public chart can reproduce the coaches' grade; its purpose is consistency, not omniscience. Offensive line: combinations and communication The open right-tackle problem makes line evaluation central, but “no sacks allowed” is insufficient. Sacks depend on quarterback timing, coverage, game situation, and whether pressure arrives from another player's assignment. A tackle can lose quickly on a completion; a quarterback can create a sack after sound initial protection. Track five-man combinations and the quarterback behind them. For each pass rep, identify the protection only when evidence supports it, then record initial set, width and depth, first meaningful contact, whether the blocker preserves the pocket's shape, and whether help was built into the call. For runs, record alignment, first-step relationship, displacement or sealing, second-level timing, and whether penetration changes the back's track. Communication failures deserve their own category. An untouched rusher may reflect a physical loss, a protection identification error, a late adjustment, or a deliberate unblocked defender in a read concept. The broadcast rarely resolves all four possibilities. Mark it “unresolved assignment” until end-zone film, replay, or credible explanation supports more. Cross-training is roster evidence. A reserve taking snaps at guard and tackle, or center and guard, may be demonstrating contingency value even if he is not the best player at either single spot. The final comparison should combine execution quality with position coverage, because the game-day roster cannot dress a separate replacement for every offensive-line position. Skill positions: function over touches Touches are opportunity, not a complete grade. The receiver and tight-end rooms must redistribute functions after Michael Pittman Jr.'s departure, while the running-back group needs complementary offensive and special-teams value behind Jonathan Taylor. Preseason can show which functions coaches are testing. For receivers, chart alignment, release, route depth, separation at the decision point, contested-catch necessity, blocking assignment, motion, and special-teams use. A player with one catch may repeatedly clear space for another route or execute difficult run-blocking assignments. A player with six catches may have been targeted on low-difficulty concepts without demonstrating an outside or vertical role. Drops matter, but so do target quality and whether the receiver reached the expected landmark on time. For tight ends, “starter” language is especially unhelpful because Tyler Warren, Mo Alie-Cox, Drew Ogletree, Will Mallory, Sean McKeon, and Carson Towt can be tested across attached, slot, backfield, motion, protection, and kicking-game jobs. Record personnel grouping and alignment before judging a depth order. A tight end who can survive several functions can change both the play menu and the number of specialists the offense must carry. For backs, separate rushing output from the work that creates game-day trust: pass-protection identification, pickup technique, route timing, ball security, kickoff return, coverage, and the ability to execute from more than one backfield alignment. A 25-yard run through a clean lane is useful evidence of burst; it says little about blitz pickup. A reserve back's path to the roster may depend more on avoiding a free rusher and covering a kick than on leading the team in preseason carries. Defense: grade the chain, not only the finish Lou Anarumo's defense and the turnover described in [[Indianapolis Colts defensive identity 2026]] make communication a preseason priority. The visible result often occurs at the end of a chain that begins with the front, travels through linebackers and safeties, and changes with motion or formation. The evaluation must preserve that chain. For the defensive front, chart alignment, get-off, gap control, edge integrity, rush lane, counter use, and whether pressure is produced individually or by a stunt or simulated pressure. A defender can execute a successful rush by forcing the quarterback toward a teammate without receiving a sack. Against the run, a player can occupy a double-team and preserve a linebacker's path without making the tackle. Production totals should follow mechanism notes, not replace them. At linebacker, record pre-snap communication when visible, run-fit entry, block response, coverage responsibility, pursuit angle, tackling finish, and special-teams phase. The post-Zaire Franklin room is not only choosing snap-takers; it is distributing calls and checks. A correct fit that spills the ball to help can be successful even when another defender makes the tackle. A tackle five yards downfield can conceal a late read. In the defensive backfield, avoid cornerback box-score grading. Targets and completions must be paired with leverage, route, coverage family when reasonably identifiable, safety help, communication, and catch-point result. One-on-one losses are informative, but preseason also needs to reveal whether the secondary passes routes, handles bunches and motion, disguises without busting, and tackles in space. Slot, outside, safety, dime, and special-teams work are separate pieces of roster value. Explosive plays require full-chain review. Ask whether the problem began with pressure containment, a fit, a coverage handoff, leverage, a missed tackle, or several failures. If the answer is unavailable, record the explosive and withhold the diagnosis. Special teams: roster evidence in four phases The [[Indianapolis Colts special teams 2026]] evaluation should connect the Blake Grupe–Spencer Shrader kicking competition, the established Luke Rhodes–Rigoberto Sanchez snap-and-hold operation, return decisions, and the reserve-player contests that fill coverage units. For placekicks, log distance, hash, environment, snap location, hold, operation quality, trajectory, and result. A make does not prove a clean operation; a miss does not always isolate the kicker. For punts, record field position, gross and net distance, hang and direction when available, return opportunity, coverage arrival, touchback, and pressure. For kick returns under the permanent dynamic-kickoff structure, compare the return with the rules-based alternative field position rather than celebrating raw return yards alone. The bottom of the roster is shaped by four-phase work: kickoff, kickoff return, punt, and punt return. Chart who appears, in what role, and whether the player repeats sound alignment, release, block fit, lane discipline, ball security, and tackling. One splash tackle is weaker evidence than correct work across several phases. A receiver or defensive back who supplies a safe second punt catcher or a linebacker who covers multiple units may have functional value invisible in offensive or defensive totals. Penalties belong to the responsible phase and mechanism. “Special-teams penalty” is too coarse. Identify whether the failure was alignment, an illegal block, holding, interference with the catch opportunity, or a late action, while acknowledging when the responsible assignment is unclear. A game-by-game workflow Before each game, freeze the official roster and availability baseline. List the questions being tested without predicting answers: quarterback participation and order; offensive-line combinations; first-unit returners; defensive communication; and multi-phase reserve use. This avoids rewriting the purpose of the evaluation around whatever becomes dramatic on television. During the game, log possessions and units rather than highlights. Note personnel, opponent level where identifiable, field situation, and the relevant mechanism. Preserve an “unknown” category. A chart that admits missing information is more reliable than a complete chart filled with guessed assignments. Within 24 hours, separate three outputs: Verified events: snap counts, alignments, results, penalties, transactions, and explicit club statements. Supported inferences: repeated role allocation or execution patterns, with the evidence named. Unresolved questions: plays without sufficient assignment context, medical questions, and roster consequences not yet made official. After the Atlanta joint-practice sequence, specifically test correction. Which problems repeated? Which appeared to change after coaching? Did a player execute the same responsibility in practice reports and the game? After Detroit, compare the final evidence with the whole month rather than allowing recency to dominate. What preseason can and cannot establish Preseason can establish official participation, observable assignments, combinations, live execution, corrections, versatility, and repeated tendencies. It can strengthen an inference that a player is being prepared for a particular job. It can expose a mechanism that deserves more testing. It cannot fully establish regular-season health, durability, opponent-adjusted quality, a complete scheme, or a permanent depth order. It cannot reveal every coach's assignment or private grade. It cannot make a small sample large by calling it “game action.” It cannot turn the initial 53 into a permanent roster, because waivers, claims, reserve designations, and practice-squad construction continue after the deadline. The strongest possible preseason conclusion is therefore usually conditional: a player repeatedly executed a named job against a described level of competition and added a particular kind of roster utility. That claim is narrower than “he won camp,” but it is also more durable. Once Indianapolis makes official moves, the framework should record the outcome without retroactively treating every earlier rep as obvious evidence of it. NFL Football Operations — 2026–27 important dates — official August 30 roster-reduction deadline. Open questions Which quarterbacks are medically and operationally cleared for each game, and how will Indianapolis divide representative situations rather than only total snaps? Which offensive-line combinations persist across practices, games, and different quarterbacks? What assignments will the Colts expose publicly in the Atlanta joint practices, and which corrections will transfer to the game? Who handles first and contingency returns, and which roster-edge players demonstrate genuine four-phase special-teams value? How will defensive communication move across linebackers and safeties when personnel changes within a series? Which observations can be independently checked with end-zone film or official snap data after each game? Will the NFL publish a 2026 rulebook change that materially alters any kickoff or roster-evaluation assumption used here?

title: Indianapolis Colts quarterback structure 2026
deck: Indianapolis enters 2026 with Daniel Jones established as its intended starter but recovering from a torn Achilles, Anthony Richardson Sr. and Riley Leonard in a declared competition for the backup job, and Easton Stick as a fourth camp quarterback; that structure is official, while the readiness, ordering, and long-term meaning are not.
headings: The official state is clearer than the available lineup
Daniel Jones: the incumbent, with recovery as the gating variable
Anthony Richardson Sr.: enormous tools, unresolved availability and operation
Riley Leonard: a real second-year challenger, not a solved projection
Easton Stick: veteran insurance and a different kind of evaluation
Scheme fit is a spectrum, not four separate playbooks
What July and August evidence can actually establish
text: Indianapolis enters 2026 with Daniel Jones established as its intended starter but recovering from a torn Achilles, Anthony Richardson Sr. and Riley Leonard in a declared competition for the backup job, and Easton Stick as a fourth camp quarterback; that structure is official, while the readiness, ordering, and long-term meaning are not. Up: [[Indianapolis Colts 2026]] Related: [[Indianapolis Colts 2026 roster map]], [[Quarterback evaluation]], [[Shane Steichen offense]] The official state is clearer than the available lineup The cleanest way to understand the Colts' quarterback room on July 9 is to separate four different questions that are often collapsed into one. Roster membership is one question. The intended Week 1 starter is another. Physical readiness for Week 1 is a third. The order behind the starter is a fourth. Indianapolis has supplied a reasonably firm answer to the first two and only partial answers to the last two. The club's roster lists four quarterbacks: Daniel Jones, Anthony Richardson Sr., Riley Leonard, and Easton Stick. A roster page is not a depth chart, but Indianapolis has also described Jones as the returning starter. Offensive coordinator Jim Bob Cooter said in May that Richardson and Leonard would compete to be the backup, and head coach Shane Steichen called that contest “50/50” during organized team activities. Stick joined the club on June 1 after Seth Henigan was waived. These transactions make Stick a participant in the room, not an announced co-favorite for QB2. Jones's recovery prevents the official hierarchy from being the same thing as an available-game hierarchy. He tore his right Achilles in December 2025. At the Colts' May 27 OTA practice, Jones performed individual work but did not participate in team periods. Jones said he expected to be ready for the regular-season opener, while Steichen emphasized the rehabilitation work rather than certifying a return date. The responsible description is therefore “intended starter in rehabilitation,” not “healthy Week 1 starter.” A July depth projection that silently converts optimism into medical certainty would outrun the evidence. The club has nevertheless made a meaningful commitment. Jones re-signed on a two-year contract after a productive 2025 season. Exact contract accounting should live in a contract ledger rather than this football note, but the term and the club's public description matter to quarterback structure: Indianapolis did not bring Jones back as a temporary camp challenger. The team has organized the room around his return. That still leaves two competitions. Richardson and Leonard are competing for the formal backup role. All three alternatives are competing, in a broader sense, to demonstrate that Indianapolis can survive a delayed Jones return or an in-season absence. Stick's path is different because the club has not publicly placed him in the 50/50 contest, but a veteran fourth quarterback can earn value through command, preseason function, and emergency reliability. The roster must also contract before the season, so four names in July need not imply four quarterbacks on the initial 53-player roster. Daniel Jones: the incumbent, with recovery as the gating variable Jones gave Indianapolis an efficient 2025 passing baseline over his 13 starts. The club's official statistics credit him with 261 completions on 384 attempts (68.0 percent), 3,101 yards, 19 touchdowns, eight interceptions, 8.1 yards per attempt, and a 100.2 passer rating. He also took 22 sacks. Those are descriptive conventional statistics rather than a complete measure of quarterback value, but they help explain why the Colts chose continuity. Ballard highlighted that Jones finished among the league's top six in completion percentage, yards per attempt, and passer rating. The context is essential. Jones started 13 games, not a complete season, and the offense's fast start did not survive intact through the year. The AP reported that he played through a hairline fracture in his left leg after the bye before the right-Achilles rupture ended his season. Thus the 2025 record supports a narrower proposition than “Jones solved quarterback”: he operated Steichen's offense efficiently over a substantial sample before injuries broke the continuity. Whether that performance is repeatable after rehabilitation is the central 2026 question. Jones's fit with Steichen is easiest to describe through operating requirements rather than a rigid scheme label. During the 2025 competition, Steichen repeatedly identified consistency, ball security, decisions, line-of-scrimmage operation, protection checks, ball placement, and moving the offense as his criteria. When he named Jones the starter, he cited those same dimensions. That tells us what the staff values even if the weekly call sheet changes by opponent. The 2025 results suggest Jones could deliver that version of quarterbacking. His 68 percent completion rate and eight interceptions over 384 attempts are compatible with the accuracy and ball-security criteria Steichen named. Yards per attempt records the outcome of passes, not their air depth or the quarterback's intended distribution, so it cannot by itself establish whether the offense was aggressive or conservative. Personnel nevertheless gave Indianapolis multiple possible answers: Alec Pierce supplied verified vertical production, Tyler Warren could align in several locations, and Jonathan Taylor anchored the run game. How Steichen combines those pieces in 2026 remains a projection until camp and game evidence reveal the actual call distribution. Jones is also mobile enough that defenses cannot treat every keeper or scramble as a non-event, but his 2026 rushing use should not be inferred from pre-injury tape alone. An Achilles rehabilitation changes the relevant question from “has he run before?” to “what movement can he execute repeatedly and safely now?” Camp may show whether the offense retains designed movement, boot action, and quarterback-run complements. It cannot prove that a reconstructed Achilles will tolerate a full regular season. The risk profile is therefore concentrated rather than mysterious. Jones must regain the lower-body function required for drops, resets, pocket escape, and throwing from imperfect platforms. He must also show that the 2025 accuracy and decision baseline survives the injury and the league's counter-adjustments. A handful of clean practice completions could confirm participation and timing progress; they could not establish durability or reproduce regular-season pressure. Anthony Richardson Sr.: enormous tools, unresolved availability and operation Richardson remains the room's highest-variance player. Indianapolis selected him fourth overall in 2023 because rare size, arm strength, and rushing ability created a path to an offense that stresses every level of a defense. Those traits have not vanished. Neither have the reasons he lost the 2025 competition. The club framed consistency and availability as the central development requirements entering that competition. In its April 2025 account of the competition, the Colts reported that Richardson had completed 47.7 percent of his passes in 2024, missed four games because of injury, and was held out of two additional starts after being benched. Jones then won the job because Steichen judged his daily operation, checks, protections, placement, and completion consistency superior. That decision is historical evidence about what Richardson had not yet demonstrated; it is not proof that improvement is impossible. His 2025 season supplied almost no new passing sample. The official team statistics list two attempts, one completion, and nine passing yards. A freak pregame eye injury eventually sent him to injured reserve, and Indianapolis did not activate him for Week 18. Richardson and his agent later requested permission to seek a trade, according to both the club and independent reporting, but no trade occurred. In May he publicly acknowledged his contractual obligation and participated in the backup competition. Richardson's best schematic argument begins with conflict creation. A defense accounting for Jonathan Taylor already has difficult run-fit choices. Add a quarterback who can keep the ball, threaten the edge, and throw vertically, and an unblocked defender can be made wrong by design. Run-pass options, zone-read elements, movement passes, and designed quarterback runs can turn Richardson's athleticism into structure rather than asking him to win only as a conventional dropback passer. His arm can also attack space behind safeties who step toward the run. But “build around the athlete” is not a sufficient NFL offense. The same play can require a correct box count, protection answer, post-snap read, throw location, and self-protection decision. Explosive traits amplify good decisions; they do not replace them. The Colts' own criteria show that Richardson's path to QB2 runs through repeatable operation: getting the offense aligned, identifying pressure, delivering catchable balls on schedule, protecting possession, and finishing practices available for the next one. Training camp can provide more evidence here than it can for a veteran with a secure role because Richardson's recent competitive sample is so thin. Repeated team periods can show whether his footwork and timing are stable across concept families, whether his short and intermediate placement lets receivers continue after the catch, and whether he handles pressure looks without turning every rep into improvisation. Preseason games can add live pass rush, contact avoidance, and drive-level operation. Even then, caution is necessary. Practice completion percentages are shaped by personnel, scripted situations, defensive installation, protection rules, and whether quarterbacks are live to contact. A spectacular deep throw does not answer the routine-down question. One interception may be a terrible read, a receiver error, an experiment encouraged by coaches, or a pressure artifact. The useful unit is a repeated pattern with context, not the day's winner declared from a reporter's tally. Riley Leonard: a real second-year challenger, not a solved projection Leonard enters his second season with a small but nonzero NFL sample. The Colts drafted him in 2025, initially placed him third behind Jones and Richardson, and eventually needed him because the room suffered a cascade of injuries. He appeared in five games and started the finale against Houston. Official club statistics credit him with 39 completions on 67 attempts (58.2 percent), 415 yards, two touchdowns, three interceptions, and a 67.7 passer rating. He added six carries for 27 yards and two rushing touchdowns. Sixty-seven attempts are enough to identify questions for camp, not enough to establish a stable professional level. His Week 18 start was encouraging in specific ways. The club reported 270 passing yards and two touchdowns, and Steichen later praised his huddle command, growing understanding of the offense, and progress through reads. Yet the full season line, including three interceptions on 67 attempts, prevents one finale from being treated as a conclusive arrival. A single start can reveal that a player is capable of executing a plan; it cannot estimate his stable level against varied opponents. Leonard's college and early professional profile makes the backup competition conceptually interesting. Like Richardson and Jones, he offers functional mobility rather than forcing the offense to abandon every quarterback-run or movement component. He is large enough to be used in short-yardage packages and showed rushing scoring value as a rookie. The fit question, however, is less about whether he can move and more about whether his processing and accuracy advance quickly enough to support the whole call sheet. A backup who enters for Jones must preserve the offense's connective tissue. He needs to communicate formations and motions, set protections, keep Taylor's run game out of bad looks, distribute to Warren and the receivers on time, and avoid giving away possessions. Leonard's command praise matters because it touches that job description. His 58.2 percent completion rate and small sample remind us that command must become consistent execution. Camp can establish whether Leonard has made a meaningful second-year leap. Watch the distribution of first- and second-team snaps, performance in third-down and red-zone periods, answers against pressure, and whether coaches trust him with adjustments rather than only simplified calls. Also watch who receives the first relief work in preseason games. Those choices are stronger evidence of organizational trust than an isolated highlight. Camp cannot fully establish how Leonard responds after opponents build a game plan around his tendencies. Nor can it tell us whether his best 2025 game is the start of a trend or the high end of a wide range. If he wins QB2, the proper conclusion will be that he outperformed Richardson under the club's summer criteria—not that his long-term starting ceiling has been proven. Easton Stick: veteran insurance and a different kind of evaluation Stick joined Indianapolis on June 1 after spending 2025 with Atlanta, primarily on its practice squad. He has seven credited NFL seasons, but his meaningful regular-season passing work is concentrated in 2023 with the Chargers. The Colts' biography lists five appearances, four starts, 111 completions on 174 attempts, 1,129 yards, three touchdowns, one interception, and an 85.6 rating that year. It also records 144 rushing yards and a touchdown on 27 carries. That history gives Stick more live NFL starting experience than his “fourth quarterback” shorthand might suggest, but it does not put him inside the declared Richardson-Leonard competition. His immediate value is practical: Jones's rehabilitation limits certainty, Richardson and Leonard are competing, and a four-quarterback camp needs enough arms to distribute repetitions. Stick can provide veteran operation in practice and preseason while giving the club another emergency option. His evaluation should therefore use a realistic standard. Does he learn the terminology quickly? Can he keep reserve-unit practices functional amid line and receiver rotation? Does he protect the ball and handle pressure? Can his mobility preserve some of the offense's movement menu? If he performs well, the club may face a roster decision. But absent an explicit change from Steichen, observers should not manufacture a four-way contest from a four-player room. Scheme fit is a spectrum, not four separate playbooks Steichen has coached offenses around quarterbacks with different strengths, but that history does not prove a fixed 2026 design. A reasonable pre-camp hypothesis is that Indianapolis will begin with Taylor's run game and seek complementary passes to Pierce, Warren, Downs, and the rest of the receiving corps. Shotgun work, play action, run-pass conflicts, and quarterback movement are possibilities supported by Steichen's prior offenses and the quarterbacks' traits, not an announced 2026 scheme spine. Camp and regular-season call distribution must test the hypothesis. Jones offers the best recent evidence of full-field, down-to-down operation in this system. Richardson offers the largest designed-run and explosive-creation ceiling but must prove routine accuracy, decision-making, and availability. Leonard offers mobility and growing command with a still-small professional passing sample. Stick offers veteran competence and emergency flexibility without an announced claim to the top two roles. This hypothesis avoids two common errors. The first is assuming the Colts must choose categorically between quarterback movement and passing. Each quarterback has recorded some rushing production, but that does not tell us how often Steichen will call designed runs or movement passes in 2026. The second is treating scheme fit as a trait checklist detached from execution. A quarterback fits only if he can perform the offense's decisions at NFL speed. Arm strength can open a concept; placement and timing complete it. The supporting cast also changes what should be demanded. Taylor can force safety involvement and create play-action opportunities. Pierce's vertical speed punishes defenses that compress. Warren can give the quarterback a large target and formation flexibility. Josh Downs can win in shorter areas. Those assets create answers, but the quarterback still must diagnose where the defense has conceded space. Camp reports should therefore track decision quality and timing, not merely the number of throws to a favored receiver. What July and August evidence can actually establish The first camp checkpoint is participation. Does Jones progress from individual work into team periods, and at what workload? Does he move without visible protection from the practice design? Participation is meaningful, but a return-to-practice designation is not equivalent to game clearance or full-season durability. The second checkpoint is role allocation. Richardson and Leonard were split evenly in OTA team work. If that remains even, the competition is still open. If one player receives sustained first relief work, two-minute periods, and the more demanding situational menu, the balance may be shifting. Repetition quality matters alongside count: ten scripted handoffs are not equivalent to ten third-down passing reps. The third is operational consistency. Track false starts or alignment corrections attributable to the quarterback, protection communication, time to initiate the play, turnover-worthy decisions that can be established from credible observation, and whether completions arrive in rhythm. Public observers rarely have the call, so humility is required when assigning blame. Coaches' explanations and multiple independent reports are stronger than a single sideline angle. The fourth is translation under contact. Preseason football gives a more realistic pocket and tackling environment than non-live practice, but vanilla defenses, rotating personnel, and small samples limit inference. A backup can strengthen his case by sustaining drives and avoiding negative plays; he cannot prove regular-season quality in two quarters against reserves. Finally, camp cannot resolve the franchise's long-term quarterback future. Jones is under contract beyond 2026, but recovery and performance will determine the value of that commitment. Richardson's future is clouded by the unsuccessful trade exploration and his development path. Leonard is only entering Year 2. The correct summer conclusion may be as modest as “the Colts have identified their safest available order.” That would still be important. It would not be the same as finding a decade-long answer.
