How can studies report numerical mixing in a metric that is comparable across spectral, finite-volume, finite-difference, and finite-element cores? When does a tracer-specific effective K_{zz} remain useful for retrievals despite demonstrably non-diffusive global transport? Which combinations of passive lifetime sweeps and reactive networks best separate circulation uncertainty from kinetic uncertainty? How long must deep and long-lived tracers be integrated before hot-Jupiter and sub-Neptune transport statistics lose initialization memory? Can future phase-resolved spectra constrain a transit-time distribution rather than only one retrieved abundance or mixing coefficient?

title: Transmission spectroscopy
deck: Transmission spectroscopy measures the wavelength-dependent fraction of starlight blocked during transit; atmospheric composition is a model-dependent inference from the effective occulting area of the planet’s limb.
headings: Why the slant path is powerful
The star is part of the spectrum
Where measurement ends and retrieval begins
text: Transmission spectroscopy measures the wavelength-dependent fraction of starlight blocked during transit; atmospheric composition is a model-dependent inference from the effective occulting area of the planet’s limb. Up: [[Exometeorology research frontier 2026]] Why this method matters When a planet transits, its opaque body blocks part of the stellar disk while a thin annulus of atmosphere filters starlight along long, grazing paths. At wavelengths where gases, aerosols, or atoms are more opaque, the atmosphere becomes opaque at a higher altitude and the apparent planet is slightly larger. Repeating a transit measurement across wavelength produces a transmission spectrum . The technique has exceptional leverage because the slant path through the limb is much longer than a vertical path. It can reveal spectral modulation from trace absorbers even when the atmosphere contributes essentially none of the system’s total luminosity. But the detector does not observe a molecule, pressure, temperature, cloud, or wind directly. It observes time- and wavelength-dependent counts. Calibration and light-curve fitting yield transit depths. A forward model then connects those depths to an effective radius, and a retrieval estimates which combinations of atmospheric, stellar, orbital, and instrumental parameters are compatible with the data. That evidence ladder is essential: Measured: calibrated relative fluxes and fitted wavelength-dependent transit depths, with uncertainties and covariance. Retrieved: abundances, temperature, cloud properties, or reference radius inferred under a stated forward model and priors. Simulated: limb structure, circulation, chemistry, or clouds generated by a physical model. Interpreted: a proposed atmospheric story connecting measurements, retrievals, and simulations. Forecast: an unmeasured prediction for another wavelength, epoch, or instrument. “Water detected” is shorthand for evidence favoring opacity shaped like water within a model comparison. It should not erase this chain. Transit-depth geometry For a uniformly bright star and an opaque circular planet, the transit depth is approximately D(\lambda)\simeq \left[\frac{R_{\rm eff}(\lambda)}{R_*}\right]^2, where R_* is stellar radius and R_{\rm eff}(\lambda) is the planet’s wavelength-dependent effective occulting radius. Real transit fitting includes orbital geometry and stellar limb darkening: the planet blocks different surface brightnesses as it crosses the disk. The measured spectrum is often a vector of radius ratios or transit depths after jointly or sequentially fitting a transit model and an instrument/systematics model. If atmospheric opacity shifts the effective altitude by \Delta z\ll R_p , the spectral modulation is \Delta D\simeq \frac{2R_p\Delta z}{R_*^2}. The geometry explains target selection. A large planet around a small star gives a larger signal. A low-gravity, hot, hydrogen-rich atmosphere has a large pressure scale height, H=\frac{k_B T}{\mu m_H g}, where T is temperature, \mu is mean molecular weight in hydrogen masses, and g is gravity. Strong molecular bands can span several scale heights in an ideal clear atmosphere, giving a rough feature amplitude of 2R_p N H/R_*^2 for N effective scale heights. This is an observing heuristic, not an abundance measurement: N depends logarithmically on opacity and is changed by clouds, refraction, composition gradients, and limb structure. Why the slant path is powerful Consider a ray with impact parameter b passing through a spherical atmosphere. Its optical depth is \tau_\lambda(b)=\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty}\sum_i n_i(s)\,\sigma_{i,\lambda}[T(s),p(s)]\,ds, with number density n_i , cross section \sigma_{i,\lambda} , and distance s along the ray. The occulted area is not simply the disk below the altitude where \tau=1 . Rays are partially attenuated, so the effective area is an integral over impact parameter, \pi R_{\rm eff}^2(\lambda)=\pi R_0^2+2\pi\int_{R_0}^{\infty}\left[1-e^{-\tau_\lambda(b)}\right]b\,db. This expression assumes the disk below R_0 is fully opaque; R_0 must therefore be chosen deep enough to serve as the lower boundary of the calculation. In an isothermal, hydrostatic atmosphere with an exponential density profile, a grazing ray near altitude z samples a slant column enhanced over the vertical column by roughly \sqrt{2\pi R_p/H} . For a hot Jupiter this factor can be tens. Effective transit altitude therefore occurs where the slant optical depth is of order unity, often at much lower pressure than a vertical optical-depth estimate suggests. Analytic treatments show that effective altitude varies approximately as the logarithm of opacity. For opacity \sigma(\lambda) and otherwise fixed conditions, z(\lambda)\sim H\left[C+\ln\frac{\sigma(\lambda)}{\sigma_{\rm ref}}+\ln\frac{X}{X_{\rm ref}}+\ln\frac{P_0}{P_{\rm ref}}+\ldots\right], where X is mixing ratio, P_0 is the pressure assigned to the reference radius, the reference quantities make the logarithms dimensionless, and C groups those reference choices with geometry and thermodynamic factors. Only changes and parameter combinations have physical meaning; taking a logarithm of a dimensional cross section or pressure by itself would not. A power-law scattering cross section \sigma\propto\lambda^\alpha then gives the idealized slope \frac{dz}{d\ln\lambda}=\alpha H. The relation explains why a resolved Rayleigh-like slope can constrain the product of temperature and inverse mean molecular weight if gravity and the opacity law are known. In practice, stellar heterogeneity, aerosols, non-isothermal structure, unknown particle physics, and calibration offsets can generate or alter slopes. The reference-radius problem A broadband transit light curve measures an apparent radius, but it does not label the pressure at that radius. Forward models therefore specify a pair (R_0,P_0) . Hydrostatic integration maps altitude to pressure above that boundary. Changing R_0 and P_0 shifts the atmospheric column encountered by grazing rays, and abundance changes opacity through the absorber number density. In restricted wavelength coverage these effects can compensate one another. This produces a reference-radius–reference-pressure–abundance degeneracy. In the simplest isothermal expression, the spectrum depends partly on products such as X P_0 , so the absolute mixing ratio cannot be separated from the boundary pressure without additional information. Clouds add another boundary: an optically thick cloud deck truncates the chord column below its top and can mute all bands. High-altitude haze adds a wavelength-dependent continuum. Increasing mean molecular weight or gravity shrinks H and also suppresses modulation. A flat spectrum can consequently mean no atmosphere, a compact high- \mu atmosphere, high clouds or haze, refraction, weak absorbers over the bandpass, or insufficient precision. The degeneracy is real but not absolute. Broad wavelength coverage can constrain multiple opacity sources with different shapes. Collision-induced absorption, alkali wings, Rayleigh-like scattering, resolved line structure, and continuum windows can help anchor pressure or composition. Welbanks and Madhusudhan showed with detailed retrievals of hydrogen-rich atmospheres that the radius–pressure correlation can be well characterized and need not destroy abundance constraints when optical and infrared data and appropriate opacity/cloud models are combined. Heng and Kitzmann showed why restricted WFC3-like coverage and semi-analytic assumptions leave a more severe normalization ambiguity. The apparent disagreement is a lesson about model and data scope, not permission to claim either that abundances are always precise or fundamentally unknowable. Retrievals must therefore report the parameterization, priors, opacity database, cloud prescription, reference boundary, stellar model, and sensitivity to alternative models. Posterior precision within one forward model is not the same as robustness to model misspecification. See [[Atmospheric retrieval degeneracies]] for the broader inverse-problem framework. The star is part of the spectrum Transmission spectroscopy is a differential comparison between light from the portion of the stellar surface crossed by the planet and light from the entire unresolved stellar disk. If those sources have different spectra, the inferred transit depth acquires wavelength structure that is not planetary. Suppose the transit chord has specific intensity I_{\rm chord}(\lambda) while the disk average is I_{\rm disk}(\lambda) . Schematically, D_{\rm obs}(\lambda)\simeq D_{\rm planet}(\lambda)\frac{I_{\rm chord}(\lambda)}{I_{\rm disk}(\lambda)}. Unocculted cool spots can make the star dimmer and redder than the transit chord, increasing and tilting apparent depths. Bright faculae can act in the opposite direction or imprint line-dependent structure. Occulted spots produce anomalies in the transit time series; masking or fitting them does not automatically solve the effect of unocculted regions. The distribution evolves with stellar rotation and activity. Rackham, Apai, and Giampapa termed this the transit light source effect . Their modeling shows that contamination is target-dependent: active cool stars are especially challenging because spots and faculae can cover substantial fractions of the disk and possess molecular features, while inactive FGK stars generally present weaker contamination. Stellar limb darkening is also wavelength-dependent and imperfect stellar-atmosphere models can bias fitted depths. Repeated transits, rotational monitoring, spot-crossing analysis, multiwavelength stellar constraints, and retrievals that include heterogeneity parameters can reduce but not universally eliminate the problem. A claimed planetary slope or band should therefore be tested against plausible stellar spectra, particularly for M-dwarf hosts and active stars. The measured depth belongs to the star–planet system until that test is made. Instrument and reduction systematics An ideal transmission spectrum is much smaller than the raw changes affecting many detectors. A pipeline must correct or model bias and dark signals, nonlinearity, saturation, cosmic rays, flat-field variations, background, wavelength calibration, pointing drift, detector persistence, ramp-like behavior, scan-direction offsets, and time-correlated noise. The exact list depends on instrument and observing mode. Ground-based spectra additionally face Earth’s variable telluric absorption, seeing, slit losses, and changing airmass. Analysis choices can change the result: extraction aperture, background region, spectral binning, bad-pixel treatment, limb-darkening priors, orbital parameters, baseline length, common-mode correction, and functional form for systematics. Fitting white and spectroscopic light curves sequentially can transmit uncertainty differently than a joint fit. Combining instruments or visits introduces offsets because each bandpass has distinct calibration, epochs, and stellar states. Robust work examines residuals for autocorrelation, compares plausible systematics models, performs injection–recovery tests where appropriate, propagates covariance, and checks whether a feature survives independent reductions. Error bars based only on photon noise are incomplete if nuisance-model uncertainty dominates. A spectral point is measured only with reference to its reduction and light-curve model; it is not a raw property of the atmosphere. JWST has transformed wavelength coverage and precision, but it has not removed these principles. Detector behavior, saturation strategy, trace motion, background, order overlap, and pipeline versions remain relevant. Cross-instrument agreement is powerful only when offsets and stellar variability are modeled rather than silently normalized away. Where measurement ends and retrieval begins The direct result of a conventional low-resolution analysis is a set of wavelength bins with fitted transit depths and a likelihood or covariance description. An absorption-shaped modulation is still a measurement of relative occulting area. Assigning it to H _2 O, CO _2 , Na, aerosols, or another opacity source is a model comparison. Turning that identification into an abundance requires assumptions about temperature, gravity, mean molecular weight, other absorbers, clouds, reference pressure, and often chemical uniformity. Retrieval is valuable precisely because it makes this conditional inference explicit. A forward model calculates R_{\rm eff}(\lambda) , convolves it with the instrument response, and evaluates a likelihood against the depths. Bayesian or other algorithms explore parameter combinations. Evidence ratios, posterior predictive checks, leave-one-instrument-out tests, and alternative opacity or cloud models ask different robustness questions. None converts an underdetermined spectrum into a direct atmospheric sample. High-resolution transmission spectroscopy uses time-dependent Doppler shifts to separate planet lines from stellar and telluric spectra. Cross-correlation can detect a resolved line pattern even when individual lines are too weak to detect separately. Its amplitude and velocity likewise depend on templates, line lists, temperature, abundance, clouds, rotation, limb geometry, and removal of the spectral continuum during processing. The measured velocity can mix orbital ephemeris error, rotation, morning–evening weighting, and winds. A cross-correlation peak is therefore not automatically a volume mixing ratio or a global wind speed. What spatial claims are supported Transmission primarily probes the narrow annulus near the planet’s terminator , not the dayside, nightside, or global mean. Even “the terminator” is a mixture. During most of transit, rays traverse both morning and evening limbs; ingress and egress weight them differently. The chord spans a range of latitudes and pressures. Refraction, clouds, scale height, and opacity determine which parts contribute. A one-dimensional retrieved profile is therefore an effective representation of a three-dimensional limb. Horizontal inhomogeneity creates nonlinear averaging. A hot clear limb with a large scale height can dominate spectral modulation over a cool cloudy limb even if both cover equal azimuth. Molecular dissociation or condensation may make composition different on morning and evening sides. Combining their spectra is not equivalent to evaluating one column at the mean temperature and abundance. Three-dimensional forward models have demonstrated biases when such spectra are fitted with one-dimensional retrievals. Spatial information is possible, but it demands specific data and models. Ingress–egress differences can in principle separate limbs; high-resolution line shifts and broadening can constrain combinations of orbital motion, winds, and rotation; time-resolved spectra can weight different chord regions. These signals are small and degenerate with ephemeris, stellar line distortions, limb darkening, instrumental drift, and asymmetric clouds. “Wind detected” should specify the measured Doppler quantity and the atmospheric model connecting it to circulation. Transmission spectra do not make a weather map. A single transit is a spatially integrated limb spectrum. It cannot establish temporal variability without a comparison epoch and a repeatable difference that survives instrument and stellar tests. What temporal claims are supported Repeated transits can test whether the system’s transmission spectrum changes. A credible atmospheric-variability claim requires comparable reductions, control of visit-dependent systematics, and evidence that stellar surface evolution is insufficient to explain the difference. Instrument upgrades or pipeline changes can masquerade as temporal evolution. Multiple comparisons across many wavelength bins inflate false-positive risk unless accounted for. If repeatable variability remains, transmission data may constrain changing cloud opacity, escaping gas, chemistry, or terminator structure. The causal label is still interpreted or simulated rather than measured. Atmospheric advection and cloud-evolution timescales can guide cadence, but the transit samples once per orbit and may alias faster processes. Nonrepeatability may also be informative: it can bound large changes in the effective limb over the pressures and wavelengths observed. It does not prove meteorological steadiness at unprobed levels. The conservative hierarchy is: measure epoch-specific depths; demonstrate a statistically and reduction-robust difference; test stellar and instrumental alternatives; then compare atmospheric models that predict variability. Only after these steps does the result contribute to [[What counts as weather on an exoplanet]]. Practical interpretation checklist Before treating a transmission spectrum as atmospheric evidence, ask: Which instrument, mode, wavelength range, visits, and reduction produced the depths? Are uncertainties correlated, and do independent pipelines recover the feature? Which pressures and limb regions contribute at each wavelength? Which opacity source is favored over explicit alternatives, at what model-comparison strength? How do the abundance posterior and detection significance change with clouds, reference radius, temperature structure, and opacity database? Were stellar spots, faculae, limb darkening, and epoch variability modeled? Is the claim measured, retrieved, simulated, interpreted, or forecast? What new wavelength, resolution, or epoch would distinguish the leading explanations? This discipline preserves what makes transmission spectroscopy powerful: not a direct photograph of an atmosphere, but a precise, repeatable geometric experiment whose inference chain can be tested. Place in the map This foundation links transit geometry and slant radiative transfer to [[Atmospheric retrieval degeneracies]], [[Stellar contamination in exoplanet spectra]], [[Cloud formation and transport beyond Earth]], [[High-resolution Doppler spectroscopy of exoplanet winds]], and [[What counts as weather on an exoplanet]]. It complements [[Emission spectroscopy and secondary eclipses]] and [[Exoplanet phase curves]], which weight different regions and physical quantities. Sources Brown, T. M. (2001), “Transmission Spectra as Diagnostics of Extrasolar Giant Planet Atmospheres.” Foundational primary derivation and simulated observations of wavelength-dependent transit geometry. Astrophysical Journal / arXiv manuscript . Lecavelier des Etangs, A. et al. (2008), “Rayleigh scattering in the transit spectrum of HD 189733b.” Primary analytic treatment of effective altitude and opacity slopes, plus an application whose aerosol interpretation illustrates model dependence. Astronomy & Astrophysics / arXiv manuscript . Heng, K. and Kitzmann, D. (2017), “The theory of transmission spectra revisited.” Scholarly semi-analytic account of slant geometry and the reference-radius–pressure–abundance normalization problem, especially for restricted wavelength coverage. Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society / arXiv manuscript . Welbanks, L. and Madhusudhan, N. (2019), “On degeneracies in retrievals of exoplanetary transmission spectra.” Primary retrieval experiments testing how broadband coverage, collision-induced absorption, clouds, radius, pressure, and abundance interact. Astronomical Journal / arXiv manuscript . Rackham, B. V., Apai, D., and Giampapa, M. S. (2018), “The Transit Light Source Effect.” Primary modeling of stellar photospheric heterogeneity contaminating M-dwarf transmission spectra. Astrophysical Journal / arXiv manuscript . Rackham, B. V., Apai, D., and Giampapa, M. S. (2019), “The Transit Light Source Effect II.” Primary extension to FGK host stars, demonstrating the dependence of contamination on spectral type and activity. Astronomical Journal / arXiv manuscript . MacDonald, R. J., Goyal, J. M., and Lewis, N. K. (2020), “Why is it so Cold in Here? Explaining the Cold Temperatures Retrieved from Transmission Spectra of Exoplanet Atmospheres.” Primary study of biases caused by fitting three-dimensional terminators with one-dimensional retrievals. Astrophysical Journal Letters / arXiv manuscript . Alderson, L. et al. (2023), “Early Release Science of the exoplanet WASP-39b with JWST NIRSpec PRISM.” Primary observation and reduction example showing how wide wavelength coverage constrains multiple opacity sources while retaining pipeline and model qualifications. Nature / arXiv manuscript . Open questions Which retrieval diagnostics most reliably expose bias from a two-dimensional morning–evening terminator when the data do not support a full three-dimensional model? Can coordinated stellar monitoring constrain the unocculted photosphere tightly enough for temperate M-dwarf planets, or must stellar heterogeneity remain a dominant latent variable? What minimum number and cadence of repeat transits can distinguish atmospheric variability from evolving stellar contamination for a given host activity level? Which pressure anchors—collision-induced absorption, alkali wings, or complementary emission data—most improve absolute abundance constraints for different planet classes? How reproducible are current high-precision spectra across independent reductions and pipeline versions when covariance is propagated consistently?

title: Vertical mixing and chemical quenching
deck: Vertical mixing can carry gas across temperature and pressure faster than reactions can restore equilibrium, leaving observable abundances that record a competition between transport and chemistry rather than a direct reading of local conditions.
text: Vertical mixing can carry gas across temperature and pressure faster than reactions can restore equilibrium, leaving observable abundances that record a competition between transport and chemistry rather than a direct reading of local conditions. Up: [[Exometeorology research frontier 2026]] Related: [[Disequilibrium chemistry as a tracer of circulation]] · [[Coupled chemistry circulation models]] · [[General circulation models for exoplanets]] · [[Radiative and advective timescales in exoplanet atmospheres]] The central idea Thermochemical equilibrium is a local prediction. Given pressure, temperature, and elemental inventories, it identifies the composition that minimizes the appropriate thermodynamic potential. It says nothing by itself about whether a moving atmosphere has had enough time to reach that state. A parcel rising from a hot, dense layer into a cooler, thinner layer can retain the deeper abundance of a slowly interconverting molecule. When chemical conversion becomes slower than transport, the abundance is said to be quenched . The familiar one-dimensional picture compares a chemical time with a mixing time, \tau_{\mathrm{chem}}(p,T,\{f_i\}) \sim \tau_{\mathrm{mix}} \approx \frac{L^2}{K_{zz}}, where K_{zz} is an effective vertical eddy diffusivity and L is a transport length. Below the crossing, reactions are fast enough to follow the changing equilibrium composition. Above it, transport is faster and the mixing ratio is approximately inherited from the crossing region. This is a useful organizing approximation, not a literal discontinuity or a universal law. The result matters because spectra probe pressures well above many expected quench regions. Carbon monoxide seen in a cool observable layer, for example, may have been favored deeper down and transported upward. Methane, ammonia, carbon dioxide, phosphine, or other species can behave differently because each has its own reaction network, rate-limiting pathways, and equilibrium gradient. There is therefore no single chemical quench pressure for an atmosphere. What vertical mixing means In a three-dimensional atmosphere, vertical transport can arise from resolved overturning, waves, convection, shear-driven turbulence, and correlations between vertical velocity and tracer anomalies. A one-dimensional chemistry model usually compresses all of this into the diffusive flux \Phi_i = -K_{zz} n \frac{\partial f_i}{\partial z}, for total number density n and mixing ratio f_i , sometimes with additional molecular-diffusion and settling terms. This closure is attractive because it converts an unresolved dynamical problem into a tractable coefficient. It does not mean the true motion is molecular diffusion, nor does it guarantee that one scalar K_{zz} represents every tracer, height, latitude, and chemical lifetime. A diagnosed effective diffusivity can depend on the tracer. Long-lived species sample broad circulation cells; short-lived species remain correlated with their sources and sinks. On a tidally locked planet, dayside heating and nightside cooling organize coherent ascent and descent. Photochemical production may occur only on the illuminated hemisphere, and condensates may disappear into a cold trap. Under these circumstances the global-mean vertical flux need not be proportional to the global-mean vertical gradient. An inferred K_{zz} is then a model-dependent summary of a non-diffusive circulation. Convection creates another ambiguity. Mixing-length arguments can estimate velocities and length scales in a convective interior, but those estimates need not extend through a stably stratified photosphere. Waves launched below may mix tracers without carrying heat in the same fashion as overturning convection. A retrieval that assigns one constant K_{zz} through the entire modeled column therefore makes a strong structural assumption. The quench-level approximation The timescale crossing is often described as if L were automatically the pressure scale height H . Smith's 1998 analysis showed why that shortcut can be seriously wrong. The relevant length depends on how rapidly the equilibrium abundance and chemical time change with height; it can be a fraction of H . Because \tau_{\mathrm{mix}} scales as L^2 , even a modest length-scale error shifts the inferred quench point. Nor is \tau_{\mathrm{chem}} simply the inverse rate of any convenient reaction. Net conversion between stable reservoirs such as CO and CH _4 or N _2 and NH _3 proceeds through multi-step networks. The slow controlling pathway can change with temperature, pressure, metallicity, and composition. Updated rate coefficients or a different reaction network can therefore move the quench point even when the atmospheric profile and K_{zz} are unchanged. A more complete one-dimensional calculation integrates continuity equations, \frac{\partial n_i}{\partial t} = P_i-L_i-\frac{\partial \Phi_i}{\partial z}, where P_i and L_i collect chemical production and loss. Coupled nonlinear networks are stiff because radical reactions can be extremely fast while reservoir conversion is slow. Full kinetics avoids choosing a single rate-limiting step in advance, but it remains conditional on the adopted network, rate data, boundary conditions, temperature profile, and transport closure. The simple approximation works best when one interconversion has a steep chemical timescale, vertical transport dominates, the equilibrium abundance varies smoothly, and chemistry above the crossing is weak. It weakens when photochemistry creates a second abundance region, condensation removes an element, molecular diffusion separates species, horizontal advection competes with vertical mixing, or several pathways quench at different depths. Vertical and horizontal quenching Tidally locked planets expose the limitation of a purely vertical story. Their daysides, nightsides, morning limbs, and evening limbs can have radically different equilibrium compositions. A fast equatorial jet may move gas around the planet before local chemistry adjusts. Composition then becomes horizontally quenched toward values characteristic of the hottest or fastest-reacting region encountered by the flow. Whether vertical or horizontal transport dominates is species- and regime-dependent. A useful comparison adds an advective time \tau_{\mathrm{adv}} \sim L_h/U for horizontal distance L_h and wind speed U . Yet this estimate is also a scale argument: the relevant path follows the circulation, and reaction time varies continuously along it. Three-dimensional models of hot Jupiters have found strong longitudinal homogenization for some carbon species, while polar regions or other species retain distinct patterns. Such results are simulated , not direct wind measurements. The observational consequence is geometrical. Transmission spectra mix slant paths across a terminator; emission spectra weight temperature and opacity across the visible hemisphere; phase curves change that weighting with orbital phase. A single retrieved abundance may average different quenched reservoirs. Conversely, an apparent morning–evening difference need not identify vertical mixing unless temperature structure, clouds, stellar contamination, and reduction systematics are controlled. What an abundance can constrain A measured spectrum is calibrated wavelength-dependent flux or transit depth. Molecular abundance is retrieved through an opacity and atmospheric model. A quench pressure or K_{zz} is a further inference. Keeping those levels separate prevents a common overstatement: a molecule does not directly measure a mixing coefficient. Suppose a retrieval favors more CO and less CH _4 than local equilibrium predicts. That pattern may be consistent with vigorous mixing from hot deeper layers. But the same spectrum can respond to the temperature profile, elemental metallicity, carbon-to-oxygen ratio, cloud opacity, disequilibrium photochemistry, line-list choices, and spatial inhomogeneity. Even if quenching is the correct explanation, many combinations of K_{zz} and thermal structure can yield a similar quenched abundance because both determine where the timescales cross. The most defensible inference chain is therefore conditional: The data constrain spectral features after calibration and systematics treatment. A retrieval maps those features to abundance ranges under stated opacity, cloud, temperature, and geometry assumptions. A kinetics–transport model asks which profiles and mixing prescriptions reproduce those ranges. Comparisons across multiple species test whether one thermal structure and transport field explains all of them. Pairs with different kinetic sensitivities are especially valuable. CO/CH _4 and N _2 /NH _3 conversion respond differently to temperature and pressure. A model that matches one pair but not the other may have an incomplete network, incorrect thermal profile, missing photochemistry, or an over-simple K_{zz} . Disequilibrium molecules can thus diagnose a model family more readily than they uniquely determine a single parameter. Feedback on temperature and circulation Chemistry is not always a passive tracer. CO, CH _4 , H _2 O, and other molecules contribute opacity. Transport-driven abundance changes can alter where radiation is absorbed and emitted, changing heating rates and hence winds. Clouds can remove elements, supply surfaces for reactions, and change radiative forcing. A post-processed chemistry calculation—running kinetics on a fixed circulation—captures transport's effect on composition but not composition's feedback on dynamics. Fully or partially [[Coupled chemistry circulation models]] attempt to close this loop. Chemical relaxation schemes push selected species toward equilibrium on prescribed timescales and are computationally cheaper than integrating a full network. Reduced networks evolve a small set of species and reactions inside a general circulation model. Both approaches trade completeness for cost. A reduced network can be well validated within its intended temperature–pressure domain and unreliable outside it; a relaxation scheme cannot represent pathways absent from its target equilibrium and timescale tables. This distinction is important when interpreting model spectra. A post-processed calculation may show large compositional disequilibrium but little spectral effect if the affected species contributes weak opacity in the observed band. Conversely, radiative feedback can modify temperature enough to change both equilibrium and circulation. Agreement between a spectrum and one uncoupled model is not proof that feedbacks are negligible. Boundary conditions and hidden reservoirs Quench calculations also inherit their lower and upper boundaries. A deep giant-planet model commonly assumes thermochemical equilibrium at a hot lower boundary and zero flux for many species at the top. If the modeled column does not extend beneath the true quench region, that lower condition can impose the answer instead of predicting it. An internal heat flux changes the deep adiabat and can move the equilibrium transition between carbon or nitrogen reservoirs. Condensation and rainout can remove atoms from the gas carried upward, so conserving gas-phase elemental ratios everywhere may be inappropriate. At low pressure, ultraviolet photolysis, escape, ion chemistry, and externally supplied material can create fluxes that a closed upper boundary excludes. A photochemical product transported downward can meet a thermochemical species transported upward, producing an abundance profile with more than one transition. Describing that column by one quench pressure hides the competing reservoirs. These issues suggest a practical convergence test: move the model boundaries, vary their flux prescriptions, and check whether the spectrum-forming abundance is stable. A result that changes when the bottom is extended modestly deeper or the top flux is relaxed is boundary-sensitive, even if its internal differential equations are solved precisely. Reporting vertical domain and boundary conditions is therefore as important as reporting K_{zz} . Regime dependence Hotter gas generally reacts faster, so very hot observable layers may remain closer to equilibrium for major species. Cooler giant planets and brown dwarfs can show strong quenching because reservoir interconversion becomes slow above the convective region. Warm Neptunes and sub-Neptunes introduce broader metallicity, mean-molecular-weight, haze, and interior-boundary uncertainties. Rocky atmospheres may have surface exchange, condensation, escape, or photochemistry that prevents the giant-planet K_{zz} picture from transferring cleanly. Gravity and scale height enter both transport and observation. Metallicity changes equilibrium abundances, reaction partners, opacity, and sometimes the thermal structure. Irradiation controls the day–night contrast and can move photochemical production relative to the pressure levels sampled spectroscopically. Rotation shapes jets and overturning. Thus a quoted K_{zz} should always be attached to a model domain, pressure range, tracer set, and assumed circulation regime. Brown dwarfs are valuable comparative laboratories because their rotational variability and spectra probe cloudy, convective atmospheres without stellar irradiation dominating the energy budget. Yet their unresolved disks still mix latitude, longitude, and pressure, and cloud evolution can mimic or accompany chemical variability. Solar-System giant planets provide the historical quenching logic and in situ or spatially resolved constraints, but exoplanet forcing and observability can be qualitatively different. A verification checklist When a paper or retrieval claims vertical mixing or quenching, ask: Which quantity was measured, and which abundance was retrieved? Is the temperature–pressure profile retrieved, prescribed, or self-consistent? Is K_{zz} constant, pressure-dependent, predicted by a circulation model, or merely varied over a grid? What length scale defines \tau_{\mathrm{mix}} , and is the Smith correction considered? Which kinetic network and rate coefficients set \tau_{\mathrm{chem}} ? Are photochemistry, condensation, rainout, molecular diffusion, and boundary fluxes included? Could horizontal transport dominate the relevant species? Does one transport prescription fit several chemically independent tracers? Is chemistry radiatively coupled to the circulation or post-processed? What observation would distinguish vigorous mixing from altered elemental abundance, clouds, or temperature? This checklist converts “disequilibrium detected” from a slogan into a testable chain of assumptions. Why it matters Chemical quenching is one of the few ways an unresolved spectrum can retain information about motion and deeper atmospheric layers. It links observable molecules to circulation, convection, kinetics, and thermal structure. That leverage is precisely why caution is necessary: the link is an inverse problem, not a direct anemometer. The strongest result is rarely a universal K_{zz} . It is a coherent model that explains several species, spectral geometries, and epochs with physically consistent transport and chemistry, survives alternative clouds and temperature profiles, and predicts a discriminating new observation. Quenching then becomes a bridge from photons to atmospheric process while preserving the distinction among what was measured, retrieved, simulated, and interpreted. Sources Smith, M. D. P. (2018), “Global-mean Vertical Tracer Mixing in Planetary Atmospheres. II. Tidally Locked Planets.” https://arxiv.org/abs/1808.05365 Mendonça, J. M. et al. (2018), “Three-Dimensional Circulation Driving Chemical Disequilibrium in WASP-43b.” https://arxiv.org/abs/1808.00501 Tsai, S.-M. et al. (2018), “Chemical kinetics in exoplanet atmospheres.” https://doi.org/10.3847/1538-4357/aadf43 Hobbs, R. et al. (2019), “A chemical kinetics code for modelling exoplanetary atmospheres,” MNRAS 487, 2242–2261. https://doi.org/10.1093/mnras/stz1333 Baeyens, R. et al.
